title: feat(impact): per-symbol processes field on byDepth items
body:
## Summary

`impact` already returns aggregated `affected_processes` at the top level (which entry points break, with total hit counts), but the per-symbol `byDepth` items don't say which processes each individual caller participates in. For deploy planning the per-symbol mapping matters: a single function might be hit by a cron, a webhook, and a user-facing route, each with a different deploy-risk profile.

This PR attaches a `processes: [...]` field to every `byDepth[depth][i]` item, listing the processes that specific symbol participates in. The data is already in the graph via `STEP_IN_PROCESS` edges; this is the join that wasn't being surfaced.

## Output shape

```json
{
  "byDepth": {
    "1": [
      {
        "depth": 1,
        "id": "Function:src/foo.ts:doStuff",
        "name": "doStuff",
        "filePath": "src/foo.ts",
        "relationType": "CALLS",
        "confidence": 0.85,
        "processes": [
          { "id": "proc:cron_daily", "label": "Daily cron", "processType": "cron", "step": 12 }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

The `processes` list is empty for symbols not in any process. Additive change, no breaking modifications to existing fields.

## Implementation

The existing per-process aggregation query uses `WITH p, COUNT(DISTINCT s.id) AS hits` so it has lost per-symbol info by the time it returns. The new field is populated by a second chunked Cypher pass that runs after the aggregation pass:

```cypher
MATCH (s)-[r:CodeRelation {type: 'STEP_IN_PROCESS'}]->(p:Process)
WHERE s.id IN $ids
RETURN s.id AS sid, p.id AS pid, p.heuristicLabel AS pName,
       p.processType AS pType, r.step AS step
```

Same `CHUNK_SIZE=100` and `MAX_CHUNKS` (configurable via `IMPACT_MAX_CHUNKS`, default 10) as the aggregation pass. Worst-case adds **up to 10 extra round-trips** for a maxed-out impact call.

The pass is **skipped entirely** when:
- `affectedProcesses.length === 0` (no processes affected at all, nothing to enrich)
- `summaryOnly === true` (byDepth isn't returned anyway)

so callers that don't benefit from the new field pay zero cost.

## Behavioral note

Additive. Existing consumers ignoring the new field keep working. Consumers that want it now get it inline with the impact response, no follow-up query needed.

## Verification

- Full unit suite: 298 files / 6527 tests pass / 0 failures.
- `npx tsc --noEmit`: clean.
- New unit tests cover (a) byDepth items always have a `processes: []` field even when no STEP_IN_PROCESS rows exist, (b) when rows exist the right `{id, label, processType, step}` entry appears.
- One existing test (`impact-batching-grouping`) was narrowed: its mock previously counted any STEP_IN_PROCESS query as a chunk; the new per-symbol pass also matches that pattern, so the mock now filters for the aggregation pattern (`COUNT(DISTINCT s.id)`). The per-symbol pass is asserted separately in `calltool-dispatch.test.ts`.

## Scope

3 files changed, 157 insertions, 4 deletions. No new dependencies. No new public types beyond the additive `processes` field on `byDepth` items.

title: Feature: index SQL functions (PL/pgSQL) as first-class graph nodes
body:
## Summary

GitNexus indexes 12 languages today (TS/JS/Python/Java/C/C++/C#/Go/Rust/PHP/Kotlin/Swift/Ruby per the README matrix), but SQL is absent. For Postgres-heavy codebases that put business logic in `CREATE FUNCTION ... LANGUAGE plpgsql` and invoke those functions from app code, the affected functions are invisible to `impact`, `context`, and `query`.

Concrete example:

```
$ gitnexus impact mark_items_dirty
{ "error": "Target 'mark_items_dirty' not found" }
```

`mark_items_dirty` is the hottest enqueue function in the system, called from ~15 Python sites via `supabase.rpc(...)`. Today the only way to assess blast radius is grep.

This issue is to scope a feature that would index SQL functions as first-class nodes and link the common call patterns to them.

## Why this matters beyond one codebase

The pattern (Postgres + an ORM/RPC layer + business logic in stored procedures) is common across:

- Supabase / PostgREST users invoking `supabase.rpc(\"name\", ...)`
- SQLAlchemy shops with `db.execute(text(\"SELECT name(...)\"))` or `func.name(...)`
- psycopg / asyncpg shops with raw `cursor.execute(\"SELECT name(...)\")`
- Django shops with raw SQL or stored procs

For these projects, SQL functions are usually the *highest-blast-radius* code in the system: called from many places, run inside transactions, and touch core tables. Being invisible to impact analysis is the worst combination. Once SQL is a graph citizen, `gitnexus_impact` answers \"who calls this RPC?\" the same way it answers \"who calls this Python function?\" today.

## Design questions for maintainer input

Opening this as an issue rather than a PR because three of the four decisions below are architectural and belong to the maintainer.

### 1. Parser choice

Three candidates, each with tradeoffs:

- **libpg_query** (PostgreSQL's own parser via Node binding): heavyweight, exact, native dependency. Highest fidelity but adds platform-specific builds.
- **pglast** (Python wrapper around libpg_query): same fidelity but wrong runtime for GitNexus's Node host.
- **Hand-rolled tree-sitter grammar** for top-level `CREATE [OR REPLACE] FUNCTION ... AS $$ ... $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql`: lightweight, fits the existing tree-sitter pipeline, may miss edge cases like nested $$ blocks or unusual quoting.
- **Hybrid**: tree-sitter for the top-level declaration only (name, args, return type, language tag); defer body parsing to a later phase or skip it entirely.

Recommendation request: which fits the existing analyze pipeline best? Tree-sitter feels most aligned with the current language plugins, but `pl/pgsql` is non-trivial to parse precisely.

### 2. Scope of callsite recognition

Which call patterns should the analyzer auto-recognize? Suggested initial set:

- `supabase.rpc(\"name\", {...})` (Supabase / PostgREST)
- `db.execute(text(\"SELECT name(...)\"))` (SQLAlchemy)
- `cursor.execute(\"SELECT name(...)\")` (psycopg)
- `await connection.execute(\"SELECT name(...)\")` (asyncpg)
- `func.name(...)` (SQLAlchemy core function expressions)
- Raw cross-references inside other `.sql` files (`SELECT name(...)`, `CALL name(...)`)

The Python/TS side fits the existing per-language extractor pattern. The SQL-to-SQL references fall out for free once SQL nodes exist.

### 3. Source of truth

Two ways to get the function definitions:

- **Migration files only** (`*/migrations/*.sql`): pure static analysis, matches GitNexus's current model, can drift from live DB if migrations were hot-patched in production.
- **Live DB introspection via `pg_proc`** (opt-in flag, requires connection string): exact ground truth, requires runtime credentials at index time which is unusual for a code-intel tool.
- **Both, with migrations as default and live introspection as opt-in**: hybrid that matches the static-analysis bias while giving power users an escape hatch.

Recommendation request: live-DB introspection would be a departure from GitNexus's pure-static-analysis posture. Worth it for the precision win, or out of scope?

### 4. Output node shape

Proposed:

```
SqlFunction node {
  name: string
  schema: string           // 'public' default
  language: 'plpgsql' | 'sql' | 'plpython' | ...
  returnType: string
  argSpec: string          // e.g. \"(p_org_id uuid, p_sku text)\"
  filePath: string         // migrations/NNN_add_mark_items_dirty.sql
  startLine: number
  endLine: number
  source: string           // the body, optional
}
```

Edges:

- `(caller:Function|Method)-[:CALLS]->(target:SqlFunction)` for each recognized callsite
- `(file:File)-[:DEFINES]->(target:SqlFunction)` for the definition site
- `(caller:SqlFunction)-[:CALLS]->(callee:SqlFunction)` for cross-function SQL refs

This shape would make `gitnexus impact <sql_function_name>` and `gitnexus context <sql_function_name>` work without further changes to those commands.

## Follow-on work (out of scope for this issue, depends on landing this one)

Once SQL nodes exist:

- `gitnexus dead-sql`: list SQL functions with zero recognized callers in code or other SQL. Mirrors the existing dead-code lint for Python/TS.
- `group sync` Contract Registry integration: SQL function names are exactly the kind of \"contract\" the Registry was designed to track.

## Use case prior art

For shops that already snapshot SQL function bodies from `pg_proc` (e.g., for drift detection between live and migrations), this feature would be the *call-graph* layer that sits on top: the snapshot tool answers \"has the body changed?\"; the call graph answers \"who calls it and what breaks if it does change?\" The two are complementary, not overlapping.

Happy to draft a PR for the parser choice the maintainer prefers, or to scope down to a minimum-viable shape (e.g., migration-file parsing + supabase.rpc + SQLAlchemy text() only) for the first cut.

title: test(group): fail loud on CI when tree-sitter-kotlin grammar is unavailable
body:
## Summary

Follow-up to #1855, addressing the deferred Finding 2 from Claude's review (https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/pull/1855#issuecomment-4552615253).

The Kotlin Provider tests (#1849) and Consumer tests (#1855) both gate their `it()` calls behind:

```ts
const kotlinAvailable = getPluginForFile('Probe.kt') !== undefined;
const itKotlin = kotlinAvailable ? it : it.skip;
```

Locally this is intentional — contributors on platforms where the optional `tree-sitter-kotlin` native binding can't build (or who haven't installed it) shouldn't be blocked by red Kotlin tests.

On CI it's a silent-skip hazard: if the optional dep ever fails to install (npm registry hiccup, build-toolchain drift on a runner image update, ABI bump in `tree-sitter-kotlin`) all 17+ Kotlin cases would silently skip and CI would still pass green.

## Fix

A module-load tripwire that throws only when **both** conditions hold:

- `process.env.CI` is set
- `getPluginForFile('Probe.kt')` returns `undefined`

Mirrors the existing CI tripwire pattern at [`test/integration/object-literal-owner-resolution.test.ts:55-66`](https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/blob/main/gitnexus/test/integration/object-literal-owner-resolution.test.ts#L55-L66), which guards against silent skip on missing `dist/parse-worker.js`.

The error message states what's missing, what would otherwise happen (silent skip of Provider + Consumer), where to look (`optionalDependencies` + runner toolchain), and explicitly reassures contributors that local runs are unaffected.

## Coverage

This single tripwire protects **all** Kotlin tests in `http-route-extractor.test.ts`:

- 11 `itKotlin` cases (Provider — #1849)
- 6 `itKotlinConsumer` cases (Consumer — #1855)
- Any future Kotlin tests added under the same gating pattern

## Reverse-validated four states

| Scenario | Behavior |
|---|---|
| local + grammar present | 60 / 60 pass (unchanged) |
| local + grammar absent | 43 pass + 17 skip (unchanged) |
| `CI=true` + grammar present | 60 / 60 pass (unchanged) |
| **`CI=true` + grammar ABSENT** | **tripwire throws with clear error message** (was silently green; now hard red) |

The "grammar absent" cases were exercised locally by temporarily commenting out `Kotlin = _require('tree-sitter-kotlin')` in `kotlin.ts` and running the suite under both env settings.

## Local validation

- `http-route-extractor.test.ts` — 60 / 60 ✅
- `test/unit/group` — 540 / 540 ✅
- `npm run format:check` — clean ✅

One of my CSharp project repositories contains approximately 40,000 CSharp files, **of which over 30,000 code files have types without declared namespaces.** After I set this environment variable, gitnexus analyze can work normally. **set REGISTRY_PRIMARY_CSHARP=0** ### Context **The following are the reasons analyzed by AI** _GitNexus's current C# scope-resolution mechanism, in order to support cross-file type visibility within the same namespace, pre-copies types under each namespace into the scope augmentation of each file. In a repository with 36,000 C# files and a highly concentrated namespace structure, this can result in billions of binding injections and duplicate checks, causing the 'Resolving types (Csharp — analyzing types)' process to stall for a long time and eventually leading to OutOfMemoryException._ ### Expected behavior Even after I removed the environment variable setting, gitnexus analyze could still complete the analysis normally. **set REGISTRY_PRIMARY_CSHARP=0** ### Actual behavior As shown in the screenshot, it has been stuck for over ten hours at this stage ### Steps to reproduce 1. Prepare a massive C# code repository containing approximately 30,000 C# files, where each type does not declare a namespace 2. gitnexus analyze ### Environment - OS ： Windows11 - node --version v22.14.0 - gitnexus --version 1.6.6-rc.78 ### Logs / screenshots _No response_

title: feat(java): add HTTP consumer contract extraction
body:
## Summary

Part of #1870. Adds low-complexity Java HTTP consumer extraction for common literal client patterns without taking on dynamic URL resolution.

## What changed

- Detects `RestTemplate.exchange("/path", HttpMethod.X, ...)` consumers.
- Detects Java `WebClient` short-form chains like `webClient.post().uri("/path")`.
- Detects OpenFeign interfaces annotated with `@FeignClient` plus Spring MVC method annotations.
- Detects literal Java `HttpRequest.newBuilder().uri(URI.create("/path")).GET/POST/...` request construction.
- Detects literal Apache HttpClient `HttpGet` / `HttpPost` / `HttpPut` / `HttpDelete` / `HttpPatch` request construction.
- Uses AST annotation checks for Feign interfaces so `@FeignClient` text in strings/comments is not misclassified.
- Keeps these patterns source-scan only and avoids scope-resolution / dynamic URL analysis.

## Validation

- `npx vitest run test/unit/group/http-route-extractor.test.ts` — 70 passed
- `npx vitest run test/unit/group` — 550 passed
- `npx tsc --noEmit`
- `./dist/cli/index.js detect-changes --scope unstaged --repo GitNexus` — risk low, 0 affected processes
- pre-commit hook — formatting, eslint, gitnexus typecheck passed

## Follow-up

Dynamic URL assembly, wrapper tracking, fully-qualified route annotation extraction, and broader interface-controller support are intentionally left for #1873.

title: Java Spring: follow-up HTTP consumer extraction for dynamic URLs and wrappers
body:
## Summary

Follow-up to #1870 and PR #1872. PR #1872 covers low-complexity literal Java HTTP consumer extraction. This issue tracks the remaining higher-complexity Java/Spring consumer cases that need scope-aware or data-flow-aware handling.

## Remaining scenarios

- Fully-qualified annotations, for example `@org.springframework.cloud.openfeign.FeignClient` and fully-qualified Spring MVC annotations.
- Spring controller interfaces with class/interface-level `@RequestMapping` prefixes that are not Feign clients.
- `@Value` config, constants, and string concatenation in URLs, for example `host + detailPath`.
- `UriComponentsBuilder` URL construction.
- Helper methods such as `HttpClients.buildQueryUrl(host + path, params)`.
- Thin wrapper classes around `RestTemplate`, `WebClient`, Java `HttpClient`, Apache HttpClient, or OkHttp.
- OkHttp verb inference from sibling builder calls like `.post(body)`, `.put(body)`, `.delete()` rather than defaulting to GET.
- Java / Apache HttpClient request variable tracking through `send(...)` / `execute(...)`.

## Notes

These cases were intentionally left out of #1872 to keep the first Java consumer extraction PR low-risk and independent of the ongoing scope-resolution work in #909.

title: Support CUDA source files (`.cu` / `.cuh`) as C++
body:
### Area

gitnexus (CLI / core / indexing / MCP server)

### Problem or opportunity

## Summary

GitNexus cannot extract symbols (classes, functions, methods, call graphs) from **CUDA C++** source files because `.cu` and `.cuh` extensions are not mapped to any supported language. For CUDA-heavy codebases, the knowledge graph is essentially **file-structure only** — the core simulation/engine code is invisible to MCP tools, hooks, and impact analysis.

This makes GitNexus nearly useless for projects like [GPUMD](https://github.com/brucefan1983/GPUMD), where the entire engine lives in `.cu`/`.cuh` files.

## Environment

- **GitNexus version:** 1.6.5 (local monorepo build from source)
- **OS:** Linux (WSL2)
- **Node:** v22.22.3
- **Test repo:** [GPUMD](https://github.com/brucefan1983/GPUMD) @ `3fba820a`

## Expected behavior

When indexing a CUDA C++ project, GitNexus should:

1. Recognize `.cu` and `.cuh` as C++ (or a dedicated CUDA profile)
2. Parse them with the existing C++ Tree-sitter grammar (`tree-sitter-cpp`)
3. Extract classes like `Force`, `NEP`, `Integrate`, methods, and call relationships
4. Make them queryable via `context`, `query`, `impact`, MCP tools, and Cursor hooks

## Actual behavior

### Indexing succeeds, but symbols are missing

```bash
gitnexus analyze --force --drop-embeddings
# → 3,220 nodes | 4,279 edges | 86 clusters | 105 flows
```

Looks fine on paper. But core CUDA symbols are **not in the graph**.

### Symbol lookup fails for core GPUMD types

```bash
gitnexus context Force --repo GPUMD    # → Symbol 'Force' not found
gitnexus context NEP --repo GPUMD      # → Symbol 'NEP' not found
gitnexus context Integrate --repo GPUMD # → Symbol 'Integrate' not found
gitnexus impact Force --repo GPUMD   # → Target 'Force' not found
```

These classes exist in `src/force/force.cuh`, `src/force/nep.cuh`, `src/integrate/integrate.cuh`, etc.

### Cypher confirms zero symbols from CUDA files

```cypher
MATCH (n:Function) WHERE n.filePath ENDS WITH ".cu"  RETURN count(n)  -- 0
MATCH (n:Class)    WHERE n.filePath ENDS WITH ".cu"  RETURN count(n)  -- 0
MATCH (n:Function) WHERE n.filePath ENDS WITH ".cuh" RETURN count(n)  -- 0
MATCH (n:Class)    WHERE n.filePath ENDS WITH ".cuh" RETURN count(n)  -- 0
```

Meanwhile, **147 `.cu` files** are indexed as `File` nodes (folder structure only):

```cypher
MATCH (f:File) WHERE f.filePath ENDS WITH ".cu" RETURN count(f)  -- 147
```

### What *does* get indexed in GPUMD

| Source | Result |
|--------|--------|
| Python tests/tools (`.py`) | ✅ Functions/classes found (`run_md`, etc.) |
| C++ in `tools/` (`.cpp`, `.h`) | ✅ e.g. `NEP3` in `tools/Miscellaneous/.../nep.cpp` |
| `src/` CUDA core (`.cu`, `.cuh`) | ❌ **0 classes, 0 functions** |
| `src/main_mdi/mdi_fallback.h` (only `.h` in `src/`) | ✅ 44 functions |

GPUMD `src/` breakdown:

```
147 × .cu
158 × .cuh
  0 × .cpp
  1 × .h   (mdi_fallback.h — the only parsed header in src/)
```

**~99% of GPUMD's engine code is unparseable** with current extension mapping.

## Root cause

In `gitnexus-shared/src/language-detection.ts`, C++ extensions do not include CUDA suffixes:

```typescript
[SupportedLanguages.CPlusPlus]: ['.cpp', '.cc', '.cxx', '.h', '.hpp', '.hxx', '.hh'],
// Missing: '.cu', '.cuh'
```

Files with unrecognized extensions are walked and stored as `File` nodes but **never enter the Tree-sitter parsing pipeline**, so no AST extraction, no call graph, no impact analysis.

## Impact

This affects any project where CUDA is the primary language:

- **GPUMD** — GPU molecular dynamics (entire `src/` is `.cu`/`.cuh`)
- **LAMMPS GPU packages**, custom MD/CFD kernels, ML training CUDA ops, etc.
- Users integrating GitNexus with Cursor/Claude Code get MCP + hooks that **silently skip** the most important code

From a user perspective: indexing reports thousands of nodes, tools appear to work, but asking about `Force` or `NEP` returns "not found" — very misleading.

## Suggested fix

Minimal change (likely sufficient for most CUDA C++ code):

```typescript
[SupportedLanguages.CPlusPlus]: [
  '.cpp', '.cc', '.cxx',
  '.h', '.hpp', '.hxx', '.hh',
  '.cu', '.cuh',  // CUDA C++ source & headers
],
```

CUDA C++ is syntactically close enough to ISO C++ that `tree-sitter-cpp` should handle classes, methods, namespaces, and most call sites. CUDA-specific syntax (`__global__`, `<<<>>>` launches, etc.) may parse imperfectly, but **missing 100% of symbols is worse than parsing 90%**.

Optional follow-ups:

- Add `.cuda` if any projects use that extension
- Document CUDA support level in README (best-effort via C++ grammar)
- Add a `--verbose` warning during analyze: `"N files skipped (unrecognized extension: .cu)"` so users know upfront

## Reproduction

```bash
git clone https://github.com/brucefan1983/GPUMD.git
cd GPUMD
gitnexus analyze --force

gitnexus context Force --repo GPUMD   # not found
gitnexus context NEP --repo GPUMD     # not found

gitnexus cypher 'MATCH (n:Class) WHERE n.filePath ENDS WITH ".cuh" RETURN count(n)' --repo GPUMD
# → 0
```

## Workaround (none really)

Renaming `.cu` → `.cpp` is not practical for upstream projects. Forking `language-detection.ts` locally works but shouldn't be required for a common HPC/GPU workflow.

---

**TL;DR:** Please add `.cu` and `.cuh` to the C++ extension map. Without this, GitNexus cannot analyze CUDA codebases in any meaningful way — the graph looks populated but the actual engine code is a black hole.


### Proposed solution

Treat `.cu` and `.cuh` as C++ during indexing (same pipeline as `.cpp`/`.hpp`), using the existing `tree-sitter-cpp` grammar.

**User-visible behavior after the fix:**

1. **`gitnexus analyze`** on a CUDA project (e.g. GPUMD) parses `.cu`/`.cuh` files and extracts classes, functions, methods, and call relationships — not just `File` folder nodes.

2. **CLI / MCP tools work on CUDA symbols**, same as normal C++:
   - `gitnexus context Force --repo GPUMD` → returns callers, callees, file location (`src/force/force.cuh`)
   - `gitnexus context NEP --repo GPUMD` → works
   - `gitnexus query "force potential"` → returns processes/symbols from `src/force/`, not only Python test code
   - `gitnexus impact <symbol>` → blast-radius analysis includes CUDA call chains

3. **Cursor / Claude Code integration** (MCP + hooks) can augment grep/read results with graph context for CUDA symbols — e.g. searching `NEP` or reading `force.cu` shows `[GitNexus]` caller/callee blocks.

4. **Analyze output is honest**: symbol counts reflect CUDA code; users are not misled by a "successful" index that silently skips the entire engine.

**Implementation hint (minimal):** add `.cu` and `.cuh` to `CPlusPlus` in `gitnexus-shared/src/language-detection.ts`. CUDA-specific syntax (`__global__`, `<<<>>>`) may parse imperfectly — best-effort C++ coverage is acceptable; 0% coverage is not.

**Non-goals for v1:** full CUDA kernel launch semantics, separate CUDA grammar, or perfect parsing of device-only syntax. Goal is parity with "regular C++ project" UX for `.cu`/`.cuh` files.

### Alternatives considered

_No response_

### Acceptance criteria

_No response_

### Constraints

_No response_

### Contribution

- [ ] I am willing to open a PR for this (may need design discussion first).

body:
## Summary

- Add a `.devcontainer/` that pre-installs **Claude Code 2.1.153** (via Anthropic's official Feature), **OpenAI Codex CLI 0.134.0** (pinned), and **Cursor CLI** (latest at build time) alongside the GitNexus native build chain.
- Opens via VS Code's Dev Containers extension on **Windows 11 (Docker Desktop + WSL2), macOS, and Linux** without OS-specific branches in `devcontainer.json`.
- Persistent auth and `node_modules` via per-devcontainer named volumes scoped by `${devcontainerId}` (including four sub-workspace `node_modules` volumes so tree-sitter native bindings + onnxruntime stay off the bind mount on Win/Mac).

## What changed

- `.devcontainer/Dockerfile` — base `mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/typescript-node` (multi-arch), **digest-pinned** to the `1-22-bookworm` tag; apt block matches `Dockerfile.cli`/`gitnexus/Dockerfile.test` (`python3 make g++ git curl ca-certificates bash`); pre-creates `/home/node/.claude`, `.codex`, `.cursor`, `.npm`, `/commandhistory` with `chown node:node` _before_ `USER node` so empty named volumes inherit correct ownership; installs Codex via npm-global, Cursor pinned by version + per-arch sha256 (artifact fetched directly, no remote install script); promotes build ARGs to ENV so they're visible to lifecycle scripts.
- `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` — 9 named volumes (3 credential, 1 history, 1 npm-cache, 4 sub-workspace `node_modules`); `consistency=delegated` workspace mount; `forwardPorts: [5173, 4747, 4173]` with `requireLocalPort: true` on 4747 (the gitnexus-web UI hardcodes `http://localhost:4747`); `customizations.vscode.extensions` (Claude Code, ESLint, Prettier, GitLens); `postCreateCommand` chowns the workspace `node_modules` volumes and runs installs in dependency order (gitnexus-shared builds before consumers).
- `.devcontainer/README.md` — WSL2 setup (clone _inside_ WSL2 for IO + file-watcher reliability), first-time auth flows per CLI, port-forwarding notes, LadybugDB container caveats from `AGENTS.md`, troubleshooting table, CLI version-bumping procedure.
- `.gitattributes` — extended with explicit `*.sh`/`*.bash` LF rules and native-binary markers (`*.node *.wasm *.onnx *.so *.dll *.dylib binary`). Existing `* text=auto eol=lf` and `.husky/* text eol=lf` rules preserved. `git ls-files --eol` confirmed zero CRLF/mixed blobs — no `--renormalize` needed.
- `CONTRIBUTING.md` — new "Containerized development (optional)" subsection under Development setup pointing at the devcontainer README.

## Key decisions

- **Single container, all three CLIs co-installed.** Prevailing 2026 pattern; per-tool docker-compose adds complexity without daily-driver benefit.
- **Build args promoted to runtime ENV in the Dockerfile.** Without this, `$FIREWALL`/`$CODEX_VERSION` referenced in lifecycle commands would silently no-op (Docker ARGs are build-only by default). Caught during planning's doc-review.
- **Credential paths pre-created with `chown` in the Dockerfile.** Docker copies image-side ownership onto empty named volumes on first mount, so first-run `claude login` / `codex login --device-auth` / `cursor-agent login` writes succeed without EACCES.
- **`CURSOR_API_KEY` via `${localEnv:CURSOR_API_KEY}`.** Cursor's documented headless path; falls back to interactive login when the host env var is unset.
- **Sub-workspace `node_modules` volumes.** Root-only would still leave the heavy `gitnexus/node_modules` (tree-sitter + onnxruntime) on the bind mount — the four-volume layout actually delivers the perf claim.

## Deferred (follow-up PRs)

- **Opt-in egress firewall.** Originally a fourth implementation unit (Anthropic-style iptables/ipset allowlist). Dev Containers' `runArgs` is static — clean toggling of `NET_ADMIN`/`NET_RAW` capabilities needs either a separate `devcontainer-firewall.json` profile or an `initializeCommand`-generated overlay. Keeping this PR focused on the working baseline.
- **Codespaces-specific tuning.** Works incidentally with no privileged capabilities; not actively tested.
- **Inside-container Playwright e2e.** Needs Chromium libs the base image doesn't ship.

## Test plan

- [ ] `docker build .devcontainer/` succeeds on `linux/amd64`
- [ ] `docker buildx build --platform linux/arm64 .devcontainer/` succeeds (Apple Silicon path)
- [ ] VS Code "Dev Containers: Reopen in Container" succeeds; recommended extensions install; Ports panel shows 5173, 4747, 4173 forwarded with no remap on 4747
- [ ] Inside the container as `node`: `claude --version`, `codex --version`, `cursor-agent --version` all resolve
- [ ] First-time `claude login` succeeds (browser callback via VS Code port forwarding); rebuild container; `claude` reports authenticated without re-login
- [ ] `codex login --device-auth` succeeds; rebuild; still authenticated
- [ ] Setting `CURSOR_API_KEY` on the host and rebuilding makes `cursor-agent status` report authenticated
- [ ] `cd /workspace/gitnexus && npm run test:unit` runs clean
- [ ] Husky pre-commit fires correctly on `git commit` from inside the container
- [ ] Windows 11 host: repo cloned inside WSL2 (not on Windows side) → Vite HMR works without polling
- [ ] Linux host with UID ≠ 1000: `updateRemoteUserUID: true` aligns; workspace writable without `EACCES`

## Post-Deploy Monitoring & Validation

No runtime production impact — this is dev tooling only; the production Dockerfiles (`Dockerfile.cli`, `Dockerfile.web`, `gitnexus/Dockerfile.test`) are untouched; the only CI addition is the devcontainer-scoped smoke workflow (`.github/workflows/ci-devcontainer.yml`). Failure signals are local-only: image build failures, `postCreateCommand` errors, first-time CLI login EACCES (would indicate the named-volume `chown` didn't take), or VS Code unable to reach forwarded ports. No metrics or dashboards needed.

title: JavaScript Index produces a Function and a Const for a Lambda Call
body:
### Area

gitnexus (CLI / core / indexing / MCP server)

### Summary

Given code like this:

```javascript
    // Format export data
    const exportData = accountsList.map(account => ({
      code: account.code,
      name: account.name,
      type: account.type,
      direction: account.direction,
      description: account.description || '',
      isActive: account.isActive,
      systems: accountSystemsMap[account.id]?.join(',') || '',
    }))
```

It produces a Const named `exportData` and a Function called `exportData`. 

Although the lambda itself is technically a 'Function', but its semantic meaning is not. And this behaviour doubles the count of nodes which makes the graph hard to read and slow to load. 

### Context

_No response_

### Expected behavior

One thing (a piece of code, one line) generates one node at most. In this case, a Function might be a better choice. 

### Actual behavior

Duplicated nodes are generated. 

### Steps to reproduce

1. clone a javascript code repo
2. Find a file node.
3. Check its links of Function and Const

title: feat(ingestion): resolve FastAPI include_router(prefix=...) cross-file routes
body:
## Background & Problem

A very common FastAPI pattern: sub-route files declare paths via `APIRouter`,
and the entry file mounts the whole router under a prefix using
`app.include_router(<router>, prefix='/x')`.

```python
# users.py
from fastapi import APIRouter
router = APIRouter()

@router.get("/list")
def list_users(): ...

# main.py
from fastapi import FastAPI
from . import users
from .calls import router as calls_router

app = FastAPI()
app.include_router(users.router, prefix="/users")  # Shape A: attribute access
app.include_router(calls_router,  prefix="/calls") # Shape B: named import
```

The expected routes are `GET /users/list`, `GET /calls/list`, etc.

But today both of GitNexus's route-producing paths only see the bare `/list`
declared inside the sub-route file — the `prefix` from the entry file is
completely lost:

1. **Ingestion layer** — when writing `Route` graph nodes,
   `routes.ts` uses the decorator's `routePath` directly as the URL,
   with no mechanism to thread the cross-file `prefix` in.
2. **Group layer** — `HttpRouteExtractor` only scans decorators file-by-file;
   there is no "scan the repo first to build a prefix map" pre-pass,
   so `ExtractedContract` URLs are also bare `/list`.

The direct impact: cross-repo contract matching (HTTP provider ↔ HTTP consumer)
fails to find the corresponding provider — a frontend call to `/users/list`
ends up disconnected on the graph.

## Solution

Two independent but thematically aligned changes, both centered on
"thread the cross-file `include_router(prefix=)` info onto sub-route URLs."

### 1. Ingestion layer (so `Route` graph nodes carry the correct URL)

Add extraction & cross-file aggregation for "router imports / mounts":

- **`parse-worker.ts`**
  - `ExtractedDecoratorRoute` gains `decoratorReceiver?: string` and `prefix?: string | null`
  - New `ExtractedRouterInclude` / `ExtractedRouterImport` interfaces
  - `ParseWorkerResult` adds `routerIncludes` / `routerImports` (3 init sites + `mergeResult`)
  - New `extractFastAPIRouterBindings()`: scans `app.include_router(...)`
    (both attribute and named shapes) and `from <module> import router [as <alias>]`
- **`parsing-processor.ts`**
  - `WorkerExtractedData` / `mergeChunkResults` pass the two new fields through
- **`pipeline-phases/parse-impl.ts`**
  - Cross-chunk aggregation of `allRouterIncludes` / `allRouterImports`
  - Before `return`, build `prefixesByModule: Map<moduleKey, Set<prefix>>`
  - Walk `allDecoratorRoutes`: when `decoratorReceiver === 'router'` and the
    file is `.py`, duplicate the decorator route once per matching prefix
    (mirrors FastAPI's runtime behavior when one router is mounted under
    multiple prefixes)
- **`pipeline-phases/routes.ts`**
  - Use `normalizeExtractedRoutePath(dr.routePath, dr.prefix ?? null)` to join URLs
  - Drop an unused local helper

The new `ParseWorkerResult` fields are all optional, so existing parse caches
remain readable — no forced full re-scan.

### 2. Group layer (so `ExtractedContract` carries the correct URL)

Introduce "repo-level pre-processing" capability for HTTP language plugins:

- **`http-patterns/types.ts`**
  - Introduce `RepoContext = unknown` opaque type
  - `HttpLanguagePlugin` gains an optional
    `prepareRepo({ repoPath, files, parser, readFile, parseSource })` hook
  - `scan` signature extended to `scan(tree, repoContext?, fileRel?)`
- **`http-patterns/python.ts`**
  - Split the previously combined `FASTAPI_PATTERNS` into
    `FASTAPI_APP_PATTERNS` (`@app.<verb>`, already absolute) and
    `FASTAPI_ROUTER_PATTERNS` (`@router.<verb>`, needs prefix join)
  - Add `INCLUDE_ROUTER_ATTR_PATTERNS` / `INCLUDE_ROUTER_NAME_PATTERNS` /
    `FROM_IMPORT_ROUTER_PATTERNS`
  - `prepareRepo` builds `PythonRepoContext.prefixesByModule`
  - `scan` looks up the map by file basename; falls back to the bare path
    when no entry matches (backward compatible)
- **`http-route-extractor.ts`**
  - Cache one `repoContext` per plugin to avoid rebuilding
  - Make the relevant call chain async to thread the pre-pass through
    (`getDetections`, `extractProvidersSourceScan`, etc.)

## Tests

### New

- `test/unit/group/http-route-extractor.test.ts` adds three cases:
  - Attribute shape: `@router.post(\"/assistant\")` + `include_router(ai.router, prefix=\"/ai\")` → `http::POST::/ai/assistant`
  - Named-import shape: `@router.get(\"/concurrent\")` + `include_router(concurrent_router, prefix=\"/ai\")` → `http::GET::/ai/concurrent`
  - No-prefix fallback: `@router.get(\"/standalone\")` stays as `http::GET::/standalone` when no `include_router` is configured

### Compatibility patches

- `test/unit/incremental-parse-cache.test.ts`,
  `test/unit/parse-impl-worker-lazy-cache.test.ts`, and
  `test/integration/parse-impl-quarantine-cache-skip.test.ts`:
  add `routerIncludes: []` / `routerImports: []` to existing
  `ParseWorkerResult` literals to match the new interface shape.

### End-to-end verification

Built a realistic FastAPI fixture under `/tmp/gitnexus-prefix-test`
(covering both Shape A and Shape B), ran `npx gitnexus analyze`, and
queried `Route` nodes via cypher:

```
+--------------+
| r.name       |
+==============+
| /users/list  |
| /users/create|
| /calls/list  |
+--------------+
```

Cross-file prefix joining works as expected.

### Local checks

- `tsc --noEmit`: ✅ pass
- Unit tests (298 files / 6557 tests): ✅ all green
- Tests directly related to this change (4 files / 89 cases): ✅ all green

## Impact

- **Ingestion layer**: `Route` graph node URL changes only happen for
  FastAPI projects that use `@router.<verb>` decorators AND mount the
  router with `include_router(prefix=...)` in the entry file.
  Projects without prefixes, or that decorate with `@app.<verb>` directly,
  see no behavioral change.
- **Group layer**: the two new arguments to `HttpLanguagePlugin.scan` are
  both optional, so existing plugins (PHP / TS / etc.) require no changes.
  When a plugin doesn't implement `prepareRepo`, `repoContext` is
  `undefined` and behavior is identical to before.
- **Parse cache**: the new `ParseWorkerResult` fields are all optional;
  historical cache entries continue to load (guarded with
  `if (src.routerIncludes)`), with no forced full re-scan.

Thanks for the review — happy to address any questions or suggestions.

title: feat(cpp): add CUDA (.cu/.cuh) parsing via tree-sitter-cuda
body:
GitNexus previously classified .cu and .cuh files as unsupported, so CUDA kernels and device-side headers were ingested as unparsed File nodes with zero extracted symbols. This blocked code intelligence for GPU projects such as GPUMD, where the majority of force/potential logic lives in .cu/.cuh.

Changes:

- language-detection: map .cu and .cuh to SupportedLanguages.CPlusPlus so ingestion picks them up alongside existing C++ extensions.
- c-cpp provider: register .cu/.cuh in cppProvider.extensions for entry-point heuristics and language routing during graph build.
- parser-loader: add optional `cuda` grammar source (tree-sitter-cuda); resolveLanguageKey() routes .cu/.cuh to the cuda key while other C++ files still use tree-sitter-cpp. If tree-sitter-cuda is missing or its native binding fails to build, isLanguageAvailable/getLanguageGrammar gracefully fall back to tree-sitter-cpp instead of dropping the file.
- package.json: declare tree-sitter-cuda@^0.20.5 as an optionalDependency (0.21.x is ABI-incompatible with tree-sitter@0.21.1 in this repo).
- tests: extend filename detection cases for .cu/.cuh; add parser-loader smoke tests that load CUDA grammar for sample .cu/.cuh paths.

Validation (GPUMD re-index after build):
  symbols  3,220 → 14,715
  edges      4,279 → 27,969
  .cu funcs  0     → 849
  Force → src/force/force.cuh, NEP → src/main_nep/nep.cuh resolve correctly.

Install note: optional native module may require `npm install --legacy-peer-deps` in gitnexus/ if peer resolution fails; rebuild bindings after install.

title: feat: add Objective-C ingestion support (phase 1)
body:
## Summary
- add Objective-C language support to ingestion pipeline (provider + parser wiring)
- add Objective-C tree-sitter queries and fixture coverage
- add integration tests for Objective-C parsing/definitions/calls
- extend shared language detection/types for Objective-C

## Implementation details
- new provider: `gitnexus/src/core/ingestion/languages/objc.ts`
  - language id: `SupportedLanguages.ObjectiveC`
  - extensions: `.m`, `.mm`
  - import semantics: wildcard-transitive
  - built-in filtering for common ObjC/runtime symbols
  - preprocess nullability macros (`NS_ASSUME_NONNULL_BEGIN/END`) to preserve parser stability
- parser registration: `tree-sitter-objc` wired in `parser-loader.ts`
- queries: Objective-C captures in `tree-sitter-queries.ts`
- tests:
  - fixture: `test/fixtures/sample-code/simple.m`
  - integration: Objective-C cases in `test/integration/tree-sitter-languages.test.ts`

## Dependency note
- use `tree-sitter-objc@^2.1.0`
- reason: current repo uses `tree-sitter@0.21.x`; `tree-sitter-objc@3.x` pulls peerOptional `tree-sitter@^0.22.1`, causing install conflict in this branch setup

## Validation
- full integration suite passed locally after merge/conflict resolution:
  - Test Files: 91 passed, 5 skipped
  - Tests: 3049 passed, 133 skipped

## Follow-ups (separate phase)
- Objective-C++ specific semantics and query refinements
- broader Apple framework/runtime heuristics for ObjC projects


## Incremental update

Additional follow-up has now been pushed on branch `feat/objcxx-p2-02-header-classification`:

- commit: `f3ad5c21`
- title: `fix(objcxx): honor guarded ObjC and C++ header signals`

What this follow-up fixes:
- content-aware `.h/.pch` classification now inspects compatibility-guarded branches
- `__OBJC__` sections contribute Objective-C signals
- `__cplusplus` sections contribute C++ signals
- guarded diagnostics were added for exact test assertions:
  - `objcGuardedSignals`
  - `cppGuardedSignals`

Why it matters:
- Apple-style compatibility headers often hide ObjC or C++ declarations behind preprocessor guards
- without scanning those guarded regions, mixed headers could be routed through the wrong language path during ingestion
- this preserves Objective-C routing for guarded ObjC declarations and correctly classifies guarded C/C++ compatibility headers

Validation:
- `node gitnexus/scripts/build.js`
- `cd gitnexus && npx vitest run test/unit/ingestion-utils.test.ts test/unit/sequential-language-availability.test.ts`
- result: **126 tests passed**

title: feat(group): add Kotlin Spring WebClient long-form HTTP consumer extraction
body:
## Summary

Follow-up to #1855. Adds support for the WebClient **long-form** fluent chain that #1855 explicitly deferred:

```kotlin
webClient.method(HttpMethod.GET).uri("/api/users").retrieve().awaitBody<User>()
webClient.method(HttpMethod.POST).uri("/api/orders")...
webClient.method(HttpMethod.DELETE).uri("/api/items/1")...
```

The short form (`webClient.get().uri("/x")`) was already covered in #1855. The long form remains common in Kotlin Spring 4 → 5 migrations and in codebases that prefer the fluent verb-as-enum style.

## Approach

A single deeper tree-sitter query (`WEB_CLIENT_LONG_PATTERNS`) matches the full chain structurally — both `.method(HttpMethod.X)` and `.uri("...")` are captured in one pattern, no walk-up helper needed.

```scheme
(call_expression
  (navigation_expression
    (call_expression
      (navigation_expression
        (simple_identifier) @obj (#eq? @obj "webClient")
        (navigation_suffix
          (simple_identifier) @method_call (#eq? @method_call "method")))
      (call_suffix
        (value_arguments
          . (value_argument
              (navigation_expression
                (simple_identifier) @httpMethodCls (#eq? @httpMethodCls "HttpMethod")
                (navigation_suffix (simple_identifier) @verb))))))
    (navigation_suffix (simple_identifier) @uri (#eq? @uri "uri")))
  (call_suffix
    (value_arguments . (value_argument . (string_literal) @path))))
```

Verb is captured as the `simple_identifier` under `HttpMethod`'s `navigation_suffix` (the literal field name `GET`/`POST`/...) and whitelisted to `^(GET|POST|PUT|DELETE|PATCH)$` for symmetry with the short form's `WEB_CLIENT_SHORT_TO_HTTP` map.

Receiver constraint `(#eq? @obj "webClient")` mirrors the short form and the Java plugin's heuristic.

## Out of scope (intentional)

- **Variable-bound verbs**: `val verb = HttpMethod.PATCH; webClient.method(verb)...`. Source-scan can't follow the binding without graph context. Pinned by an anti-overreach test in the consumer suite.
- **HEAD / OPTIONS / TRACE**: not in `WEB_CLIENT_SHORT_TO_HTTP` either — keeps polyglot symmetry with `java.ts` and the short form.

## Tests

4 new cases under `consumer extraction — fetch patterns`, gated by tree-sitter-kotlin grammar availability.

**Positive (3)**
- long form GET
- long form POST / PUT / DELETE / PATCH (4 verbs in one fixture)
- no double-emit: a long-form chain emits exactly one consumer, not one from each query

**Anti-regression (1)**
- variable-bound verb does NOT match (graph-aware concern)

The previous `'does NOT match Kotlin WebClient long form (deferred to follow-up)'` test from #1855 is replaced by these — the deferred state is now resolved.

## Reverse validation

Temporarily disabling the long-form emit makes exactly the 3 positive tests fail; the variable-bound-verb anti-regression test continues to pass (it pins behavior independent of the emit being on or off — exactly the right shape).

## Local validation

- `http-route-extractor.test.ts` — 66 / 66 ✅
- `test/unit/group` — 546 / 546 ✅
- `npx prettier --check` (changed files) — clean ✅
