title: fix(eval): stop discarding completed benchmark sessions as unverifiable
body:
## What was broken

The skill-evolution loop has not produced a promotion decision on merit since it went online, and a run gave no sign of life until it exited. Four things, all found in the artifact of the last green run ([`29907431284`](https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/actions/runs/29907431284) — 14h45m, ≈$110 of benchmark sessions).

**The scheduled lane never ran.** `vars.GITNEXUS_EVOLUTION_ENABLED` was never set, so the job `if:` was false and both scheduled invocations (`30143231476` on 2026-07-25, `30683251591` on 2026-08-01) skipped in seconds — while the EventBridge schedule still started the runner for the day. The variable is now set to `true`.

**The gate could not reach a verdict.** That run excluded 5 of its 18 runs, and promotion requires *zero* excluded runs in both paired arms:

```
[gen 0] candidate_workflow: insufficient_evidence — inv-bug-pdg-note: needs at least 3 valid
runs per arm (got 1/3); inv-bug-pdg-note: promotion requires zero excluded runs in both paired
arms (got 2/0); ...
```

## 1. Trailing background-task events invalidated complete sessions (3 runs)

Claude Code drains background-task bookkeeping *after* the final `result` event. From the captured stdout of `inv-feature-list-repos-filter / candidate_workflow / run0` — exit code 0, complete `result` with `total_cost_usd` and full `usage`:

```
{... "num_turns":103, "total_cost_usd":5.5727, "usage":{...}, "terminal_reason":"completed"}
{"type":"system","subtype":"background_tasks_changed","tasks":[]}
{"type":"system","subtype":"task_updated","task_id":"bdw43oy7j","patch":{"status":"killed",...}}
{"type":"system","subtype":"task_notification","task_id":"bdw43oy7j","status":"stopped",...}
```

`run_claude` required the result to be the literal last event, so these sessions were recorded as `session-error` with `evidence_diagnostics: ['unverifiable parent event stream: final result event is not the last event in the captured stream']`.

Trailing `type: "system"` events are now tolerated. They carry no `tool_use`/`tool_result`/`usage` payload, so they cannot forge skill or cost evidence; any other event after the result still fails closed, and the existing `test_final_result_event_must_be_last` (which appends an `assistant` event) still passes.

## 2. The per-session ceiling was below real `workflow`-arm work (2 runs)

`inv-bug-pdg-note / workflow / run0` and `run2` died on `SIGTERM` at the 3600s ceiling (`process_state: 'timeout'`, `returncode: -15`) with a Bash verification step still emitting heartbeats. Successful `workflow` rows in the same run finished in ~1600–2600s across both sessions, so the ceiling moves to 5400s — headroom over observed work, not over the timeout. `runner.py` and `evolve.py` now share `runner_sessions.SESSION_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` instead of two argparse defaults that could drift.

## 3. A task neither arm can solve vetoed every promotion

The quality floor demanded that the candidate resolve every valid run of *every* selected task regardless of the incumbent's score. `inv-feature-list-repos-filter` fails its hidden oracle on 100% of runs in **both** arms (incumbent 0/2, candidate 0/1), so the floor could never be met while it stayed in the set — and its cost comparison, which ranks who spent more while failing the same oracle, also fed the per-task regression cap and the median.

A task that both arms measured cleanly (≥ `min_runs` valid runs, zero exclusions) and that neither ever resolved now reports as `gated: false` with a named reason and an `ungated_tasks` list, and is left out of the floor, the cap, and the median. It still runs, and its failures still feed the proposer: an unsolved task is the loop's target, not its veto.

The floor is unchanged wherever it has signal — a candidate that goes 2/3 where the incumbent goes 1/3 is still rejected as unreliable — and a generation where nothing resolved anywhere is now `insufficient_evidence` instead of an efficiency verdict over runs that all failed. `promotion.json` goes to `schema_version: 4`, since task rows changed meaning and a stale v3 binding must not be applied under the new rule.

## 4. A run reported nothing until it exited

Every line of that 14h45m run carries the same timestamp — `00:02:59.32`, as the process exited. The step's stdout is a pipe, so CPython block-buffered it, and there was no way to tell a live run from a wedged one:

```
2026-07-23T00:02:59.3222017Z selected 3 task(s): trivial-version-alias, inv-bug-pdg-note, ...
2026-07-23T00:02:59.3225096Z [gen 0] proposing…
2026-07-23T00:02:59.3226455Z [gen 0] benchmarking candidate…
2026-07-23T00:02:59.3231117Z [gen 0] candidate_workflow: insufficient_evidence — ...
```

- `PYTHONUNBUFFERED` for the driver (workflow step) and for the benchmark subprocess (its env is an explicit minimal dict and inherits nothing).
- `run_managed` grows `echo_stdout`, a passthrough that streams a child's stdout to stderr as it arrives while leaving the bounded tail intact. `evolve.py` enables it for the benchmark sweep — the multi-hour phase, whose per-run lines previously surfaced only as a tail, and only on failure. It stays off everywhere else: a Claude session's stdout is the evidence stream and is written out only after redaction.
- The sweep announces each cell as it starts and reports `took=` and `error_kind=` when it finishes, so an excluded run — the thing that actually blocks promotion — is visible live instead of only in `results.jsonl`. The proposer's duration, turns, and cost are reported once the proposal lands.

```
[inv-bug-pdg-note][workflow][run 0] starting (7/18, 214m elapsed)
[inv-bug-pdg-note][workflow][run 0] resolved=False in=200 out=41053 cost=$n/a took=3990.8s error_kind=session-error
```

## Validation

- `uv run --locked --extra dev python -m pytest tests/` → 333 passed, 12 skipped
- `npx vitest run test/unit/skill-evolution-workflow.test.ts` → 10 passed

---

## 5. The sweep ran 18 cells one at a time

97.4% of a generation is the benchmark sweep — 18 cells at ~48 min each (min 27, max 67), strictly serial:

```
job wall clock        14.74 h
proposer session       0.06 h   (3.4 min)
18 benchmark cells    14.36 h   ← 97.4%
setup/builds/clones/graph/verify/oracle/cache   0.32 h
```

The cells are independent — 3 tasks × 3 runs × 2 arms, with `min_runs=3` the gate's own floor — so the wall clock was a scheduling choice, not a measurement requirement. This matters less for EC2 cost (the box is 1.3% of a run's spend) than for headroom: at 14.7h the run sits against the 19h step cap with 29% margin, `include_expensive: true` (+6 cells, ~+4.8h) already overflows it, and a second generation is impossible.

`--workers` (default 1) runs the cells of one task concurrently; tasks stay sequential, so the sanitized graph snapshot each task builds before its cells stays single-writer. Threads, not processes: cells are subprocess-bound and `run_managed` keeps every piece of ownership state local to its own call.

Three design points that are load-bearing:

**Waves, not one fan-out.** The outage breaker counts *consecutive* systemic failures, and "consecutive" means nothing in completion order — folding as futures landed would make the trip point flaky between identical runs. Each wave is folded in submission order once complete, and the next wave starts only if the breaker held, so it overruns by at most `workers - 1` cells rather than a whole task.

**`--workers 1` never leaves the calling thread.** Not an optimisation: an async `KeyboardInterrupt` is delivered only to the main thread, so a cell on a worker thread is outside the reach of `process_control`'s ownership cleanup that kills its sandboxed process tree. The default stays exactly what it is today, Ctrl-C included.

**All bookkeeping stays on the main thread** — the `results.jsonl` append, per-arm accumulation, progress prints, streak fold. No lock anywhere, no counter race, no interleaved prints, and `results.jsonl` keeps its canonical order.

Landed as three commits: the cell body becomes `run_cell(ctx, run_idx, arm)` with a frozen `TaskCellContext` (a pure refactor, and the first test coverage that body has ever had — 6 tests); then the wave driver `sweep_task_cells` (6 more tests, including a `threading.Barrier` that deadlocks if a wave is not genuinely concurrent, and one asserting `workers=1` stays on the calling thread); then the `--workers` plumbing through `evolve.py` and a dispatch input.

### Turning it on

The workflow input defaults to `'1'` and the contract test pins that default, so the lane cannot start running 3-way on a 2-vCPU box by accident. Enabling it is:

1. Resize the runner — it is stopped, so this is clean and reversible with the same call:
   ```
   aws ec2 modify-instance-attribute --instance-id i-084d230b97e53ca55 \
     --instance-type '{"Value":"m6i.2xlarge"}' --region us-east-1
   ```
2. `workflow_dispatch` with `workers: 3`, watched live.
3. Judge it against the serial baseline: **mean cell 48 min** and **zero excluded runs**. A stretched mean means contention is pushing cells toward the 5400s session ceiling, and every ceiling hit is an excluded run.
4. If clean, flip the input default to `'3'`. Expected: **14.4h → ~5h**.

Rollback at any point is `--workers 1`, which restores the serial path exactly.

title: assertDeclaredPair aborts on the first undeclared pair, not all of them
body:
## Problem

`assertDeclaredPair` (`gitnexus/src/core/lbug/rel-pair-routing.ts`) throws on the **first** undeclared FROM/TO pair it meets, aborting `analyze` immediately. The emit pass is already walking every edge, so the remaining undeclared pairs in the same run are never reported.

The cost is not theoretical — **PR #2793 is the proof**. Four undeclared pairs were live simultaneously at that branch's head:

| pair | trigger |
|---|---|
| `Method→Annotation` | Spring `@Bean` + `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` (Java and Kotlin) |
| `Method→File` | Vue Options-API `methods:` handler bound to a child-component event |
| `Namespace→Record` | COBOL `DECLARATIVES` / `USE AFTER STANDARD ERROR ON <file>` |
| `Class→Tool` | `@mcp.tool()` applied to a class |

Each had to be found by constructing a separate reproduction repo, because the run dies at the first one. A user with three missing pairs today files three bug reports across three releases — which is roughly the shape of #2740 → #2769/#2781 → #2783 → #2789/#2791 → #2792/#2793.

## Proposal

Accumulate undeclared pairs during the emit pass (skip the edge, count it), then throw **once** at `RelPairRouter.close()` / sink finalize with the complete list.

Same abort semantics, same "no partial index", same fail-loud contract — one round trip instead of N. This does not touch the throw-vs-degrade question below; the run still fails.

## Related, worth deciding at the same time

`rel-pair-routing.ts`'s docblock argues for throwing on the grounds that *"silently writing such a CSV lets COPY fail late and can drop an otherwise valid edge during fallback."* That is an argument against the pre-#2203 status quo, not against skip-and-warn — skip + count + non-zero exit + a named list is neither silent nor fatal.

The throw is still probably right, but for a reason the docblock does not state: GitNexus's product is graph completeness, and a dropped `CALLS` edge produces a wrong `impact` answer, which is worse than no index. That reasoning is **relation-type-scoped** though — dropping a `CONDITIONAL_ON` evidence edge corrupts no query. If the policy is ever revisited, the principled split is by relation type, not global. Worth recording in the docblock so the next reader doesn't re-derive it from the weaker COPY argument.

## Context

Surfaced by the multi-engine review of #2793 (which fixed all four pairs above by generating the surface rather than hand-listing it).

title: No non-Go fixture exercises a compound (field) interface receiver, so the shared Case 0 path is ungated outside Go
body:
`scope-resolution/passes/receiver-bound-calls.ts` is shared, language-nameless code consumed by all 14 languages. #2829 changed its Case 0 path (adding interface-dispatch fan-out, then walking the subtype closure), yet **every test added for that change is Go**.

The gap is not theoretical. Measured on a two-implementor non-generic TypeScript fixture calling the same interface method through a **field** and through a **parameter** side by side:

| call shape | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `runField → save` (field, Case 0) | 1 edge | **3 edges** |
| `runLocal → save` (parameter, Case 4) | 3 edges | 3 edges |
| total CALLS | 4 | **6** |

The new edges are the real `UserRepo.save` / `MockRepo.save` implementations — correct behaviour, the change doing what it intends. But nothing outside Go pins it, so a regression here is uncatchable.

**Why the existing corpus cannot see it**

All four pre-existing non-Go `*-interface-dispatch` fixtures (`csharp-`, `typescript-`, `java-`) use **bare-name** receivers — `_repo.Save()`, `action.execute()`, `repo.find(1)` — which take Case 4, and Case 4 already had the fan-out. No non-Go fixture anywhere exercises an interface-typed **field**. That is the same blind spot that hid the original Go bug for so long.

It is also what would have caught the sub-interface/abstract-base defect found during review of #2829: that one reproduces in plain Java and was invisible to the Go-only suite.

**Suggested work**

Add one field-receiver fixture per collapse class, since the edge accounting differs:

- **Java, C#** — set `collapseMemberCallsByCallerTarget`, so fan-out is bounded by distinct (caller, target) pairs.
- **TypeScript, Kotlin, Go** — do not, so fan-out is per call **site**.

Assert both the targets and the count, so a future cap/collapse/dedup change is visible rather than silent.

Follow-up from #2829.

title: Interface dispatch emits a self-loop CALLS edge for the Go decorator pattern — decide and pin the semantics
body:
The canonical Go decorator / middleware shape now emits a **self-referential** `CALLS` edge.

**Reproduced:**

```go
type Repository interface{ DeleteItem(id string) error }

type SqlRepo struct{ dsn string }
func (s *SqlRepo) DeleteItem(id string) error { return nil }

type loggingRepo struct{ next Repository }          // holds the delegate in a FIELD
func (l *loggingRepo) DeleteItem(id string) error { return l.next.DeleteItem(id) }
```

```
CALLS  loggingRepo.DeleteItem -> loggingRepo.DeleteItem   (interface-dispatch)   <- self-loop
CALLS  loggingRepo.DeleteItem -> Repository.DeleteItem    (global)
CALLS  loggingRepo.DeleteItem -> SqlRepo.DeleteItem       (interface-dispatch)
```

Both #2829 changes are required to produce it: before, `loggingRepo` (pointer receivers) did not implement `Repository`, and a field receiver never fanned out at all. The decorator shape was immune *precisely because* it holds its delegate in a field.

**This is not obviously a bug.** Interface dispatch is an over-approximation by design — "the receiver is typed `I`, so any implementor of `I` could be the runtime target" — and `next Repository` genuinely can hold another `loggingRepo`; nested middleware is a real pattern. `emitInterfaceDispatchFor` excludes only the *primary* target, never the caller.

**But it should be a decision, not an accident.** Downstream consumers may not expect a self-recursive `CALLS` edge in what is one of the most common Go structural patterns:

- cycle detection (`check --cycles`) will report a cycle that does not exist in any concrete execution;
- `impact()` shows the method as its own caller;
- community clustering and `process-processor.ts`'s "avoid cycles" truncation both see it.

**Suggested work**

Pick one and pin it with a fixture:

1. Accept it — document that dispatch is an over-approximation and self-loops are legitimate for self-implementing decorators.
2. Exclude the enclosing caller's own owner from the fan-out when it coincides with an implementor.
3. Keep the edge but make it distinguishable so cycle-detection consumers can filter it.

Follow-up from #2829.

- [x] `.github/` (workflows, actions)
- [x] `eval/` or other tooling
- [x] Docs / agent config

## Scope & constraints

**In scope**

- Objective-C headers and implementations
- Classes, categories, protocols, properties, methods, functions, imports, calls, inheritance, and protocol edges
- Receiver-aware Objective-C message dispatch through the shared scope-resolution pipeline
- Optional grammar installation and prebuild behavior across supported platforms
- Objective-C unit, integration, regression, and real-project validation

**Explicitly out of scope / not done here**

- Full Swift semantic support
- Xcode build-setting evaluation
- Bridging-header and module-map semantics
- Compiler-grade macro expansion beyond parser-visible facts

## Implementation notes

- Language-specific behavior is isolated behind the existing language-provider and scope-resolver extension points; shared ingestion code does not add Objective-C-specific branching.
- The Objective-C grammar follows the repository's existing optional vendored-grammar lifecycle.
- Existing-language behavior is guarded by the full regression suite and targeted cross-language scope-resolution tests.

## Testing & verification

Validated on Node.js 22.18.0:

- [x] Objective-C targeted suite: **17 files, 184/184 tests passed**
- [x] Changed-test suite: **46 files, 688/688 tests passed**
- [x] `cd gitnexus-web && npm test`: **34 files, 391/391 tests passed**
- [x] `cd gitnexus && npx tsc --noEmit`
- [x] `cd gitnexus-web && npx tsc -b --noEmit`
- [x] Production build
- [x] ESLint: 0 errors (existing warnings only)
- [x] Prettier: every changed file passed
- [x] Real Objective-C iOS project indexing: **94,492 nodes, 210,931 edges, 1,370 clusters, 324 flows**

Core full-suite result: **821 files passed and 16,495 tests passed**. Seven local-environment failures were investigated:

- Four Linux-only `/proc/self/fd` provenance tests on macOS
- One GNU `timeout` dependency absent on macOS
- One local `javac` version limitation for Java records/local enums
- One isolated-home fixture setup issue; the targeted rerun passed 5/5

The repository CI matrix remains the authoritative cross-platform check.

## Risk & rollout

Graph impact analysis reports **CRITICAL** breadth, expected for parser and scope-resolution work: 161 files, 668 symbols, and 135 processes affected.

Recommended rollout:

1. Merge behind the normal optional-grammar availability behavior.
2. Run the repository CI matrix, including Linux and supported Node versions.
3. Refresh indexes for Objective-C repositories after upgrading.
4. Monitor grammar prebuild availability per platform and architecture.

## Checklist

- [x] PR body meets the repository minimum length
- [x] Change is scoped to Objective-C support and shared extension contracts
- [x] No secrets, tokens, machine-specific paths, generated indexes, or test artifacts are committed
- [x] Existing-language regression coverage was run
- [x] Documentation and tests are included
- [x] Graph impact and change detection were reviewed
- [ ] Repository CI matrix passes

*A broad, cross-cutting code intelligence change centered on Objective-C language support and scope resolution. Its graph reach is shallow, but its surface area spans parsing, ingestion, embeddings, pipeline infrastructure, documentation, and editor-facing code.*

**🔴 CRITICAL blast radius. An Objective-C code intelligence change reaching across language detection, scope resolution, parsing infrastructure, and related UI and documentation areas, with no graph dependents.**

The core changes land in `gitnexus-shared/src/language-detection.ts` through `EXTENSION_MAP`, `SYNTAX_MAP`, `AUXILIARY_SYNTAX_MAP`, `getLanguageFromFilename`, and `getSyntaxLanguageFromFilename`. New scope-resolution contracts in `gitnexus-shared/src/scope-resolution/language-classification.ts`, `gitnexus-shared/src/scope-resolution/parsed-file.ts`, `gitnexus-shared/src/scope-resolution/reference-site.ts`, `gitnexus-shared/src/scope-resolution/symbol-definition.ts`, and `gitnexus-shared/src/scope-resolution/types.ts` define `LanguageClassifications`, `ParsedFile`, `ReferenceSite`, `SymbolDefinition`, `ImportEdge`, and `Scope`. The change also passes through `Passes`, `Ingestion`, `Embeddings`, `Scope-resolution`, `Pipeline`, and `Graph-bridge`, with 28 affected execution flows.
