title: perf(kotlin): index import resolution instead of scanning per import
body:
## Summary

Kotlin import resolution walked the entire workspace on every import, across a cascade of four tiers, making it O(imports × files). This replaces the scans with three maps built once per file set and memoized on its identity, so each tier is O(1). Resolution behaviour is unchanged and gated by a fingerprint whose committed baseline is the value the pre-index implementation produces.

## Motivation / context

`resolveKotlinImportTarget` tried four tiers in cascade — exact/suffix, directory child, package fan-out, progressive prefix strip — and each one ran `for (const raw of allFilePaths)` with a `replace(/\\/g, '/')` and several string scans per entry. One unresolved import therefore cost two to four full passes over the workspace.

Once a repository reaches tens of thousands of Kotlin files that is on the order of 10^10 string operations on a single thread. It does not present as a hot loop, which is what makes it hard to spot: `analyze` sits at exactly 1.00 core with a completely flat heap and emits nothing for hours, because every allocation is a short-lived string and nothing accumulates to hint at progress. Small repositories hide it entirely — at a few hundred files each pass is free, which is why the existing test suite never noticed.

This is the same shape #1918 fixed for Python (issue #1741, "analyze gets stuck at 'Resolving calls'") and #2788 fixed for C++; neither touched the Kotlin path. I found it with a CPU profile that put 99.5% of self-time in `resolveKotlinImportTarget` under `makeEdgeDrafts`.

The bench added here reproduces it from scratch, so the cost is checkable without my profile: at only 400 files and 12.8k imports the pre-index resolver already spends 2.2 s where the index spends ~6 ms, and at 1600 files the gap is 33.0 s against ~24 ms — 3.737 versus ~1.0 on the scaling ratio. Both numbers come from the same corpus in the same harness; swapping one module specifier reproduces the first row.

I could not find an existing upstream issue for the Kotlin path specifically — happy to open one and re-title this PR if you would prefer the usual `(#NNNN)` reference.

## Areas touched

- [x] `gitnexus/` (CLI / core / MCP server)
- [ ] `gitnexus-web/` (Vite / React UI)
- [x] `.github/` (workflows, actions) — one step added to the existing `benchmarks (GITNEXUS_BENCH)` job
- [ ] `eval/` or other tooling
- [ ] Docs / agent config only

## Scope & constraints

**In scope**

- `languages/kotlin/import-target.ts`: three lookup maps (`exactByStem`, `suffixByStem`, `dirChildren`) built once per `allFilePaths` Set and memoized in a `WeakMap` keyed on its identity, mirroring Python's `getPythonFileIndex`.
- `languages/kotlin/index-stats.ts`: the build counter, mirroring `python/index-stats.ts`.
- `bench/kotlin-import-target/`: identity + scaling gate, wired into the existing benchmarks job next to the C++ (#2788) and Python (#1918) guards.
- Parity and index-reuse tests, named and placed to match the Python pair.

**Explicitly out of scope / not done here**

- **The directory-match rule is preserved as-is, including its bug.** The old scan tested `startsWith` and then used `indexOf`, so it only ever considered the FIRST occurrence of `/dir/`. Fixing it belongs in its own change with its own fixtures: it would move edges in every Kotlin repository, and that is a behaviour change that should not ride along with a performance one. The shape it actually breaks is narrower than it first looks — executed against a standard Gradle layout, `com.example.data.Repo`, `com.example.data.helper` and `data.Repo` all resolve correctly; only a bare single-segment key whose package sits at the repository root and collides with an ancestor directory name (`data.helper`) fails. Real Kotlin files under `…/com/example/data/` declare `package com.example.data`, so real imports take the multi-segment path that works. A follow-up issue should be scoped to that narrow shape.
- **Go, Dart and Ruby have the same defect and are left alone**, having no repository at hand to verify a change against:
  - `go/import-target.ts` — `findRootPackageFiles` and `findAllFilesInPkgDir` scan unmemoized, and the GOPATH fallback calls the latter once per path segment but the last, so one import can trigger several full passes. Most Go imports are external and always run the whole cascade, so this is likely the worst of the family;
  - `dart/import-target.ts` — the `package:` branch scans once per candidate path (`lib/<rel>` and bare `<rel>`), and `resolveRelative` scans again in its suffix fallback;
  - `ruby/import-target.ts` — rebuilds the entire `buildSuffixIndex` on every `require`, unmemoized at any layer.
- **C# is a partial case**: `getWorkspaceFileIndex` is already memoized, but it is only reached when a `.csproj` is found; the no-csproj path hands the raw Set to `resolveDirectMatch` and `resolveByProgressiveStripping`, which scan past it.
- Happy to file these as issues if you would rather track them that way than in this description.

## Implementation notes

The tie-breaks in this resolver were expressed only through Set-iteration order, so they are the part most at risk in a rewrite, and each is reproduced deliberately:

- an **exact match anywhere beats a suffix match found earlier** — the scan returned on the first exact hit but merely *remembered* the first suffix hit, which is why these are two maps rather than one lookup;
- **"first match" means first in set-iteration order**, so both stem maps keep the earliest path inserted per key;
- `suffixByStem` is keyed per **component-suffix of the stem**, not per basename, so a multi-segment import (`com/example/User`) hits one bucket instead of filtering a `User` bucket.

Rather than assert equivalence, the PR gates it. `bench/kotlin-import-target/measure.mjs` fingerprints every `fileSet | fromFile | targetRaw -> result` record over an exhaustive branch matrix plus a deterministic fuzz, resolving **each file set in both iteration orders** — a single-order corpus would score an implementation that keeps the *last* match identically. The committed baseline is the value the **pre-index implementation** produces: pointing the harness's module specifier at the old file and re-running prints the same `ebf1790b…` over the same 20,106 cases, 13,256 of them non-null. `--check` asserts all three together, because a hollowed corpus yields a perfectly valid fingerprint over a smaller surface.

The second arm is `(t_large/t_small)/(1600/400)` over a synthetic Kotlin monorepo whose imports are ~40% unresolvable, because only a miss drives all four tiers and that is where the scan was worst. Measured on a 12-core dev box:

| implementation | small (400 files, 12.8k imports) | large (1600 files, 51.2k imports) | ratio |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| pre-index scan | 2207.8 ms | 33003.5 ms | **3.737** |
| this change | 5.9 ms | 24.0 ms | **~1.02** |

so the budget of 1.6 separates them by a wide margin in both directions. The **ratios** are the comparable pair — each implementation's two arms are measured identically. Take the absolute times as an order of magnitude only: the pre-index row is a single cold run, because best-of-seven against a quadratic implementation costs minutes of wall time, while the index row is best-of-seven after two warmups. Both rows are author-measured; what CI reproduces is the index row and the budget. (Independent runs during review put the pre-index floor at 3.905–4.297 and the index between 0.95 and 1.08, so the separation is not an artifact of my machine.)

`--check` asserts three more things a single ratio cannot see, each added in response to review:

- a **depth ratio** — same file count, paths ~3× deeper. `scaling_ratio` divides the file count out, so it is scale-invariant and structurally blind to a cost that grows with path depth instead, which is exactly what both loops here do.
- an **absolute ceiling on the small arm**. A ratio cannot see a constant factor: a full workspace scan reintroduced on 1-in-32 imports scores 1.490, inside the budget, while running 2.8× slower.
- **`non_null` alongside `cases`**, so a corpus that stops resolving anything is not a valid baseline.

The memory cost is modest — I had overstated it in the first revision of this description. The index holds roughly `2 × (depth − 1)` map entries per Kotlin file, which measures **8.1 MiB at 10k files, 30.3 MiB at 50k and 60.1 MiB at 100k** (depth 8; 104.2 MiB at 100k with depth 12). It is released with the Set after each run — `allFilePaths` is a local in `runScopeResolution` (`scope-resolution/pipeline/run.ts`), captured only by the `finalizeScopeModel` closure, so the WeakMap entry does not survive the run and `gitnexus serve` cannot accumulate indexes across analyses.

Worth stating plainly because an inflated number invites the wrong optimization. Review built the obvious alternative — a Python-style basename-bucket index — proved it byte-identical in output, and measured it at ~66% less memory but **7.3× slower per query** on a repeated-basename corpus, failing this PR's own 1.6 scaling budget at ~2.0. I have recorded that in the code next to the `suffixByStem` description so the next reader does not re-derive it.

## Testing & verification

- [x] `cd gitnexus && npm test` — ran; see the note on pre-existing failures below
- [x] `cd gitnexus && npx vitest run test/integration` — covered by the full run above
- [x] `cd gitnexus && npx tsc --noEmit`
- [ ] `cd gitnexus-web && npm test` *(web not touched)*
- [ ] Manual / Playwright E2E *(not applicable)*

Also run:

```
cd gitnexus
npx prettier --check .                                            # clean
node --import tsx bench/kotlin-import-target/measure.mjs --check   # PASS

npx eslint \
  src/core/ingestion/languages/kotlin/import-target.ts \
  src/core/ingestion/languages/kotlin/index-stats.ts \
  bench/kotlin-import-target/measure.mjs \
  test/unit/scope-resolution/kotlin/kotlin-import-target-parity.test.ts \
  test/integration/kotlin-import-index-reuse.test.ts             # no errors, no warnings
```

Every mutation named in this description was re-run against the gate after the fix, not assumed: capping suffix-key depth at 7, skipping the `dirChildren` suffix loop above depth 8, capping a bucket at 17 entries, and the corpus edit that gutted two documented cases — all four now move the fingerprint, where all four previously passed. The two test mutations (relaxing the `indexOf` position check to `>= 0`, and `raw.lastIndexOf` for `norm.lastIndexOf`) now fail the unit suite, where both previously passed 18/18.

`npm test` is not green on my machine: 30 failures across 10 files (`resolvers/go`, `resolvers/typescript`, `analyzer-identity`, `evidence-provenance-helper`, `review-agent-workflow`, `cli-limit-e2e`, `analyze-index-lock-concurrency`, and three FTS-dependent suites). None are from this branch — I checked out a clean `main` and ran exactly those ten files, which produced exactly the same 30 failures. Kotlin is not among them, and the 20 tests this PR adds all pass. If they are green in your CI, they are environment-specific to me and worth ignoring.

Beyond the suites above, the change was exercised end to end: a large Kotlin codebase that previously could not finish `analyze` at all now completes and produces a full graph. The reproducible part of that claim is the bench — it derives the same asymptotic difference from a synthetic corpus anyone can run.

## Risk & rollout

No contract changes: `resolveKotlinImportTarget`'s signature, the `WorkspaceIndex` shape, graph node/edge shapes and persisted IDs are all untouched. No index refresh is required for correctness — the resolver returns the same targets — though Kotlin repositories that previously could not finish `analyze` will now produce a graph where they produced none.

Rollback is a straight revert; nothing persists state that would outlive it.

The one thing to watch after merge is the new benchmarks step: its fingerprint arm is deterministic and a failure there is always a behaviour change, but its scaling arm is a timing gate on a shared runner and should be re-run on an idle machine before it is investigated. Both rules are written into `baselines.json`.

On the `.github/` edit: it is one additive `run:` step in the existing `benchmarks (GITNEXUS_BENCH)` job — no new job, no permissions, secrets, triggers or `concurrency` change, and the command is a local `node --import tsx …` with no network access. I included it because a perf fix whose gate is not wired in is a gate that silently stops existing, and because #1918 and #2788 both shipped their bench and its CI step together. If you would rather take the code change first and wire the bench separately, say so and I will split it — the bench passes standalone either way.

## Checklist

- [x] PR body meets repo minimum length
- [x] `AGENTS.md` / overlays not changed
- [x] No secrets, tokens, or machine-specific paths committed

title: Go: a signature naming any type from outside the repository (`context.Context`, any stdlib/third-party type) is treated as *incompatible*, so IMPLEMENTS is never emitted and `impact()` returns a confident `0`
body:
Follow-up to #2766 / #2813. This is a self-contained repro against `1.6.10-rc.174`, and I think it explains the "inconsistent at scale" behaviour I reported in #2813 without any of the ambiguity that report had. The interface-typed-field story turned out to be a symptom; the cause is in signature normalization.

## TL;DR

`qualifyGoSignatureTypes` returns `undefined` when a package qualifier in a signature has no entry in `importQualifiers`. `signatureContextForFile` only populates `importQualifiers` from import edges whose `targetFile !== null` — i.e. imports that resolve to a file **inside the repository**. Every stdlib and third-party import is therefore absent, so any signature mentioning `context.Context`, `time.Time`, `sql.Tx`, `http.Request`, … normalizes to `undefined`, and both `parameterTypesCompatible` and `returnTypesCompatible` treat `undefined` as *not compatible*.

`ctx context.Context` is the first parameter of essentially every idiomatic Go method, so in practice Go interface satisfaction only succeeds for the small minority of interfaces whose signatures are builtin-only.

## Repro

Two files, no dependencies. `go vet` clean.

`go.mod`
```
module example.com/gnrepro

go 1.22
```

`repro.go`
```go
package repro

import "context"

// ---- Control: signature uses only in-repo/builtin types. IMPLEMENTS is emitted.
type LocalPayload struct{ ID string }

type LocalStore interface {
	Get(p LocalPayload) error
}

type LocalStoreImpl struct{}

func (l *LocalStoreImpl) Get(p LocalPayload) error { return nil }

// ---- Case A: one parameter type comes from the stdlib. No IMPLEMENTS.
type CtxStore interface {
	Delete(ctx context.Context, id string) error
}

type CtxStoreImpl struct{}

func (c *CtxStoreImpl) Delete(ctx context.Context, id string) error { return nil }

// ---- Case B: stdlib type in the RETURN position only. No IMPLEMENTS.
type RetStore interface {
	Ctx() (context.Context, error)
}

type RetStoreImpl struct{}

func (r *RetStoreImpl) Ctx() (context.Context, error) { return nil, nil }

// ---- Consequence: a call through an interface-typed field never reaches the impl.
type Handler struct {
	store CtxStore
}

func (h *Handler) Remove(ctx context.Context, id string) error {
	return h.store.Delete(ctx, id) // real caller of (*CtxStoreImpl).Delete
}
```

```
gitnexus analyze --index-only .
gitnexus cypher "MATCH (a)-[r:CodeRelation]->(b) WHERE r.type='IMPLEMENTS' RETURN a.name AS impl, b.name AS iface ORDER BY impl"
```

**Observed**

| impl | iface |
| --- | --- |
| LocalStoreImpl | LocalStore |

**Expected** — all three, per the Go spec's structural satisfaction rules:

| impl | iface |
| --- | --- |
| CtxStoreImpl | CtxStore |
| LocalStoreImpl | LocalStore |
| RetStoreImpl | RetStore |

The three declarations are identical in shape. The only variable is whether a type in the signature is qualified by a package that lives inside the repo. Note Case B: the parameter list is empty, so this is not a parameter-matching problem — one stdlib type anywhere in the signature is sufficient.

## Consequence for `impact()`

`Handler.Remove` calls `(*CtxStoreImpl).Delete` through the interface-typed field. With no IMPLEMENTS edge there is nothing to dispatch through:

```
gitnexus impact --uid "Method:repro.go:CtxStoreImpl.Delete#2" --depth 1 --summary-only
```
```json
{
  "impactedCount": 0,
  "risk": "LOW",
  "epistemic": "exact",
  "summary": { "direct": 0, "processes_affected": 0, "modules_affected": 0 }
}
```

This is the #2813 complaint, now with a mechanism. And note the epistemics interaction, which I think is the more important half: the `lower-bound` hedge added in #2747 is derived from the dispatch boundary, and the dispatch boundary is derived from IMPLEMENTS. When detection *succeeds*, a comparable symbol correctly reports `epistemic: "lower-bound"` with a boundary note naming interface dispatch. When detection **fails**, there is no boundary to notice, so the same query reports `epistemic: "exact"`. **The hedge is strongest exactly where it is least needed and silent exactly where the answer is wrong.**

## Why CI is green — the two-line falsifier in your own suite

`test/fixtures/lang-resolution/go-structural-interface-dispatch/repository.go` is a single file with **no imports at all**. Every signature it asserts on is builtin-only:

```go
Find(id string) User
Save(user User) error
Read() error
Touch()
```

That is exactly the case that works, so `go.test.ts` → *"emits signature-checked structural IMPLEMENTS edges only for valid implementors"* has never exercised a qualified type. I believe this is why #2813 looked resolved by #2829 — that PR genuinely did fix the pointer-method-set half, and nothing in the suite could show the remaining half.

Adding one import and one parameter to that fixture should turn the existing assertion red:

```diff
+import "context"
+
 type Repository interface {
 	Find(id string) User
-	Save(user User) error
+	Save(ctx context.Context, user User) error
 }
```

…with the same `ctx context.Context` added to `SqlRepository.Save` and `MemoryRepository.Save`. Expected result: `MemoryRepository → Repository` and `SqlRepository → Repository` disappear from the asserted edge set, while `File → Reader`, `FileBase → Reader`, `File → ReadCloser` and `PointerOnlyThing → PointerOnly` survive — because those four are the interfaces with no qualified types in their signatures.

**Provenance, so you can weigh it:** the standalone repro above I built and ran against rc.174; the outputs are copied verbatim. This fixture diff I derived from reading `go.test.ts` and the fixture — I did not build your repo to execute it, so treat it as a prediction rather than a measurement. If it does not go red, the mechanism I describe is wrong and the repro above is the artifact worth trusting.

## Root cause

`gitnexus/src/core/ingestion/languages/go/interface-impls.ts`

1. `signatureContextForFile` (~L739) builds `importQualifiers` only from in-repo imports:

```ts
for (const edge of importEdges) {
  if (edge.kind !== 'namespace' || edge.targetFile === null) continue;   // <-- stdlib/vendor dropped
  const qualifier = packageQualifierForFile(edge.targetFile);
  if (qualifier !== undefined) importQualifiers.set(edge.localName, qualifier);
}
```

`import "context"` has no `targetFile`, so `context` never lands in the map.

2. `qualifyGoSignatureTypes` (~L718) turns that miss into a hard `undefined`:

```ts
if (source[offset + token.length] === '.') {
  const qualifier = context.importQualifiers.get(token);
  if (qualifier !== undefined) return qualifier;
  unresolvedQualifier = true;                    // <-- "I don't know this package"
  return token;
}
...
return unresolvedQualifier ? undefined : qualified;
```

3. `parameterTypesCompatible` (~L689) and `returnTypesCompatible` (~L704) read `undefined` as a mismatch:

```ts
return actualType !== undefined && requiredType !== undefined && actualType === requiredType;
```

So "I could not normalize this qualifier" is collapsed into "these signatures differ" — and it happens symmetrically, on both the interface side and the implementation side, so even two *textually identical* signatures compare unequal.

## Suggested direction

The information needed is already present: for an unresolved qualifier the token is unambiguous **within its file**, and both sides of the comparison carry their own `SignatureContext`. A few options, roughly in order of how much I'd trust them:

- **Resolve out-of-repo qualifiers to the import path.** Normalizing `context` to `context` (or `std/context`) rather than failing makes the comparison exact rather than merely permissive, and is the fix I'd expect to be correct in every case. It is also the most work: `ImportEdge` (`gitnexus-shared/src/scope-resolution/types.ts:329`) carries `localName` and `targetFile` but no raw import specifier, so the path isn't recoverable where `signatureContextForFile` runs today — this needs the specifier threaded through, not just a fallback branch. You'll know better than I do whether that's cheap on your side.
- **Make unresolved-but-identical compare equal.** If both sides normalize to `undefined` and the raw compacted text matches, treat as compatible. Cheap, but it will produce false positives across packages that alias different imports to the same local name.
- **At minimum, propagate the uncertainty.** If a required or actual signature could not be normalized, the resulting non-implementation is an *unknown*, not a *no*. Feeding that into the `epistemic` channel so `impact()` degrades to `lower-bound` would fix the dangerous half of this even if the edges stay unresolved — which is the same ask I made in #2813, and it stays independently valuable.

`GO_BUILTIN_TYPES` (~L766) is effectively the current allowlist of "types we can compare", which is why builtin-only interfaces are the ones that survive.

## Environment

- `gitnexus` 1.6.10-rc.174 (npm `latest` is still 1.6.9, so this is `@rc` only)
- Go 1.26 · Node v22.22.3 · Darwin arm64 (Apple Silicon)
- `GITNEXUS_SKIP_OPTIONAL_GRAMMARS=1` at install · indexed with `--index-only`

title: perf(go): resolveGoImportTarget scans the whole workspace on every import
body:
Follow-up from #2872, which fixed the same shape in Kotlin (and #1918 in Python, #2788 in C++).

`resolveGoImportTarget` walks all of `allFilePaths` on every import, with nothing memoized:

- `findRootPackageFiles` (`gitnexus/src/core/ingestion/languages/go/import-target.ts`) iterates the whole set, normalizing each path with `raw.replace(/\\/g, '/')`.
- `findAllFilesInPkgDir` does the same, plus an `includes` and an `indexOf` per entry.
- The GOPATH fallback calls `findAllFilesInPkgDir` once per path segment except the last: `for (let i = 0; i < parts.length - 1; i++)`. For a typical `github.com/org/repo/pkg` import that is three full passes; for a deeper path, more.

So a single unresolved import costs several full workspace scans, and resolution overall is O(imports × files).

This is likely the worst of the family, because most Go imports are external (stdlib, third-party modules) and therefore always run the whole cascade to completion before returning null — the fast path never triggers. Measured during review of #2872: scaling ratio **4.00**, ~370 µs per import at 1600 files.

### What it looks like when it bites

It does not present as a hot loop. `analyze` sits at exactly 1.00 core with a flat heap and no output, because every allocation is a short-lived string. Small repositories hide it entirely.

### Suggested fix

The same shape as `getKotlinFileIndex` (#2872) and `getPythonFileIndex` (#1918): build the lookup tables once per `allFilePaths` Set, memoized on the Set's identity in a `WeakMap`, so each query is O(1).

Two things that turned out to matter in the Kotlin change and would apply here:

1. The adapter must pass the Set **through**. A defensive `new Set(allFilePaths)` hands a fresh WeakMap key per call and rebuilds the index every import, restoring the original behaviour — Python shipped exactly that bug and it was caught in review (#1918 P1). Worth an integration test asserting the index builds once across many imports.
2. Go's resolution has implicit tie-breaks (`findRootPackageFiles` sorts, `findAllFilesInPkgDir` does not) and the GOPATH fallback returns on the first non-empty result. Those need to be reproduced exactly, or edges move in every Go repository. A differential harness against the current implementation, plus a fingerprint bench in the `benchmarks (GITNEXUS_BENCH)` job, is what made that checkable in #2872 — `bench/kotlin-import-target/` is a working template.

title: perf(csharp): the no-csproj path bypasses the memoized workspace index
body:
Follow-up from #2872.

`csharp/import-target.ts` already has the right machinery — `getWorkspaceFileIndex` is memoized on the `allFilePaths` Set identity via a `WeakMap`, added for #1881. But it is only reached inside the `csharpConfigs.length > 0` branch, and that branch returns unconditionally. When no `.csproj` is found, resolution falls through to:

- `resolveDirectMatch(ctx.allFilePaths, pathLike)` — a raw `for (const raw of allFilePaths)` scan;
- `resolveByProgressiveStripping(ctx.allFilePaths, pathLike)` — nested loops over `allFilePaths` via `findDirectChild`.

Both take the raw Set and scan past the index that is sitting right there. An unresolved four-segment `using` can trigger up to eight full workspace passes.

Measured during review of #2872: scaling ratio **3.43**, ~359 µs per import at 1600 files.

There is a second-order effect worth flagging: the #1881 namespace-evidence gate fails open when the namespace scan is truncated, and truncation is most likely on exactly the large repositories where this cost hurts most. So the slow path and the degraded-accuracy path coincide.

### Suggested fix

Route the no-csproj path through `getWorkspaceFileIndex` as well, rather than adding a second index. The index already carries `normalized`, `all` and a `SuffixIndex`, which is most of what `resolveDirectMatch` recomputes per call.

Care needed on tie-breaks: `resolveDirectMatch` returns the first exact match but only remembers the first *suffix* match, so an exact match found later still wins. That ordering is expressed only through Set-iteration order and has to be preserved, or edges move. In #2872 a differential harness against the pre-change implementation plus a fingerprint bench in the `benchmarks (GITNEXUS_BENCH)` job made that verifiable; `bench/kotlin-import-target/` is a template.

title: perf(dart): resolveDartImportTarget scans the workspace once per candidate path
body:
Follow-up from #2872.

`dart/import-target.ts` scans all of `allFilePaths` per import, unmemoized, on both of its paths:

- the `package:` branch builds two candidate paths (`lib/<rel>` and bare `<rel>`) and runs a full `for (const fp of allFilePaths)` loop for each. For an external package both miss, so both loops always run to completion;
- `resolveRelative` tries an O(1) `allFilePaths.has(target)` first, but its suffix fallback is another full scan.

Measured during review of #2872: scaling ratio **4.05**, ~89 µs per import at 1600 files. The per-import constant is lower than Go or C# because the loop body is cheap, but the asymptotic shape is the same.

### Suggested fix

Same pattern as `getKotlinFileIndex` (#2872) / `getPythonFileIndex` (#1918): one index per `allFilePaths` Set, memoized on the Set's identity in a `WeakMap`.

Dart's rules are simpler than Kotlin's — the match is `fp === candidate || fp.endsWith('/' + candidate)`, so a stem/suffix map covers both — but the first-match-in-iteration-order tie-break still needs preserving, and the two candidates must keep their priority (`lib/<rel>` before bare `<rel>`). A differential harness against the current implementation plus a fingerprint bench in `benchmarks (GITNEXUS_BENCH)` is what made that checkable in #2872; `bench/kotlin-import-target/` is a template.

Also worth keeping in mind from that review: the adapter must pass the Set through without copying, or the `WeakMap` key changes per call and the index rebuilds on every import (#1918 P1).

title: perf(ruby): resolveBare rebuilds the whole suffix index on every require
body:
Follow-up from #2872.

`resolveBare` in `ruby/import-target.ts` does this per bare `require`:

```ts
const normalizedFileList = [...allFilePaths].map((f) => f.replace(/\\/g, '/'));
const allFileList = [...allFilePaths];
const index = buildSuffixIndex(normalizedFileList, allFileList);
```

That is two full array materializations from the Set plus a complete `buildSuffixIndex` — which itself walks every file and inserts one entry per path suffix into `exactMap`, one into `lowerMap`, and one into `dirMap` — and it is thrown away as soon as the call returns.

This is a worse constant factor than the plain scans in the sibling resolvers: Go and Dart re-scan, Ruby re-*builds*. Every `require` in the repository pays for indexing every Ruby file in the repository.

`buildSuffixIndex` is shared (`import-resolvers/utils.ts`) and used by C#, Vue and TypeScript as well, so it is worth checking whether any of those call sites are also inside a per-import path rather than hoisted.

### Suggested fix

Memoize on the `allFilePaths` Set identity, the same way `csharp/import-target.ts` already wraps `buildSuffixIndex` in `getWorkspaceFileIndex`, or as `getKotlinFileIndex` (#2872) and `getPythonFileIndex` (#1918) do. Since `buildSuffixIndex` is deterministic in its inputs, this should be a pure hoist with no behaviour change — but the same caveats apply:

- the adapter must pass the Set through without copying, or the `WeakMap` key changes per call and nothing is saved (#1918 P1);
- worth an integration test asserting the index builds once across many `require`s, and a fingerprint bench so a future per-import rebuild does not slip back in. `bench/kotlin-import-target/` is a template.

title: fix(kotlin): a root-level package colliding with an ancestor directory name does not resolve
body:
Split out of #2872, which preserved this behaviour deliberately rather than changing it inside a performance PR.

Kotlin package resolution decides whether a file is a direct child of a package directory using a rule inherited from the original per-import scan: it tests `startsWith` first, and otherwise takes the **first** occurrence of `/dir/` via `indexOf`. It never looks for a second one.

The result is that a directory name appearing twice in a path is only ever matched at its first occurrence. Given:

```
data/src/main/kotlin/com/example/data/Repo.kt
```

`import data.helper` does not resolve, because the first `/data/` is the module root, not the package directory, and the check stops there.

### Scope

Narrower than it first looks, and worth stating precisely so this is not over-fixed:

- `com.example.data.Repo` resolves
- `com.example.data.helper` fans out correctly
- `data.Repo` resolves
- `data.helper` — a bare single-segment key whose package sits at the repository root and collides with an ancestor directory name — does **not**

Real Kotlin files under `…/com/example/data/` declare `package com.example.data`, so real imports take the multi-segment path that works. The broken shape is a root-level package whose name repeats higher in the module tree.

### Why it was not fixed in #2872

That PR is behaviour-preserving by construction: its gate is a fingerprint whose committed baseline is the output of the pre-index implementation, over ~20k cases in both file-set iteration orders. Changing this rule moves edges in every Kotlin repository that has the colliding shape, which is a behaviour change and needs its own fixtures and its own review.

### Notes for whoever picks this up

- The rule and the reason it was preserved are documented in `getKotlinFileIndex` in `gitnexus/src/core/ingestion/languages/kotlin/import-target.ts`.
- Two cases pin the current behaviour: one in `test/unit/scope-resolution/kotlin/kotlin-import-target-parity.test.ts` and the branch matrix in `bench/kotlin-import-target/measure.mjs`. Both will fail on a fix — that is expected, and the bench fingerprint will need a deliberate re-baseline with the change explained, not adjusted to make CI green.
- The bench's `_provenance` and `_gate_controls` fields describe how the baseline was derived and which mutations it catches; the same harness can show exactly which edges a fix moves, by diffing the resolved output before and after.

title: Python: `from <pkg> import <submodule>` classified as named import, not namespace — receiver-bound calls unresolved
body:
## Summary

`interpretPythonImport` in `src/core/ingestion/languages/python/interpret.ts` classifies **every** `from X import Y` as `kind: 'named'` (a symbol import). It doesn't disambiguate the case where `Y` is actually a **submodule** of package `X` — e.g. `from . import accounts` or `from mypkg import accounts` where `accounts` is `mypkg/accounts.py`, not a function/class defined in `mypkg/__init__.py`.

Downstream, `receiver-bound-calls.ts` resolves `X.method()` receiver-bound calls only via `collectNamespaceTargets` (`scope/namespace-targets.ts`), which only considers imports tagged `kind === 'namespace'`. Because the `from`-import submodule case is always tagged `'named'`, `accounts.load_chain(...)` never resolves to `accounts.py`'s `load_chain`, at any depth, regardless of CLI flags.

## Repro

```
# pkg/__init__.py
# (empty)

# pkg/accounts.py
def load_chain(name):
    return [name]

# pkg/adapter.py
from . import accounts

def build(name):
    return accounts.load_chain(name)   # <-- CALLS edge to load_chain is NOT emitted
```

`gitnexus impact load_chain -f pkg/accounts.py` reports 0 upstream callers from `adapter.py` (only same-file/bare calls to `load_chain` resolve, if any exist).

Compare with the two *already-covered* namespace forms, which resolve correctly:
- `import accounts` / `import accounts as acc` (plain/aliased — `test/fixtures/lang-resolution/python-function-local-namespace-import/`, `python-class-body-namespace-import/`)

Neither existing fixture covers `from X import <submodule>`.

## Root cause

`src/core/ingestion/languages/python/interpret.ts`, `interpretPythonImport`, `case 'from':` (~line 53):

```ts
case 'from': {
  // `from m import x`
  if (sourceCap === undefined || nameCap === undefined) return null;
  return {
    kind: 'named',
    localName: nameCap.text,
    importedName: nameCap.text,
    targetRaw: sourceCap.text,
  };
}
```

This treats `x` as a plain symbol unconditionally. To fix, this needs to detect when `x` resolves to an actual file in the target package (i.e. `<package-dir>/<x>.py` or `<package-dir>/<x>/__init__.py` exists) and emit `kind: 'namespace'` in that case instead, mirroring the `plain`/`aliased` branches above it.

## Impact

For codebases whose dominant intra-package convention is `from . import <submodule>` / `from <pkg> import <submodule>` followed by `submodule.func()` (a very common Python style, e.g. Django app conventions, `from . import models` / `from . import views`), `impact`/blast-radius queries silently undercount or miss real callers entirely — with no warning, no degraded-confidence marker, just a clean low/zero-risk result. This is a bit dangerous given `impact` is positioned as the "run this before editing" safety check for AI agents.

## Environment

- gitnexus 1.6.9
- Node v25.9.0
- macOS

Happy to help narrow this down further or test a fix if useful.

title: feat(route): resolve vendor-derived Spring mapping annotations by suffix
body:
## Problem

Frameworks commonly wrap Spring's built-in mapping annotations with company-specific variants. In our vendor monorepo (healthcare, ~25.7k Java files) controllers are annotated with `@WinPostMapping` / `@WinGetMapping` / `@WinRequestMapping` — each meta-annotated with the corresponding Spring built-in, with the definition living inside a vendor JAR. Since the meta-annotation cannot be read statically, the exact-name map in `spring-shared.ts` (`METHOD_ANNOTATION_TO_HTTP`) matches none of them:

- source contains **2,760 `@Win*Mapping` annotation sites** across 483 controller files
- the index extracts only **88 Routes** (the handful of controllers that happen to use plain Spring annotations)

`api_impact` / `route_map` are effectively blind on repos built on any vendor-wrapped annotation convention.

## Approach

Resolve vendor-derived annotations **by naming suffix**: `WinPostMapping` → `PostMapping`, `WinRequestMapping` → `RequestMapping`. This matches the universal Java convention of naming a derived annotation with the base name as a suffix. The false-positive risk is negligible — a non-HTTP annotation whose simple name ends in `GetMapping`/`PostMapping`/… is unprecedented in mainstream Java.

Notes on scope and safety:

- `SPRING_MAPPING_NAMES` is sorted longest-first so the alias resolver prefers the most specific suffix.
- Folding (`@PostMapping(ApiPathConstants.X)` constant resolution, #2980) and alias recognition compose — neither implies the other.
- Class-level vendor aliases (`@WinRequestMapping("prefix")` on the controller) are resolved too, and contribute URL prefixes exactly like class-level `@RequestMapping` does.
- Registered-prefix handling from the review pass is included.

## Results

On the 25.7k-file vendor monorepo: **88 Routes → ~2,800 Routes** recovered (2,760 `@Win*Mapping` sites, deduped against shared paths), each still resolvable through constant folding.

## Testing

- `spring-vendor-annotation-alias.test.ts` — 20 tests (suffix resolution per verb, longest-first, class-level alias prefixes, non-suffix annotations left untouched, composition with constant folding)
- existing suites green: `java-spring-route-ingestion` (9), `data-route-table` (8), `api-file-route` (10), wider route face (198 across 7 files)
- `tsc --noEmit` clean, prettier clean

title: fix(scope-resolution): include C# Record implementors in interface dispatch
body:
## Problem

After #2871 makes `Record` definitions resolve to their canonical graph nodes, C# record `IMPLEMENTS` / `EXTENDS` edges can reach interface-dispatch fan-out. The consumer still excludes records while building `graphIdToClassDef`:

```ts
if (def.type !== 'Class' && def.type !== 'Struct' && def.type !== 'Interface') continue;
```

As a result, calls through an interface reach the interface method but do not fan out to the implementing C# record method. Callers and `impact` therefore under-report.

Discovered in the review of #2871: https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/pull/2871#discussion_r3736079701

Java record dispatch is blocked earlier because Java records emit no inheritance captures; that CRITICAL-impact producer change is tracked separately in #2900.

## Proposed fix

- Replace the hard-coded `Class | Struct | Interface` predicate in `receiver-bound-calls.ts` with the existing `isClassLike(def.type)` helper.
- Add a C# record-interface dispatch integration regression.
- Verify ordinary class/struct/interface dispatch remains unchanged and fan-out limits still apply.

## Acceptance criteria

- C# interface calls fan out to implementing record methods.
- Existing receiver-bound call and C# resolver suites pass.
- No schema or parse-cache change is required.

title: feat(jvm): synthesize Lombok and Kotlin JVM accessor methods
body:
## Problem

Lombok generates getter/setter methods at compile time; they are absent from the Java AST. Kotlin `val`/`var` properties similarly compile to JVM `get*`/`set*` methods that the Kotlin AST does not surface as `Method` nodes. Calls such as `obj.getOrderId()` therefore never bind, so impact and trace queries miss those edges.

## Solution

Language adapters discover candidate members; a shared JVM synthesizer (`gitnexus/src/core/ingestion/languages/jvm/accessor-synthesis.ts`, `beanspec.ts`) emits virtual `Method` nodes, `HAS_METHOD` edges, and matching scope captures. Java and Kotlin plug in through `LanguageProvider.synthesizeStructureMembers` so synthetic accessors take the same graph, registry, and call-resolution path as handwritten methods. Kotlin graph tags stay `kotlin-jvm`.

### Java (Lombok)

Walks `@Getter` / `@Setter` / `@Data` (plus field-level annotations) and emits accessors Lombok would produce:

| Field | Getter | Setter |
|-------|--------|--------|
| `String name` | `getName()` | `setName(String)` |
| `boolean active` | `isActive()` | `setActive(boolean)` |
| `Boolean active` | `getActive()` | `setActive(Boolean)` |

ABI details this PR pins:

- Collision index is **case-folded** (same name ignoring case + same arity), matching Lombok. Do not switch to exact-name collisions.
- Boolean `is` prefix: third character is non-lowercase (`=== toUpperCase()`), including digits (`is1` → `is1` / `set1`).
- Explicit `@Getter` / `@Setter` win over `@Data` regardless of annotation order.
- Field `@Accessors` **replaces** class-level fluent/chain (including explicit `false`); it is not a sticky OR.
- Provenance is limited to `lombok` / `lombok.experimental` FQNs.
- Skip existing methods, `AccessLevel.NONE`, static fields, and setters on `final` fields. Nested classes and multi-declarator fields are covered.

### Kotlin (kotlinc JVM ABI)

`val`/`var` properties (including data-class constructor properties and custom accessors) emit the same JavaBeans get/set Methods. Collision matching is **exact** JVM name + arity. Body-less interface property accessors are `isAbstract: true`; default implementations with a `function_body` stay concrete. `@JvmName` renaming is suppressed until custom names are modeled.

### Cache and benches

`SCHEMA_BUMP` is **86** so warm caches cannot replay pre-synthesis or pre-`isAbstract` worker output. Java/Kotlin accessor benches and Kotlin scope-capture fingerprints are pinned in CI.

**Out of scope:** `@Builder` and related generated APIs.

## Test plan

- [ ] Java Lombok synthesizer units (collision, boolean naming, `AccessLevel.NONE`, nested/multi-declarator, Data vs Getter order, field `@Accessors`)
- [ ] Kotlin accessor synthesizer units (is-prefix, interface abstract vs default impl, exact-name collisions)
- [ ] Parse-cache pin at schema 86 (cold/warm/historical)
- [ ] CI `--check` accessor benches + Kotlin scope-capture fingerprint

title: feat(java): resolve SpringContextUtil.getBeans(X.class) dynamic lookups
body:
## Problem

Java frameworks commonly provide static accessors that retrieve all Spring beans of a given type at runtime:

```java
// Winning Health (WiNEX)
Map<String, IClinicalOrderConverter> beans = SpringContextUtil.getBeans(IClinicalOrderConverter.class);

// Spring native
Map<String, Plugin> plugins = applicationContext.getBeansOfType(Plugin.class);
```

These are the **programmatic equivalent** of `@Autowired List<X>`: both express "inject all implementations of interface X". But while `@Autowired List<X>` is already resolved by GitNexus's Spring DI resolver (PR #2200), `getBeans(X.class)` calls resolve to nothing — the receiver (`SpringContextUtil`) is a static utility in a binary JAR, invisible to the static call graph.

**Impact**: In the WiNEX medical platform alone, **60+ files** use this pattern across **40+ distinct interfaces** — representing hundreds of invisible dependency paths that impact/trace queries cannot follow.

## Solution

A post-resolution heuristic that detects `*.getBeans(Type.class)` patterns and emits INJECTS edges to all implementers:

1. **Scans** Function/Method source text for the regex pattern `(\w+)\.(getBeans|getBean|getBeansOfType)\s*\(\s*(\w+)\.class\s*\)`
2. **Filters** by known receiver names (`SpringContextUtil`, `applicationContext`, `ctx`, etc.) to minimize false positives
3. **Resolves** `Type` to an Interface/Class node via the graph
4. **Walks** IMPLEMENTS edges to find all implementers
5. **Emits** INJECTS edges: `caller Function → each implementer Class`

### Confidence levels
| Method | Cardinality | Confidence |
|--------|------------|------------|
| `getBeans(X.class)` | Collection | 0.8 |
| `getBeansOfType(X.class)` | Collection | 0.8 |
| `getBean(X.class)` | Single | 0.6 |

### Safety features
- ✅ **Receiver filtering**: Only known Spring context names trigger detection
- ✅ **`.class` argument requirement**: Ignores `getBean(String)` overloads
- ✅ **Ambiguous type names skipped**: If multiple interfaces share a simple name, no edges are emitted (fail closed)
- ✅ **Self-injection excluded**
- ✅ **Deduplication**: Edge IDs encode source+target, duplicates collapse automatically

### Why regex (not AST)?
This runs in `emitPostResolutionEdges`, which operates on graph nodes — not raw AST nodes. The graph stores `filePath`, `startLine`, `endLine` for each Function/Method, so we extract the source range and scan it. This is the same approach used by other post-resolution hooks.

## Files
| File | Type | Lines |
|------|------|-------|
| `languages/java/spring-dynamic-lookup.ts` | NEW | ~170 |
| `languages/java/scope-resolver.ts` | MOD (+2) | Import + hook call |
| `test/unit/spring-dynamic-lookup.test.ts` | NEW | ~160 |

## Tests
| Category | Tests | Status |
|----------|-------|--------|
| getBeans collection detection | 4 | ✅ |
| getBean single detection | 1 | ✅ |
| getBeansOfType variant | 1 | ✅ |
| Receiver filtering | 2 | ✅ |
| Negative cases (String arg, no arg, unrelated methods) | 3 | ✅ |
| Multi-lookup in one function | 1 | ✅ |
| Stream-style usage | 1 | ✅ |
| **Existing Java/Spring tests** | **73** | **✅ No regression** |

title: MCP server crashes with ENOENT on registry.json.tmp when multiple instances prune the registry concurrently
body:
## Summary

`writeRegistry()` performs an atomic tmp+rename using a **fixed** temp filename
(`registry.json.tmp`). With no per-process suffix, no cross-process lock, and no
retry on failure, two GitNexus MCP instances starting at the same time can race:
both write the same tmp path, the first `rename()` wins and moves the file away,
and the second gets `ENOENT`. The rejection is unhandled, so the whole MCP server
process exits during `init` and the client reports "Server disconnected".

## Environment

- gitnexus 1.6.9 (installed via `npx -y gitnexus@latest mcp`)
- Node.js v24.13.0, macOS (arm64)
- Three MCP clients on the same machine each spawning their own `gitnexus mcp`
  process against the same `~/.gitnexus/registry.json`

## Stack trace

```
Error: ENOENT: no such file or directory,
  rename '/home/user/.gitnexus/registry.json.tmp' -> '/home/user/.gitnexus/registry.json'
    at async Object.rename (node:internal/fs/promises:782:10)
    at async writeRegistry (gitnexus/dist/storage/repo-manager.js:551:5)
    at async listRegisteredRepos (gitnexus/dist/storage/repo-manager.js:1229:9)
    at async LocalBackend.refreshRepos (gitnexus/dist/mcp/local/local-backend.js:592:25)
    at async LocalBackend.init (gitnexus/dist/mcp/local/local-backend.js:583:9)
    at async mcpCommand (gitnexus/dist/cli/mcp.js:61:5)
  errno: -2, code: 'ENOENT', syscall: 'rename'
```

## Root cause

`src/storage/repo-manager.ts` (line ~1103 on `main`):

```ts
const writeRegistry = async (entries: RegistryEntry[]): Promise<void> => {
  const dir = getGlobalDir();
  await fs.mkdir(dir, { recursive: true });
  const target = getGlobalRegistryPath();
  const tmp = `${target}.tmp`;              // <-- fixed name, shared by every process
  await fs.writeFile(tmp, JSON.stringify(entries, null, 2), 'utf-8');
  await fs.rename(tmp, target);             // <-- ENOENT if another process won the race
};
```

The tmp+rename is atomic *with respect to readers* — it does prevent the
truncated-registry problem it was added for (#2106 R9) — but it is **not safe
against concurrent writers**, because every process uses the same tmp path.

The write is reached from startup: `LocalBackend.init` → `refreshRepos` →
`listRegisteredRepos`, which writes only when entries were pruned:

```ts
if (valid.length !== entries.length) {
  await writeRegistry(valid);
}
```

That conditional is why this looks intermittent. The registry only needs writing
when it contains stale entries (e.g. after deleting a worktree or repo whose
index is gone). Once one process successfully prunes, the registry is stable, no
further writes happen, and the crash stops reproducing — which makes it look like
a transient connection problem rather than a bug.

## Reproduction

Deterministic on a machine where the registry has entries whose `storagePath` no
longer exists:

1. Add N stale entries to `~/.gitnexus/registry.json` pointing at deleted paths
   (this is exactly the state left behind by removing a git worktree that had
   been analyzed).
2. Start several MCP servers simultaneously:

   ```sh
   for i in $(seq 1 8); do
     node "$(npm root -g)/gitnexus/dist/cli/index.js" mcp < /dev/null 2> "rep$i.err" &
   done
   ```

3. `grep -l ENOENT rep*.err`

Observed on gitnexus 1.6.9: **1 of 8 instances crashed** with the trace above.
Control run with a clean registry (nothing to prune, so `writeRegistry` is never
called): **0 of 8 crashed**. Raising the number of stale entries or of concurrent
instances increases the hit rate.

## Suggested fix

Give each writer its own tmp file so no two processes can collide:

```ts
const tmp = `${target}.${process.pid}.${randomUUID()}.tmp`;
await fs.writeFile(tmp, JSON.stringify(entries, null, 2), 'utf-8');
try {
  await fs.rename(tmp, target);
} catch (err) {
  await fs.rm(tmp, { force: true });   // don't leak tmp files on failure
  throw err;
}
```

This keeps the atomicity guarantee that motivated the original change while
removing the cross-process collision. Two further hardening options, if wanted:

- Treat a failed registry write as non-fatal during `init` — a stale registry
  entry is far less harmful than an MCP server that refuses to start.
- Serialize the prune-and-write with a lockfile (e.g. `proper-lockfile`) so
  concurrent starters don't each recompute and rewrite the same result.

`saveMeta()` uses the same fixed-tmp pattern and looks like it has the same
exposure whenever two processes touch one project's metadata concurrently.

feat(java): resolve @FeignClient method calls as CALLS edges
body:
## Summary

`@FeignClient` interfaces have no source-level implementation — Spring Cloud creates a dynamic proxy at runtime. The scope resolver cannot resolve the receiver to any concrete symbol, so calls on injected Feign fields produce zero CALLS edges, completely breaking impact analysis across RPC boundaries.

## Approach

New module `spring-feign-rpc.ts` runs in `emitPostResolutionEdges`:

1. **Identify Feign interfaces**: Scans source text for `@FeignClient` annotations.
2. **Build method index**: Maps Feign interface name → method node IDs from the graph.
3. **Detect field declarations**: Finds `@Autowired/@Resource/private` fields of Feign types.
4. **Scan for calls**: For each Function/Method node, regex-matches `fieldName.methodName()` patterns.
5. **Emit edges**: Creates `CALLS` edges (confidence 0.85) from caller to Feign interface method.

## Test coverage

12 unit tests: single/multiple methods, multiple Feign interfaces in same class, `@Autowired`/`@Resource`/no-annotation injection, duplicate suppression, self-reference filtering, uncalled fields, multi-function files, value-quoted service name.

body:
## Summary

`deduplicateTraces` in `gitnexus/src/core/ingestion/process-processor.ts` decides whether one execution trace is a sub-path of another by joining both to strings and testing `String.prototype.includes`. That test is not anchored to step boundaries, so a match can begin in the middle of a node id.

```js
['X', 'AA', 'B'].join('->').includes(['A', 'B'].join('->'))
// 'X->AA->B'.includes('A->B')  ->  true
```

The trace `A -> B` is discarded as redundant against `X -> AA -> B`, a chain it does not appear in. `A` is not a step of that chain at all — the match starts inside `AA`.

## Where

`gitnexus/src/core/ingestion/process-processor.ts`, the subsumption loop in `deduplicateTraces`:

```ts
const isSubset = uniqueKeys.some((existingKey) => existingKey.includes(traceKey));
```

Long-standing — the same predicate is on `main` (pre-#2856, as `unique.some((existing) => existing.join('->').includes(traceKey))`). #2856 only changed how often it is reached.

## Measured impact: zero on every corpus I could test

Worth stating up front so this is not over-prioritised. I applied the fix and measured rather than assuming it mattered:

- **Real corpus** — `gitnexus/src`, 11,490 symbols: **936 processes / 4,648 STEP_IN_PROCESS with and without the fix.** Identical.
- **Synthetic** — all sixteen `shape × scale × sink-variant` combinations from an A/B harness (`shallow_wide`, `deep_chain`, `mixed_cycles`, `flat_pairs` × 5k/25k callables × sinks on/off): every process count and step count identical.

The collision requires one node id to be a proper suffix of another **at a `->` boundary**. Ids are shaped `Function:<path>:<name>:<line>`, so that needs two symbols agreeing on file and line while one name is a strict suffix of the other — which does not occur in practice. The bug is real as a predicate and inert as a defect.

## Why fix it anyway

The predicate does not mean what the surrounding code says it means, and nothing pins that. It is one line, it costs nothing at runtime, and it removes a silent-wrong-answer mode from a function whose entire job is deciding what to delete. It also makes the invariant testable, which it currently is not — there is no test covering a boundary case in `test/unit/process-processor.test.ts`.

## Suggested fix

Pad both keys with the separator so `includes` can only match whole steps:

```ts
const traceKey = `->${trace.join('->')}->`;
```

Both sides are already built once per surviving trace, so padding adds two characters per key and no extra work. Verified against the existing suite: 41/41 pass across `process-processor.test.ts`, `route-process-linking.test.ts`, `tool-process-linking.test.ts` and `ingestion/pipeline-phase-registry.test.ts`.

Worth adding alongside it: a unit test asserting `A -> B` survives against `X -> AA -> B`. That is the assertion that would have caught this, and it pins the invariant going forward.

## Note on a related hazard

The separator `->` is assumed absent from node ids. A symbol named `operator->` (C++) would break the join-based encoding regardless of padding. Out of scope here, but worth knowing the encoding has that assumption baked in.

---
Found while investigating the call-flow slowdown in #2856. Deliberately kept out of that PR — it is pre-existing and unrelated to the regression there.

title: CI: a failing bench --check aborts the benchmarks job, so every guard after it silently never runs
body:
## Summary

Every step in the `tests / benchmarks (GITNEXUS_BENCH)` job is fail-fast, so the first `--check` that fails aborts the job and **every guard declared after it never executes**. Those later guards then report as `skipped`, which reads identically to "nothing to do" in the checks UI — not as "this was never verified".

A skipped guard is not a passing guard, and right now nothing distinguishes them.

## Evidence

`.github/workflows/ci-tests.yml`, the benchmarks job spans lines 462-593. Grepping that range for `if:` or `continue-on-error:` returns nothing — there is no `if: always()` anywhere in the job (the only two in the file are at lines 72 and 134, both in other jobs).

The three tail steps:

| line | step |
|---|---|
| 558 | Emit-persistence throughput / byte-identity guards (#2203) |
| 567 | Streaming PDG-emit byte-identity / bounded-RSS guards (#2202) |
| 576 | Cross-language pipeline benchmarks (GITNEXUS_BENCH, serial) |

## How this actually played out

On the branch for #2856, the emit-persistence baseline was stale for the life of the PR. Result, audited across every benchmark-job run on that branch (jobs `92659525436`, `92716925200`, `92725814265`, `92734685285`, `92739585125`, `92817491828`, `92884400117`, `92923296393`, `92937498727`, `92941732433`, `92969156952`, `93062865688`, `93074242346`):

- the benchmarks job **succeeded zero times**
- step 12 executed **zero times**
- step 13 executed **zero times**

So the streaming PDG-emit byte-identity guard and the eight-language pipeline benchmarks had no result at all for the entire PR, while the checks UI showed them as skipped. Two full reviews of that PR read the checks summary and did not catch it. Both guards in fact pass — I ran them locally after fixing the baseline (`[stream-pdg-emit --check] PASS`; pipeline benchmarks 8 files / 13 tests) — but that was luck, not verification.

The failure mode is worst exactly when it matters most: a change broad enough to trip an early guard is a change you most want the later ones to have run against.

## Suggested fix

Roughly in order of effort:

1. **`if: always()` on each `--check` step after the first**, so one stale baseline reports one red step instead of masking three. Cheapest change, keeps the current single-job shape.
2. **Split the bench guards into a matrix job** keyed on the bench directory, so each guard is an independent check with its own pass/fail. Also parallelises what is currently ~7 minutes of serial work.
3. **A job-level summary step** (`if: always()`) that fails when any guard's result is `skipped`, so "never ran" can never be mistaken for "fine".

(1) alone would have surfaced this. (3) is what makes the distinction visible in the UI rather than only in the step list.

## Related

Found while fixing the red benchmarks job on #2856. Same class of problem as the baseline-guard blind spot in that PR: the guard existed, was correct, and nobody could see its state.

title: processes phase: the parse-output sink wiring is only ever exercised through its fail-open catch branch
body:
## Summary

`processesPhase` reads `allFetchCalls` / `allORMQueries` off the parse output to build the R3-6 sink set, wrapped in a `try/catch` that falls open to "no sinks". **Every phase-level test omits `parse` from the deps map, so all of them take the catch branch.** The success path — parse output present, sites read, sinks passed to `processProcesses` — has no coverage at all.

The consequence is that the wiring can break silently. `getPhaseOutput` is a raw `as T` cast, so if the field names on `ParseOutput` ever drift, the phase detects zero sinks and every test still passes, because zero sinks is exactly what the tests already assert.

## Evidence

All four `processesPhase.execute(...)` call sites, and what their deps `Map` contains:

| call site | deps passed |
|---|---|
| `test/unit/route-process-linking.test.ts:102` | no `parse` |
| `test/unit/route-process-linking.test.ts:169` | no `parse` |
| `test/unit/route-process-linking.test.ts:240` | no `parse` |
| `test/unit/tool-process-linking.test.ts:118` | `structure`, `communities`, `routes`, `tools` — no `parse` |

`grep -n parse test/unit/route-process-linking.test.ts` returns nothing. `tool-process-linking.test.ts` does build a `parse` phase result at `:66`, but passes it to `toolsPhase.execute`, not to `processesPhase.execute`.

No test asserts `processesPhase.deps` contains `'parse'` either — `test/unit/ingestion/pipeline-phase-registry.test.ts` checks membership and ordering, and only that no always-included phase lists a pdg-gated dep.

## What IS covered

The sink logic itself is well tested at the unit level, so this is a wiring gap and not a logic gap:

- `buildSinkFunctionSet` directly, including innermost-enclosing-function attribution — `test/unit/process-processor.test.ts:723`, `:736`
- the R3-6 behaviours through `processProcesses` — the `sink-terminated flows (R3-6)` describe block, `:639` onward

## Suggested fix

One phase-level test that passes a `parse` entry carrying real `allFetchCalls` / `allORMQueries` and asserts a sink-terminated Process comes out — the assertion that fails if the field names drift or the read is dropped. Worth pairing with an assertion that `processesPhase.deps` includes `'parse'`, so the declaration and the read can't diverge.

## Related

Noted while fixing the call-flow regression in #2856, which introduced this read. Kept out of that PR since it is test coverage rather than the regression itself.

title: fetch/ORM extraction yields zero sites on this repo, so R3-6 sink-terminated flows can never fire
body:
## Summary

The R3-6 sink feature added in #2856 lets an execution flow end where the program reaches outward — a fetch call or an ORM query — instead of only at a call-graph leaf. It derives that set entirely from the parse phase's `allFetchCalls` and `allORMQueries`.

On this repository both are **empty**, so the feature is inert here: no flow can ever be sink-terminated, and the sink-first ranking rule never changes an ordering.

This is not an objection to the feature. It is that the signal it depends on produces nothing on a TypeScript codebase that plainly does perform outward calls, which points at a gap in fetch/ORM extraction rather than in the flow walk.

## Evidence

Live index (`/workspace`), both edge types that these facts produce:

```
MATCH ()-[r:CodeRelation]->() WHERE r.type IN ['FETCHES','QUERIES'] RETURN r.type, count(*)
-> []
```

Zero rows for both. `ormPhase` returns early on an empty `allORMQueries` and otherwise emits one `QUERIES` edge per de-duplicated entry, so zero edges implies zero sites.

Running the real pipeline over `gitnexus/src` (793 files, 11,490 symbols) and reading the parse output directly:

```json
{"repoPath":"/workspace/gitnexus/src","symbolCount":11490,"fetchCallSites":0,"ormQuerySites":0,"outwardActionSites":0}
```

And the resulting flows are byte-identical with and without sinks wired in:

```json
{"variant":"pr(real sinks)","processes":936,"stepEdges":4648,"avgSteps":4.966}
{"variant":"pr(no sinks)",  "processes":936,"stepEdges":4648,"avgSteps":4.966}
```

Meanwhile `grep -c 'fetch('` over `gitnexus/src`, `gitnexus-web/src` and `gitnexus-shared/src` finds 48 occurrences, so the calls exist — they are just not being extracted as fetch sites.

## Why it matters

Two separate consequences:

1. **The measured deepening in #2856 is entirely the BFS→DFS change, not sinks.** Average step count went 4.104 → 4.966 and the histogram now reaches 10, with zero sinks in play. Worth knowing when attributing that PR's effect, and worth correcting in its description, which reads as though sinks are doing work on this repo.
2. **`explain` / taint and anything else keyed on `FETCHES` / `QUERIES` is equally blind here.** The sink feature is just the newest consumer of a signal that appears to be broadly under-firing.

## Suggested next step

Establish whether this is repo-specific or general: run the extraction over a fixture that definitely contains `fetch(` / `axios` / an ORM call and check whether sites are produced. If they are, work out what about this codebase's call shapes evades it (wrappers? `await fetch` inside methods? re-exported clients?). If they are not, the extractor itself has regressed and the 0-edge count on a repo this size is the symptom.

Either way it would be good to have a guard that fails when a corpus known to contain outward calls yields zero sites — the current failure is completely silent.

## Related

Found while measuring the call-flow regression in #2856.

title: perf(import-target): index the workspace once per run for go/csharp/dart/ruby
body:
Closes #2877, closes #2878, closes #2879, closes #2880.

Four import-target resolvers answered their lookups with a full `allFilePaths` scan per import, so import resolution cost **O(imports × files)**. Each now reads an index memoized on the `allFilePaths` Set identity — the shape `getPythonFileIndex` (#1918) and C#'s own `getWorkspaceFileIndex` (#1881) already used.

| | before | now |
|---|---|---|
| **go** #2877 | `findRootPackageFiles` / `findAllFilesInPkgDir`, the latter once per path segment on the GOPATH fallback. Most Go imports are external, so the whole cascade ran to completion before returning `null` — the fast path never fired. | one package-dir index per run |
| **csharp** #2878 | the no-csproj leg took the raw Set past the memoized index the csproj leg was already using — up to eight passes for a four-segment `using` | both legs read the same two per-run indexes |
| **dart** #2879 | one scan per candidate path; for an external package both candidates miss, so both always ran to completion | one basename index per run |
| **ruby** #2880 | a complete `buildSuffixIndex` **rebuilt and discarded per `require`** — every require paid to index every file in the repo | shared workspace index, hoisted |

## Measured

`bench/import-target/measure.mjs`, 8 imports/file, ~5 in 8 imports external (they run every leg to completion — a mostly-resolving corpus measures the wrong half of the function). The two columns are at different scales: the "after" column is the shipped gate at 400 → 1600 files, the "before" column was measured against the pre-change implementations on the same corpus **shape** at 150 → 600 files (recorded in `_floor` in `baselines.json`). `scaling_ratio` divides the file count out, so it is scale-invariant and the two are comparable:

| | scaling ratio before (150 → 600) | after (400 → 1600) |
|---|---|---|
| go | 3.36 | 0.984 |
| csharp | 4.10 | 1.138 |
| dart | 3.32 | 0.787 |
| ruby | 3.87 | 1.123 |

1.0 is linear; ~4 is quadratic at a 4× scale gap. The "before" column does **not** reproduce the exact ratios reported in the issues (4.00 / 3.43 / 4.05) — different corpora — but the two sets independently confirm the same quadratic behaviour. Ruby's absolute cost at 1600 files fell from *unfinished after 2 minutes* to 86 ms.

## Two shared modules

- `import-resolvers/workspace-file-index.ts` — normalized list + `SuffixIndex` + a normalized→raw map (C#, Ruby). C#'s local copy moved here; the new `normToRaw` answers "is there a file whose **whole** path is X", which `index.get` cannot, because the suffix map conflates a whole-path hit with a `…/X` suffix hit.
- `import-resolvers/package-dir-index.ts` — "which files live directly inside a directory ending with `<path>`" (Go, C#). Candidates are bucketed by the directory's **last segment** rather than by indexing every directory suffix: a suffix map costs O(files × depth) entries, which is the memory this codebase runs out of at kernel scale (#2649).

## Behaviour is unchanged, including the invisible tie-breaks

These are expressed only through Set-iteration order and `indexOf` positions, so nothing in the type system or the existing tests could see them move:

- Go's root leg is **sorted**; its package leg is **not** — it keeps Set order, and multi-directory matches are merged back onto it.
- Go and C# both take the **first** occurrence of `/<segment>/`, so `a/pkg/b/pkg/x.go` does **not** answer `pkg`. Dropping that looks like a cleanup and moves edges in every repo that nests a directory name inside itself (`internal/…/internal`, `Models/…/Models`).
- C#'s `resolveDirectMatch` lets a whole-path match win over a suffix match found **earlier** in iteration order; `resolveByProgressiveStripping` takes whichever comes first.
- Dart tries `lib/<rel>` fully before bare `<rel>`, and matches **raw** paths — normalizing backslashes here would start resolving imports that previously returned `null`.

Verified two independent ways:

1. **`test/unit/scope-resolution/import-target-index-parity.test.ts`** keeps verbatim copies of the pre-change implementations and diffs against them over a deterministic corpus (40 layouts × every target shape, per language) plus hand-built layouts for each tie-break above. Six mutations of the new code were each confirmed to fail it — dropping the first-occurrence rule, dropping the order merge, sorting Go's package leg, dropping C#'s exact-wins lookup, normalizing Dart's paths, and flipping Dart's candidate priority.
2. **Byte-identical fingerprints.** The bench corpus was run against the pre-change resolvers and this branch at both 400 and 1600 files: all seven sha256s match exactly.

The same file also asserts the index is built **once per file set**, by counting traversals of the Set. Go 1, Dart 1, Ruby 1, C# 2.

That arm catches a rescan reintroduced *inside* a resolver, but it calls the resolvers directly, so it does **not** cross the adapter boundary — which is exactly where #1918 review P1 lived (a defensive `new Set(allFilePaths)` in an adapter hands a fresh `WeakMap` key per call and silently restores the quadratic behaviour). `test/integration/{go,csharp,dart,ruby}-import-index-reuse.test.ts` cover that layer, resolving through `<lang>ScopeResolver.resolveImportTarget` the way Kotlin's and Python's existing guards do. Each was verified to fail under the copy it exists to catch.

## CI

New always-on step in `benchmarks (GITNEXUS_BENCH)`. The final `--check` gates eight arms per language, not two: the output fingerprint **at every scale** (small, large, deep, collide), the scaling budget (1.8), the per-language `depth_ratio` budget, the per-language `collide_scaling_ratio` budget, the absolute `small_ms_ceiling`, the absolute retained-heap ceiling, `deep.resolved === small.resolved`, and `deep.fingerprint !== small.fingerprint` — **plus the corpus shape at every scale** (files / imports / resolved / distinct outcomes, asserted exactly), because a fingerprint alone cannot tell a legitimate resolution change from a corpus quietly shrunk below the size at which the timing arms can see anything.

The step is placed **last** in the `benchmarks` job on purpose until #2895 lands: a failing `run:` step aborts every step after it, so the newest and least-proven gate must not be in a position to mask the eight established guards behind it.

## Also checked, no change needed

#2880 asks whether the other `buildSuffixIndex` call sites are inside a per-import path. TypeScript (`typescript/scope-resolver.ts`) and Vue (`vue/import-target.ts`) already hoist theirs behind a pass cache keyed on the Set identity; `group/extractors/include-extractor.ts` builds one per extraction run, not per import.

## Out of scope, worth a follow-up

`php/import-target.ts` re-materializes `[...allFiles].map(…)` per call at two sites (lines 185 and 220) — the same shape as #2880, not covered by any of these four issues.

## Test status

`tsc` clean, lint clean. 27/27 in the new parity file; 243/243 across the go/csharp/dart/ruby scope-resolution unit suites; 592 passing in the integration resolver suites. Two integration files (`resolvers/ruby.test.ts` and one sibling) failed locally with `Worker pool failed to start: Replacement worker did not report ready within 5000ms` — the #1741 host-load flake, in `beforeAll` before any resolution runs. Nothing in this PR touches worker startup. CI is the arbiter.

---

## Update: merged `main`, and Kotlin folded in

`main` now carries #2872, which did the same hoist for Kotlin. Merge conflict was one benchmark step both branches add at the same place in the `benchmarks` job — kept both. (The new step was also renamed to `(#2877/#2878/#2879/#2880/#2872)`: a space before `#` starts a YAML comment inside a plain scalar, so the original spelling truncated the step name to `Import-target resolution guards (#2877`.)

Kotlin now runs in the shared corpus, and #2872's review surfaced two arms a scaling ratio alone cannot carry, so all five languages get them:

- **`depth_ratio`** — deep arm at a **fixed** file count with ~6× the path components. `scaling_ratio` divides the file count out, so it is scale-invariant and structurally cannot see cost growing with path *depth* instead — and `buildSuffixIndex` (C#, Ruby) and Kotlin's `suffixByStem` each emit one entry per component. Measured go 1.06, dart 0.88 (depth-free indexes), ruby 1.48, kotlin 2.20, csharp 3.45. Budget is per language: one global budget would have to sit at 5.0 and would let Dart go 0.88 → 4.9 unnoticed.
- **`small_ms_ceiling`** — absolute, at 4× the measured arm, because a constant-factor regression that grows both scale arms equally passes every ratio.
- The deep arm must resolve **exactly** what the small arm resolves — padding was supposed to change depth and nothing else; a deep arm that stopped resolving would be timing the null path.

The five fingerprints are unchanged by that commit, verified against the previous baseline before rewriting it — adding the Kotlin arm and the deep scale did not perturb the four languages' output.

Kotlin also joins the Set-iteration counter in the parity test. Its own guard (`kotlin-import-index-reuse.test.ts`) counts index **builds**, which a scan added beside a reused index does not move.

### One measured blind spot, documented rather than papered over

A full workspace scan reintroduced on **1-in-32 imports passes every timing arm** here — dart scored 1.458 against the 1.8 scaling budget and 1.736 ms against a 4 ms ceiling. At 1-in-8 the scaling arm catches it (2.414). What *narrows* the gap is not a timing gate: the traversal counter reads **14 instead of 1** for that same mutation, deterministically, for all five languages. It does not close it — the counter watches the Set, while the resolvers hold materialized arrays of the same list (`WorkspaceFileIndex.normalized`/`.all`, Dart's basename buckets, `PackageDirIndex.filesByDir`), so a scan over one of those is still invisible to both gates. Tightening the ceilings toward the noise floor to chase that case would only buy flaky CI. Recorded in `_blind_spot` in `baselines.json` so nobody has to rediscover it.

`bench/kotlin-import-target/` stays. It fingerprints both file-set iteration orders and probes the four-tier cascade shape by shape; this corpus does neither, so it is a second corpus, not a replacement.



---

## Update: review round

Addressed the findings from the two-engine review (Claude swarm + ce personas, Codex `gpt-5.6-sol`, review [#4889364193](https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/pull/2898#pullrequestreview-4889364193)). The resolver logic itself came through clean — 6,402,319 old-vs-new differential comparisons with 0 divergences, and **all five output fingerprints are byte-identical after every change below**, which is the proof that none of it altered behaviour.

**One real cost regression, now inverted.** `filesDirectlyInPkgDir` re-spread its accumulator per matching directory, O(files × dirs²). Where many services share a package directory (`svcN/internal/pkg`, which Go's GOPATH cascade queries by two-segment tail) the index was **13.4× slower than the scan it replaced** at k=1600. Appending once and sorting once makes it **4.1× faster** there; output byte-identical at every k. The same edit is what the simplicity lane independently asked for.

**Three holes in this PR's own gate.**
- `--check` computed three fingerprints per language and compared one. `DEEP_PAD = 16 → 0` deleted the whole depth arm and still printed PASS. Every scale is asserted now, plus `deep.fingerprint !== small.fingerprint` so the padding's *effect* is pinned rather than just its output.
- The corpus minted unique directory names, so max bucket cardinality was **1** — and that is the only non-constant term the index has, so the `dirCount > 1` merge branch had never executed in any arm. The new `collide` arm reaches 9,269 multi-directory merges per run, up to 34 at once. Go/C#/Dart legitimately score above the linear budget on shared-leaf layouts and get their own; Ruby and Kotlin stay at 1.8 because their keyed maps are collision-immune and that immunity is the assertion.
- No arm measured memory. A retained-heap arm on the `bench/cfg` pattern (including its loud failure when `--expose-gc` is missing, rather than a silent skip) measures **csharp 73.62 MiB / ruby 55.26 MiB at 32k files**. Its ceiling is **1.5×, deliberately not the 4× the timing arms use** — the measurement is byte-stable to 0.00085% across processes, so 4× would discard the gate. `_arms_note` records why, so it does not get "harmonised" back.

**The reuse guard did not guard the layer its own docstring named.** Inserting `new Set(allFilePaths)` into all four `<lang>/scope-resolver.ts` adapters left the parity test 28/28 green and `--check` PASS. Kotlin and Python already had adapter-level integration guards; go/csharp/dart/ruby now do too, each proven to fail under that exact mutation. `CountingSet` also now counts `forEach`/`values`/`keys`/`entries`, not just `[Symbol.iterator]` — a rescan spelled `allFilePaths.forEach(…)` was previously invisible.

**`depth_ratio`, added by this PR, flaked ~1-in-20** (go peaked 1.748, dart 2.043, against a 1.6 budget) — both are ratios of two sub-3 ms minima. Fixed at the estimator, not the threshold: `REPS` 5 → 15, matching `bench/cfg`, `schema-pairs` and `callable-value-flow`. 22/22 PASS, every arm now at 70–78% of its budget with a ≤1.26× swing, **no budget widened**; the measured distributions are in `_arms_note` so the headroom is visibly earned.

**Four fixtures pinned the guard next door** to the one their title named — the Dart "matched RAW" case asserted `null === null`, C# and Ruby had no backslash target at all, `normToRaw`'s first-wins rule had no normalization twin, and the Go nested-package case was decided by the `endsWith` half. Each now kills the mutation it exists for.

Also corrected three copies of the claim that the parity test *closes* the 1-in-32 blind spot (it narrows it), and `_floor`'s claim that its ratios "match" the issues' (different corpora, both quadratic).

### Still out of scope, with numbers attached

- `languages/php/import-target.ts:185/220` — materializes the workspace twice per import and passes no index: **95 ms per import at 20k files**. The last language without a per-pass memo; `getWorkspaceFileIndex` makes it a small change.
- `import-resolvers/csharp.ts:81` — per-import linear scan on the **csproj** leg, ~0.95 ms/import at 50k `.cs`. Bounded: the root-namespace gate at `:32-42` means BCL/NuGet usings never reach it.
- `buildSuffixIndex`'s `dirMap` is **15.7% (C#) / 20.3% (Ruby)** of retained bytes, and Ruby, TypeScript, Vue and the include-extractor never read it — building it lazily is behaviour-identical and worth ~34 MiB at 100k Ruby files. Left alone here rather than widening this PR into shared `utils.ts`.

title: fix: close the nine follow-up review findings from #2856 (routes, receiver typing, truncation honesty)
body:
Follow-up to #2856, which upstream asked to keep for a second PR. Nine review findings, each reproduced before it was fixed and mutation-checked after.

Two of the nine turned out **not to reproduce**. They are reported as closed-with-evidence rather than quietly dropped, because the structural observations behind them were correct — only their consequences were absent.

---

## Measured on a real repo

`crypto-trading-bot` — 982 files, 619 JavaScript + 255 TypeScript. Both sides analyzed under identical conditions: **BEFORE** is `main` at `c6b24162` (i.e. with #2856 already merged), **AFTER** is this branch. So this table is wave 2's own contribution, not a re-run of #2856's.

### Routes

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| routes detected | 75 | 76 |
| **verb-qualified** | 39 (52%) | **55 (72%)** |
| **attributed to `apiRouteTable.js`** — a membership test, not a handler | **28** | **12** |
| `researchRunRoutes.js` | 2 | **16** |
| `catalogRoutes.js` / `liveDecisionRoutes.js` | 4 / 2 | 5 / 3 |
| `positionReplayRoutes.js` | 0 | 1 |
