title: fix(storage): give every registry write its own tmp path (#2888)
body:
Fixes #2888.

## The bug

`writeRegistry` staged the global registry through a **fixed** `~/.gitnexus/registry.json.tmp`. The rename is atomic with respect to readers, but the tmp path is not private to the writer, and `registry.json` is the one file every gitnexus process on the machine writes. Two processes starting together stage through the same inode: B's `writeFile` overwrites A's bytes, B's `rename` moves that inode onto `registry.json`, and A's own rename finds nothing at the source:

```
ENOENT: no such file or directory, rename '<home>/registry.json.tmp' -> '<home>/registry.json'
```

That lands on the MCP startup path (`mcpCommand` → `LocalBackend.init` → `refreshRepos` → `listRegisteredRepos({validate:true})`), where nothing catches, so the client only sees "Server disconnected".

`withRegistryLock` (#2716) serializes the callers and hides this in the normal path, but it deliberately degrades to **unlocked** after a 5s `IndexLockTimeoutError` — availability over serialization — so the window is still live on `main` today. Measured on the parent commit, 12 concurrent processes pruning a stale registry while another process held the registry lock: **4/12 crashed** with the trace above; 24 processes with no lock contention: 0/24. The write itself has to be collision-proof rather than leaning on the lock.

## The fix

- **`writeFileAtomic(targetPath, data, mode = 0o600)`** in `storage/fs-atomic.ts`, beside the `retryRename` it uses: random tmp suffix, `'wx'` + explicit mode, write, `retryRename`, and `unlink` of the tmp before rethrowing on any rejection. With a fixed name a leaked tmp was self-limiting (the next writer overwrote it); a random suffix would drop a fresh orphan on every failed publish, so the cleanup is part of the fix, not polish.
- **`writeRegistry` calls it.** That is the whole of #2888.
- **Three existing writers were byte-identical copies** of that sequence — `writeMetaFile` (repo-manager), `writeBridgeMeta` (group/bridge-db), `writeContractRegistry` (group/storage) — none of which cleaned up its tmp on failure. They now call the same helper instead of a fourth copy being added, which also retro-fits the cleanup to all three. Net −45 lines of duplication.
- **The prune write in `listRegisteredRepos({validate:true})` no longer throws.** It is housekeeping, not the caller's request: every caller consumes the returned `valid` array and the prune set is recomputed from scratch on the next validating read, so a failed write costs a retry, never correctness — while rethrowing took down the whole MCP server. Catching it also covers the read-only-home and full-disk variants of the same startup death.

## Verification

Five new tests in `test/unit/repo-manager-registry-atomic-write.test.ts`, all deterministic (a hooked `fs.rename` drives the interleaving; no sleeps, no spawned processes):

| test | on parent commit |
|---|---|
| rival publishes `registry.json` between our write and our rename | ENOENT, `registerRepo` rejects |
| same window via `unregisterRepo` (fix lives in `writeRegistry`, not one caller) | ENOENT |
| every transaction gets its own tmp path in the registry dir | both renames stage from the same fixed path |
| tmp removed when the rename fails, previous registry intact | `registry.json.tmp` left behind |
| validating read still serves when the prune write fails | throws out of `listRegisteredRepos` |

All five fail on the parent commit, four of them with the exact error from the issue, and pass here. The process-level repro from the issue goes 4/12 → 0/12 crashes with the registry lock held.

`test/unit/group/insecure-tempfile.test.ts` structural guards were retargeted at `fs-atomic.ts`, where the `randomBytes` / `'wx'` / `0o600` sequence now lives, plus a new guard for the tmp cleanup and per-writer guards that they route through the helper. Full unit suite: 12183 passed; the 3 unrelated failures on this box are the local untracked `.claude/skills/gitnexus/*` copies and the known `skip-git-cli` child-process timeout.

## Note for reviewers

`registry.json` is now created `0o600` — it inherited the umask before (typically `0o644`), and this matches what `gitnexus.json` has always used. Existing installs tighten on the next rewrite. Flagging it in case a deployment reads `~/.gitnexus/registry.json` as a different user.

Deliberately out of scope, all latent rather than live: `parse-cache.ts` and `parsedfile-store.ts` still use fixed tmp names, but they are per-repo paths covered by the analyze index lock, which throws on timeout instead of degrading; `bridge.lbug.bak` uses a fixed set-aside name; `saveCLIConfig` writes `~/.gitnexus/config.json` in place with no atomicity at all. Happy to fold any of them in if you'd rather they ride along.

title: fix(go): resolve out-of-repo package qualifiers, and stop reporting an undecided interface check as a decided negative (#2873)
body:
Fixes #2873.

## The bug

Go structural interface satisfaction compares method signatures after normalizing package qualifiers. `signatureContextForFile` built its qualifier map only from import edges that resolved to a file **inside the repository**:

```ts
if (edge.kind !== 'namespace' || edge.targetFile === null) continue;   // stdlib/third-party dropped
```

`import "context"` resolves to no file, so `context` never entered the map, `qualifyGoSignatureTypes` collapsed the whole signature to `undefined`, and both `parameterTypesCompatible` and `returnTypesCompatible` read `undefined` as *these signatures differ*. That happens symmetrically — interface side and implementation side — so two **textually identical** methods compared unequal.

`ctx context.Context` opens nearly every idiomatic Go method, so satisfaction only ever succeeded for the minority of interfaces whose signatures are builtin-only.

The knock-on effect is the one that actually hurts: with no `IMPLEMENTS` edge there is no dispatch boundary, so a call through an interface-typed field stops at the interface declaration and `impact()` on the real implementation reports a confident `0` callers — the #2813 complaint, with a mechanism.

Reproduced on `origin/main` (`18bc51dfd`) with the reporter's repro. Before:

```
IMPLEMENTS: ["LocalStoreImpl → LocalStore"]
CALLS:      ["Handler.Remove -> CtxStore.Delete [global]"]
```

After:

```
IMPLEMENTS: ["CtxStoreImpl → CtxStore","LocalStoreImpl → LocalStore","RetStoreImpl → RetStore"]
CALLS:      [..., "Handler.Remove -> CtxStoreImpl.Delete [interface-dispatch]"]
```

## The fix

The identity such an import needs was already parsed — `ParsedImport.targetRaw` holds the import path — it just was not carried onto the finalized `ImportEdge`. `signatureContextForFile` now falls back to it for any local name the in-repo pass did not claim:

- **In-repo wins.** The existing edge pass runs first and still supplies the package directory; the fallback only fills gaps, so nothing that resolved before changes.
- **Keyed on the path, not the local name.** `net/http` and `example.com/x/http` stay distinct even though both spell their qualifier `http`, while `import c "context"` in one file still matches plain `context.Context` in another.
- **Namespaced `extern:<path>`.** In-repo qualifiers are package directories, which never contain `:`, so the two spaces cannot collide.
- **Still conservative where it must be.** A qualifier with no import directive at all remains `undefined` — unresolved, not silently equal.

No shared type changed; `ImportEdge` is untouched.

### Major-version import paths

The extractor derives an unaliased import's local name from the last path segment, which for a module at v2+ is the *version*: `github.com/foo/bar/v2` gives `v2` while source writes `bar.Config`, and `gopkg.in/yaml.v3` gives `yaml.v3` while source writes `yaml.Node`. Keying only on that name would have left #2873 unfixed for every v2+ dependency — and one such parameter is enough to poison a whole method.

So the path-derived package name is registered alongside the extractor's local name, both pointing at the same `extern:<path>`. Only for **unaliased** imports: an alias already names the token the source uses, and minting the derived name for it would let one major version claim the token a sibling spells natively — `import v1 "…/bar"` next to `import bar "…/bar/v2"` must keep `bar` on v2. A package whose name diverges from its path for any other reason needs source that is by definition outside the repo; those stay unresolved.

One more precedence detail: an in-repo import now claims its local name even when the target is a repo-**root** package, whose file has no directory to be named by. Behavior is unchanged there (no qualifier either side can agree on), but the map no longer labels a genuinely in-repo package as external.

## Tests

New fixture `test/fixtures/lang-resolution/go-extern-qualified-signatures/`:

- cross-package interface + implementation whose signatures name `context.Context` in both parameter and return position → `IMPLEMENTS` emitted, and the interface-typed field call fans out to the implementor (`interface-dispatch`);
- a same-method-name struct with a mismatched signature that must stay excluded;
- packages `alpha` and `beta` importing two **different** out-of-repo packages that share the last segment `client` → must *not* match.

The fixture also carries a `github.com/foo/bar/v2` method, so the version-suffix path is proven end to end through the real extractor, not just against a hand-built directive.

Unit tests in `go-hooks.test.ts` cover the parameter position, the return position across packages, an aliased import against its unaliased spelling, the colliding-basename negative, in-repo-wins precedence, dot-imports registering nothing, the `/v2` and `gopkg.in/….v3` recovery, and two majors of one module staying distinct.

**Mutation-checked, each guard individually:** reverting the fallback fails 3 unit + 2 integration tests; deleting the in-repo precedence guard fails exactly the precedence test; dropping the version-strip fails the `/v2` unit test and all 3 integration tests; dropping the unaliased-only guard fails the two-majors test. No guard in the diff is unpinned.

Local runs: `go.test.ts` 179/179, all 9 Go unit files 124/124, `go-pipeline-benchmark.test.ts` green, `tsc --noEmit` clean. The Go captures golden was regenerated additively (+20 lines, one new fixture's entries).

`generateSyntheticInterfaceData` in `go-pipeline-benchmark.test.ts` gained `parsedImports: []` — that test double casts through `as ParsedFile[]`, so the missing required field was invisible to `tsc` and would have thrown at runtime on the new pass.

---

# Part 2 — the epistemic half

The first half above removes the dominant *cause* of a wrong-and-confident answer. This half removes the *confidence*: the analyzer now distinguishes "no type implements this interface" from "we could not tell", and carries the second all the way to `impact`.

#2921 removed the dominant *cause* of a wrong-and-confident answer. This one removes the *confidence*: the analyzer now distinguishes "no type implements this interface" from "we could not tell", and carries the second all the way to `impact`.

## Why a graph probe cannot fix this

The existing hedge (`computeEpistemicBoundary`) finds a dispatch boundary by counting IMPLEMENTS edges. An undecided check mints no edge — so there is nothing left for it to notice. The evidence a graph probe would need is precisely what went missing. That is why the reported symptom is a *confident* zero and not merely a low one:

```
impact --uid "Method:repro.go:CtxStoreImpl.Delete"
{ "impactedCount": 0, "risk": "LOW", "epistemic": "exact" }
```

## The tri-state

`satisfied | unsatisfied | undecided`, propagated from the one place a type spelling decides anything up to the candidate loop.

| verdict | edge | recorded |
| --- | --- | --- |
| satisfied | IMPLEMENTS | — |
| unsatisfied | none | none — a decided "no" is trustworthy |
| **undecided** | **none** | **yes** |

`undecided` deliberately mints no edge. A speculative IMPLEMENTS would fan out through `emitReceiverBoundCalls` into fabricated CALLS, and wrong callers in a blast-radius tool are their own kind of lie. Note `go/types` folds the same case the *other* way — `hasAllMethods` returns `true` for an invalid type, commented *"we don't know anything about V, assume it implements T"* — because a type checker's job is to avoid cascading errors, not to bound a change. Soot is conservative upward (phantom → true) but its *downward* `getSubclassesOf` has no such guard, which is exactly the "who implements this" direction `impact` asks in.

Two propagation rules keep unknown from swallowing everything:
- **A decided mismatch dominates.** A type that provably lacks a required method does not implement the interface however many other methods went unread.
- **One matching overload settles its method.** Unknowns on the siblings cannot unsettle it — the same rule Pyright uses to suppress partially-unknown when a resolvable path exists.

Two pre-existing assumptions surfaced on the way. An absent parameter-type list read as **compatible** — a bare guess that could mint an edge between signatures nobody compared; it is now `undecided`, except where both sides declare zero parameters and absence is the honest shape of `Close() error`. A required method with no verifiable signature read as *does not match*; that is missing information too.

## Where the record lives

`RepoMeta`, beside `unresolvedReceiverMembers`, for its reasons: the fact is about the **analysis** rather than the code; it is additive metadata so `SCHEMA_FINGERPRINT` does not move and no re-analyze is forced; and it stays invisible to all nine IMPLEMENTS consumers (MRO, METHOD_IMPLEMENTS derivation, dispatch fan-out, clustering, DI, Spring AOP, the impact walk, the retention sink) — none of which should see a question as an edge.

Both sides of each pair are recorded. Asking about the **implementation** is the case the issue reports, and an interface-keyed record alone leaves exactly that query unhedged: the walk starts at a method whose owner has no heritage edge. A method matches through its declaring type — one Cypher hop, asked only for methods.

## What `impact` now returns

A fourth `causes` slot. The three that existed count decided facts that could not be *attributed*; this one counts questions never *answered*, and it is the only cause that shortens a result without leaving a trace in the graph:

```jsonc
{ "impactedCount": 0,          // unchanged — this invents no callers
  "epistemic": "lower-bound",  // was "exact"
  "causes": { "receiverTyping": 0, "dispatchBoundary": 0,
              "externalBoundary": 0, "undecidedSatisfaction": 1 },
  "boundaries": ["`CtxStoreImpl` was a candidate implementation for 1 interface the analyzer could not decide, …"] }
```

A cleanly-decided symbol in the same index still reports `exact`. The hedge has to stay rare to mean anything — Pyright's `Unknown` is always tracked but its diagnostics default to off outside strict mode, for the same reason.

## Performance

Measured best-of-N at three sizes, against this same branch with the tri-state reverted:

| pairs | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 200×200 = 40k | 94–95 ms | **87–89 ms** |
| 800×800 = 640k | 2367–2767 ms | **2140–2357 ms** |

Faster, because a decided parameter mismatch now short-circuits before the return-type comparison. (The suite's `scaling < 1.5` gate fails identically with and without these commits on this machine — it is not a regression introduced here.) The query side adds one metadata read, already loaded on the same path, plus one gated Cypher hop for methods only.

## Tests

- Unit: the undecided channel fires for an unresolvable qualifier, stays silent for a decided mismatch, and a hard "no" beats an unknown in the same method set.
- Unit: the summary records both sides, keeps true totals beside the capped window, and ranks deterministically (the tiebreak decides which entries survive the cap).
- Integration, end to end: a dot-import fixture — no qualifier at all — reports `Drawer` undecided with `Canvas` as its candidate, while `Label → Named` still emits in the same file.
- Integration, query side: `impact` on the implementation method returns `lower-bound` with `undecidedSatisfaction: 1`; on the interface, `2`; a clean leaf in the same index stays `exact`.

Go integration 182/182, all scope-resolution units 1803 passing, tsc clean.

## Follow-up, not in this PR

Go publishes `api/go1*.txt` — every exported stdlib symbol including full interface method sets, generated and enforced by the Go release process. Consuming it would turn "does `MyType` implement `io.Reader`" from undecidable into decided, shrinking the unknown set to genuine third-party interfaces. Complementary to this change, not a replacement.

## Not in this PR

Go publishes `api/go1*.txt` — every exported stdlib symbol including full interface method sets, generated and enforced by the Go release process. Consuming it would turn "does `MyType` implement `io.Reader`" from undecidable into decided, shrinking the unknown set to genuine third-party interfaces. Complementary to this change, not a replacement.

title: fix(skills): publish gitnexus-plan artifacts on macOS without an interpreter (#2905)
body:
Fixes #2905.

## The problem

`requireDescriptorAnchoring()` hard-gated `process.platform !== 'linux'`, so on macOS the safe generated-plan writer refused before doing anything. The gate was not incidental: the helper resolves every name through `/proc/self/fd/<fd>/<child>`, and published with `renameat2(RENAME_NOREPLACE)`. macOS has neither.

The issue reports `write-plan`. Two more commands were affected. `read-plan` goes through the same parent walk, so `gitnexus-work` could not load a plan either. `snapshot` fails whenever a materialized path is absent, via `materializeRecord` -> `recordAnchoredAbsence` — deleted files, rename sources and missing cited paths all reach it, which the suite's own fixture does.

## What the platform actually allows

Two things were measured on real runners rather than argued from documentation.

**macOS `/dev/fd/<fd>` is not a substitute for `/proc/self/fd/<fd>`.** With an open directory descriptor on macos-latest:

```
stat /dev/fd/11            ok, isDirectory true
realpath /dev/fd/11        "/dev/fd/11"      <- not the directory's path
lstat  /dev/fd/11/child    ENOENT
open   /dev/fd/11/child    ENOENT
create /dev/fd/11/child    ENOENT
mkdir  /dev/fd/11/child    ENOENT
```

The same probe on ubuntu-latest traverses fine, and after renaming the directory away and planting an impostor at the same name, reading through the descriptor path still returns the original file. That is the anchoring property, and it has no Node-reachable equivalent on macOS: `node:fs` exposes no `dir_fd` parameter anywhere, `fs.Dir` cannot open a child, and there is no FFI. `fcntl(F_GETPATH)` does not help either — XNU reconstructs that string from the name cache at call time and any later use re-walks from the root by name.

**`link(2)` is a portable no-replace publish.** On macOS, Linux, and a 9p mount:

```
link publishes                     "new"
link over an existing destination  EEXIST, destination intact
link onto a symlinked destination  EEXIST, symlink target untouched
same, through /proc/self/fd/<fd>/  identical results, nlink 1 after unlink
```

That is exactly what `RENAME_NOREPLACE` and `RENAME_EXCL` were being used for, and it is reachable from `fs.linkSync`.

## What changed

Publication is now `link(2)` on both platforms, and the writer spawns no interpreter and loads no native code.

That removes the interpreter from Linux entirely, because `/proc` was already doing the resolving there, and removes `ctypes`, `libSystem`, `renameatx_np`, `RENAME_EXCL` and the `ENOTSUP` handling from macOS. Deleted along with them: the trusted-executable validation, the held-descriptor exec and its two-tier probe, the capability probe, the JSON request protocol, and both embedded Python programs. The helper goes from 3047 to 2327 lines.

macOS keeps the part that genuinely cannot be done in Node, and now does it in-process: a lexical `O_NOFOLLOW` walk that holds an open descriptor on every directory in the chain for the operation's lifetime, and re-proves the chain either side of every step. The pinning is load bearing rather than tidy — an open descriptor keeps its inode number from being recycled, and without it a freed directory's inode can be reclaimed by the next `mkdir` and satisfy a recorded identity. That was reproduced during review, first try, on ext4.

## The guarantees are not symmetric, and the docs say so

On Linux a parent swapped between a check and its use cannot redirect the operation, because names are resolved against the descriptor rather than re-walked. On macOS the same swap is detected by the check that follows and the operation aborts having written nothing — but it is detection rather than prevention. `references/evidence-provenance.md` states this in those words, under a heading that says it.

## Verification

The suite had been silently skipping on every non-Linux runner (`process.platform === 'linux' ? describe : describe.skip`), which is why this shipped. It now admits darwin and is registered in `scripts/cross-platform-tests.ts`, so it runs on the `macos-latest` matrix.

Because the backend no longer needs an interpreter or `/proc`, it is fully portable — spoofing `process.platform` exercises the real macOS code path on Linux CI instead of leaving it unrun. Three tests were added on that basis: a full write/read round trip under a spoofed darwin that asserts no `/proc/` path reaches the test hooks (proving the Darwin backend was actually selected), the `afterParentOpen` rename-and-symlink attack refused through the pinned chain, and a publish test asserting the published file is the same inode as the temporary with no `.tmp` left behind and a symlinked destination refused.

154 tests green locally. 29 fixtures that drove the deleted Python program directly were removed with it.

## Also fixed

The writer failed on 9p mounts every time, because `renameat2(RENAME_NOREPLACE)` returns `EINVAL` there. `link(2)` succeeds, so publication now works on WSL2 9p checkouts.

## History note

This PR started with a Python-based `openat` backend for macOS, which is why the earlier commits describe one. Two adversarial review passes and four quality passes ran against that design and their findings are folded in — the inode-recycling pin, in-backend identity proof for descriptor-returning operations, and the Windows realpath fix in `assertRepository` (`snapshot` is not platform-gated, and 8.3 short names made it reject a worktree root by quoting that same directory back). The interpreter was then removed entirely in favour of `link(2)`.

Out of scope, noted for the record: `eval/workflow_bench/promotion_apply.py` carries the same Linux-only `renameat2` and `/proc/self/fd` pattern, but it is a separate program, not a caller of this helper.

Thanks to @koriyoshi2041 for confirming the reproduction on native macOS and for pinning down that the blocker was the descriptor-path backend rather than missing open flags.

title: feat(impact): tell an undecided interface check apart from a decided negative (#2873)
body:
Completes #2873. **Stacked on #2921** — review that first; this branch contains its commits.

#2921 removed the dominant *cause* of a wrong-and-confident answer. This one removes the *confidence*: the analyzer now distinguishes "no type implements this interface" from "we could not tell", and carries the second all the way to `impact`.

## Why a graph probe cannot fix this

The existing hedge (`computeEpistemicBoundary`) finds a dispatch boundary by counting IMPLEMENTS edges. An undecided check mints no edge — so there is nothing left for it to notice. The evidence a graph probe would need is precisely what went missing. That is why the reported symptom is a *confident* zero and not merely a low one:

```
impact --uid "Method:repro.go:CtxStoreImpl.Delete"
{ "impactedCount": 0, "risk": "LOW", "epistemic": "exact" }
```

## The tri-state

`satisfied | unsatisfied | undecided`, propagated from the one place a type spelling decides anything up to the candidate loop.

| verdict | edge | recorded |
| --- | --- | --- |
| satisfied | IMPLEMENTS | — |
| unsatisfied | none | none — a decided "no" is trustworthy |
| **undecided** | **none** | **yes** |

`undecided` deliberately mints no edge. A speculative IMPLEMENTS would fan out through `emitReceiverBoundCalls` into fabricated CALLS, and wrong callers in a blast-radius tool are their own kind of lie. Note `go/types` folds the same case the *other* way — `hasAllMethods` returns `true` for an invalid type, commented *"we don't know anything about V, assume it implements T"* — because a type checker's job is to avoid cascading errors, not to bound a change. Soot is conservative upward (phantom → true) but its *downward* `getSubclassesOf` has no such guard, which is exactly the "who implements this" direction `impact` asks in.

Two propagation rules keep unknown from swallowing everything:
- **A decided mismatch dominates.** A type that provably lacks a required method does not implement the interface however many other methods went unread.
- **One matching overload settles its method.** Unknowns on the siblings cannot unsettle it — the same rule Pyright uses to suppress partially-unknown when a resolvable path exists.

Two pre-existing assumptions surfaced on the way. An absent parameter-type list read as **compatible** — a bare guess that could mint an edge between signatures nobody compared; it is now `undecided`, except where both sides declare zero parameters and absence is the honest shape of `Close() error`. A required method with no verifiable signature read as *does not match*; that is missing information too.

## Where the record lives

`RepoMeta`, beside `unresolvedReceiverMembers`, for its reasons: the fact is about the **analysis** rather than the code; it is additive metadata so `SCHEMA_FINGERPRINT` does not move and no re-analyze is forced; and it stays invisible to all nine IMPLEMENTS consumers (MRO, METHOD_IMPLEMENTS derivation, dispatch fan-out, clustering, DI, Spring AOP, the impact walk, the retention sink) — none of which should see a question as an edge.

Both sides of each pair are recorded. Asking about the **implementation** is the case the issue reports, and an interface-keyed record alone leaves exactly that query unhedged: the walk starts at a method whose owner has no heritage edge. A method matches through its declaring type — one Cypher hop, asked only for methods.

## What `impact` now returns

A fourth `causes` slot. The three that existed count decided facts that could not be *attributed*; this one counts questions never *answered*, and it is the only cause that shortens a result without leaving a trace in the graph:

```jsonc
{ "impactedCount": 0,          // unchanged — this invents no callers
  "epistemic": "lower-bound",  // was "exact"
  "causes": { "receiverTyping": 0, "dispatchBoundary": 0,
              "externalBoundary": 0, "undecidedSatisfaction": 1 },
  "boundaries": ["`CtxStoreImpl` was a candidate implementation for 1 interface the analyzer could not decide, …"] }
```

A cleanly-decided symbol in the same index still reports `exact`. The hedge has to stay rare to mean anything — Pyright's `Unknown` is always tracked but its diagnostics default to off outside strict mode, for the same reason.

## Performance

Measured best-of-N at three sizes, against this same branch with the tri-state reverted:

| pairs | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 200×200 = 40k | 94–95 ms | **87–89 ms** |
| 800×800 = 640k | 2367–2767 ms | **2140–2357 ms** |

Faster, because a decided parameter mismatch now short-circuits before the return-type comparison. (The suite's `scaling < 1.5` gate fails identically with and without these commits on this machine — it is not a regression introduced here.) The query side adds one metadata read, already loaded on the same path, plus one gated Cypher hop for methods only.

## Tests

- Unit: the undecided channel fires for an unresolvable qualifier, stays silent for a decided mismatch, and a hard "no" beats an unknown in the same method set.
- Unit: the summary records both sides, keeps true totals beside the capped window, and ranks deterministically (the tiebreak decides which entries survive the cap).
- Integration, end to end: a dot-import fixture — no qualifier at all — reports `Drawer` undecided with `Canvas` as its candidate, while `Label → Named` still emits in the same file.
- Integration, query side: `impact` on the implementation method returns `lower-bound` with `undecidedSatisfaction: 1`; on the interface, `2`; a clean leaf in the same index stays `exact`.

Go integration 182/182, all scope-resolution units 1803 passing, tsc clean.

## Follow-up, not in this PR

Go publishes `api/go1*.txt` — every exported stdlib symbol including full interface method sets, generated and enforced by the Go release process. Consuming it would turn "does `MyType` implement `io.Reader`" from undecidable into decided, shrinking the unknown set to genuine third-party interfaces. Complementary to this change, not a replacement.

body:
Fixes #2907.

Both problems in the issue reproduce on `main` (verified at 135bcae03 by driving the real `generateAIContextFiles` against throwaway git repos).

## Problem 1 — the injected block churns tracked files

`AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md` are the agent guides teams commit, and the block carries live counts. Any code change moves them, so every reindex rewrote a tracked file:

```
-This project is indexed by GitNexus as **Demo** (5384 symbols, 10483 relationships, 281 execution flows)...
+This project is indexed by GitNexus as **Demo** (5385 symbols, 10483 relationships, 281 execution flows)...
```

**The write is now skipped when the volatile counts are the only delta.** Counts are substituted with placeholders rather than deleted before the comparison, so `--no-stats` *removing* the parenthetical is still a material change that writes through — only a numbers-only difference is suppressed. The verbose path and the `gitnexus:keep` path share the rule; a project rename, a template change, or a `base_ref` change still rewrites exactly as before. Live counts stay available from `gitnexus status` and `gitnexus://repo/{name}/context`, which is where the issue suggested they belong.

Two smaller churn sources found while reproducing, fixed here too:

- The file was **created** without a trailing newline while every update path writes `.trim() + '\n'`. So the analyze right after committing a freshly created `AGENTS.md` dirtied it at unchanged counts, purely to append that newline.
- `--no-stats` left the per-cluster `(N symbols)` counts in the skills table — as volatile as the header parenthetical the flag exists to remove, and reachable via `analyze --skills --no-stats`.

## Problem 2 — the stale-index nudge recommends the invasive variant

`formatAnalyzeCommand()` returned a bare `gitnexus analyze`, so an agent following the nudge verbatim reindexed with the doc-rewriting flags. It now takes `indexOnly`, and every routine-reindex message names `--index-only`:

- `gitnexus/hooks/claude/gitnexus-hook.cjs` (+ the byte-identical plugin copy)
- `gitnexus/hooks/antigravity/gitnexus-antigravity-hook.cjs`
- the injected `> Index stale?` line in `ai-context.ts`
- `re_index:` in the MCP context resource (`resources.ts`) — a fourth site the issue did not name

Full `analyze` stays the documented way to refresh the docs and skills. Both `resolve-analyze-cmd.cjs` copies remain byte-identical (enforced by `resolve-invocation.test.ts`).

## Tests

- count-only reindex leaves both files **byte-identical** and reports `preserved`
- a rename still rewrites; `--no-stats` still strips the parenthetical from an already-injected block
- created files end with a trailing newline
- keep-marker blocks follow the same rule (preserved on counts, updated on rename)
- `--no-stats` drops the per-cluster count
- `formatAnalyzeCommand({ indexOnly: true })` → `analyze --index-only [--embeddings]`

Existing keep-path tests were seeded with a stale project *name* so they still exercise a real write (CRLF handling, custom-prose preservation) now that a counts-only delta is a no-op.

`npx tsc --noEmit`, eslint and the touched unit + integration suites pass locally (207 passed / 2 skipped across the 7 affected files).

title: fix(storage): strip credentials from remote URLs before they are persisted (#2914)
body:
Fixes #2914.

## Problem

`getRemoteUrl` returns `git config --get remote.origin.url` verbatim. When the checkout was configured with an HTTPS token remote (`https://x-access-token:<token>@github.com/owner/repo`, the shape CI checkouts and credential helpers produce), that string is written to `~/.gitnexus/registry.json` and to the per-repo meta, and MCP `list_repos` returns it unchanged. Repository discovery doubles as credential disclosure.

Reproduced on `main` (`d3687259d`) with a fake credential:

```
getRemoteUrl        = https://x-access-token:example-secret@github.com/example/project
registry.json       contains the secret
listRegisteredRepos = {"remoteUrl":"https://x-access-token:example-secret@github.com/..."}
```

A second, smaller bug fell out of the same path: the existing host lower-casing regex treats `user:pass@host` as one host span, so a mixed case token was persisted lower cased (`ExAmPle-SECRET` became `example-secret`).

## Fix

One helper, applied at three edges:

* `stripUrlCredentials(url)` removes `user[:password]@` userinfo from http(s) URLs. `ssh://git@host/...` and SCP like `git@host:owner/repo` are deliberately untouched, that is an SSH user name rather than a secret, and rewriting it would repoint the sibling clone fingerprint (#2054) for every already registered repo. The match is bounded by the authority and greedy to the last `@` in it, so a password containing `@` is removed whole.
* `getRemoteUrl` strips at capture, before the host lower-casing, so nothing credentialed is ever written and the token case is no longer mangled.
* The registry sanitizes on read and on write. Capture time stripping only covers what this version writes, so a `registry.json` written by an older version, or a legacy per-repo meta that a re-register copies forward, is neither emitted by `list_repos` nor rewritten back to disk with the credential still in it.

Also stripped from the mismatch error in `assertRemoteMatchesRequestedUrl`, which is echoed to API callers and to the server log.

Sanitized values compare equal to a freshly captured remote on both sides, so sibling matching, drift checks, `--name` inference and group sync behave exactly as before.

## Acceptance criteria

* Sanitize HTTPS remote URLs before registry persistence: yes, at capture and at the write edge.
* Sanitize legacy registry values before any API or MCP output: yes, at the read edge.
* Preserve normal HTTPS, SSH and SCP like remote URL behaviour: yes, covered by tests.
* Regression coverage with an obviously fake credential: 9 new tests, all use `ExAmPle-FAKE-SECRET`.
* Focused unit tests and TypeScript compilation verified.

## Tests

`gitnexus/test/unit/git-utils.test.ts` (5 new)
* HTTPS userinfo and username only forms are stripped at capture.
* Plain HTTPS, `ssh://git@...`, SCP like and an `@` inside the path are untouched.
* A password containing `@` is removed whole, no tail left behind.
* A credentialed clone and a clean clone of the same repo still fingerprint identically.

`gitnexus/test/unit/repo-manager.test.ts` (4 new)
* A legacy on-disk entry is sanitized before `listRegisteredRepos` returns it.
* A credentialed `meta.remoteUrl` never reaches `registry.json`.
* A legacy entry that this run does not touch is scrubbed, not dropped, when another repo registers.
* Sibling matching still holds after sanitization.

All 9 fail on `main` and pass here. `npx tsc --noEmit` is clean, and the surrounding registry, git util, git clone, remove and skip-git suites pass (252 tests).

## Note

The credential also sits in the repo's own `.git/config`, which is where it came from, and a legacy `.gitnexus/gitnexus.json` written before this change keeps its copy until the next analyze. Neither is a new exposure and neither is read back out to an API or MCP surface, so this PR does not rewrite them. The propagation path into the global registry and `list_repos` is what is closed here.

title: fix(scope-resolution): resolve a package whose directory name repeats higher in the path (#2881)
body:
Fixes #2881.

Four commits. The first fixes the reported Kotlin shape; the second finds the same rule live in
Java, Go and C# and removes it there too; the third is an output-identical optimization of the
Kotlin index; the fourth applies a four-lens review of the first three. A fifth group of commits
responds to PR review — see [Review response](#review-response).

## The bug

`getKotlinFileIndex` builds its `dirChildren` buckets under two guards, both inherited from the
pre-index per-import scan rather than from anything Kotlin requires:

```ts
if (norm.startsWith(`${suffix}/`)) continue;
if (norm.indexOf(`/${suffix}/`) === dir.length - suffix.length - 1) { ... }
```

`suffix` is `dir.slice(i + 1)` taken at each `/`, so `dir` ends with `/suffix` **by construction** —
the file always is a direct child of a directory named `suffix`. Both guards therefore only ever
drop legitimate buckets, and each drops a different shape:

| file | import | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `data/src/main/kotlin/com/example/data/Repo.kt` | `data.helper` | `null` | fans out |
| `top/data/mid/data/Repo.kt` | `data.helper` | `null` | fans out |
| `data/src/main/kotlin/com/example/data/Repo.kt` | `data.*` | `null` | resolves |
| `src/main/kotlin/com/example/data/Repo.kt` (control) | `data.helper` | fans out | unchanged |

The issue names the `startsWith` shape. The `indexOf` first-occurrence check is a **second,
independent** mechanism that the issue's example never reaches, because `startsWith` fires first and
short-circuits it. A fix that drops only `startsWith` leaves every mid-path repeat broken; there is
a gate control for exactly that below.

Only the fan-out tier was affected. `data.Repo` answers from `suffixByStem`, which carries no such
guard, which is why the blast radius looked narrow enough for #2872 to preserve rather than change
inside a performance PR.

## The fix

Both guards are deleted; the loop is now a bare per-component-suffix insert.

The rule stays "the parent directory is named `s`", not "`s` appears somewhere in the path" —
`top/data/mid/Repo.kt` is still not a child of `data`, and a case pins that so the fix cannot be
widened by accident.

**The same rule was live in three more places, and this PR removes it from all of them.** #2881 was
reported against Kotlin, but the rule was never Kotlin's — it is what the pre-index per-import scan
happened to compute, and every resolver built to reproduce that scan inherited it. Verified by
running the real resolvers, not by reading:

```
java   data/src/main/java/com/example/data/Repo.java  `import data.*`   => null
java   top/data/mid/data/Repo.java                    `import data.*`   => null
csharp Models/src/App/Models/User.cs                  `using Models;`   => null
csharp a/Models/b/Models/User.cs                      `using Models;`   => null
go     a/internal/auth/b/internal/auth/svc.go   import "internal/auth"  => null
```

Controls (`top/data/Repo.java`, `a/b/internal/auth/svc.go`) resolve, so this is the rule firing
rather than an unrelated miss.

Four sites, all reduced to "the file's parent directory ends with the queried path":
`import-resolvers/package-dir-index.ts` `matchingDirs` (Go, Java, C# without csproj),
`import-resolvers/csharp.ts` `matchingDirPositions` (csproj step 3), `csharp.ts` csproj step 2, and
the legacy `go.ts` scan the parity harness copies as its spec. Kotlin's own `dirChildren` is the
fifth.

Two things worth reviewer attention:

- **The two C# csproj sites must move together.** Fixing only step 3 makes `Lib.Models` return step
  3's superset instead of step 2's segment-aligned answer.
- **Step 2's empty-`dirPrefix` case must keep `indexOf`.** Its needle is a bare `/`, and step 3
  answers that query from `singleSegmentDirs` ("exactly one directory deep"), which only the first
  occurrence expresses. Without the guard, step 2 accepts every `.cs` in any directory and diverges
  from step 3 — caught as a real failure in `csharp-csproj-parity.test.ts`, not hypothesised.

**Risk is not symmetric.** Go's consumer is a fan-out list and the finalize pass materializes one
`IMPORTS` edge per element, so widening only *adds* edges. Java and C#-without-csproj commit to a
single file through `firstFileDirectlyInPkgDir` with no downstream filter, so a widened bucket can
also change which file an already-resolving import binds to — Java's collide fingerprints moved
while its resolved count did not, which is exactly that.

**Go was not gated at all, and the corpus had to change.** Its nested slice repeated only the last
segment (`src/pkg{d}/internal/pkg{d}`) while a Go query addresses the whole package path, so the
directory never ended with the query and the rule was never reached — every Go arm sat unchanged
through the resolver fix. Shipping like that would have re-baselined C# and Java for a change Go
received silently. The corpus now repeats the shape at the granularity Go queries. C# and Java hit
the same collide-arm trap Kotlin did, and the same-workload assertion caught both.

The three parity harnesses keep verbatim copies of the pre-change scans as their specification, so
each copy moved with the resolver.

## Two claims earlier revisions of this description got wrong

Both were disproved in review. They are corrected here rather than quietly dropped, because each one
was load-bearing in the original argument for the change.

### 1. "A bucket that is too wide is filtered downstream" — false for File→File `IMPORTS` edges

The `localDefs` filter of #1759 is **def-level only**. It decides `targetDefId` / `BindingRef`; it
never removes a candidate file.

`gitnexus-shared/src/scope-resolution/finalize-algorithm.ts:395` mints **one draft per candidate**,
each keeping its own `targetFile`:

```ts
const targetFiles = Array.isArray(targetFile) ? targetFile : [targetFile];
```

A draft whose imported name is not exported by its candidate never finalizes, and the SCC sweep then
stamps it `{ ...draft.base, linkStatus: 'unresolved' }` — `draft.base` still carries the non-null
`targetFile`. The one File→File filter downstream,
`gitnexus/src/core/ingestion/scope-resolution/graph-bridge/imports-to-edges.ts:35-36`, tests only:

```ts
if (edge.targetFile === null) continue;
if (edge.targetFile === sourceFile) continue;
```

It never reads `linkStatus`, and emits at `confidence: 1.0`.

**So every extra bucket member becomes an unconditional File→File `IMPORTS` edge.** Measured: one
`import data.load` on an Android-style layout goes from 5 edges to 6, the added one `unresolved`.
That is a real cost, and it is paid deliberately — a *missing* bucket is an edge nothing later can
recover, while a wide one is a precision loss on an edge type that is already a coarse
file-level summary. But "filtered downstream" was not true, and the design question it was papering
over is filed separately rather than answered here.

### 2. "Zero results were dropped" — true of bucket membership, not of the resolver's output

Bucket membership is monotone by construction: removing a `continue` can only add members, and the
record-level diff confirms zero buckets lost one. That is what the sentence was measuring, and it
still holds.

It does not follow that no *answer* was lost, because the tiers are a cascade and a newly non-empty
tier 3 preempts tier 4. Measured on the real resolver, BASE `0fa547ccd` against HEAD:

```
files   ['data/src/main/kotlin/com/example/data/Repo.kt', 'common/helper.kt']
import  data.helper
BASE    "common/helper.kt"                                  (tier 4, bound)
HEAD    ["data/src/main/kotlin/com/example/data/Repo.kt"]   (tier 3, fans out)
```

The tier-4 progressive-prefix-strip answer `common/helper.kt` is gone, and the file that replaces it
need not export `helper` at all. The mid-path variant behaves the same way
(`['top/data/mid/data/Repo.kt', 'common/helper.kt']` → `"common/helper.kt"` becomes
`["top/data/mid/data/Repo.kt"]`).

The original census classified the 235 moved records by null-ness (54 `null` → resolved, 149
reselections, 32 wider fan-outs), a taxonomy that is entirely shape-preserving and therefore has no
bucket for this class at all. Re-run with a shape classifier, the `string → array` count over this
bench's corpus is:

**Zero — and the zero is the finding, not a reprieve.**

The shape reproduces by hand in both iteration orders, and this bench's own generator at 4000
repositories (~198 600 distinct records) hits it 4–12 times per seed — an expectation of about *one*
over this corpus's 19 968. So the fingerprint does not gate this class, which is the same blindness
the go arm carried until this branch widened its corpus: a gate cannot catch a shape its corpus
cannot express. Adding a case is a deliberate fingerprint move and belongs in its own change, so the
class is pinned by a unit test instead (`kotlin-import-target-parity.test.ts`, "tier 3 preempts
tier 4").

The full classification behind the 235 records now lives in `_provenance`: 149 `string → string`,
38 `null → string`, 16 `null → array`, 32 `array` grew, and zero of every other transition. The old
54/149/32 taxonomy reappears exactly (38 + 16 = 54), and its structural claims check out directly —
all 32 growths are order-preserving supersets, no bucket lost a member, and all 149 reselections keep
a parent directory whose name is a segment of the import.

This is a defensible trade — tier 4 is a last-resort heuristic and tier 3 is directory evidence —
but it is a trade, not a free widening, and the earlier wording said otherwise.

## Re-baselining, and what the drift actually is

Both Kotlin benches gate on a correctness fingerprint that says, in the file, never to re-baseline it
to make CI green. This change re-baselines them on purpose. The drift was measured, not accepted: the
corpus was dumped from the pre-fix and post-fix resolvers and diffed record by record.

**`bench/kotlin-import-target`** — 235 of 19968 distinct records moved:

- 54 `null` → resolved. This is the fix, and it is exactly the `+54` in `non_null` (13256 → 13310).
- 149 single answers that changed within a now-larger bucket, where the first-child tier picks a
  different member.
- 32 fan-out arrays that gained entries.
- **Zero** buckets lost a member, and in all 149 reselections the new answer's parent directory is
  the queried package segment. (What that does *not* say is covered in correction 2 above.)

The corpus itself is untouched, so `cases` is unchanged at 20106 — the new fingerprint covers the
same surface as the value it replaces.

**`bench/import-target`** — **20 fingerprints moved, across four languages**, and two of them needed a
corpus edit beside the new numbers:

| language | arms | `resolved` small → | `resolved` large → |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| kotlin | small, large, deep, collide, collide_large | 1100 → 1153 | 4456 → 4681 |
| java | small, large, deep, collide, collide_large | 1100 → 1153 | 4456 → 4681 |
| go | small, large, deep, collide, collide_large | 979 → 1153 | 4064 → 4681 |
| csharp | small, large, deep, collide, collide_large | 979 → 1153 | 4064 → 4681 |

`csharp_csproj` is unchanged at 979 / 4064.

Each collide arm asserts that it resolves exactly as many imports as its `small` arm, so the two time
the same workload. Kotlin's, Java's and C#'s `d % 7` slices each imported a namespace that exists
nowhere (`com.example.vendor{d}`, `com.svc{d}.vendor`, `App.Src{d}.Vendor`), purely to mirror the
unique arm's nested-slice **miss**. With that slice now resolving, leaving the mirrors alone would
have left collide at 1100 or 979 against small's 1153. The invariant assertion is what caught all
three; each slice now uses the same spelling as the rest of its arm, which is why Kotlin's
`distinct_outcomes` falls (2775 → 2744, 11087 → 10961): one shared target instead of one per `d`.

## Gate controls, re-run against the new baseline

The baseline is only worth having if a plausible regression still moves it. All values are against
the current baseline (guards removed + per-directory key memo + bucket compaction):

| mutation | fingerprint | `non_null` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| half fix — drop `startsWith`, keep `indexOf` | `836977b83bf0…` | 13310 → 13282 |
| skip the `dirChildren` suffix loop above depth 8 | `41bb550b76d4…` | 13310 → 12800 |
| cap a `dirChildren` bucket at 17 entries | `a7681945b752…` | unchanged — fingerprint is the only arm that sees it |
| cap `suffixByStem` key depth at 7 | `d24b8a2bd822…` | unchanged |
| key the new `dirKeys` memo on the directory's LAST SEGMENT | `36a4e9dad313…` | 13310 → 13305 |
| corpus-only: drop the competing file from the exact-beats-suffix case | `44df5093ee…` | — |

The half fix is the one this change makes newly plausible, and it is caught. The bucket cap is
re-run *after* the compaction pass, since compaction rewrites those same buckets.

## Commit 3 — two measured optimizations, one measured rejection

| | effect | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| per-directory key memo | **−18.4% to −21.7%** build, 0 retained | ship |
| bucket compaction on freeze | **−5 397 768 B, −11.20%** retained | ship |
| merging the two build loops | −0.10% / +0.23% / +0.40% — inside a −2.3%/+3.1% noise floor | **dropped** |

The loop merge was implemented and benchmarked before being dropped: the scan it deletes is exactly
the scan the memo makes rare. Only its provably free half is kept (`stem.lastIndexOf` for
`norm.lastIndexOf`).

Compaction skips `length === 1` deliberately — a bucket that never grew is already exact, and on
single-file packages the unguarded form costs 31% of the build to save zero bytes.

**Neither optimization is visible to the correctness fingerprint, which is the point and also the
risk.** The fingerprint observes the index only through the four resolver tiers, so a key-order move
no corpus query reaches would survive it. `fingerprint`, `cases` and `non_null` are unchanged by this
commit.

> **Corrected in review.** This section previously claimed correctness rested on "a structural
> comparison of all three maps … over 1234 corpora in both iteration orders: 14 808 comparisons, zero
> failures". That probe was a throwaway and was never committed — no such differential exists in the
> tree, and the same sentence had also been left standing in `_gate_controls`. Both are now replaced
> by what actually ships, with its limits measured: see the review response below.

## Rejected with measurement: reusing the shared index

`package-dir-index.ts` is the obvious consolidation target once the rule is gone, and it is
**output-identical** — 0 divergences over 107 948 answers, byte-identical fingerprint — for **26.2%
less memory** (12.18 MiB at 32 000 files). It is not taken, because it costs 13.5× per first-child
query, 409× per fan-out, and **8114× on `import data.*` at 200 matching directories** — the exact
shape #2881 exists for — for 3.1×–5.7× end to end.

`bench/kotlin-import-target` passes that swap at 1.37×–1.50×. Its scaling corpus gives every module a
unique package leaf, so it structurally cannot see a cost that grows with the number of directories
sharing a queried segment. That blind spot is now written into `_blind_spot` with the measurements,
the memory the trade would buy, and the corpus arm that already exists to gate it
(`bench/import-target`'s kotlin `collide`, where the swap scores 3.465 against a 1.8 budget).

## Commit 4 — a four-lens review of the first three, applied

Correctness, simplification, reuse/altitude and gate-integrity passes. **Correctness found no defect
in the shipped resolvers** — the `endsWith` rewrites, the C# empty-prefix guard, the memo's purity,
the `stem`-vs-`norm` derivation, the Map re-`set` during iteration and Go's `substring` arithmetic
were each attacked with running code and each held. Everything applied is a gap in what the change
*asserts, measures or claims*.

**Two behaviour changes were shipping ungated.**

- `import-resolvers/go.ts` had no test at all, and the shared bench drives Go's *indexed* leg rather
  than this one — a revert was caught by nothing. New
  `test/unit/import-resolvers/go-package-resolve.test.ts` pins the rule and, more usefully, pins that
  Go's two independent legs agree on it. They disagreed before #2881.
- The memo and the compaction are output-identical, so no fingerprint sees them and reverting either
  leaves both benches green. New `test/unit/scope-resolution/kotlin/kotlin-index-internals.test.ts`
  narrows that gap. The comment claiming this was already "asserted structurally" pointed at nothing
  in the repo — a real false claim. Review then established that the replacement does not close the
  gap either, and the honest bounds are now recorded in the test's own header: a **mis-keyed** memo
  is caught, a **deleted** one is not (it is output-identical by construction), and the compaction is
  invisible to every assertion because a JS array's backing-store capacity has no reflective surface.
  The compaction is instead gated by a bench heap ceiling, added in the review response.

**Gates.**

- Six ratio budgets had gone slack — the measurements they bound got faster and the numbers were left
  alone. Tightened to hold their original headroom: `bench/import-target` `depth_budget` kotlin
  3.4 → 2.8, go 1.6 → 1.4, csharp 2.2 → 2.0, java 2.2 → 2.1; `collide_scaling_budget` kotlin
  1.8 → 1.65, go 5.5 → 5.1. Absolute ms ceilings deliberately untouched: those carry
  runner-contention headroom, and a ratio is runner-speed-invariant where a millisecond is not.
- **The `csharp_csproj` heap re-baseline is reverted.** Base and branch both measure ~73.10e6, three
  runs each — the recorded `73703384` was never reproducible, and re-recording it would have dropped
  that language's derived floor 0.8% for no reason belonging to this change. `heap_reading_bytes`
  stays at `73703384`.
- Kotlin's collide arm was blind to the rule it had been re-baselined for: a full revert of the
  Kotlin guards left both its fingerprints unmoved. Deepened so it repeats the whole queried path;
  exactly two fingerprints moved. **The same deepening on the Java and Kotlin unique arms was
  measured and reverted** — ten more fingerprints, Java's heap reading up 43%, and no coverage
  gained, because progressive stripping lands those queries on the same file either way.

**Claims that were wrong, now corrected.** `package-dir-index.ts` said "the four resolvers agree
again" — it is six, and the sixth is the evidence: `jvm.ts` has answered the same question with
`lastIndexOf` since #488, so before this change Java's and Kotlin's two resolution hooks disagreed
about what a package contains. The `uniqueDir` docblock claimed the last segment *is* the query
granularity for C#/Java/Kotlin; they query the whole dotted path first, which is why the
partial-revert control fires on the Go arm alone. Three parity harnesses described themselves as
verbatim copies of the pre-change implementations after this branch edited them. And `measure.mjs`
plus `_heap_bound_note` still counted nine bounded languages where `HEAP_BOUNDED` derives to three —
this branch had dutifully updated a Kotlin bound inside a list no gate reads.

**Simplification.** `go.ts` states the predicate as ends-with like its three siblings. C# csproj step
2's direct-child filter is dead for a non-empty prefix (zero rejections over 12 008 pairs) and only
the empty-prefix case remains. `addChild` had one call site left and is inlined; the duplicated V8
byte accounting now lives only in the baselines note; four copies of one ternary in the csproj
harness collapse onto a hoisted `dirTrail`.

Both baselines are also re-serialized to preserve each note's original escaping, undoing ~20 KB of
no-op churn an earlier revision of this branch introduced by round-tripping the JSON.

## Two heap gates moved with the code

Neither is required to make CI green — both pass either way — but leaving them would have let a gate
drift.

- **kotlin heap baseline, twice.** `heap_reading_bytes` and `heap_ceiling_bytes` re-recorded together
  each time, as `_heap_reading_note` requires. First the resolver fix: 48 073 096 → 48 200 224 bytes
  (+0.264%). Then commit 3's bucket compaction: 48 200 224 → **42 802 456** (−11.20%), with the
  ceiling re-derived alongside it. (The ceiling is revisited again in the review response below —
  it is the one entry in that file that has to gate a size *reduction* being preserved rather than a
  footprint not growing, so the file-wide 1.5× convention is the wrong shape for it.) The note
  records *why* the first number is small,
  so it is not misread as evidence the change is cheap: the heap corpus uses `HEAP_PAD = 8`, which
  prefixes every path with `d0/…/d7/`, so no path can begin with a suffix of its own directory and
  the leading-segment half of the old rule is structurally invisible to that arm. Read +0.264% as the
  arm's ceiling on the effect, not the effect.
- **`bench/kotlin-import-target` `depth_budget` 2.4 → 2.2 → 2.0.** Two per-depth changes, two moves.
  Guard removal deleted two string comparisons per directory component and took the depth band from
  1.44–1.51 to 1.27–1.40; the per-directory key memo turned the whole component walk from
  once-per-file into once-per-directory and took it to 1.20–1.26. The budget moved with the band both
  times, holding the ~1.6× headroom over the band's top that 2.4 expressed against the original; left
  at 2.4 it would quietly have become 1.9×. Explicitly *not* tightened far enough to fail a revert of
  this PR — a revert scores ~1.5 and passes, and that is correct: a revert restores a resolution bug,
  which is the fingerprint's job, not a timing arm's.

## What the widening does and does not guarantee

Tier 3 hands the finalize pass a candidate list, and the finalize pass picks the file whose
`localDefs` export the imported name (#1759) **for the purpose of `targetDefId`**. It does not drop
the other candidates, and File→File `IMPORTS` emission does not consult the result — see correction 1.

The tier-1 first-child fallback is not filtered at all: it commits to `children[0]`, and that is
where most of the change lands — 149 of the 235 moved records are a different first child against 32
wider arrays. Both are intended. Keeping a narrower bucket for the first-child tier alone would hold
its answers byte-identical, but it would also leave `import data.*` — a wildcard, which strips to
`data` and lands on exactly that tier — resolving to null on the very shape this fixes, so there is no
version of the bucket that is right for one consumer and wrong for the other.

Since #2881 the first child can be an *earlier* file than the pre-index scan returned, never a later
one: the guards that fell take members away from no bucket, so a bucket only ever gains, and a gained
member lands wherever set iteration puts it.

## Review response

Four commits — `0bc8ede47`, `d1e70eca5`, `3d2ad2189`, `465256b61` — answer a two-engine review of
this branch. **Nothing about the fix itself changed**: the resolvers behave identically and the
correctness fingerprint `d91110bee389…` is unmoved. What changed is what the branch *asserts*, plus
the gaps the review found in what watches it.

**Three shipped claims were false and are corrected.** Two of them were load-bearing.

1. *"Widening is filtered downstream for tier 3"* — corrected above as correction 1. No filtering is
   added here; whether an unresolved candidate should produce that edge at all is a graph-bridge
   design question, filed separately.
2. *"`import-resolvers/jvm.ts` … it is live, wired as `importResolver`"* — wired, but never read.
   `provider.importResolver` is consumed at exactly two lines, both inside
   `import-target-adapter.ts`, whose exports have no importer outside their own unit test — while its
   docblock claims it is threaded through `finalizeScopeModel`, and the one production caller of
   `finalizeScopeModel` does not pass it. That makes `jvm.ts` evidence about how the predicate was
   *written*, not about live behaviour, and it means `resolveGoPackage` has no production caller
   either. The argument that the rule was accidental survives on the pre-index-scan derivation.
3. *"…correctness rests on a structural comparison … over 1234 corpora"* — no such probe exists in
   the tree. `_gate_controls` now names the test that does exist, lists what it actually pins, and
   states that key insertion order is unasserted by design because `dirChildren` is only read via
   `.get(key)`.

**Three gates were missing and now exist.**

- The bucket compaction had none anywhere: deleting `bucket.slice()` moved no fingerprint, no count
  and no test — only retained heap, +12.57%. Note the direction, which is why this was missed —
  compaction *reclaims*, so losing it makes the reading **grow**, and no floor can see that.
  `heap_ceiling_bytes.kotlin` tightens 64 203 684 → 46 000 000, with the band derived from first
  principles (~61 000 buckets × 11 spare slots at Node 22's 1→19 growth step) so it can be
  re-checked rather than trusted.
- None of the 149 first-child reselections was pinned, because every widened-shape test used a
  one-file corpus — the tier that commits to `children[0]` unfiltered had no test that could see
  which file it commits to. Kotlin and Java now pin the choice absolutely, in both insertion orders.
- The C# empty-`dirPrefix` filter this branch calls load-bearing could be deleted with the whole
  1869-test suite green. It has an arm now, verified to fail with the guard removed and pass with it
  restored.

**One performance regression this branch introduced is undone.** `resolveGoPackage`'s rewrite left
the `'/' + path` cons that the old `includes` guard used to short-circuit, and the first `endsWith`
forces V8 to flatten it once per file — 2.5× slower per file than the code it replaced. Working on
the raw path with an explicit start index is 4.8× faster than that and 1.78× faster than the pre-PR
code. Separately, the two surviving `endsWith` membership tests each minted a decorated copy of the
directory per candidate, and the decoration cancels algebraically — verified over 132 496 string
pairs with 0 divergences and the match count reported beside it, because two predicates that agree on
`false` everywhere also show 0 divergences. Worth 3.96× on `matchingDirs`.

**Two review findings did not survive re-measurement and are recorded as retracted**, rather than
quietly dropped:

- *"the 2-argument `endsWith` overload leaves V8's fast path, 20×"* — its baseline was a 1-argument
  call that early-exited on the length precheck. On identical work the three forms land together:
  8.15 ns one-arg, 8.55 ns two-arg, 8.54 ns `startsWith`.
- *"unsorted `glob` order reaches the resolver, so two machines can produce different edges"* — glob
  is unsorted, but `filesystem-walker.ts` canonicalizes at the scan boundary ("Filesystem/glob
  traversal order is not stable … Canonicalize once"), pinned by `filesystem-walker-order.test.ts`.

**Also corrected:** the C# `getDirMap` derivation was wrong in both directions (`src/X.cs` satisfies
the stated rule and emits no empty key; `a//X.cs` violates it and does) though its conclusion stands;
step 2's suppression of step 3's unanchored leg is now stated; `measure.mjs` loses a paragraph that
contradicted the paragraph below it and the code, where acting on it would resolve the `csproj` arm
to zero; V8's array growth steps were re-measured (1 → 19 → 46 → 86, growing at lengths 2/20/47/87,
not 1 → 17 → 41, which under-counted the slack at 40 files by 6×); `SuffixIndex.getFilesInDir` states
the segment-alignment its callers now rely on; and `finalize-algorithm.ts` annotates `targetFiles`
`readonly` so `Array.isArray`'s `any[]` predicate can no longer widen a frozen cached bucket into
something `.sort()` compiles against.

**Measured while gating the compaction, and recorded rather than fixed:** the `csharp` collide arm is
*not* blind to #2881 — its fingerprint already moves — but **both `csharp_csproj` arms are**, because
`getFilesInDir` keys on segment-aligned directory suffixes and neither nested slice is one. Closing
that needs a corpus redesign plus four re-baselines.

Verification for these commits: `npx tsc --noEmit` clean in both packages; `npx vitest run
test/unit/import-resolvers test/unit/scope-resolution` → 117 files, **1880** tests (11 added);
`test/integration/{kotlin,csharp,java}-import-index-reuse` → 11 tests; both bench `--check` gates
PASS with `fingerprint d91110bee389…`, `cases 20106`, `non_null 13310` unchanged.

## Filed, not fixed here

- **#2931** — `languages/swift/target-grouping.ts:70` carries the same first-occurrence mechanism and
  reproduces (`vendor/SubModules/Core/shim/Modules/Core/Thing.swift` misses target `Core`). It is a
  verbatim-duplicate module under a byte-identical-with-legacy constraint, with three consumers behind
  a first-target-wins `break`, so it needs its own fixtures.
- **Two more sites of the same defect class, on id parsing rather than paths** —
  `scope-resolution/passes/return-shape-members.ts:83` (false negative) and
  `passes/unique-name-properties.ts:304` (false positives *and* a false negative — it fires at the
  pass's first tier, the one whose comment says nothing can outrank it). Both reproduce; issues to be
  filed.
- **The dormant-resolver question** — `provider.importResolver` is read at exactly two lines, both
  inside `import-target-adapter.ts`, and that module has no importer outside its own unit test. So
  `jvm.ts`'s `resolveJvmWildcard` and `import-resolvers/go.ts`'s `resolveGoPackage` have no production
  caller. Delete or wire is a decision this PR should not make, and `package-dir-index.ts` now says so
  where it used to claim `jvm.ts` was live.
- **The design question behind correction 1** — should a candidate that does not export the imported
  symbol produce a File→File `IMPORTS` edge at `confidence: 1.0`? This PR only corrects the comment
  that said it did not.

## Verification

Commands, and what each one is actually asserting:

| command | asserts |
| --- | --- |
| `npx vitest run test/unit/scope-resolution test/unit/import-resolvers` | the four parity harnesses (their verbatim pre-change copies moved with the resolvers), plus the two new files below |
| `npx vitest run test/integration/kotlin-import-index-reuse.test.ts` | the per-file-set memo is still built once per run, not once per import |
| `node bench/kotlin-import-target/measure.mjs --check` | `fingerprint d91110bee389…`, `cases 20106`, `non_null 13310`; `scaling_budget 1.6`, `depth_budget 2.0`, `small_ms_ceiling 40` |
| `node bench/import-target/measure.mjs --check` | 20 re-baselined fingerprints + counts per arm per language, the six tightened ratio budgets, the kotlin heap reading/ceiling pair, and the `--check` inventory arm reconciling `LANG_REGISTRY` against `SCOPE_RESOLVERS` in both directions |
| `npx tsc --noEmit` | — |

New test files in commit 4:

  pins the rule and pins that Go's two independent legs agree on it.

  compaction directly, since no fingerprint can see either.

title: fix(mcp): stop scaling the detect_changes query with the diff's hunk count (#2915)
body:
Fixes #2915.

## Problem

`detect_changes` built one OR'd condition pair per diff hunk into a single `WHERE` clause, one query per changed file:

```js
const overlapConditions = fileDiff.hunks
  .map((_, i) => `(n.startLine <= $hunkEnd${i} AND n.endLine >= $hunkStart${i})`)
  .join(' OR ');
```

A machine generated file (a cache JSON, a lockfile, a golden fixture) diffs at thousands of hunks with `-U0`, and the expression tree that produces is deep enough to overflow LadybugDB's recursive evaluator copy on a TaskScheduler worker thread.

Reproduced on `main` with `@ladybugdb/core` 0.19.1. On Linux the engine gets an 8 MB thread stack, so I ran it with macOS sized stacks (`ulimit -s 512`, glibc uses RLIMIT_STACK for pthread defaults) and the threshold lands on the reporter's numbers:

| hunks | exit |
|-------|------|
| 1000 / 2000 / 2500 | 0 |
| 3333 | 139 (SIGSEGV) |
| 4000 / 5000 | 139 |

A one hunk diff under the same `ulimit` exits 0, so the crash follows the hunk count, not the stack limit. On a roomier stack the same query does not crash but goes quadratic (5,000 hunks 12s, 10,000 hunks 65s, 20,000 over 2 minutes), tripping the 30s query timeout. That path is worse than the crash: the failure is swallowed, the result comes back `partial: true` with `changed_count: 0`, and the CLI printed `No changes detected.` and exited 0 while missing a real edit in the same diff.

## Fix

The overlap test no longer goes into Cypher at all.

* `coalesceHunks(hunks)` sorts a file's hunks and merges only the ones that overlap or abut (`next.startLine <= current.endLine + 1`), so the union covers exactly the lines the raw hunks covered. No widening, no gap heuristic.
* `hunksOverlapRange(coalesced, start, end)` binary searches those disjoint ranges. Matching happens in JS on rows the query returns.
* The per file query became a batched one, with a per file `[lo, hi]` span:

```cypher
UNWIND $bounds AS b
MATCH (n) WHERE (n.filePath = b.path OR n.filePath ENDS WITH b.suffix)
  AND NOT n.id STARTS WITH 'BasicBlock:'
  AND n.startLine IS NOT NULL AND n.endLine IS NOT NULL
  AND n.startLine <= b.hi AND n.endLine >= b.lo
RETURN b.path AS diffPath, n.id AS id, ...
```

Query text and parameters are now identical whether a file changed in 1 place or 100,000. The same repro repo, still under `ulimit -s 512`, maps a 100,001 hunk diff in 2.1s.

The span matters on its own: without it the query returned every symbol of every changed file and filtered them in JS. Measured on a 25k node index, 400 file batch: **546ms / 13,870 rows before, 84ms / 1,555 after**, with the kept set verified identical. Depth stays constant (two comparisons per file, not per hunk), so this cannot revive the crash, and `hunksOverlapRange` still rejects symbols landing in the gaps between hunks. The struct list parameter was probed against `@ladybugdb/core` 0.18.3 and 0.19.1 before the rewrite (the index subscript form `$paths[i]` does not parse).

Batches run a few at a time. `executeParameterized` checks a connection out of the 8 connection per repo pool for the duration of a query, so parallel calls never share one, which is why ~15 other queries in this file already run under `Promise.all`. `allSettled`, so one failed batch degrades the result to `partial` instead of discarding the batches that succeeded beside it.

## Three more bugs in the same path

**Line base.** Graph rows are 0-based (#2377) and git hunk lines are 1-based, and the overlap compared them raw. Every symbol was shifted one line up, so an edit to a symbol's last line reported nothing changed. On the shipped build, for a two line function:

```
edit line 1 (def hello():)  -> Changes: 1 files, 1 symbols
edit line 2 (return 42)     -> No changes detected.
```

Both edits are inside `hello`. Grouping and the conversion now happen once in `coalesceHunksByPath`, at the parse boundary: `parseDiffHunks` stays faithful to git, consumers compare graph native values.

**Path matching.** `ENDS WITH` is a plain string suffix, so a diff touching `lib/a.py` also matched an indexed `src/mylib/a.py` and reported a symbol from a file the diff never touched. Proven against a real index:

```
bare ENDS WITH  ["a@lib/a.py","b@src/mylib/a.py"]
anchored        ["a@lib/a.py"]
```

The match is anchored on the separator, with an equality arm for a path that is the indexed value. This is the form `explain` already uses.

**Double counting.** One node matched by two changed paths was pushed once per match (169 duplicates in 13,870 rows on a real 400 file diff), and `changed_files` counted a path twice when a diff reported it twice (a rename alongside an edit). Both deduplicated.

## Reporting honesty

`formatDetectChangesResult` never read the `partial` flag the backend sets when a graph query is swallowed (#2283), so a degraded run rendered as a clean pre-commit check. It now prints the note in both branches, and both `partial` and the new `symbols_truncated` are documented in the `detect_changes` tool description, since the MCP client is the main consumer of this gate and was getting them as undocumented raw keys.

The listing is capped at 1,000 symbols with `symbols_truncated: {listed, total}` — a repo wide diff otherwise puts an unbounded array in one MCP payload, where the CLI has `--limit` and an MCP client has nothing. Counts are never capped, so the risk level and the CLI's "... and N more" still see the true total.

## The same shape elsewhere

`detect_changes` was not the only place building query text from a caller sized array. `core/wiki/graph-queries.ts` interpolated a module's whole file list into four `IN [...]` literals. Flat breadth rather than nested depth, but the same unbounded shape, and the one the repo's own `DELETE_FILES_CHUNK_SIZE` precedent already chunks elsewhere. All four are batched now, with the membership arms handled carefully and documented where it happens — in particular `getInterModuleCallEdges` keeps the same batch list in its `NOT` arm, because `NOT null IN [...]` is null and a JS only filter would have started admitting nodes with no `filePath`.

`chunk` / `mapBatches` / `LBUG_QUERY_BATCH_SIZE` now live in `core/lbug/query-batch.ts` with the measured batch size recorded where it is defined, replacing three same valued constants under three names and the hand rolled slice loops in `lbug-adapter.ts`, `embeddings/http-client.ts` and `run-analyze.ts`. No batch size changed.

`toOneBasedLine` joins `toZeroBasedLine` in `ingestion/utils/line-base.ts`, so that module owns both directions, and the four CFG/PDG join sites plus two backend sites call it instead of open coding `+ 1`. It is deliberately not `toDisplayLine`, which is a response boundary converter with an `undefined` passthrough; the `Number.NaN` guards for an absent line are kept verbatim.

## Tests

* `test/unit/detect-changes-hunk-scale.test.ts` — 25 tests. Drives the real `detect_changes` against a real temp git repo with the query layer mocked, so it inspects the exact Cypher the engine would receive: query text identical for a 1 hunk and a 3,000 hunk diff, `bounds` carrying 0-based spans and anchored suffixes, 250 files producing 3 queries rather than 250, the last line edit reported, a symbol one line above the hunk not reported, the dedup, and the listing cap with true counts.
* `test/integration/detect-changes-path-anchoring.test.ts` — the same tool against a real engine, seeded with `lib/a.py` and `src/mylib/a.py`. Fails 3/3 with the un-anchored predicate.
* `test/unit/query-batch.test.ts`, `test/unit/line-base-conversion.test.ts`, `test/unit/wiki-graph-queries-batching.test.ts` — the new helpers, including the wiki batching oracle running the pre-#2915 single query text against the same fixture.

Verified the behaviour tests fail with the old implementation restored. `tsc --noEmit`, eslint and prettier clean. The PDG/CFG/taint/impact suites (96 files, 1,973 tests) pass unchanged, as do the delete/importer/embedding suites whose assertions pin the batch progress and chunk index values.

<!-- gitnexus-pr-summary:v1:start -->

---

### 📝 Summary by GitNexus

## Summary

*A broad, cross-cutting GitNexus change focused on `detect_changes`, with implementation work alongside updates to operational documentation and skills. Its reach is wide within the repository, but the graph shows no outward dependent chain.*

**🔴 CRITICAL blast radius. A broad GitNexus change centered on `detect_changes`, spanning the MCP local backend, CLI and core code, documentation, and skill files across 80 changed files.**

The implementation hotspot is `gitnexus/src/mcp/local/local-backend.ts`, while related changes extend through the `Cli`, `Local`, `Wiki`, `Extractors`, `Ingestion`, and `Embeddings` modules. The report traces 26 affected flows, so review the local backend first, then the CLI files that format and expose `detect_changes`, including `gitnexus/src/cli/detect-changes-format.ts` and `gitnexus/src/cli/tool.ts`.

The graph found no dependents beyond the changed symbols, and every changed file is classified LOW risk with no HIGH or CRITICAL risk files. Given the PR title, verify the query behavior and its handling of diff hunk counts in the MCP and CLI paths before reviewing the broader documentation and skill updates.
