title: Group cross-impact never fires for manifest-declared links (+ 4 related defects)
body:
**Version:** gitnexus 1.6.7 · macOS arm64 · Node 24.15.0 · LadybugDB via `@ladybugdb/core`

## Context

A two-repo group (`demo`): a NestJS **GraphQL** API (`demo/api`) and a TypeScript client
(`demo/web`). GitNexus has no GraphQL extractor, so I declared the API↔client contracts manually
in `group.yaml` — one link per SDL root field, ~280 of them. The declared data lands in
`contracts.json` **exactly as intended**, but `group impact` never reports a cross-repo hit.

Root defect first, then four smaller ones found along the way. All names and paths below are
anonymised placeholders; the shapes and error strings are verbatim.

> A companion feature request covers the underlying gap (a first-class GraphQL extractor) — it is
> filed separately since it is not a defect. Defect 2 below is what forces the `type: topic`
> workaround described there.

---

## 1. Cross-impact does not join manifest-declared contracts (main issue)

`CY_NEIGHBORS_UPSTREAM` (`core/group/cross-impact.ts`) requires three conditions:

```cypher
WHERE provider.repo = $localRepo
  AND provider.symbolUid IN $uids
  AND provider.role = 'provider'
```

All three are satisfiable in my data, yet the result is always `cross=0`.

**Stored contract** (`~/.gitnexus/groups/demo/contracts.json`):

```json
{ "repo": "demo/api", "role": "provider",
  "contractId": "topic::getWidget",
  "symbolUid": "Method:src/modules/widget/graphql/widget.resolver.ts:WidgetResolver.getWidget#1" }
```

**Local impact** on a method the resolver depends on returns that same uid at depth 1:

```console
$ gitnexus impact 'Method:src/modules/widget/service/widget.service.interface.ts:IWidgetService.findById#1' -r demo-api
  → byDepth."1" includes
    Method:src/modules/widget/graphql/widget.resolver.ts:WidgetResolver.getWidget#1
```

**Group impact, same target, immediately after a fresh `group sync`:**

```console
$ gitnexus group impact demo \
    --target 'Method:src/modules/widget/service/widget.service.interface.ts:IWidgetService.findById#1' \
    --repo demo/api
Group impact for "demo" (demo/api): risk=HIGH
  direct=10 processes=0 cross=0        ← expected cross≥1
```

So: `provider.repo` matches the `--repo` group path, `role` is `provider`, and the uid is in the
impacted set — but no `ContractLink` neighbour comes back. My guess is that either the bridge
never materialises `ContractLink` edges for `matchType: 'manifest'` links, or `$localRepo` is
bound to the registry alias (`demo-api`) rather than the group path (`demo/api`); I could not
narrow it further from the shipped `dist/`.

## 2. `type: custom` emits Cypher that LadybugDB cannot parse

`manifest-extractor.ts` `resolveSymbol()` for `custom`:

```console
[manifest-extractor] resolveSymbol failed for custom:updateWidget in demo/web:
Prepare failed: Parser exception: Invalid input
<MATCH (n:Function|Method|Class|Interface|Struct|Enum|Trait|Constructor|TypeAlias|Impl|Macro>:
expected rule oC_SingleQuery (line: 1, offset: 86)
```

The parser stops at `Macro` — the 21-label alternation exceeds what it accepts. Consequence:
**`type: custom` never resolves a symbol, in any repo**; every custom link silently degrades to a
synthetic `manifest::…` uid on both endpoints. It fired ~560× in a single sync (~280 links × 2
repos).

Workaround I'm using: `type: topic`, whose 4-label query
(`MATCH (n:Function|Method|Class|Interface)`) parses fine and resolves 100% on the provider side.
That is a semantic abuse of `topic` and it forces `detect.topics: false`.

## 3. `bridge.lbug` cannot be reopened after the first read

Reproducible: `group sync`, then `group impact` (works), then `group impact` again:

```console
Could not open bridge.lbug read-only (schema 1). Run gitnexus group sync.
```

Every subsequent call fails until another `group sync`. A `bridge.lbug.wal` (34 B) and
`bridge.lbug.shadow` remain in the group dir, so it looks like the read handle is not released.

## 4. `group sync` resolves repos by first-match, with no ambiguity error

`core/group/sync.ts`:

```ts
const e = allEntries.find((en) => en.name === registryName);
```

Registry names are **not** unique — `analyze` derives them from the directory basename, so a
second clone of the same repo elsewhere on disk registers under the same name. `group.yaml`
references repos by name, so the group can silently bind to a stale clone. I hit this with an
index 400+ commits behind; nothing in `group sync`, `group status` or `group list` surfaced it.

`resolveRegistryEntry` already does this correctly for `remove` (path tier first, then
`RegistryAmbiguousTargetError` on duplicate names) — `group sync` should reuse it, or at minimum
warn. Allowing an absolute path as a `repos:` value would also solve it.

## 5. `--name` is silently ignored when the index is already up to date

```console
$ gitnexus analyze --index-only --name demo-web <path>
  Already up to date            ← alias NOT applied, exit 0, no warning
$ gitnexus analyze --index-only --name demo-web --force <path>
  Repository indexed successfully   ← alias applied
```

The short-circuit returns before `registerRepo`, so a rename needs a full re-index. Either apply
the rename on the fast path, or warn that `--name` was ignored.

title: Feature request: first-class GraphQL contracts for cross-repo groups
body:
**Version:** gitnexus 1.6.7

## The gap

GitNexus ships extractors for `http`, `grpc`, `thrift`, `topic`, `shared_libs` and `includes`, but
none for GraphQL — there is no `tree-sitter-graphql` grammar among the 16 ingested languages, and
no occurrence of "graphql" anywhere in the published `dist/`.

For a group pairing a GraphQL API with its client, that means **zero auto-detected cross-links**.
In my case `group sync` extracted 230 contracts and produced 0 cross-links: the REST routes the
`http` extractor does find are third-party webhooks, while the actual API surface — the resolvers
— is invisible.

## Why this should be cheap to add

Both halves already exist as patterns in the codebase:

- **provider** — NestJS `@Query()` / `@Mutation()` / `@Subscription()` decorators. This is the
  same tree-sitter decorator walk that `extractors/http-patterns/node.ts` already performs for
  `@Controller` / `@Get`, so the traversal is a copy with different decorator names.
- **consumer** — root selections in the client's `.graphql` operation documents. The `graphql`
  package parses these directly, so no new tree-sitter grammar is strictly required for the
  consumer side.
- **contractId** — `graphql::query::<field>` slots straight into the existing `runExactMatch`
  cascade with no changes to the matching layer, and **both** endpoints anchor on real symbols.

## Why the join key is reliable

NestJS names the resolver method exactly like the schema field, and a client operation's root
selection uses that same identifier:

```
api     src/modules/widget/graphql/widget.resolver.ts   async getWidget()      ← Method node
schema  schema.gql                                      type Query { getWidget }
web     src/api/widget/getWidget.graphql                query GetWidget {
                                                          getWidget { … }      ← same identifier
```

In my repos that is an exact match on **279 of 279** root fields, verified by intersecting the SDL
root fields with the indexed resolver method names.

## What I do today, and why it is not enough

I generate ~280 manifest links into `group.yaml` from the SDL. That anchors 279/279 on real
provider symbols, which proves the join key works — but it has two problems that a real extractor
would remove:

1. It has to use `type: topic`, because `type: custom` emits Cypher LadybugDB cannot parse (filed
   separately as a defect). `topic` is semantically wrong here and forces `detect.topics: false`.
2. A manifest link carries a single `contract` string shared by both endpoints, so only one side
   can anchor on a real symbol. The client's generated symbols are named `useGetWidgetQuery` /
   `GetWidgetDocument`, which do not match the field name — so the consumer endpoint degrades to a
   synthetic uid. A native extractor would anchor the consumer on the `.graphql` document (or the
   generated hook) and give both ends real symbols.

Happy to test a branch against a real NestJS + TypeScript-client pair if that helps.

title: watch mode for automatic incremental re-indexing on source changes
body:
### Area

gitnexus (CLI / core / indexing / MCP server)

### Problem or opportunity

GitNexus already supports incremental analyze, but keeping the knowledge graph current during an active development session still requires an explicit re-analysis trigger.

For AI-agent and IDE workflows, the graph can become stale immediately after a developer or agent edits source code.

It would be useful to have an opt-in long-running watch mode that detects relevant working-tree changes and automatically performs a debounced incremental re-index.

### Proposed solution

Add something like:
gitnexus watch
or:
gitnexus analyze --watch

Expected behavior:

1. Watch indexed source/config files for create, modify, rename, and delete events.
2. Debounce/batch rapid editor writes so a save burst produces one refresh.
3. Feed only changed/affected files into the existing incremental-analysis path.
4. Keep the existing graph readable while the update is being prepared.
5. Ignore .gitnexus, .git, dependencies, generated files, build artifacts, and existing ignored paths.
6. If changes arrive while indexing is running, coalesce them into the next update instead of starting concurrent writers.
7. Report files changed, files re-parsed, affected dependents, duration, and last successful refresh.

Ideally MCP/server consumers could use the same mechanism so AI agents always query the latest graph without manually invoking gitnexus analyze.


### Alternatives considered

_No response_

### Acceptance criteria

* Opt-in watch command/mode exists.
* Creating, modifying, renaming, or deleting a relevant source file triggers an incremental refresh.
* Rapid writes are debounced/coalesced.
* Multiple graph writers cannot run concurrently.
* Ignored/generated directories do not trigger unnecessary indexing.
* A small change uses the incremental path whenever safe.
* Changes made while indexing is in progress are processed afterward.
* The previous usable graph remains available if a refresh fails.
* MCP/daemon consumers can observe the refreshed graph without requiring a complete restart, once hot-reload support is available.

### Constraints

_No response_

### Contribution

- [ ] I am willing to open a PR for this (may need design discussion first).

title: Incremental analyze: deterministic "Failed calling LOWER: Invalid UTF-8" on .py-bearing writable sets — inputs ASCII, no concurrent writers, store LOWER-sweeps clean (1.6.9)
body:
### Area

CLI / core indexing — incremental analyze + LadybugDB FTS writeback (Windows x64)

### Environment

- gitnexus **1.6.9** (npm global install — current `latest` as of 2026-08-22), Node **v26.4.0**, Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26200
- Repo: private mixed Python + JS/React codebase, ~74.5k symbols; store = **201,305 nodes / 294,860 edges** after a clean full rebuild (345 s)
- Embeddings **disabled** (`stats.embeddings: 0`); FTS in use and healthy after full builds
- No concurrent writers: every crashing run analyzed a settled git commit; nothing rewrites the changed files while analyze runs

### Summary

Incremental `analyze` fails with

```
  Analysis failed: Runtime exception: Failed calling LOWER: Invalid UTF-8.
```

immediately after the incremental plan lines, **whenever the writable set contains symbol-bearing Python files**. Every `.py`-bearing incremental attempted on 1.6.9 has failed (0 of 3 succeeded, across disjoint change sets — two as the LOWER exception, one as a native access violation). A docs-only (`.md`) incremental on the same store passes. Full rebuilds (`--force`, or the `incrementalInProgress` crash-marker recovery) are consistently green — 3/3, reproducing an identical graph.

This is the same crash signature as #2546, but the evidence below rules out both explanations on the table so far — #2546's concurrent-writer torn-read theory and #2889's dirty-source-bytes / sanitization-gap mechanism — and localizes the defect to the incremental symbol-row delete/rewrite + FTS side-structure update itself. In other words, this is the "exact original source of the invalid content" that the #2546 close-out comment said was still unresolved and asked reporters to help pin down.

### Failure output

From the 2026-08-22 run (changed = `trader.py` + 2 × `.md`):

```
Incremental: changed=3, added=0, deleted=0 (skipping wipe + unchanged file rows preserved)
Incremental: +28 importer(s) added to writable set

  Analysis failed: Runtime exception: Failed calling LOWER: Invalid UTF-8.
```

The failure lands immediately after the importer-set line every time.

### All observed runs

| Date | Changed set | Writable set | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-08-18 | routine incremental | symbol-bearing | **native crash, exit 3221225477 (0xC0000005)** mid-incremental; the marker-forced *full* rebuild that followed was green |
| 2026-08-21 | 2 × `.json` + 1 × `.py`, all pure ASCII (the `.py` is a leaf module — no importers pulled in) | those 3 files | `Failed calling LOWER: Invalid UTF-8` |
| 2026-08-22 | `trader.py` + 2 × `.md` — run on a freshly rebuilt, verified-clean store (see below) | +28 importers | `Failed calling LOWER: Invalid UTF-8` |
| 2026-08-22 | `.md` only | docs only | ✅ completes |
| ×3 | — | full rebuild (`--force` / crash-marker recovery) | ✅ green, identical graph |

Two disjoint Python populations trigger it (one isolated leaf script; `trader.py` plus its importer closure), so it is not one cursed file — it's the Python symbol-rewrite path generally. A **single leaf `.py` in the writable set is sufficient**.

### What the evidence rules out

**1. Concurrent writers / torn reads (#2546's theory).** All crashing runs analyzed settled commits; nothing rewrites those files during analyze. The crash is deterministic, not occasional. And a full rebuild ingests the *same* file content minutes later without complaint.

**2. Invalid bytes in the source inputs (#2889's mechanism).** The changed files are pure ASCII; a repo-wide byte-level scan decodes every candidate input as valid UTF-8; filenames are plain ASCII; embeddings are off. ASCII is invariant under every encode/sanitize step, so no string-level vs byte-level sanitization gap can manufacture invalid UTF-8 out of these inputs.

**3. Poison resident in stored rows (our own first theory — disproved).** After the 08-21 crash we moved aside the `lbug` store **and both parse caches** (`parse-cache/`, `parsedfile-cache/`) and rebuilt from scratch: green, 201,305 nodes / 294,860 edges. We then ran a Cypher sweep forcing `LOWER()` over **every string property of every node and CodeRelation edge** (never-matching `CONTAINS` predicates) — clean end to end. Note also that on 1.6.9 a green full rebuild already implies the full FTS index build over all stored rows succeeded, since pre-#2548 an FTS build failure aborts the run. The very next `.py`-bearing incremental on that verified-clean store crashed identically.

### Inference

The invalid UTF-8 reaching `LOWER` is **manufactured during the incremental writeback itself** — the symbol-row delete/rewrite for the writable set and/or the FTS side-structure update that accompanies it — not read from source files and not resident in row columns (column-level LOWER over the whole store passes). Taking the #2546 close-out description at face value (FTS indexes rebuilt from all stored rows on every run), the only new material in a crashing run is the symbol rows the incremental itself just rewrote — pointing at the incremental row-write path, or the native FTS update over those rows. That is consistent with the #2546 close-out suspicion that the source may be internal to the bundled LadybugDB FTS layer.

The 2026-08-18 occurrence — an access violation at the same point in the run instead of the runtime exception — suggests the same defect can corrupt memory rather than throw, i.e. a native-side memory-safety bug with two masks.

Docs-only incrementals passing fits the same picture: `.md` changes rewrite file rows but no Function/Method/Property/Variable symbol rows, and they don't crash.

### Why this matters even after #2548

- #2548 (degrade FTS instead of aborting) is merged but **unreleased** — npm `latest` is still 1.6.9, so released users get the hard abort on every routine incremental of a Python repo.
- Once #2548 ships, this defect means keyword search would be **silently skipped on essentially every incremental** in a Python repo (nearly every real change set touches a `.py`) — permanent FTS degradation rather than an occasional skip.
- The 0xC0000005 sibling suggests the underlying writeback path can corrupt memory, which graceful degradation doesn't make safe.

Adjacent-but-different, for cross-reference: #2841 (incremental + FTS *extension load* failure — our extension loads fine and full builds are green), #1160 (FTS index-creation segfault, rc era), #2409 (a different deterministic incremental-writeback failure on 1.6.8 — that path has history).

### Workaround

Our refresh wrapper now appends `--force` to every analyze, so every refresh is a full re-index (~2 min warm on this repo). Reliable, but it abandons the incremental path entirely.

### Repro (as observed — repo is private)

1. `gitnexus analyze --force` on a mid-size Python repo → green.
2. Make an ASCII-only edit to any symbol-bearing `.py` (a leaf module with no importers suffices), commit.
3. Incremental `gitnexus analyze` → `Failed calling LOWER: Invalid UTF-8` right after the importer-set line.
4. Same store, `.md`-only change → incremental completes.

We can reproduce on demand (any `.py` touch triggers it) and are happy to run an instrumented build or extra tracing to capture the exact string handed to `LOWER`.

title: rename preview under-reports its own edits; impact returns 0 callers for a hub function; incremental index drops live symbols (1.6.9, Python repo)
body:
**Environment:** gitnexus 1.6.9 via `node .gitnexus/run.cjs analyze` (index of a ~6.8k-symbol Python/Streamlit repo), MCP tools `impact`, `rename`, `detect_changes`, run from git worktrees on macOS (Darwin 25.5), Python 3.14.

**Observed (2026-08-23, three independent sessions on the same repo):**

1. **`rename` preview vs apply.** Renaming `_sqlite_backup` → `sqlite_online_backup` (one def, one same-file call site, one cross-file import alias) previewed fewer edits than it applied — the same-file call site was missing from the preview but correctly rewritten on apply. Same shape on a second rename (`_course_mirror_values` → `course_to_deal_course_values`: 3 edits previewed, 6 applied). A post-apply `grep` was needed to trust the result.
2. **`impact` false negative on a hub.** `impact({target: "open_session", direction: "upstream"})` returned 0 callers / LOW. `grep -rn "open_session(" app tests` finds ~40 call sites, and `detect_changes --compare main` on the same branch reported 300/300 flows affected through it. The MUST-gate that keys off `impact`'s risk level therefore under-reported a CRITICAL-scale change.
3. **Incremental index drops a live symbol.** After a commit that moved a function between modules, the next incremental `analyze` could not resolve the moved symbol by name; a clean full re-analyze fixed it. Repeated once more after a different commit (symbols `save_card`, `save_assumptions` unresolvable until a forced full run).

**Expected:** preview == apply for `rename`; `impact` upstream counts to match direct call sites for a plain function; incremental indexing to keep moved/new symbols resolvable.

**Repro hints:** any repo where a function has a same-file caller (1); a function called from many modules via `from x import f` (2); move a function between modules and re-run incremental analyze (3).

title: npm install -g gitnexus` fails on install due to onnxruntime-node postinstall (HTTP 302 not followed)
body:
### Area

gitnexus (CLI / core / indexing / MCP server)

### Summary

A fresh npm install -g gitnexus@latest fails on machines where the onnxruntime-node postinstall script hits a redirecting response (HTTP 302). The error is produced by onnxruntime-node's install script, which uses Node's native https.get() and treats any non-200 status as a hard error — it does not follow redirects.

This is upstream onnxruntime-node's bug (see microsoft/onnxruntime#...), but it blocks a clean install of this package for many users, so I'd like to track it here and suggest mitigations.

### Context

_No response_

### Expected behavior

it can be install.

### Actual behavior

npm error command failed
npm error command sh -c node ./script/install
npm error /.../onnxruntime-node/script/install-utils.js:57
npm error           reject(new Error(`Failed to download build list. HTTP status code = ${statusCode}`));
npm error Error: Failed to download build list. HTTP status code = 302
Note: curl -L downloads the same URLs fine, and npm config get proxy is empty — so this is not a proxy misconfiguration on our side; the feed (NuGet / GitHub release CDN) simply returns 302 and the script doesn't follow it.

### Steps to reproduce

npm install -g gitnexus@latest --onnxruntime-node-install=skip

### Environment

OS: Linux x64
Node.js: v22.23.2, npm 10.9.8
gitnexus: 1.6.9
onnxruntime-node (transitive dep): 1.27.0

### Logs / screenshots

title: Bare package specifiers silently resolve to the wrong file via suffixResolve (wrong edges, not missing ones)
body:
# Bare package specifiers silently resolve to the wrong file via `suffixResolve` (wrong edges, not missing ones)

**Version:** gitnexus 1.6.7 (global install, macOS arm64, Node 24.14.0)

## Summary

When a repo declares no tsconfig path aliases, imports of a workspace package
subpath fall through to `suffixResolve`, which strips leading path segments and
takes the **first basename match anywhere in the repo**. When some unrelated file
happens to share that basename, the import edge is attached to it.

The result is not a missing edge — it is a **wrong edge**, recorded at full
confidence. That is considerably worse than no data, because both directions of
the graph become misleading and nothing signals it:

- the real module reports **0 inbound importers** → `impact --direction upstream`
  returns `impactedCount: 0, risk: "LOW"`, i.e. "safe to edit", for a module with
  many live callers
- the unrelated same-named file accumulates **phantom importers** that exist
  nowhere in source, inflating its apparent blast radius

Because the fallback only misfires when a basename collides, the failure looks
random: within one repo some package subpaths resolve exactly while others
resolve to zero, with no visible pattern until you inspect the edges directly.

## Minimal reproduction

```
repro/
  package.json                       {"workspaces": ["apps/*", "packages/*"]}
  packages/lib/package.json          {"name": "@scope/lib",
                                      "exports": {"./widget": "./src/widget/index.ts"}}
  packages/lib/src/widget/index.ts   export { doThing } from './impl';
  packages/lib/src/widget/impl.ts    export function doThing() {}
  server/widget.ts                   // decoy: unrelated file, same basename
  apps/web/src/App.ts                import { doThing } from '@scope/lib/widget';
                                     doThing();
```

No `compilerOptions.paths` anywhere.

```bash
gitnexus analyze -f
gitnexus cypher "MATCH (a)-[r:CodeRelation {type:'IMPORTS'}]->(b) WHERE a.filePath = 'apps/web/src/App.ts' RETURN b.filePath"
```

**Expected:** `packages/lib/src/widget/index.ts`
**Actual:** `server/widget.ts`

Consequently:

```bash
gitnexus impact doThing -d upstream --summary-only
# impactedCount: 0, direct: 0, risk: "LOW"   ← despite a live caller in apps/web
```

Delete `server/widget.ts`, re-analyze, and it resolves correctly.

## Root cause

Two compounding behaviours, both in the fallback path.

**1. The segment-stripping loop lets any file in the repo compete.**
`suffixResolve` (`src/core/ingestion/import-resolvers/utils.ts`) walks
`pathParts` from the left, so the package scope is discarded entirely:

```
@scope/lib/widget  →  lib/widget  →  widget      ← matches server/widget.ts
```

By the final iteration the specifier has been reduced to a single bare segment
with no remaining tie to the package it came from.

**2. Within one iteration, `.ts` is tried before `/index.ts`.**
In `EXTENSIONS`, `.ts` sits at index 2 while `/index.ts` sits at index 11. So even
at the same suffix depth, a same-basename *file* outranks the correct barrel
*directory*: `widget.ts` beats `widget/index.ts`. Reaching the right answer
requires both the right depth and the right extension, and the ordering actively
works against it.

**Why the fallback runs at all:** `loadTsconfigPaths`
(`src/core/ingestion/language-config.ts`) tries `tsconfig.json`,
`tsconfig.app.json`, `tsconfig.base.json` and returns the first with
`compilerOptions.paths`. A workspace monorepo that resolves purely through
`package.json` `exports` + workspace symlinks — a completely normal setup, and
the one npm/pnpm/yarn recommend — declares none, so `tsconfigPaths` is `null`,
the alias branch in `standard.ts` no-ops, and every bare specifier lands in the
fuzzy path.

## Suggested fixes

In rough order of value:

1. **Resolve workspace packages properly.** Before the suffix fallback, match a
   bare specifier against workspace `package.json` `name` + `exports`/`main`.
   This is the actual resolution algorithm and would fix the class of bug rather
   than one symptom.
2. **Never strip the package scope.** For a specifier starting with `@scope/` or
   any bare (non-relative) specifier, constrain `suffixResolve` to candidates
   under the resolved package root. Stripping down to a single bare segment
   should not be reachable for scoped specifiers.
3. **Prefer `/index.*` over `.*` for the final segment** of a bare specifier,
   reversing the current `EXTENSIONS` precedence in that case.
4. **Mark fallback edges as low confidence.** `CodeRelation` already carries a
   `confidence` property, but suffix-fallback guesses appear indistinguishable
   from exact resolutions. Emitting them below 1.0 would let `impact`'s existing
   `minConfidence` filter exclude them, and make the guessing visible.
5. **Warn when `tsconfigPaths` is null** in a repo with workspaces — a one-line
   analyze warning would make this debuggable instead of invisible.

## Workaround (for anyone hitting this)

Declare the aliases so the fallback never runs. A solution-style root
`tsconfig.json` (`"files": []`, nothing extends it) is a good host because it is
inert for `tsc`, builds and typecheck:

```jsonc
{
  "files": [],
  "compilerOptions": {
    "baseUrl": ".",
    "paths": {
      "@scope/lib/*": ["packages/lib/src/*"],
      "@scope/lib": ["packages/lib/src/index.ts"]
    }
  },
  "references": [...]
}
```

Two caveats worth documenting, both easy to get wrong:

- **Glob keys must precede their bare counterpart.** The alias loop in
  `standard.ts` takes the first prefix that matches, so listing `"@scope/lib"`
  first rewrites `@scope/lib/widget` to `packages/lib/src/index.ts/widget`.
- **App-relative aliases must not be hoisted here.** A per-app `@/*` meaning
  `apps/<app>/src/*` cannot be expressed in one repo-root map; adding it points
  every app's `@/` at a single app.

With the map declared and `analyze -f` re-run, previously-zero package subpaths
pick up their real inbound edges, subpaths that already looked correct gain the
importers that had been mis-bound elsewhere, and the phantom edges on
same-basename files disappear.

title: Directories named env/ or generated/ are silently skipped at discovery, hiding real source files
body:
## Summary

Directories whose path contains a segment named `env` or `generated` are silently excluded at file-discovery time, along with every `*.d.ts`. On our repo that drops **18 tracked, non-git-ignored TypeScript source files** — 13 of them hand-written application code.

Because the files are never parsed, their symbols have no node at all. `impact` and `context` on them return nothing, and — more dangerously — symbols they *call* report caller lists with the missing files silently absent. That reads as "unused", which is the same class of false-safe answer as #3038.

Reproduced on **v1.6.10-rc.215** (and identically on 1.6.7).

## Repro

The excluded paths on our repo:

```
apps/{admin,admin-new,client,contractor}/src/shared/env/applyEnvChrome.ts
apps/{admin,admin-new,client,contractor}/src/shared/env/getAppEnv.ts
apps/{admin,admin-new,client,contractor}/src/shared/env/EnvironmentBanner.tsx
packages/ai/src/generated/bundle.ts
apps/{admin,admin-new,client,contractor}/vite-env.d.ts
apps/admin/src/vite-env.d.ts
```

`shared/env/` is an ordinary app directory — environment *banner*, app-env getter, favicon/title chrome. Nothing virtualenv-shaped.

```bash
npx gitnexus@1.6.10-rc.215 cypher \
  "MATCH (n) WHERE n.filePath STARTS WITH 'apps/client/src/shared/env/' RETURN DISTINCT n.filePath AS f"
# []   — three real .ts/.tsx files live there
```

Full diff of source files vs indexed nodes:

```bash
npx gitnexus@1.6.10-rc.215 cypher "MATCH (n) WHERE n.filePath IS NOT NULL RETURN DISTINCT n.filePath AS f" > graph.txt
find apps convex packages -type f \( -name '*.ts' -o -name '*.tsx' \) \
  -not -path '*/node_modules/*' -not -path '*/_generated/*' | sort
# 1928 source files, 18 absent from the graph
```

The paths are also absent from `fileHashes` in `.gitnexus/meta.json`, which is what points at file discovery rather than parsing. They are tracked in git and `git check-ignore` reports nothing.

## It is segment matching, not substring

`packages/domain/src/appEnv.ts` contains `env` in its basename and indexes fine, so the rule is matching a path *segment* named exactly `env` / `generated`.

## Why it bites

`envFaviconHref` in `packages/domain/src/appEnv.ts` is called by all four `applyEnvChrome.ts` files. The graph shows:

```
context({name: "envFaviconHref"})
→ Called by: appEnv.test.ts
```

One caller, and it is the symbol's own test — a textbook "dead code, safe to delete" signal for a function four production entry points depend on.

## Suggestion

`env` and `generated` look like they are aimed at Python virtualenvs and build output, which is reasonable for those ecosystems but costly in a TS monorepo where both are ordinary directory names. Options that would fix it for us, roughly in order of preference:

1. Scope those two patterns to the languages/ecosystems they are meant for, or to a repo-root-relative position (`/env/`, `/generated/`) rather than any depth.
2. Respect `.gitignore` as the source of truth for build output, and drop the hardcoded `generated`.
3. At minimum, make the exclusion list configurable via `.gitnexusrc`, and **report skipped files** — the large-file skip already prints a notice (`Skipped 2 large files…`), which is how it should feel. A silent skip is what made this take a while to find.

Happy to test a patch against this repo — we have a 1,928-file TS/Convex monorepo that has now surfaced three of these.

title: impact() reports epistemic: "exact" with 0 callers for Convex functions, where anyApi indirection leaves no edge for the #1858 probe to key on
body:
### Area

gitnexus (CLI / core / indexing / MCP server)

### Summary

`impact()` on a Convex function returns `impactedCount: 0` with `epistemic: "exact"` and no `causes` or `boundaries`, while the symbol has live call sites. This is the same shape as #2708 / #2744 / #2766 / #2813 / #2873, but from a cause the #1858 probe cannot currently see: the indirection leaves **no edge and no drop record at all**, so there is nothing for it to key on.

Closest open sibling is #3015 — `impact` fail-opening when analyze dropped a file. Same end state (a confident answer that is silently incomplete), different trigger.

### Context

Convex addresses its backend functions through `anyApi`, a runtime Proxy:

```js
// convex/_generated/api.js
import { anyApi } from 'convex/server';
export const api = anyApi;
```

A caller writes `useMutation(api.client.eshop.updateDraft)` — a property-access chain on an opaque object. Nothing statically links that expression to `convex/client/eshop.ts`, so no `CALLS` or `IMPORTS` edge is emitted. That part is expected and not what I am filing; it is a property of how Convex addresses functions, and I do not think a static analyser can fix it.

What I am filing is that the result does not say so. `epistemic` exists to carry exactly this signal, and here it actively vouches for the empty answer.

### Expected behavior

`epistemic: "lower-bound"` for a symbol whose only callers bind through a dynamic-dispatch boundary, with a boundary note naming the cause — the same treatment an interface-typed caller gets today.

### Actual behavior

```
$ gitnexus impact updateDraft -f convex/client/eshop.ts -d upstream --summary-only
{
  "impactedCount": 0,
  "risk": "UNKNOWN",
  "epistemic": "exact",
  "summary": { "direct": 0, "processes_affected": 0, "modules_affected": 0 }
}
```

Ground truth — 4 production call sites, plus 5 in tests:

```
apps/client/src/features/eshop/EshopUnlockedOrder.tsx:113
apps/client/src/features/eshop/EshopGraveIdentityStep.tsx:90
apps/client/src/features/eshop/wizard/useEshopWizardDraft.ts:27,89
```

No `causes` and no `boundaries` key is present — not a zeroed count, the fields are absent.

### Steps to reproduce

Any Convex repo. In ours (private, 1,928 TS files) every public endpoint reproduces it:

```bash
gitnexus impact <convexFnName> -f convex/<module>.ts -d upstream --summary-only
grep -rn "api\.<module path>\.<convexFnName>" apps convex packages   # the real callers
```

The graph confirms nothing inbound exists — only structural edges:

```cypher
MATCH (a)-[r:CodeRelation]->(b) WHERE b.filePath = 'convex/clients/create.ts'
RETURN r.type AS type, count(*) AS n
-- CONTAINS 1 | DEFINES 4
```

### Environment

- gitnexus `1.6.10-rc.215`
- macOS 15 (darwin arm64), Node 24
- TS monorepo, npm workspaces, Convex backend

### Notes

**Why the probe misses it.** `computeEpistemicBoundary` looks for materialized evidence of indirection — `EPISTEMIC_HERITAGE_RELATION_TYPES` (`IMPLEMENTS` / `METHOD_IMPLEMENTS` / `EXTENDS`) plus unresolved-receiver notes. When it finds no boundary node it returns `epistemicFrom(droppedBoundaries)`, which is bare `exact` if there are no notes. `anyApi` produces neither an edge nor an unresolved-receiver record, so the probe correctly finds nothing and reports `exact`.

The probe is additive and fail-open by design — it returns `exact` on query error too, so it can only add signal. That is right for a probe, but it means *"no evidence of indirection"* and *"indirection that leaves no evidence"* collapse into the same answer, and the second case is the dangerous one.

**Suggested fix.** Detect the Convex wrapper shape rather than the `convex/` path — `export const X = query|mutation|action|internalQuery|internalMutation|internalAction({ ... })`. That is more precise than a directory convention and survives repos that put functions elsewhere. Framework-aware detection already lives in the same function (`queryClassBeanMetadata`, `querySpringAopMetadata`), so this would sit alongside rather than introduce a new concept.

I would reuse the existing `lower-bound` value rather than adding a `partial` — it already means what is needed here, and needs no consumer changes.

**One thing that compounds it:** `direction: "downstream"` on the same symbols also returns 0, because the body's `CALLS` attach to the inner `handler` node rather than the exported `Const` (and only the first `handler` per file appears to get a node — a file of ours with 5 exported queries and 4 `requireAdmin` calls has 1 handler node and 1 `CALLS` edge). So `epistemic: "exact"` is currently vouching for two empty answers rather than one. Happy to file that separately if it is not already known — say the word and I will, with a reduced case.

title: Same-named nested functions (Convex handler:) collapse to one node; CALLS from every handler are re-attached to the first, and downstream impact returns 0
body:
### Area

gitnexus (CLI / core / indexing / MCP server)

### Summary

In a file declaring several `export const x = query({ handler: async (…) => … })`, all the `handler` arrow functions collapse into a **single** graph node, and every `CALLS` edge from every handler is re-attached to that one node — the first one in the file.

Two consequences, the second worse than the first:

1. `impact(direction: "downstream")` on any of the exported functions returns `0`, because none of them owns the node the edges hang off.
2. The surviving node is credited with calls made by *other* functions. This is a wrong edge at full confidence, not a missing one — the same shape as #3038.

Duplicate callees across handlers are also deduplicated, so a helper called by four of the nine functions appears once.

### Context

Convex declares every endpoint as an exported const wrapping an object with a `handler` property. Nine exported functions in a file therefore mean nine arrow functions all named `handler`. It looks like node identity is keyed on `(name, filePath)`, so they collide and the first wins — but that is a hypothesis from the outside; I have only observed the result.

This is separate from #3040 (which is about `epistemic` vouching for the empty *upstream* answer). Together they mean a Convex symbol reports `0` in both directions.

### Expected behavior

Each `handler` gets its own node, with its own `CALLS` edges, and `impact(direction: "downstream")` on the exported const reaches them.

### Actual behavior

`convex/orders/get.ts` — 9 exported functions, 9 `handler:` properties in source:

```bash
$ gitnexus cypher "MATCH (n) WHERE n.filePath = 'convex/orders/get.ts' AND n.name = 'handler' RETURN count(*) AS n"
# 1
```

That one node is at line 19, inside the first export (`getById`). It carries three `CALLS`:

```bash
$ gitnexus cypher "MATCH (a)-[r:CodeRelation {type:'CALLS'}]->(b) WHERE a.filePath = 'convex/orders/get.ts' RETURN a.startLine AS from_line, b.name AS callee"
# 19 | requireAdmin
# 19 | dicByGraves
# 19 | resolveOrderWpidForOrder
```

Where those calls actually live in source:

```
line  21  inside getById               -> requireAdmin
line  38  inside getAll                -> requireAdmin
line  53  inside getByGrave            -> requireAdmin
line  75  inside getInvoicesByOrder    -> requireAdmin
line 133  inside resolveWpidInternal   -> resolveOrderWpidForOrder
line 183  inside allByGraveIdInternal  -> dicByGraves
```

`getById` does not call `dicByGraves` or `resolveOrderWpidForOrder` — those belong to functions 150+ lines further down. And four `requireAdmin` call sites became one edge.

Downstream impact on each of the nine returns nothing:

```bash
$ for fn in getById getAll getByGrave getInvoicesByOrder …; do
    gitnexus impact $fn -f convex/orders/get.ts -d downstream --summary-only
  done
# every one: impactedCount 0, risk LOW
```

Pinning to the handler node instead returns a real answer, but it is always the first function's — silently, with no `ambiguous` status and no candidate list:

```bash
$ gitnexus impact handler -f convex/clients/create.ts -d downstream --summary-only
# impactedCount 10, direct 2, risk CRITICAL     (single-export file: correct)
$ gitnexus impact handler -f convex/clients/get.ts -d downstream --summary-only
# impactedCount 3                                (5-export file: getById's, presented as the answer)
```

### Steps to reproduce

Any file with two or more same-named nested functions; a Convex module is the natural case.

```ts
export const first  = query({ handler: async (ctx) => { helperA(ctx); } });
export const second = query({ handler: async (ctx) => { helperB(ctx); } });
```

Expected: two handler nodes, `first → helperA`, `second → helperB`.
Observed: one handler node at `first`, carrying edges to both `helperA` and `helperB`.

Reproduced on three files in our repo — 5, 9 and 9 exports respectively, each yielding exactly 1 handler node.

### Environment

- gitnexus `1.6.10-rc.215`
- macOS 15 (darwin arm64), Node 24
- TS monorepo, npm workspaces, Convex backend

### Notes

The misattribution is what I would prioritise. A missing edge under-reports; this one tells a caller that `getById` depends on a helper it has never referenced, which is exactly the failure mode #3038 was about — and unlike the `anyApi` limitation in #3040, nothing about this is forced by the framework. The information is in the AST.

Reporting `ambiguous` when a `-f` lookup matches several nodes of the same name would also help, independently of the identity fix.

title: Route: a method-agnostic route (@All) donates its handler to a same-URL filesystem Route node
body:
## Summary

A method-agnostic route (`@All`, a Django function view, a verb-less dispatch-guard route) keys its identity by **URL alone**. Filesystem routes (Next.js / Expo / PHP) are pre-seeded straight into `routeRegistry` and never pass through `claim()`. When both produce the same URL in one repo, the result is not a missing route — it is a **fabricated** one: the filesystem `Route` node ends up carrying the *other* framework's handler as its `handlerSymbolId`, and the method-agnostic route gets no node at all.

`ARCHITECTURE.md` states the rule this breaks: *"A missing route is a coverage limit; an invented one is a lie."*

Found during the review of #3017, which does not introduce the flaw — `@All` is just a new and much easier way to reach it.

## Reproduction

Two files:

```ts
// app/api/venues/route.ts       (Next.js filesystem route -> /api/venues)
export async function GET() {
  return new Response('next handler');
}
```
```ts
// src/venues.controller.ts      (NestJS -> /api/venues)
@Controller('api')
export class VenuesController {
  @All('venues')
  handleEverything() {
    return 'nest handler';
  }
}
```

Run the pipeline over that repo and dump every `Route` node with its resolved handler:

```
ROUTE method=undefined url=/api/venues
   handler=handleEverything in src/venues.controller.ts
```

One node. It is the **Next.js** route (`method=undefined` — the filesystem entry carries no verb), and its handler is the **NestJS** controller method. The NestJS route itself is gone.

### Controls

Both run against the same harness, same commit.

**A — Next.js route alone** (delete `src/`):
```
ROUTE method=undefined url=/api/venues
   handler=undefined in undefined
```
Correct: one node, no handler.

**B — `@Get('venues')` instead of `@All('venues')`**:
```
ROUTE method=undefined url=/api/venues
   handler=undefined in undefined
ROUTE method=GET       url=/api/venues
   handler=handleEverything in src/venues.controller.ts
```
Correct: two nodes, each with the right handler (or none).

So the donation is specific to the method-agnostic identity, and control B shows the intended behaviour the `@All` case fails to produce.

## Mechanism

Verified line by line:

1. **`routeNodeKey` drops the method for a wildcard.** `route-extractors/route-path.ts` — `method && method !== '*' ? \`${method} ${url}\` : url`. So an `@All` route's identity is the bare URL, deliberately, so filesystem and `resource`-style routes stay byte-identical to their pre-#2289 ids.

2. **Filesystem routes never enter `claimed`.** `pipeline-phases/routes.ts` writes Next.js / Expo / PHP entries directly into `routeRegistry`. `resolveRouteHandlerSymbols` (`call-processor.ts`) builds its `claimed` set from `extractedRoutes` and `decoratorRoutes` only — it starts empty and never sees a filesystem URL.

3. **So the `@All` route claims that URL unopposed** and writes its handler into the returned map under the URL-only key.

4. **Back in the routes phase, `addRoute` finds the key already present** — the filesystem entry got there first — so `duplicateRoutes++; return;`. The NestJS route is dropped.

5. **`routes.ts` then builds the node for the surviving filesystem entry and reads `routeHandlerSymbols.get(routeKey)`** — same URL-only key — getting the NestJS handler, and stamps it on.

The two sides agree on the key and disagree on who owns it. `claim()`'s own comment says it *"mirrors the routes phase `addRoute` first-writer-wins so the handler we stamp always belongs to the route that actually won the Route node"* — that invariant is exactly what breaks here, because one of the two registries is populated before either loop runs.

## Blast radius

Narrow but not theoretical: it needs a method-agnostic route at a URL a filesystem route also produces, in the same repo. A Next.js app with a NestJS backend in one monorepo is the obvious shape, and it is a common one. Django function views (`'*'`) and verb-less dispatch-guard routes can reach it the same way.

The output is a wrong fact, and `api_impact`'s documented job is to be run **before** modifying a route handler — so it answers with a handler in the wrong application.

## Suggested fix

Either would close it; the first is smaller:

1. **Pre-seed the filesystem keys into `claim`'s `claimed` set.** `resolveRouteHandlerSymbols` would need the filesystem URLs passed in (they are computed in the routes phase before it runs). The wildcard route then finds the key taken, claims nothing, and the filesystem node stays handler-less — which is correct, since nothing resolved it.

2. **Have `routes.ts` skip `routeHandlerSymbols` for entries whose `source` is `*-filesystem-route` / `php-file-route`.** A filesystem route's handler is the file's own default export, not something another framework's decorator resolved.

Neither restores the dropped `@All` route — that is the separate, deliberate consequence of URL-only identity — but both stop the fabricated attribution, which is the part that reports something untrue.

## Test that would have caught it

`test/integration/multi-verb-route-identity.test.ts` covers same-URL multi-verb splitting but has no case where a filesystem route and a decorator route collide. A fixture with both, asserting each Route node's `handlerSymbolId`, is the missing tier — the same tier that already exists for every other route extractor.

Release notes

Sourced from github/codeql-action/init's releases.

v4.37.7

  • Update default CodeQL bundle version to 2.26.3. #4085
Changelog

Sourced from github/codeql-action/init's changelog.

CodeQL Action Changelog

See the releases page for the relevant changes to the CodeQL CLI and language packs.

[UNRELEASED]

No user facing changes.

4.37.9 - 26 Aug 2026

  • Update default CodeQL bundle version to 2.26.4. #4106

4.37.8 - 21 Aug 2026

No user facing changes.

4.37.7 - 13 Aug 2026

  • Update default CodeQL bundle version to 2.26.3. #4085

4.37.6 - 04 Aug 2026

  • Changed the default filepath for the new remote file address format that was introduced in CodeQL Action 4.37.0 / 3.37.0 to .github/codeql-config.yml to align it with the suggested path that is used elsewhere. #4070

4.37.5 - 03 Aug 2026

  • Fixed a bug where a network error while streaming the download of the CodeQL bundle could terminate the init Action instead of falling back to downloading the bundle before extracting it. #4061

4.37.4 - 29 Jul 2026

  • This version of the CodeQL Action adds support for the tools input for the codeql-action/init step to be specified using a github-codeql-tools repository property. This feature will gradually be rolled out following the release of this version. Once rolled out, this allows for the CodeQL CLI version that is used in GitHub-managed workflows, such as Default Setup, to be set to a custom value. For example, customers who run into issues with rate limits when a new CodeQL CLI version is released can set the value to toolcache to always use the CodeQL CLI version that is available in the runner toolcache. For Advanced Setup workflows, the value provided for tools in the workflow definition always takes precedence unless the value of the repository property starts with !. #4037
  • Update default CodeQL bundle version to 2.26.2. #4051

4.37.3 - 22 Jul 2026

No user facing changes.

4.37.2 - 21 Jul 2026

  • The new address format for the config-file input that was introduced in CodeQL Action 4.37.0 is now enabled by default. In addition to the format described there, the remote= prefix can now be used to explicitly indicate that the input refers to a remote file. All previous input formats continue to be accepted as well. #4023
  • The CodeQL Action can now make use of configured private registries in Default Setup to retrieve CodeQL configuration files from remote repositories that require authentication. This will allow customers to store their CodeQL configuration in a single repository that can then be referenced by Default Setup workflows in other repositories. We expect to roll this and other, related changes out to everyone in July. #4007

4.37.1 - 16 Jul 2026

  • Upcoming breaking change: Add a deprecation warning for customers using CodeQL version 2.20.6 and earlier. These versions of CodeQL were discontinued on 1 July 2026 alongside GitHub Enterprise Server 3.16, and will be unsupported by the next minor release of the CodeQL Action. #3956
  • Update default CodeQL bundle version to 2.26.1. #4019

4.37.0 - 08 Jul 2026

  • Update default CodeQL bundle version to 2.26.0. #3995

title: feat(group): resolve Kotlin constant-based route paths (@PostMapping(ApiPaths.X))
body:
## Summary

Adds a Kotlin binding for the language-agnostic constant resolver, so constant-referenced route paths such as `@PostMapping(ApiPaths.ORDERS)` resolve on Kotlin sources the way they already do on Java, JavaScript/TypeScript and Python.

## Motivation / context

`route-extractors/constant-resolver.ts` is the shared core for folding constant references into literal route paths. Bindings exist for Java (#2980), JavaScript/TypeScript (#3008) and Python. Kotlin had none, so byte-for-byte equivalent Spring code produced a `Route` on Java and **nothing** on Kotlin — a silent gap rather than a reported one, which is the failure mode that makes an empty result unreadable.

This is the fourth instance of an established pattern, not a new mechanism. `java-const-resolver.ts` is the model throughout, because Kotlin shares the JVM package/import model.

## Areas touched

- [x] `gitnexus/` (CLI / core / MCP server)
- [ ] `gitnexus-web/` (Vite / React UI)
- [ ] `.github/` (workflows, actions)
- [ ] `eval/` or other tooling
- [ ] Docs / agent config only

## Scope & constraints

**In scope**

- `route-extractors/kotlin-const-resolver.ts` — `resolveKotlinImport` (import specifier → file path), `extractKotlinModuleConstants` (parse tree → `ModuleConstants`), and pre-bound wrappers (`parseKotlinConstOperands` / `foldKotlinOperands` / `resolveKotlinConstant`) so callers stay language-neutral, mirroring how `spring.ts` consumes `parseJavaConstOperands`.
- `http-patterns/kotlin.ts` — the group-layer plugin builds a repo constant map in `prepareRepo` and folds constant operands in `scan`. Both are slots the `HttpLanguagePlugin` interface already declares optional; no shared wiring changed.
- Kotlin declaration forms: top-level `const val`, `object` members, `companion object` members (keyed under the **enclosing class**, since `Companion` never appears in a reference), import aliases, single-line raw strings, and `+` concatenation chains.
- A class-level `@RequestMapping` whose prefix is an unfoldable constant now **suppresses** the routes under that class, matching the rule `java.ts` already applies.

**Explicitly out of scope / not done here**

- **Ingestion-side Kotlin route extraction.** The ingestion fold (`pipeline-phases/parse-impl.ts`) runs only over `decoratorRoutes`, and `languages/kotlin.ts` declares no `extractDecoratorRoutes` because `route-extractors/spring.ts` is built on `tree-sitter-java` node types (`method_declaration`, `element_value_pair`, `marker_annotation`). Declaring the constant hooks there today would harvest a map on every Kotlin file that nothing consumes. A Kotlin ingestion-side route extractor is the prerequisite, and it would need no change to this binding. The reasoning is recorded in the new module's header.
- **The Java `@FeignClient` interface-prefix divergence.** While testing parity, the Kotlin suppression rule turned out to reach interfaces (tree-sitter-kotlin models `interface` as a `class_declaration`) while Java's does not: `java.ts`'s `findEnclosingClass` skips `interface_declaration`, yet its `@RequestMapping` arm still records the interface in `typesWithUnfoldablePrefix`, so `feignPrefixByInterfaceId` falls back to `['']` and the consumer is emitted at an unprefixed — that is, wrong — remote URL. Kotlin is the correct side here. Aligning Java changes Java's emitted graph and belongs in its own change; this PR only documents the divergence at the guard so it is not read as an oversight.
- **Fold-state reuse across route sites.** `newFoldState` rebuilds its index on every top-level fold and `resolveKotlinImport` scans it twice per import, which is linear on each axis and so quadratic when a repository grows both. Threading prepared state through `prepareRepo` touches the plugin contract, so it is deliberately left to its own change rather than bundled here.
- **The inheritance view.** `scanProject` emits a `SharedSpringType` carrying `classPrefixes: []` when the controller's own `@RequestMapping` is a constant, so an inherited route still publishes unprefixed. Measured identical with and without this PR, and `java.ts` shares the shape.
- **Forms that skip rather than guess:** string templates (`"$BASE/orders"` — joining the content runs would publish `/orders`), multi-line raw strings, `var`, custom getters, delegates, `val` in a plain class body, wildcard imports, and an `Owner.NAME` reference that collides with a same-named top-level constant. Parenthesized operands are not unwrapped either, because `parseJavaConstOperands` has no parenthesis arm and adding one to a single binding would break parity.

## Implementation notes

- **Import resolution is unique-or-nothing at every tier.** Tier 1 matches the `<package>/<Name>.kt` convention; tier 2 falls back to the unique constant-defining file in the package directory, because Kotlin does not require a file to be named after the declaration it holds. An ambiguous import returns `null`. A wrong resolution creates a false edge, which is worse than no edge.
- **Unmarked member imports are tried both ways rather than guessed.** `import a.b.C.F` is byte-identical in shape to a type import, and inferring the intent from identifier casing would be a convention-based guess, so both readings are attempted.
- **Grammar assumptions were verified against the vendored grammar rather than assumed:** `A + B + C` nests left-associatively (always two named children, so chains fold by recursion), escape sequences stay inside one `string_content` node with no silent de-escaping, templates expose `interpolated_identifier`, and `-` shares `additive_expression` with `+`. Tests pin three-plus-operand chains and `-` rejection, neither of which was previously exercised on any binding.
- No `String` type gate on declarations — the initializer decides, which matches how Kotlin is actually written.

## Testing & verification

- [x] `cd gitnexus && npm test` — **18735 passed, 2 failed.** Both failures are environmental and pre-existing: `hooks.test.ts` (the `ps`-shaped LadybugDB owner guard) and `review-agent-workflow.test.ts` (the retry script calls GNU `timeout`, which macOS does not ship). I confirmed this rather than assumed it — checking out the base commit (31c9d922) clean and running just those two files reproduces both failures there. `hooks.test.ts` is `ps`-dependent, so *which* of its cases fail varies between runs; the file fails either way. Neither file references Kotlin, route extraction or constant resolution.
- [ ] `cd gitnexus && npm run test:integration` — not run locally; this change is confined to the group-layer plugin and the new resolver, and the integration suite's route coverage is Java-side. CI should be the gate here.
- [x] `cd gitnexus && npx tsc --noEmit` — clean
- [ ] `cd gitnexus-web && npm test` — web untouched
- [ ] `cd gitnexus-web && npx tsc -b --noEmit` — web untouched
- [ ] Manual / Playwright E2E — not applicable

New tests: `test/unit/kotlin-route-const-resolver.test.ts` and `test/unit/group/kotlin-const-route-fold.test.ts`. After the review round these two files plus `test/unit/group/` run **57 files / 1210 tests**, all passing.

**Verification method, after the review round.** Findings were reproduced and fixes confirmed on paired base-vs-head worktrees, driving `prepareRepo` + `scan(tree, ctx, rel)` the way `http-route-extractor.ts` does, over 82 cases in both POSIX and Windows key styles. Reading the diff was not sufficient: two full passes of a lane-based review found nothing, while the differential fixtures found four P1s and, later, three regressions the P1 fixes themselves introduced.

The bound tests are pinned from **both** sides against a live-imported `MAX_FOLD_LENGTH` rather than asserting a bare `null`: output doubles per level while depth only increments, so 13 doublings of a one-character leaf land exactly on the limit and 14 overrun it; a 30-link reference chain resolves where a 40-link one hits the cross-file cap; an 80-term `+` chain hits the operand-parse cap where a 60-term one folds; and a 30-level shared-descendant DAG folding inside a 5 s budget pins the success memo that keeps the walk out of `O(2^depth)`. Those guards were inherited from the Java binding but nothing held them in place.

## Risk & rollout

**One behaviour change to expect, and it will look like a regression if unannounced.** `HttpRouteExtractor` runs during `group sync` (`sync.ts:297`), not on re-index — an earlier version of this section said otherwise. After a sync, a Kotlin Spring service **stops** emitting routes from classes whose `@RequestMapping` prefix is an unresolvable constant. Those routes were emitted *unprefixed*, at paths the application never served, because the literal-prefix pattern did not match a constant prefix and left `prefixByClassId` empty.

**A correction to what this section originally claimed.** It said the drop "removes wrong routes, not right ones". That was falsified in review: Kotlin permits `@RequestMapping("/lit", ApiPaths.BASE)`, and the first version of the rule dropped every route under such a class, including the ones derivable from the literal element that *is* resolvable. Suppression now fires only when **no** argument yields a usable literal prefix, and an empty path array is treated as "no prefix" rather than "an unresolvable prefix" — a second shape of the same mistake, found later by differential testing. Both are pinned by tests that assert the surviving route, not just the absent one.

No schema, CLI, MCP or `gitnexus-shared` change. Rollback is a plain revert: the new module has no callers outside the Kotlin plugin.

## Checklist

- [x] PR body meets repo minimum length
- [x] `AGENTS.md` / overlays unchanged, so no header or changelog update is due
- [x] No secrets, tokens, or machine-specific paths committed

## Summary

*A focused Kotlin HTTP route extraction change with a low and localized blast radius. The implementation is concentrated in route-pattern handling, with unit coverage for constant-based route resolution.*

**🟢 LOW blast radius. A Kotlin HTTP route extraction change for constant-based paths such as `@​PostMapping(ApiPaths.X)`, concentrated in `gitnexus/src/core/group/extractors/http-patterns/kotlin.ts` and reaching one direct dependent.**

The main implementation surface is `gitnexus/src/core/group/extractors/http-patterns/kotlin.ts`, including `kotlinFirstStringArg`, `inferKotlinOkHttpMethod`, `scanKotlinProject`, and related Kotlin controller and annotation helpers. The change also adds `gitnexus/src/core/ingestion/route-extractors/kotlin-const-resolver.ts`, with coverage in `gitnexus/test/unit/group/kotlin-const-route-fold.test.ts` and `gitnexus/test/unit/kotlin-route-const-resolver.test.ts`. The affected area is the `Http-patterns` module.

title: feat(storage): add configurable index storage and content retention tiers
body:
## Summary

Adds configurable index artifact storage and generation-time content retention tiers.

The storage and retention changes make index generation easier to operate in managed environments: callers can centralize generated artifacts in a chosen directory and control how much source-derived content is persisted.

Objective-C semantic indexing is **not** in scope here. That work landed on `main` in #3179.

## Motivation / context

GitNexus currently writes index artifacts under the source checkout by default. That works well for local usage, but managed or short-lived workspaces often need index outputs to live outside the checkout so they can be collected, retained, promoted, or cleaned up by an external orchestrator.

This PR adds `GITNEXUS_STORAGE_PATH` so a repository index can write its artifacts to a caller-selected absolute directory. That enables centralized management of index artifacts while preserving the existing default of `<repo>/.gitnexus/`.

It also adds `GITNEXUS_STORAGE_ROOT` so multiple repositories can share one external root, with an isolated `<repo-basename>-<canonical-path-hash>/` slot per repository. When both variables are set, `GITNEXUS_STORAGE_PATH` takes precedence.

`GITNEXUS_CONTENT_RETENTION=full|symbol|none` lets callers choose the generation-time content tier: keep full source text, keep only symbol-level snippets, or persist graph structure without source body text. That reduces disk usage without changing graph-oriented CLI, MCP, and UI workflows.

## Areas touched

- [x] `gitnexus/` (CLI / core / MCP server / storage resolver)
- [x] `gitnexus-web/` (source-unavailable UI when retention or missing checkouts hide file text)
- [x] Plugin hooks (registry lookup for externally stored indexes)
- [x] Docs (`README.md`, `gitnexus/README.md`) and plugin metadata

## Scope & constraints

**In scope**

- Add `GITNEXUS_STORAGE_PATH` for selecting the absolute output directory for one repository index.
- Add `GITNEXUS_STORAGE_ROOT` for a shared external root with per-repository isolated slots.
- Route graph data, metadata, parse caches, locks, branch indexes, and related index artifacts through the resolved storage path.
- Add `GITNEXUS_CONTENT_RETENTION=full|symbol|none` to control how much source-derived text is persisted during index generation.
- Persist storage and retention compatibility metadata so indexes are rebuilt when semantics change.
- Surface unavailable source content clearly in CLI, MCP, HTTP API, and Web UI flows when retention settings or missing checkouts prevent full source reads.

**Explicitly out of scope / not done here**

- Objective-C language support (shipped in #3179).
- External lifecycle orchestration such as checkout management, index promotion/rollback policy, authorization, or publication.
- Treating `GITNEXUS_STORAGE_PATH` as a shared multi-repository graph database; it is one storage directory for one repository index.

## Implementation notes

- External storage is opt-in. Without `GITNEXUS_STORAGE_PATH` or `GITNEXUS_STORAGE_ROOT`, GitNexus continues to write to `<repo>/.gitnexus/`.
- Retention tiers preserve graph structure while changing persisted source text: `full` keeps file and symbol text, `symbol` keeps symbol snippets without full file content, and `none` keeps structural graph data without source body text.
- README updates stay small; detailed behavior and non-goals are captured in this PR description.

## Testing & verification

- [x] `cd gitnexus && npm test -- test/unit/storage-resolver.test.ts test/unit/content-retention.test.ts test/unit/repo-manager.test.ts test/unit/clean-command-ownership.test.ts`
- [x] `cd gitnexus && npm test -- test/integration/external-storage-content-retention.test.ts test/integration/local-backend-calltool.test.ts`
- [x] `cd gitnexus && npx tsc --noEmit`
- [ ] Full `npm test` suite
- [ ] Manual / Playwright E2E

## Risk & rollout

Existing behavior remains the default because both storage path selection and retention tiers are opt-in. Users who do not set the new environment variables continue writing to `<repo>/.gitnexus/` with full content retention.

The main compatibility risk is reopening an index with a different storage or retention profile. The implementation records compatibility metadata and forces rebuilds when the persisted semantics no longer match the current configuration.

Rollback is straightforward: unset `GITNEXUS_STORAGE_PATH` / `GITNEXUS_STORAGE_ROOT` / `GITNEXUS_CONTENT_RETENTION` and rebuild the index with the default settings.

## Checklist

- [x] PR body meets repo minimum length
- [ ] If `AGENTS.md` / overlays changed: headers, scope block, and changelog updated per project conventions
- [x] No secrets, tokens, or machine-specific paths committed

title: fix(ingestion): treat an empty constant fold as a resolved route path, not a skip
body:
## Summary

`foldJavaOperands` returned `null` for a constant that folds to the empty string, so `@GetMapping(ROOT)` with `static final String ROOT = "";` produced no route while the literal `@GetMapping("")` on the same controller produced one. `null` from that function is the skip floor — "a piece was unresolvable" — and an empty result is not that case.

## Motivation / context

Found by the review bot on #3059 (which adds the Kotlin binding). Investigating it showed the collapse is an anomaly in one function rather than a deliberate rule, on four independent counts:

1. **The shared core does not collapse.** `resolveOperands` in `constant-resolver.ts` returns `foldExpr(...)` unfiltered, so every language that reaches the fold through the language-agnostic path — JavaScript, Python, anything without a provider hook — already treats `""` as a result.
2. **The sibling function does not collapse.** `resolveJavaConstant` returns `""` for an empty constant, and that is already pinned by an existing test: the 30-level shared-descendant DAG case added with #2980 asserts `toBe('')`, its every intermediate value being the empty string.
3. **The literal branch does not drop it.** `java.ts:608-610` skips only when `unquoteLiteral(...) === null`, so `@GetMapping("")` is kept.
4. **The doc comment says otherwise.** It reserves `null` for "when any piece is unresolvable (skip floor)".

So the binding disagreed with the core, with its own sibling, with the literal path it is meant to mirror, and with its own documentation.

## Areas touched

- [x] `gitnexus/` (CLI / core / MCP server)
- [ ] `gitnexus-web/` (Vite / React UI)
- [ ] `.github/` (workflows, actions)
- [ ] `eval/` or other tooling
- [ ] Docs / agent config only

## Scope & constraints

**In scope**

- Drop the `out === '' ? null : out` filter in `foldJavaOperands`, and explain in the doc comment why an empty fold is a success.
- Unit coverage for the new behaviour, its multi-operand form, and — as a control — that a genuinely unresolvable operand still returns `null`, so the two outcomes stay distinguishable.
- A group ↔ ingestion parity case asserting that the constant spelling now behaves like the literal one on each side.

**Explicitly out of scope / not done here**

- **The trailing-slash divergence between the two sides.** Writing the parity test surfaced that an empty method path renders as `/api/v1/` from the group extractor (`joinPath` inserts the separator ahead of an empty path) and as `/api/v1` from ingestion. This reproduces on `main` with the **literal** spelling, with no part of this change involved — I measured it before adjusting the test. It is a separate defect, so the test pins both strings as current behaviour rather than asserting the divergence away. Happy to open it as its own issue or PR.
- **The Kotlin binding.** `foldKotlinOperands` in #3059 mirrors this function line for line, including the filter. That PR will be updated to match once the shape here is agreed, so the two bindings never diverge.

## Implementation notes

An empty method path is meaningful precisely when the type carries the prefix: `@RequestMapping("/api/v1")` on the class and an empty path on the method is how Spring spells "the collection root". Dropping the route lost a real endpoint rather than avoiding a wrong one, which inverts what the skip floor is for.

The three call sites need no change — `http-patterns/java.ts`, and the ingestion hook wired at `languages/java.ts:245` — because each already branches on `=== null` and then uses the string as-is, which is exactly how they treat a literal empty path today.

## Testing & verification

- [x] `cd gitnexus && npm test` — **18697 passed, 4 failed.** All four failures are environmental and pre-existing on my macOS machine, in `analyze-index-lock-concurrency.test.ts`, `hooks.test.ts` and `review-agent-workflow.test.ts`; none references route extraction or constant resolution. The last two reproduce on a clean checkout of the base commit.
- [ ] `cd gitnexus && npm run test:integration` — not run separately; the integration specs ran as part of the suite above, after `npm run build`.
- [x] `cd gitnexus && npx tsc --noEmit` — clean
- [x] `npx prettier --check` and `npx eslint` on the three changed files — clean (eslint reports only pre-existing non-null-assertion warnings elsewhere in the file)
- [ ] `cd gitnexus-web && …` — web untouched

## Risk & rollout

**This changes the graph Java emits**, which is why it is not folded into #3059. Re-indexing a Spring service that uses an empty-valued constant as a method path will now emit a route where it previously emitted none. title: feat: Make long HTTP embedding jobs resumable
body:
## Problem

Large repositories lose hours of HTTP embedding work when one accelerator request times out. `analyze --embeddings` rebuilds the structural index, so a late endpoint failure prevents the partially inserted vectors from becoming the registered index.

Timeouts are intentionally terminal today. Some local accelerators (observed with FastFlowLM on Ryzen AI XDNA2) release the device lock when the client disconnects and succeed on the next request, so an opt-in retry is useful without changing cloud/default behavior.

## Change

- Add `GITNEXUS_EMBEDDING_RETRY_TIMEOUTS=1`; it routes per-attempt timeouts through the existing bounded retry loop (`GITNEXUS_EMBEDDING_MAX_ATTEMPTS`). Default remains off.
- Add `gitnexus embeddings sync [path]`, alongside the existing `embeddings install` command.
- `embeddings sync` writes directly into a healthy existing LadybugDB index. Each successful batch is durable; reruns load content hashes and skip matching vectors.
- Refuse to run against an index carrying `incrementalInProgress`.
- Update metadata's embedding count only after a complete pass.

## Verification

- `npx tsc --noEmit`
- `npm test -- --run test/unit/http-embedder.test.ts test/unit/cli-index-help.test.ts` — 80 passed
- `npm test -- --maxWorkers=4` — 18,728 passed, 73 skipped
- Manual interruption proof: first run timed out after persisting 1 vector; second run reported `Checkpointed vectors already present: 1` and completed 5/5 without structural re-analysis.

title: 远程 Neo4j MCP 工具可见性收敛
body:
# 规格：远程 Neo4j MCP 工具可见性收敛

## 问题陈述

GitNexus 的远程 Neo4j Docker 部署通过内嵌 MCP 端点供 LLM 查询代码知识图谱。当前部署暴露完整工具面，其中包含原始 Cypher、重命名、分组同步和跨组路由等不适合该查询型服务的能力。即使这些能力不被正常使用，它们仍增加模型选择错误工具、生成越权调用和维护复杂度的机会。

## 解决方案

仅在远程 Neo4j Docker 部署中显式启用现有 MCP 只读策略。该策略会在工具发现阶段隐藏不允许的能力，并在工具调用阶段拒绝绕过发现列表的直接调用；保留已有的只读查询工具面。

本地 stdio MCP、独立 MCP HTTP、CLI 命令和普通 Web/API 运行方式保持当前行为。Neo4j 仅继续作为存储后端选择，不作为全局 MCP 权限开关。

## 用户故事

1. 作为使用远程 GitNexus MCP 的 LLM，我希望只看到可安全查询的工具，以便减少选择错误或不可用工具的概率。
2. 作为使用远程 GitNexus MCP 的 LLM，我希望能够继续列出仓库、查询代码、查看符号上下文、分析影响范围和追踪调用路径，以便完成代码理解任务。
3. 作为远程服务管理员，我希望即使客户端手工提交隐藏工具名称，服务仍拒绝调用，以便工具收敛不是仅靠客户端界面约定。
4. 作为远程服务管理员，我希望原始 Cypher、重命名和分组管理能力不出现在远程查询 MCP 的工具列表中，以便降低操作性风险。
5. 作为本地 GitNexus 用户，我希望 stdio MCP、CLI 和本地开发行为不因远程 Neo4j 部署策略而改变，以便维持既有工作流兼容性。
6. 作为维护者，我希望 Neo4j 存储后端配置与 MCP 权限策略保持解耦，以便未来可在任意存储后端按部署需求启用只读 MCP。
7. 作为测试维护者，我希望现有只读策略的发现与调用拒绝行为继续作为回归基线，以便部署配置变更不会削弱安全边界。

## 实现决策

- 以远程 Docker 部署配置为唯一实现 seam，显式启用现有只读 MCP 策略。
- 不新增按工具名称配置的白名单，不新增新的 MCP 策略类型，不改动工具注册、dispatch 或 Neo4j backend 判断逻辑。
- 保持既有只读策略定义的查询工具可见性；其隐藏、资源清理、group 路由限制和调用拒绝语义均保持不变。
- 只影响远程部署经内嵌 MCP 端点提供的工具面；不改变本地和其他运行模式的默认环境变量。
- 远程部署可以在未来按独立需求叠加仓库 allowlist/default repo，但本次不改变仓库范围策略。

## 测试决策

- 以 MCP 协议外部行为为准：工具发现不包含被隐藏能力，直接调用被隐藏能力被拒绝，允许的查询工具仍正常可发现和调用。
- 复用现有只读 MCP 策略测试作为主要行为覆盖，避免为 Docker 配置复制工具注册或 dispatch 测试。
- 增加或更新部署配置验证，确认远程 Neo4j 服务会向运行容器传递只读策略环境变量。
- 验证范围覆盖远程部署配置解析与现有 MCP 只读策略；不启动真实远端服务、不调用生产仓库、不测试 LLM 本身。

## 范围外

- 不引入精确的工具名称 allowlist。
- 不改变工具实现、Neo4j 查询逻辑、MCP HTTP 协议、认证机制或资源模型。
- 不修改 stdio MCP、独立 HTTP MCP、CLI 或普通 Web/API 的默认工具可见性。
- 不配置仓库 allowlist、默认仓库或单仓库限制。
- 不在本次处理中部署、提交或推送。

## 补充说明

现有只读策略已覆盖发现层与调用层，因此优先复用该机制比新增“隐藏列表”更能防止客户端绕过。该策略由远程部署显式启用，避免把存储类型误当作权限模型。

title: Feature: portable index output/import for isolated exact-commit builds
body:
## Problem

Governed consumers need to index an immutable commit in an isolated checkout, validate the complete
result, and only then replace the canonical index. This prevents dirty integration-worktree bytes
from masquerading as the target commit and keeps a failed build away from the last readable index.

GitNexus 1.6.10's atomic full-rebuild swap and opt-in atomic incremental are valuable progress.
However, the public contract still appears bound to `<repo>/.gitnexus`, and the Windows path may
fall back to in-place construction. That does not let an orchestrator build in a detached checkout
and promote/import the result for the canonical repository identity.

## Requested capability

Please expose one supported provider contract:

1. `analyze --output <path>` plus a path-independent repository identity manifest; or
2. `index export <path>` / `index import <path>` for a complete, closed index.

The contract should:

- bind source repository identity and the exact indexed commit;
- keep `--index-only` semantics and avoid consumer instruction/config writes;
- avoid changing the canonical registry/index until promotion;
- validate format, completeness, readability, and functional open before promotion;
- atomically promote on the same volume, with no in-place fallback when atomic mode is required;
- leave the prior canonical index byte-identical after any build/validation/promotion failure;
- report whether full or incremental construction actually ran;
- work on Windows as a fail-closed guarantee, not best effort.

## Acceptance sketch

- Build from a detached clean checkout while the canonical integration checkout is dirty.
- Prove the output binds the requested commit, not working-tree overlays.
- Kill/fail construction before promotion; the old index remains readable and byte-identical.
- Promote once; existing readers reopen onto the new complete index.
- Reject wrong repository identity, wrong commit, incompatible format, cross-volume promotion, and
  a Windows rename failure without falling back to in-place mutation.

If 1.6.10 already has a supported seam for this, documentation pointing to that API would be enough.
The request is intentionally about provider capability; consumers should not copy `.gitnexus`
directories and hope path identity is feeling cooperative that day.

title: feat(wiki): add grok local CLI provider
body:
## Summary

Add `gitnexus wiki --provider grok` so wiki generation can use the local Grok Build CLI login (`grok --prompt-file` + JSON `.text`) instead of an HTTP API key.

```bash
gitnexus wiki --provider grok
gitnexus wiki --provider grok --model grok-build
```

## Motivation / context

Wiki already supports local CLIs (`cursor`, `claude`, `codex`, `opencode`) that skip the API-key prompt. Grok Build is a local CLI with a different spawn contract (prompt file, not stdin/`-p`), so it needs a dedicated client rather than `runLocalCLI`.

## Areas touched

- [x] `gitnexus/` (CLI / core / MCP server)
- [ ] `gitnexus-web/` (Vite / React UI)
- [ ] `.github/` (workflows, actions)
- [ ] `eval/` or other tooling

## Scope & constraints

**In scope**

- Dedicated `grok-client.ts`: spawn `grok` with `--prompt-file`, `--output-format json`, `--max-turns 15`, tool denylist, `--sandbox strict`, empty temp `--cwd` (do not ingest repo `AGENTS.md`)

- Timeout: wait for child `close` (SIGKILL grace, then hard deadline) before `fs.rm` of the temp sandbox; skip `rm` if `close` never fires
- Parse: require non-empty JSON `text` and `stopReason=end_turn` (case-insensitive). Incomplete/missing/unknown reasons throw distinct errors

**Explicitly out of scope / not done here**

- Index format / MCP tool / workflow / env-var changes (N/A for this PR)
- `CHANGELOG.md` Unreleased hunk (DoD: release process owns that file)

- Cursor-shaped dedicated client, not stdin `runLocalCLI`.
- Never `--yolo` / `--always-approve`. Non-zero exit and JSON `{type:"error"}` throw with stderr so `grok login` failures surface.

- [ ] CI Gate + Windows platform-sensitive shards on this head SHA (was previously green only on `4376ba3`)

- Local process spawn of `grok`; no index schema, MCP, or persistence format change. Existing `~/.gitnexus/config.json` is unchanged until the user passes `--provider grok`.
- Rollback: revert the PR; wiki HTTP and other local providers are untouched.
- No secrets, tokens, or machine-specific paths.
