title: Read-only commands do not default to the repo containing cwd, though the resolver already uses cwd to disambiguate duplicate names
body:
### Area

gitnexus (CLI / core / indexing / MCP server)

### Summary

Read-only graph commands refuse to run without an explicit `repo` whenever more than one repo is registered — even when invoked from inside a registered repo — although the resolver already uses cwd to disambiguate duplicate names.

### Context

Verified on **1.6.10** (npm latest), isolated `GITNEXUS_HOME`, two indexed repos.

This is not a request for multi-repo workspace support (#2193, #1308). It is about the *default* when the caller is unambiguously standing inside one indexed repo.

What makes it odd is that cwd-awareness already exists on this path. With two registry entries sharing a name, `-r <name>` now resolves correctly by cwd — I confirmed a symbol present only in repo B is found from B and reports `Target not found` from A. So the resolver can identify the cwd repo; it just won't use it as the default when `repo` is omitted.

The asymmetry is visible within the CLI: `gitnexus status` resolves from cwd (`findRepo(process.cwd())`), while `impact` / `context` / `query` / `cypher` / `detect-changes` do not.

Compounding it: the block `analyze` writes into CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md prescribes repo-less calls — `impact({target: "symbolName", direction: "upstream"})` — i.e. exactly the call that cannot work for any user with a second repo indexed. An agent following the generated instructions hits this on its first call.

`GITNEXUS_MCP_DEFAULT_REPO` covers the MCP server but has no CLI equivalent, and pins a single repo rather than following cwd.

### Expected behavior

With no `repo` argument and >1 repo registered, resolve to the registered repo containing `process.cwd()` (longest-prefix match). Error only when cwd is outside every registered repo. An explicit `repo` always wins.

### Actual behavior

```
$ cd /path/to/indexed-repo-a
$ gitnexus impact crypto.ts -d upstream
{
  "error": "Multiple repositories indexed. Specify which one with the \"repo\" parameter. Available: ..."
}
```

Same cwd with `-r <name>` or `-r <abs path>` succeeds. `gitnexus status` in that same directory resolves fine.

### Environment

gitnexus 1.6.10 (npm), macOS 24.6.0, node 20, stdio MCP + CLI. Two repos registered in an isolated `GITNEXUS_HOME`.

title: impact: a repo-relative file path never resolves (basename does), and the miss still returns impactedCount 0 / risk UNKNOWN
body:
### Area

gitnexus (CLI / core / indexing / MCP server)

### Summary

`impact` resolves a file by **basename** but not by the repo-relative **path** the graph itself stores, and the miss returns a normal-shaped `impactedCount: 0` / `risk: "UNKNOWN"` body alongside the error.

### Context

Verified on **1.6.10** (npm latest) against a 1,480-file TypeScript/JS repo.

A repo-relative path is the most natural way for an agent to name a file, and it is exactly the string the graph reports back in `target.filePath`. Feeding that same string back in as a target fails.

Related but distinct: #3015 covers `impact` fail-opening when *analyze dropped a file*. Here the file is indexed correctly and the node exists — only the target lookup misses. 1.6.10 also added a generated-prompt line ("MUST treat `risk: UNKNOWN` as unresolved, not as low"), which mitigates the consequence via prompt text but not the resolution miss itself.

Mechanism, as far as I could trace it on 1.6.3 source (`resolveSymbolCandidates`, `mcp/local/local-backend.ts`): a target containing `/` or `:` is treated as already-qualified and matched with `WHERE n.id = $sym OR n.name = $sym`. A File node's id carries a `File:` prefix and its `name` is only the basename, so a bare repo-relative path can match neither. `n.filePath` is consulted only in the separate `hints.file_path` branch, where it is ANDed onto a name match.

### Expected behavior

A repo-relative path that matches a File node's `filePath` resolves to that node — the same node the basename resolves to. If a target cannot be resolved, the result should not also carry a `0` / `UNKNOWN` blast radius that reads as a real answer.

### Actual behavior

```
$ gitnexus impact supabase/functions/_shared/crypto.ts -r <repo> -d upstream
{
  "error": "Target 'supabase/functions/_shared/crypto.ts' not found",
  "target": { "name": "supabase/functions/_shared/crypto.ts" },
  "direction": "upstream",
  "impactedCount": 0,
  "risk": "UNKNOWN"
}

$ gitnexus impact crypto.ts -r <repo> -d upstream
{
  "target": { "id": "File:supabase/functions/_shared/crypto.ts",
              "name": "crypto.ts",
              "filePath": "supabase/functions/_shared/crypto.ts" },
  "impactedCount": 25,
  "risk": "MEDIUM",
  "summary": { "direct": 13, "processes_affected": 0, "modules_affected": 0 }
}
```

Same node, same repo, same flags — 25 dependants or 0, depending only on how the file was named.

### Environment

gitnexus 1.6.10 (npm), macOS 24.6.0, node 20. Repo: ~1,480 files, TS/JS/JSX/Python.

title: impact risk is not comparable across target types: a File can never trip the processes/modules thresholds, so wider blast radius scores lower
body:
### Area

gitnexus (CLI / core / indexing / MCP server)

### Summary

`risk` is not comparable across target types: two of its four inputs are structurally unreachable for a File target, so a file with a *wider* blast radius scores lower than a function with a narrower one.

### Context

Verified on **1.6.10** (npm latest), one repo, one module, four targets, all `--direction upstream` at the default depth:

| target | kind | impactedCount | direct | processes | modules | risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `crypto.ts` | File | **25** | 13 | 0 | 0 | **MEDIUM** |
| `getEncryptionKey` | Function | 15 | 2 | 4 | 2 | **HIGH** |
| `decryptToken` | Function | 17 | 3 | 4 | 2 | **HIGH** |
| `encryptToken` | Function | 3 | 3 | 0 | 0 | LOW |

The file that contains `getEncryptionKey` and `decryptToken` scores *below* both of them while impacting more.

The scorer is a flat disjunction over `direct`, `processes_affected`, `modules_affected` and total, with no branch on target kind. `processes_affected` and `modules_affected` are always `0` for a File target — process participation is recorded for symbol-level nodes, so a File can never accumulate those two axes. A File is therefore scored on two of four axes while a Function is scored on four, and the two thresholds that most easily reach HIGH/CRITICAL are the ones a File can never trip.

Related to #2975 (wording/thresholds vs runtime), but distinct: that is about documented thresholds disagreeing with the scorer, this is the scorer's inputs being unreachable for a whole class of target.

### Expected behavior

Either score File and symbol targets on a common basis, or make the scale explicit in the result so a consumer can tell that a File's `risk` is not comparable to a Function's.

### Actual behavior

As tabulated above — more impact, lower label.

**One caution for whoever picks this up.** The obvious fix — bridging File→symbol via `DEFINES` so a File inherits the processes/modules of the symbols it defines — was tested here and over-inflates badly: sampling 10 files with exactly one importer, 8 of 10 moved from LOW to HIGH or CRITICAL under the current thresholds, because `modules` is capped at 20 and CRITICAL sits at `processes >= 5` / `modules >= 5`, so the bridged axes saturate immediately. Threshold recalibration is a prerequisite for that approach, not a follow-up. Reporting the defect rather than proposing that patch.

### Environment

gitnexus 1.6.10 (npm), macOS 24.6.0, node 20. Repo ~1,480 files, 22.4k nodes / 55.3k edges.

title: Generated CLAUDE.md block gates every imperative on an edit, so read-only sessions never invoke the tools (measured 0/9 runs)
body:
### Area

Documentation / developer experience

### Summary

Every imperative in the generated `<!-- gitnexus:start -->` block is conditioned on an edit, so a read-only task trips none of them and the MCP tools go entirely unused — measured at 0 tool calls across 9 runs.

### Context

Verified on **1.6.10** (npm latest). The rendered block carries 7 imperative lines; 6 are explicitly gated on edit / commit / rename:

- MUST run impact analysis **before editing**
- MUST analyze graph changes **before committing**
- MUST warn the user ... **before proceeding with edits**
- NEVER **edit** a function, class, or method before ... impact analysis
- NEVER **rename** symbols with find-and-replace
- NEVER **commit** before ... graph change analysis

The 7th ("never read `UNKNOWN` as an all-clear") is only reachable once `impact` has already been run. The read-path guidance is two non-imperative "When exploring ..., use ..." bullets. Nothing imperative attaches to a read-only action.

**Measurement.** I benchmarked this as one arm of a controlled 27-run comparison on a 274k-LOC repo: three read-only codebase questions (transitive module dependents, top-level functions in a 4,444-line file, a cross-layer trace), 3 repetitions, sonnet, `--strict-mcp-config`, hooks neutralised identically across arms.

In the GitNexus arm the agent made **0 gitnexus tool calls in 9 of 9 runs** — it never even enumerated the tools. All 13 were connected and listed; the block was present in CLAUDE.md. It answered every question with `grep`. The comparison arm, a different graph tool whose session directive is unconditional rather than edit-gated, was invoked in 8 of 9 runs on identical questions. Same deferred-tool mechanism, same model, opposite outcome — the difference is the framing.

This is a real cost: the index was built and current, and the agent went around it. It also compounds #3073 — the block's prescribed calls omit `repo`, which cannot work once a second repo is indexed.

Distinct from #2954, which asks *where* the block is injected; this is about what it says.

### Expected behavior

At least one imperative that fires on a read. Something of the shape: *"MUST use `query`/`context`/`impact` instead of grep when asked who calls, what breaks, what imports, or how a flow works — the graph has edges, grep has strings."*

### Actual behavior

Read-only sessions never invoke the tools. 0/9 runs, as above.

### Environment

gitnexus 1.6.10 (template text); benchmark arm run against a 1.6.3 index, Claude Code stdio MCP, 13 tools connected.

title: `status` reports "stale" for modifications to files the index does not track
body:
### Area

gitnexus (CLI / core / indexing / MCP server)

### Summary

`gitnexus status` reports an index as stale whenever the working tree contains any modified or untracked file, including files the index does not cover, and the prescribed remedy of re-running `gitnexus analyze` cannot clear the condition. The only way back to `up-to-date` is to commit, stash, or delete the offending file.

### Context

`isUpToDate` in `dist/cli/status.js` is a four-way AND:

    currentCommit === activeMeta.lastCommit
      && runnerIdentityIsCurrent
      && incompleteReasons.length === 0
      && (currentCommit === '' || !isWorkingTreeDirty(repo.repoPath))

On a real repository of mine, `status --json` shows the first three conjuncts
passing and only the dirty check failing:

    status:               stale
    indexed commit:       <COMMIT>
    current commit:       <COMMIT>       (identical)
    runnerIdentityStatus: current
    incompleteReasons:    []

The single dirty entry was one modified tracked file in an agent-tooling
directory that GitNexus does not index. `meta.json` carries a `fileHashes`
map of the 210 files the index actually covers, and that directory is absent
from it. Hashing all 210 recorded entries against disk:

    indexed files: 210
    hash matches on disk: 210 | differ: 0 | missing: 0

So the index is byte-current with every file it covers, and is reported stale
because of a file it has never looked at.

`isWorkingTreeDirty` in `dist/storage/git.js` already excludes the tooling
paths that churn during normal use (`.gitnexus`, `.claude`, `.cursor`,
`.agents`, `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`), which suggests this class of false
positive is known. The exclusion list is an allowlist of specific tools, so
any other tool directory, or any untracked file at all, reintroduces it.

Two aggravating details:

1. `isWorkingTreeDirty` runs `git status --porcelain` without `-uno`, so a
   single untracked file is sufficient. A scratch file, a build artifact, or
   an editor swap file permanently pins the repository to "stale".
2. The message printed alongside the verdict is `re-run gitnexus analyze`,
   but `analyze` does not and cannot clear a dirty working tree. The advice
   is not actionable.

Suggested direction: `meta.fileHashes` already holds everything needed to answer this precisely. Comparing those
recorded hashes against disk would treat the index as current when they all match, instead of consulting a repo-wide dirty boolean that covers files the index never reads.

### Expected behavior

`gitnexus status` reports `up-to-date` when the index reflects the current
state of every file it covers.

If a dirty working tree must keep producing a `stale` verdict, then either
`gitnexus analyze` should be able to clear it, or the message should say what
would actually resolve it rather than prescribing a command that has no effect
on the condition.

### Actual behavior

Any modified or untracked file anywhere in the working tree, whether or not
the index covers it, forces `status` to report:

    Status: stale (re-run gitnexus analyze)

Running `gitnexus analyze` completes successfully, reports `changed=0`, writes
fresh metadata, and leaves the verdict unchanged. The verdict clears only when
the file is committed, stashed, or deleted.

### Steps to reproduce

Verified on a fresh single-file repository, not only on a large one.

1. Create and index a clean repository:

       git init . && printf 'export function a(){return 1;}\n' > a.js
       git add -A && git commit -m init
       gitnexus analyze

2. Confirm the baseline:

       gitnexus status
       # Status: up-to-date

3. Create one untracked, non-source file:

       touch notes.txt

4. Check status:

       gitnexus status
       # Status: stale (re-run gitnexus analyze)

5. Run the prescribed remedy:

       gitnexus analyze
       # Incremental: changed=0, added=3, deleted=0
       # Repository indexed successfully (7.7s)

6. Check status again:

       gitnexus status
       # Status: stale (re-run gitnexus analyze)     <-- unchanged

7. Remove the file:

       rm notes.txt
       gitnexus status
       # Status: up-to-date

Steps 4 through 6 loop indefinitely. No invocation of `analyze` reaches a
state that satisfies `status` while the file exists.

### Environment

- OS: Windows 11 Home, build 10.0.26200
- Node: 24.13.1
- gitnexus version: 1.6.10.
- git: invoked as `git status --porcelain` via execFileSync

### Logs / screenshots

_No response_

title: PHP: detect generated-client Request(method, host . resourcePath) consumer shape
body:
## Summary

openapi-generator-php / swagger-codegen PHP clients build every operation as:

```php
$resourcePath = '/foo/bar';
...
$request = new Request($method, $host . $resourcePath);
```

The existing PHP consumer patterns only match `$client->verb('/literal/path')` — a
generated client built this way (or `\GuzzleHttp\Psr7\Request` behind a `use` import)
produces zero consumer contracts today, even though `$resourcePath` is always a plain
string literal assigned a few lines above the call. This is exactly the gap the
module's own docblock already flags as a follow-up ("URLs built via binary
concatenation... require constant-folding the surrounding scope").

- Adds a pattern for `new [Qualified\]Request(...)` constructor calls.
- Resolves the path via a conservative, single-scope backward constant fold: the
  last variable in the path argument's concatenation chain is resolved to a
  `$var = '<literal>';` assignment found earlier in the same enclosing
  function/method body (searched level by level through `if`/`try`/`foreach`
  nesting, never crossing into a different function). A miss just leaves the
  endpoint undetected — never a wrong one.
- The HTTP verb is often itself a parameter in generated clients, not a literal
  at the call site — when unresolved, the detection reports a wildcard method
  (`'*'`), matching this project's own manifest-link convention for a contract
  whose verb isn't pinned.
- `hasConsumerSignals` is widened to stay a proven superset of what `scan()` now
  detects (its own documented contract, checked by `http-consumer-signals.test.ts`).
- Docblock notes this is a deliberately narrow, single-scope fallback — not this
  language's entry into the shared cross-file constant-fold the other languages
  use (`constant-resolver.ts` via `java-const-resolver.ts` / `python-const-resolver.ts`
  / `js-const-resolver.ts`). PHP has no such binding yet; adding one is a separate,
  larger project (this repo's PHP import resolution for `use`-statements is its
  own multi-file subsystem built for symbol/scope resolution, not constant
  extraction) and is intentionally out of scope here.

## Test plan

- [x] 9 new `scan()`-level unit tests in `test/unit/group/php-guzzle-request-ctor.test.ts`:
      member-access host resolution, fully-qualified class name, purely literal call,
      negative (different function scope), negative (non-`Request` constructor),
      negative (non-HTTP literal), last-of-3 concatenation, parenthesized right
      operand (regression), enclosing-`if`-block resolution + function-boundary
      negative (regression).
- [x] 2 new `hasConsumerSignals` cases + 1 negative in `http-consumer-signals.test.ts`,
      verifying the widened regex stays a superset of what `scan()` detects.
- [x] `tsc --noEmit` clean.
- [x] `eslint` clean.
- [x] Full `test/unit/group` suite green (1035+/1037 — 2 pre-existing native `EBUSY`
      failures on a `.lbug` file in `bridge-meta-swap-window.test.ts`, unrelated
      subsystem, reproduces in isolation on unchanged `main` too on this machine —
      Windows-specific file-lock flake, not caused by this change).

title: analyze overwrites committed .claude/skills/gitnexus/*/SKILL.md with older bundled copies, and --skip-agents-md does not protect them
body:
### Area

gitnexus (CLI / core / indexing / MCP server)

### Problem

A full index build rewrites every `.claude/skills/gitnexus/*/SKILL.md` from the bundled templates, discarding whatever the repository has committed there. In our case the regenerated files were **older** than the ones in git: 6 files changed, **76 insertions and 165 deletions**, and the content that disappeared was the guidance GitNexus's own generated `CLAUDE.md` tells agents to follow.

`--skip-agents-md` does not cover it. Its help text is:

```
--skip-agents-md   Skip updating the gitnexus section in AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md
```

which reads like "do not touch my checked-in agent instructions" — but the skills are agent instructions too, and they are rewritten anyway. We only noticed because `git status` was dirty after an analyze run we had explicitly told to leave our agent files alone.

Concretely, `gitnexus-cli/SKILL.md` lost this:

```diff
-Commands below use `node .gitnexus/run.cjs <command>` — the project-local runner `gitnexus analyze` drops next to the index. It auto-selects an available runner at call time (global `gitnexus`, else `pnpm dlx`, else `npx`), so no package-manager assumption and no global install is required.
-
-> **Not analyzed yet, or `node .gitnexus/run.cjs` reports `Cannot find module`** … On **npm 11.x**, if `npx` crashes during install (`node.target is null`), install once with `npm i -g gitnexus` … See [#1939](https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/issues/1939).
+All commands work via `npx` — no global install required.

-node .gitnexus/run.cjs analyze
+npx gitnexus analyze
```

Two things make this more than cosmetic:

1. **It reintroduces a documented failure.** The removed paragraph is the npm 11 `npx` workaround for #1939. After the overwrite, an agent following the skill runs `npx gitnexus analyze` and hits the crash that paragraph exists to route around.
2. **It contradicts the `CLAUDE.md` GitNexus itself maintains.** That file still says *"Run `node .gitnexus/run.cjs analyze` from the project root"*, while the regenerated skill says to use `npx`. One analyze run leaves the two sets of agent instructions disagreeing about how to invoke the tool.

### Reproduction

gitnexus 1.6.3, node v22.6.0, macOS 26.5.2. In a repo that commits `.claude/skills/gitnexus/`:

```bash
git clone --depth 1 <repo> /tmp/t && cd /tmp/t
gitnexus analyze --skip-agents-md
git status --short          # 6 modified SKILL.md files
```

The trigger is a **full index build**, which makes this hit exactly the cases where a human is least likely to be watching:

| Run | Clobbers? |
|---|---|
| First analyze in a fresh clone, checkout or **git worktree** | **yes** |
| `analyze --force` | **yes** |
| Incremental analyze with an existing `.gitnexus/` | no |

The worktree case is the one that bit us: every new worktree is a first analyze, so a repo that maintains its skills gets them silently reverted on every branch it works on.

### Expected

A full build should not discard committed skill files, or at minimum `--skip-agents-md` should mean what it appears to mean and leave every agent-facing file alone.

### Proposed solution

Any one of these would be enough for us, roughly in order of preference:

1. Do not overwrite a `SKILL.md` whose content differs from the bundled template unless a flag asks for it — write only when the file is absent or byte-identical to a previous generation.
2. Extend `--skip-agents-md` to cover generated skills (or add the `--skip-skills` flag proposed in #656, which asks for the same switch from the duplication angle).
3. Regenerate only the delimited GitNexus section of a skill file, the way `AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md` sections are handled, so local additions survive.

Related: #656 (skip skill generation, framed as duplication rather than data loss), #2540 (skills instructing `run.cjs` after Hub adoption — this is the same divergence in the other direction), #2104.

### Workaround

`git checkout -- .claude/skills/gitnexus/` after every full build, and check `git status` after any analyze in a fresh worktree.

title: fix(impact): make File risk comparable via shared axes (#3075)

## Summary
- File `impact` risk only scored on import/direct/total axes, so a File with a wider blast radius could rank below a Function in the same file that also tripped process/module HIGH/CRITICAL.
- Shared `scoreImpactRisk` keeps the existing HIGH/CRITICAL thresholds. File and `skipEnrichment` targets now expose `riskScale` and `riskSharedAxes` so agents can compare like with like.
- Function/Method/Class scoring is unchanged. No DEFINES-bridge of File→symbol processes/modules.

title: fix(status): judge freshness by covered files, not a dirty working tree
body:
Closes #3077

## The problem

`gitnexus status` reported `stale (re-run gitnexus analyze)` whenever the working tree held any modified or untracked file — including files the index never reads. Because `analyze` cannot commit, stash or delete such a file, the remedy it printed could not clear the verdict. The only way back to `up-to-date` was to remove the file.

Reproduced end to end on the issue's exact steps before changing anything:

```
step2  baseline .......................... up-to-date
step4  touch notes.txt .................. stale (re-run gitnexus analyze)
step5  gitnexus analyze ................. Incremental: changed=0, added=3, deleted=0
step6  gitnexus status .................. stale (re-run gitnexus analyze)   <-- unchanged
```

The reporter's real-world case reproduced too: with one modified tracked file under a tool directory the indexer skips (an ignored `.lock` extension, absent from `meta.fileHashes`), every covered file hash-matched disk byte for byte and `status` still said stale.

## The fix

`meta.fileHashes` already records the exact set of files a run covered, so the question is answered directly instead of via a repo-wide dirty boolean.

The new `detectIndexContentDrift` reuses **analyze's own** `walkRepositoryPaths`, `computeFileHashes` and `diffFileHashes`, so `status` and `analyze` agree on coverage by construction rather than by convention — ignore rules, dotfile handling and the large-file cap cannot drift apart.

| Scenario | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Freshly indexed repo | up-to-date | up-to-date |
| Untracked scratch file present | stale, unclearable | stale, and `analyze` clears it |
| Same, after running `analyze` | stale (the loop) | **up-to-date** |
| Modified tracked file the index doesn't cover | stale, unclearable | **up-to-date** |
| Modified file the index does cover | stale | stale, and now names the file |

The untracked-file case still reports stale at step 4 deliberately: `analyze` really does index `notes.txt` (it reported `added=3`), so the index genuinely lacked a file it covers, and reporting up-to-date would trade this bug for a worse one — certifying an index that is missing a file. What goes away is the unclearable part, which is the issue's own stated fallback ("either `gitnexus analyze` should be able to clear it").

## Notes for review

- **`isWorkingTreeDirty` behavior is unchanged.** Impact analysis rates it HIGH (direct callers `runFullAnalysisInner` and `statusCommand`), so it only sources its pathspecs from the new shared constant. The eight existing tests pinning its exclusion semantics — including the `.agentsrc` prefix-collision and nested `subdir/.agents/` cases — still pass. It survives in `status` purely as the fallback when the per-file comparison cannot run (metadata predating `fileHashes`). analyze's fast-path gate is untouched, which is fine: a false "dirty" there costs only a hash diff that finds nothing.
- **One shared exclusion list.** A first cut reported a freshly indexed repo as stale with `2 added: AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md` — analyze rewrites those stats blocks *after* recording hashes, so they read as `added` on a first run and `changed` on every run after. The two checks held separate copies of that list; they now share `GITNEXUS_MANAGED_PATHS`, so a path added to one cannot silently become a permanent stale verdict in the other.
- **Cost.** The scan runs only once the cheap metadata checks already agree, so a stale-by-commit repo answers without scanning (~1.8s on this repo, `contentDrift: "not-checked"`). When it does run it is ~1.4s here (2242 files, 30MB).
- **Diagnosability.** `status` now names the drifted files, and `--json` gains an additive `contentDrift` field (`current` / `drifted` with counts and a capped sample / `unmeasurable` / `not-checked`). `schemaVersion` stays `1` — existing consumers read `status` and are unaffected.
- `walkRepositoryPaths` gains an optional `quiet` flag so `status` does not inherit analyze's large-file warnings; the default is unchanged.

## Test plan

- [x] New `test/unit/index-content-drift.test.ts` (13 tests) against real temp directories: uncovered-file edits stay `current`, covered edits/additions/deletions report `drifted`, GitNexus's own output is ignored on both sides, missing hashes are `unmeasurable` rather than `current`, and re-recording coverage clears the verdict.
- [x] New `test/unit/status-content-drift.test.ts` (7 tests) for the verdict order, the working-tree fallback, and the skip when metadata alone decides.
- [x] `git-utils.test.ts` + `list-status-branch.test.ts` unchanged and passing — 76 tests green across the four files.
- [x] `npx tsc --noEmit`, prettier and eslint clean.
- [x] Manual end-to-end run of the issue's steps 1–7 against the built CLI, plus the uncovered-tracked-file case and a covered-source-edit control.

title: fix(impact): resolve repo-relative file paths via filePath (fixes #3074)
body:
Fixes #3074

Same File node resolved by basename (`crypto.ts` → 25 deps, MEDIUM) but missed when named repo-relative (`supabase/functions/_shared/crypto.ts` → 0/UNKNOWN).

title: loadParsedFilesForPaths forces a full GC every 8 shards regardless of shard size — ~2,000 full GCs per analyze when parse shards are small
body:
### Area

gitnexus (CLI / core / indexing / MCP server)

### Summary

loadParsedFilesForPaths (gitnexus/src/storage/parsedfile-store.ts) calls forceGc() on a fixed cadence — if ((i & 7) === 7) — while streaming ParsedFile shards back for scope-resolution. The cadence implicitly assumes shards close to the default 8 MiB worker sub-batch. When shards are small (many small source files, or GITNEXUS_WORKER_SUB_BATCH_MAX_BYTES lowered so that a worker timeout can be attributed to a single file), the loader performs hundreds of full-heap collections per language pass while reclaiming almost nothing, and scope-resolution wall time becomes GC-dominated.

### Context

We run GitNexus as the indexing backend of a code-review service on Java-dominant monorepos. To attribute worker timeouts to exactly one file we set GITNEXUS_WORKER_SUB_BATCH_MAX_BYTES=1 (one file per worker job), which yields one shard per file. Measured on 1.6.10-rc.205; dist/storage/parsedfile-store.js is byte-identical in 1.6.10.

### Expected behavior

GC frequency during shard loading should track the transient bytes actually deserialized (the comment above forceGc cites "~5 GB of avoidable transient" as the thing being reclaimed), not the shard count. Loading a ~480 MiB store should cost a handful of full GCs per pass.

### Actual behavior

On a ~6.3k-file monorepo (Java plus two single-file languages; ~91k nodes / ~242k edges):
- 5,751 data shards, median 28 KiB, mean 86 KiB, ~480 MiB of JSON in total.
- loadParsedFilesForPaths runs once per language, so three passes over the store.
- Each pass triggers ~718 forced full GCs (5,751 / 8); ~2,154 per analyze. Every one scans the full retained heap analyze has already built, so each GC is expensive precisely when it has nothing to reclaim.
- With everything else equal, replacing the fixed cadence by a byte budget took the warm-parse-cache analyze from 366.1 s to 71.1 s (−295 s). Node/edge output hashes identical; peak RSS differed by ~19 MB.

### Steps to reproduce

1. A Java repo with ~5k+ source files.
2. GITNEXUS_WORKER_SUB_BATCH_MAX_BYTES=1 gitnexus analyze --force <repo> (cold; populates parsedfile-store/ and durable parsedfile-cache/).
3. Run it again (warm parse cache: durable shards restored, scope-resolution streams them back).
4. Count forceGc calls during scope-resolution (NODE_OPTIONS=--trace-gc or a temporary counter): ≈ shards / 8 per language pass; "Linking symbols" wall time scales with shard count rather than bytes.

At the default 8 MiB sub-batch the cadence works out to ~64 MiB per GC and the problem is invisible; it appears as soon as shards get small.

### Environment

Linux x86_64 (glibc 2.38), Node v22.22.0, gitnexus 1.6.10-rc.205 (loader unchanged in 1.6.10)

### Logs / screenshots

### Proposed fix (what we run locally)

Keep the GC, size it by bytes:

- accumulate `Buffer.byteLength(raw)` of every shard read;
- call `forceGc()` only when the accumulated bytes since the last GC reach a budget (we use 128 MiB — far below the ~5 GB transient the comment describes, and well within the default heap), then reset the counter;
- still yield to the event loop (`setImmediate`) every 128 shards so pending I/O and incremental GC can run;
- a single shard larger than the budget triggers a GC right after it is read.

Retained set, JSON as source of truth and the fallback semantics are untouched; only GC timing changes.

### Logs
Can attach `--trace-gc` output and a CPU profile on request.

title: `loadParsedFilesForPaths` deserializes the whole ParsedFile store on every language pass before filtering by path — a 3-language repo JSON.parses the same ~480 MiB three times
body:
### Area

gitnexus (CLI / core / indexing / MCP server)

### Summary

`loadParsedFilesForPaths(storagePath, wantPaths)` (`gitnexus/src/storage/parsedfile-store.ts`) reads every `*.json` shard in `parsedfile-store/`, `JSON.parse`s it through the interning reviver, and only then keeps the entries whose `filePath` is in `wantPaths`. Scope-resolution calls it once per language (`loadStoreFor(paths)` in `gitnexus/src/core/ingestion/scope-resolution/pipeline/phase.ts`), so a repo with N languages deserializes the entire store N times — even when a language owns two files. Since 1.6.10 the parse phase calls it again for data-route-table files (`parse-impl.ts`), which adds one more full pass whenever such files exist.


### Context

Same deployment as #3086: GitNexus as the indexing backend of a code-review service, Java-dominant monorepos, one file per worker job (`GITNEXUS_WORKER_SUB_BATCH_MAX_BYTES=1`). Measured on 1.6.10-rc.205; `parsedfile-store.ts` and `phase.ts` are unchanged in 1.6.10.


### Expected behavior

A language pass should open only the shards that contain at least one wanted path. The cost of loading ParsedFiles for a language should be proportional to that language's files, not to the store size.


### Actual behavior

On a ~6.3k-file monorepo (Java plus two languages with a single file each):

- 5,751 shards, ~480 MiB of JSON.
- The two single-file languages each deserialize all 5,751 shards to keep one entry; Java does it a third time.
- Before we changed anything else, the Java resolver's own work was ~28 s per pass while shard deserialization took over ten minutes per analyze — the outer JSON loop, not resolution, dominated "Linking symbols".
- With a per-shard path index in place (and our other local cache changes applied), removing only the index costs +8.3 s (63.3 s → 71.6 s); the remaining load is bounded by the shards that actually contain wanted paths. Output node/edge hashes identical.


### Steps to reproduce

1. A Java repo with ~5k+ files that also contains a couple of files in other languages (e.g. one Python and one shell script).
2. `GITNEXUS_WORKER_SUB_BATCH_MAX_BYTES=1 gitnexus analyze --force <repo>`, twice (second run warm).
3. Instrument `loadParsedFilesForPaths` (count `readFile` calls per invocation): every language pass reads `shards.length` files regardless of `wantPaths.size`.
4. Compare wall time of the minor-language passes with the Java pass: they are dominated by the same full-store deserialization.


### Environment

- Linux x86_64 (glibc 2.38), Node v22.22.0
- gitnexus 1.6.10-rc.205 (loader and per-language call site unchanged in 1.6.10)


### Logs / screenshots

### Proposed fix (what we run locally)

Persist a per-shard path list next to each shard (`<shard>.json.paths`, one `filePath` per line) from both shard writers (`persistParsedFileChunk` / `persistParsedFileChunkSync`), and carry it along in `restoreDurableParsedFileShard`. The loader reads the sidecars first, opens only shards with at least one wanted path, and falls back to reading a shard whenever its sidecar is missing or corrupt — so stores written by older builds behave exactly as today and can be backfilled lazily. Shard JSON is untouched.

An equivalent alternative is a store-level `index.json` (path → shardId) written when the parse phase completes; the per-shard sidecar is simpler to keep consistent with the durable content-addressed cache.

### Logs

Can attach a `readFile`-count trace per language pass and the timing breakdown on request.

title: parse cache: chunk granularity scales with the worker pool (16 MiB chunks on 8 workers → a one-line edit re-parses the whole repo), and adding/deleting a file shifts every later chunk's key
body:
### Area

gitnexus (CLI / core / indexing / MCP server)

### Summary

The parse cache is keyed per chunk, and chunks are formed in `parse-impl.ts` by sorting parseable files by path and cutting them sequentially at a byte budget of `max(2 MiB, effectivePoolSize × 2 MiB)`. Two consequences make the cache miss far more often than `parse-cache.ts` documents ("a change to a single file invalidates only that file's chunk — typically 1 of ~50 chunks on a 1000-file repo"):

1. On an 8-worker machine the budget is 16 MiB, so a mid-size repo is 1–2 chunks and any edit re-parses (almost) everything. The chunk layout — and therefore the cache keys — also differ between machines with different core counts.
2. Chunk membership depends on a file's position in the sorted list and on the cumulative bytes before it, so adding, deleting or renaming a file shifts the boundary of every later chunk. A single added file can invalidate 100 % of the chunks even though no other file changed.

### Context

Same deployment as #3086 (GitNexus as an indexing backend for code review; per-push re-analyze of large Java monorepos). Pushes routinely add/delete/rename files, so in practice the warm parse cache rarely helps. Reproduced below on a public repo with stock 1.6.10.

### Expected behavior

As documented in `parse-cache.ts`: a change to one file invalidates only that file's chunk, and a warm re-analyze after a small change is close to free. Cache keys should not depend on how many workers the machine has.

### Actual behavior

Reproduced on `alibaba/spring-ai-alibaba` @ `f82da0b` (2,615 parseable files, 1,607 of them Java), stock gitnexus 1.6.10, `--index-only`:

**Default budget (8 workers → 16 MiB chunks)**
- Cold analyze: 34 s, **2 chunks** for the whole repo.
- Append one comment line to one Java file, re-analyze: 1 chunk invalidated = **2,193 files / 180 MiB of ParsedFile shards re-parsed**; warm run 34 s — identical to cold.

**`GITNEXUS_CHUNK_BYTE_BUDGET=262144`, `--workers 1` (47 chunks, to make the shift visible)**
- No change: 0 / 47 re-parsed, 20 s.
- Edit the content of one file: 1 / 47 (the documented behavior — content edits are fine).
- Add one 148 KiB file that sorts first: **47 / 47** re-parsed, 63 s (cold run: 62 s).
- Delete it again: **46 / 47**.
- Delete one existing 20 KiB file early in sort order: **4 / 47** (the shift propagates until the cumulative bytes realign with a boundary).

### Steps to reproduce

1. `git clone https://github.com/alibaba/spring-ai-alibaba && cd spring-ai-alibaba`
2. `gitnexus analyze --force . --index-only` twice; note the number of entries under `.gitnexus/parsedfile-cache/` (one per chunk) — 2 on an 8-core machine.
3. Append a comment to any Java file, re-analyze: one new entry appears whose shards contain ~2.2k ParsedFiles; wall time equals the cold run.
4. `GITNEXUS_CHUNK_BYTE_BUDGET=262144 gitnexus analyze --force . --index-only --workers 1` twice (47 entries).
5. Create a ~150 KiB Java file at the repo root (sorts first), re-analyze: 47 new entries; delete it, re-analyze: 46 new entries.

### Environment

- macOS (Apple Silicon), Node v26.7.0, gitnexus 1.6.10 (stock, no patches)
- Same behavior observed on Linux x86_64 / Node 22 with 1.6.10-rc.205 in our deployment


### Logs / screenshots

### Proposed fix (what we run locally)

Make chunk membership a function of the file itself, not of its neighbours or of the machine:

- Assign each file to one of N stable buckets by `(language, hash(path)) mod N` (we use N = 128), then apply the byte budget *inside* each bucket. Adding, deleting or renaming a file only touches its own bucket; content edits still invalidate one chunk; ordering inside a bucket stays sorted so results are reproducible.
- Decouple the cache-key granularity from `effectivePoolSize`: worker utilisation is already handled by the sub-batch dispatch, so the chunk budget used for cache keys can stay at the 2 MiB default regardless of core count — which also makes caches portable between machines.
- N is part of the cache layout: changing it naturally produces different chunk hashes, so old entries miss (and are pruned) instead of being reused incorrectly.

We have run this behind an env switch for several weeks; parse results and graph output are byte-identical, only the hit rate changes.

### Logs

Cache-entry counts per step above were taken by diffing `ls .gitnexus/parsedfile-cache/` before and after each run (the newly created entries are exactly the re-parsed chunks). Can attach the script and the per-run logs on request.

title: keep a `v8.serialize` sidecar next to ParsedFile and parse-cache JSON shards — `JSON.parse` + reviver is ~5× slower than `v8.deserialize` on the same object graph
body:
### Area

gitnexus (CLI / core / indexing / MCP server)

### Problem or opportunity

Both on-disk stores that feed scope-resolution round-trip through JSON with a custom reviver: ParsedFile shards (`parsedfile-store.ts`, `makeInterningReviver` — string interning plus per-shard def dedup) and parse-cache chunk results (`parse-cache.ts`, `mapReviver` for `Scope.bindings` / `typeBindings`). Every warm run pays the full deserialization cost again.

Measured on a ~6.3k-file Java-dominant monorepo (same setup as #3086):

- ParsedFile store, ~480 MiB of JSON: `JSON.parse` + reviver 32.8 s vs `v8.deserialize` of the same object graph 6.35 s.
- parse-cache, 17 worker-result shards, ~218 MiB: `JSON.parse` + `mapReviver` 9.36 s vs `v8.deserialize` 1.79 s.

End-to-end on our warm-path matrix (other local cache changes applied): removing the ParsedFile sidecar costs +27.4 s (63.3 s → 90.7 s); removing the parse-cache sidecar +4.7 s (63.3 s → 68.1 s). Graph output identical in both cases.

### Proposed solution

Best-effort binary sidecar, JSON stays canonical:

- After a shard's object graph exists (worker write for ParsedFiles; `saveParseCache` for chunk results), also write `<shard>.json.v8` = `v8.serialize(graph)` with a small header carrying the Node major / `process.versions.v8`.
- Readers try the sidecar first; on a missing file, header mismatch, size mismatch or any deserialization error they silently fall back to the JSON + reviver path (the current code, unchanged).
- The durable ParsedFile restore copies sidecars together with the JSON; parse-cache `save`/`prune` carry them in lockstep with the surviving keys, so a sidecar can never outlive its JSON.
- Because the interning reviver also dedups strings, the v8 path should serialize the *revived* graph (post-intern), so retained memory after load is the same as today.

Any failure in the binary path only loses speed; cache hits, content addressing and graph semantics are unaffected.

### Alternatives considered

- MessagePack / CBOR: adds a dependency and still needs custom Map/Set handling; `v8` is built in and already understands Map/Set.
- Replacing JSON entirely with v8: loses cross-Node-version compatibility and the human-readable recovery format; the sidecar keeps JSON as the source of truth.
- Making the reviver cheaper: the interning is what keeps the heap bounded (#1983), so the per-token cost is inherent to JSON.

### Acceptance criteria

- Byte-identical graph output with and without sidecars (we verified node/edge hashes on our matrix).
- Warm run with sidecars present measurably faster on a large repo; sidecar missing/corrupt/mismatched → same result as today, at most a debug log line.
- Sidecars pruned/copied exactly alongside their JSON; no orphan `.v8` files after `prune`.


### Constraints

- Disk: roughly doubles the size of the two stores (the v8 payload is about the size of the JSON).
- `v8.serialize` wire format is not stable across Node majors — the header check is mandatory, and a mismatch must be a silent fallback rather than an error.

### Contribution

- [ ] I am willing to open a PR for this (may need design discussion first).

title: restore durable ParsedFile shards into the run store with hardlinks instead of `copyFile` (hundreds of MiB copied on every warm analyze)
body:
### Area

gitnexus (CLI / core / indexing / MCP server)

### Problem or opportunity

On a warm parse-cache hit, `restoreDurableParsedFileShard` (`gitnexus/src/storage/parsedfile-store.ts`) byte-copies every file of the chunk from the content-addressed `parsedfile-cache/<chunkHash>/` into the run-scoped `parsedfile-store/` with `fs.copyFile`. Both directories live under the same `.gitnexus/`; the durable store is treated as read-only, and the run store is deleted wholesale after scope-resolution.

On a ~6.3k-file Java-dominant monorepo with one file per worker job (same setup as #3086) that is ~5,750 shard groups per warm run — ~480 MiB of JSON alone, ~900 MiB once the path/v8 sidecars from #2/#3 exist. The warm `parse` phase measured 27.5 s, almost all of it this copy.

### Proposed solution

Link instead of copy:

- For each file in the chunk directory, `fs.link(src, dst)`; run the links with bounded concurrency (they only write directory entries, no data blocks).
- Fall back to `fs.copyFile` per file on `EXDEV`, `EPERM`, `ENOTSUP`, `EMLINK` or any other error, so cross-device layouts and filesystems without hardlinks behave exactly as today.
- Nothing else changes: the run store is still only ever read and then unlinked, so cleanup just drops a link count and never touches the durable cache; content addressing is unchanged.

Measured end-to-end on our warm-path matrix (other local cache changes applied): sequential copy 73.6 s → concurrent copy 71.7 s → hardlink 63.3 s, i.e. −10.3 s vs today's sequential copy. Output identical.

### Alternatives considered

- `copyFile` with `COPYFILE_FICLONE` (reflink): free only on CoW filesystems (btrfs/XFS-reflink/APFS); on ext4 it degrades to a full copy. Could be tried before the plain copy in the fallback chain.
- Symlinks: fragile if the durable directory is pruned while a run is in flight.
- Read directly from the durable directory without restoring: a larger change to the loader and to the "run store is cleared at parse start" invariant.

### Acceptance criteria

- Restored shard bytes identical; loader behavior unchanged.
- Fallback path covered by a test (simulate `EXDEV`).
- After run cleanup the durable cache directory is byte-for-byte intact (link count back to 1).

### Constraints

- Assumes the two stores share a filesystem for the fast path; the fallback keeps correctness everywhere else.
- Windows: NTFS supports hardlinks, other filesystems fall back to copy.

### Contribution

title: `--skip-fts` / `GITNEXUS_SKIP_FTS=1` to skip FTS index creation for consumers that bring their own retrieval
body:
### Area

gitnexus (CLI / core / indexing / MCP server)

### Problem or opportunity

`gitnexus analyze` always loads the FTS extension and builds the BM25 search indexes (`buildSearchIndexesOrDegrade` in `gitnexus/src/core/run-analyze.ts`). The only way to not pay for it is for the extension to be unavailable, which is logged as a degradation. Consumers that read the graph through Cypher / the MCP tools and run their own keyword or semantic retrieval (we keep vectors in a separate store) rebuild an index nobody queries, on every analyze.

Measured on a ~6.3k-file Java-dominant monorepo: the FTS phase costs ~24 s of a 63 s warm analyze (63.4 s → 87.8 s when enabled) and inflates the LadybugDB file from 153.6 MB to 440.7 MB; on the full graph of the same repo the database grows from ~352 MiB to ~676 MiB. For short-lived per-review indexes that is the single largest avoidable cost after the parse caches.


### Proposed solution

An explicit opt-out, default unchanged:

- `gitnexus analyze --skip-fts` and the equivalent `GITNEXUS_SKIP_FTS=1` (env for callers that cannot change the command line), documented in the README environment-variable table.
- Skips only the FTS extension load and index creation in the "Creating search indexes" phase. Graph load, communities, processes, embeddings, meta, parse caches and registry are untouched.
- Meta records `capabilities.fts.status = "unavailable"` with `skipReason = "disabled-by-flag"` (or `disabled-by-env`), so the query side degrades exactly as it does when the extension is missing, and status/`search` report "disabled" rather than a failure.
- A later analyze without the flag rebuilds the indexes as usual.

### Alternatives considered

- Relying on the extension-unavailable degrade path: requires breaking the environment and produces warnings on every run.
- Dropping the indexes after analyze: the time is already spent.
- `--index-only`: addresses agent-guide writes, not search indexes.

### Acceptance criteria

- With the flag: no FTS extension load, no FTS index tables, meta shows the explicit skip reason, `search` reports FTS disabled.
- Without the flag: byte-identical behavior to today.
- README env table row for `GITNEXUS_SKIP_FTS`.

### Constraints

- Must not be confused with a failed index build in diagnostics (`ftsFailureIsFatal` paths unaffected).
- Interaction with `serve`/MCP: a database indexed with the flag should answer `search` with a clear "FTS disabled for this index" message.

### Contribution

title: perf(scope-resolution): six provably-equivalent redundancies on the Java emit path (~5 s combined on a 6.3k-file repo)
body:
### Area

gitnexus (CLI / core / indexing / MCP server)

### Problem or opportunity

After the cache-level fixes in #3086 / #2 / #3 / #4, profiling scope-resolution + graph write on a ~6.3k-file Java-dominant monorepo leaves ~5 s spread across six spots where the same work is done twice or through an avoidably expensive shape. Reverting all six together costs +4.7 s on our warm-path matrix (71.1 s → 75.8 s); none of them changes pass order, graph semantics or persisted formats. Listed in profile order:

1. **`collectDeferredIndirectSites` runs twice per pass on identical inputs** — once in `runScopeResolution` (`scope-resolution/pipeline/run.ts`, feeding the free-call/reference passes) and again inside `emitCallableValueFlow` (`passes/callable-value-flow.ts`) with the same ParsedFiles and scope indexes.
2. **callable-value-flow rescans every `parsed.referenceSites` to build its call-signature index** right after the orchestrator has scanned the same sites for deferred indirect calls; the first scan can populate the index and hand it down.
3. **Owner registries key every lookup on a template string** — `method-registry.ts` / `field-registry.ts` / `type-registry.ts` build `` `${ownerNodeId}\0${name}` `` for each `get`/`register`; Java reference, receiver and free-call resolution call these hundreds of thousands of times (>1 s cumulative across the three registries in the profile). A nested `Map<owner, Map<name, defs>>` keeps registration order, array identity, the frozen empty result and `clear` semantics.
4. **`resolveDefGraphId` (`graph-bridge/ids.ts`) re-derives position / qualified-name / arity / parameter-shape keys for the same definition on every pass**, although it is a pure function of `(def, filePath, nodeLookup)`; a `WeakMap` keyed by `nodeLookup` (so a rebuilt lookup after heritage never reuses stale results) removes the repeat work for Java's multi-pass emit.
5. **`csv-generator.ts` re-runs the binary scan and `content.split('\n')` for every symbol of a file**, and its 3,000-entry source cache maintains LRU order with `Array.indexOf` + `splice` (O(n) per hit). Preparing lines / binary flag / File FTS text once per cached file and keeping LRU order in `Map` insertion order makes both O(1) without changing snippet or CSV output.
6. **`analyzer-identity.ts` spawns a Node subprocess to re-verify the install tree once `requests.length >= 128`**, and this happens twice per analyze (start and before the metadata commit). On a read-only install the existing synchronous per-item check is equivalent; an opt-in in-process mode avoids two process spawns per run.

### Proposed solution

Six small, independent changes (each is a few dozen lines): pass the already-computed deferred-site set into `emitCallableValueFlow`; fill the call-signature index during the first `referenceSites` scan; nested-Map owner registries; per-`nodeLookup` memo for `resolveDefGraphId`; per-file prepared content + Map-ordered LRU in the CSV generator; in-process identity guard mode. We run all six behind env switches with the upstream path as default; upstream could simply make them the default.

### Alternatives considered

- Leave as is: ~1.5 % of the end-to-end time on this repo, but each item is also a code-clarity fix (one computation instead of two).
- Fold into larger refactors of the emit pipeline — larger blast radius for the same gain.


### Acceptance criteria

- Graph output identical (we verified node/edge hashes with all six enabled).
- Combined ≥ 4 s on the reference repo; no persisted format touched.
- Unit tests covering registry semantics (order, identity, `clear`) and the memo invalidation on lookup rebuild.

### Constraints

- Item 6 must stay opt-in or detect a read-only install tree; the subprocess exists to catch install mutation.

### Contribution

title: fix(parse): stabilize parse-cache chunks and cheapen ParsedFile loads
body:
## Summary
- Stabilize parse-cache membership with `(language, sha256(path) mod 128)` buckets and a pool-independent 2 MiB (or explicit) in-bucket byte budget so one-line edits, adds, and deletes no longer shift later sequential chunks.

title: fix(ruby): guard gem requires with dependency metadata
body:
## Summary

Prevent Ruby gem-style `require` paths from falling through to unrelated suffix matches when scoped dependency metadata identifies a known gem prefix.

This stops `require 'rails/generators'` from fabricating an import edge to an unrelated in-repo `lib/generators.rb`.

## Motivation / context

Ruby assembles `$LOAD_PATH` at runtime, so a bare `require` cannot always be resolved from repository paths alone. The existing suffix fallback could drop leading path segments and bind an external gem path to a coincidentally named local file.

This change adds a conservative dependency gate based on statically readable Ruby project metadata.

Fixes #2966.

## Areas touched

- [x] `gitnexus/` (CLI / core / MCP server)
- [ ] `gitnexus-web/` (Vite / React UI)
- [x] `.github/` (workflows, actions)
- [ ] `eval/` or other tooling
- [ ] Docs / agent config only (`AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.cursor/`, `llms.txt`, etc.)

## Scope & constraints

**In scope**

- Collect literal dependency names from `Gemfile` and `*.gemspec` files without executing Ruby code.
- Collect transitive dependency names from an adjacent `Gemfile.lock`.
- Resolve known local path gems only within their declared load roots, including returning `null` on a local miss.
- Return `null` before suffix matching for known external gem prefixes.
- Preserve local bare-require and `require_relative` resolution.
- Remove Ruby from the external-import conformance suite's known gaps.

**Explicitly out of scope / not done here**

- Evaluating dynamic Ruby expressions in Gemfiles or gemspecs.
- Attempting to model arbitrary runtime `$LOAD_PATH` mutations.
- Changing index schemas, public APIs, or existing resolution behavior when no declarative Ruby manifest is available.

## Implementation notes

- Dependency discovery is bounded and skips generated or vendored directories such as `.git`, `.gitnexus`, `node_modules`, `vendor`, `dist`, and `build`.
- A lockfile contributes dependencies only when its directory also contains a `Gemfile` or gemspec.
- Relative resolution runs before the dependency gate, so `require_relative` behavior is unchanged.
- Repositories without a `Gemfile` or gemspec fail open and retain the existing suffix-resolution behavior.

## Testing & verification

- [x] Pre-commit ESLint, Prettier, and typechecking checks.

### Ruby gem-boundary benchmark follow-up

- Added `bench/ruby-gem-resolution/baseline.json` and `measure.mjs`, wired into the existing CI benchmark job with `--check`.
- The runner calls production Ruby ScopeResolver hooks and the real temporary Gemfile/gemspec/lockfile loader. Exact counts and output fingerprints cover external decoys, aliases, local path gem hits/misses, relative/local imports and sibling-project isolation.

title: fix(serve): allow Bearer authentication on /api/mcp
body:
### Problem

GitNexus has two Streamable HTTP MCP surfaces with different authentication behavior:

- `gitnexus mcp --http` supports `GITNEXUS_MCP_AUTH_TOKEN` / `--auth-token` and refuses a non-loopback bind without a token;
- `gitnexus serve` mounts `/api/mcp` through `mountMCPEndpoints` without an MCP auth middleware.

`SECURITY.md` already documents the `serve` route as a pre-existing gap. The Render Blueprint contains it behind a private backend plus an edge token, but an operator running `serve` directly on a reachable interface cannot add Bearer protection specifically to `/api/mcp`. This blocks authenticated URL-only clients such as the planned Astron connector without forcing them onto the full web proxy deployment.

### Proposed solution

Reuse the existing dedicated MCP token contract for the `serve` route:

1. Resolve `GITNEXUS_MCP_AUTH_TOKEN` with the same whitespace/empty handling as `gitnexus mcp --http`.
2. When a token is present, install `createAuthMiddleware(token)` for `/api/mcp` before the global JSON body parser and before the MCP handler.
3. Keep current behavior when the variable is unset. Do not make every non-loopback `serve` invocation fail: existing private-network/edge-gated deployments rely on that topology.
4. Do not treat `GITNEXUS_SERVE_AUTH_TOKEN` as interchangeable. It belongs to the Render/web edge; `GITNEXUS_MCP_AUTH_TOKEN` protects the MCP protocol endpoint itself.
5. Update the README environment table and SECURITY notes to explain the two layers and warn that a directly reachable `serve` remains unsafe when neither MCP auth nor an authenticated edge is present.
6. Reuse constant-time Bearer comparison and JSON-RPC 401 responses from the dedicated MCP transport; do not create a second token parser.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] With no `GITNEXUS_MCP_AUTH_TOKEN`, `/api/mcp` retains current behavior for compatibility.
- [ ] With a nonblank token, a missing or incorrect Authorization header receives the existing JSON-RPC `401` envelope.
- [ ] `Authorization: Bearer <exact token>` reaches the existing MCP handler.
- [ ] Whitespace-only token values do not silently enable or disable a different policy.
- [ ] Auth middleware is registered before body parsing for `/api/mcp`, so unauthenticated request bodies are not parsed first.
- [ ] Non-MCP `serve` routes are unchanged.
- [ ] Unit tests cover absent, incorrect, valid, and whitespace token cases plus middleware order.
- [ ] README and SECURITY distinguish protocol auth from the Render/web edge token.

### Current implementation evidence

Pinned baseline: `abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus@4e51213c82249d5c235f8535d8292bd56de8c01a`

- Unauthenticated `serve` MCP mount: https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/blob/4e51213c82249d5c235f8535d8292bd56de8c01a/gitnexus/src/server/mcp-http.ts
- Mount call occurs after global JSON parsing is installed: https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/blob/4e51213c82249d5c235f8535d8292bd56de8c01a/gitnexus/src/server/api.ts
- Existing constant-time Bearer middleware and token resolver: https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/blob/4e51213c82249d5c235f8535d8292bd56de8c01a/gitnexus/src/mcp/http-transport.ts
- Public security note for the current gap: https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/blob/4e51213c82249d5c235f8535d8292bd56de8c01a/SECURITY.md

### Related

- https://github.com/iflytek/astron-agent/issues/1661 — managed Bearer credentials for authenticated Streamable HTTP MCP clients.
- https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/pull/3097 — Astron compatibility/security guide.
- #2102 is a broader team onboarding wizard and does not provide this focused in-process `/api/mcp` middleware.

title: perf(store): V8 sidecars plus hardlinked ParsedFile restore

## Summary
- Replaces ParsedFile and parse-cache JSON loading with immutable V8 envelopes; there is no JSON fallback.
- Uses envelope format 5 with runtime/version gates, exact path metadata, payload-length checks, and a SHA-256 digest over listing||payload. Existing format-4 caches cold-start once after upgrade.
- Records each durable chunk's actual persisted path coverage. A parse-cache hit skips workers only after every indexed shard validates and the complete generation is snapshotted into the per-run store.

title: Incremental writeback with streamed graph emit produces corrupted Class rows (reproduced)
body:
# Incremental writeback with streamed graph emit produces corrupted Class rows (reproduced)

## Summary

While stress-testing GitNexus on a large Java monorepo (25k files, ~605k nodes, 3.6GB-RAM box), we locally enabled streamed structural graph emit for **incremental** runs via an env-gated patch modeled on #2680. The upstream code deliberately refuses `streamGraphEmit` on incremental runs — the test suite calls this "a soundness boundary, not a preference" (`test/unit/stream-graph-emit-config.test.ts:4`). We reproduced the corruption it guards against, deterministically, and are documenting the failure mode since it is subtle and silent (exit 0, no warnings about the corruption itself).

## Reproduction (deterministic)

1. Clean full rebuild (healthy index, verified: 0 corrupted rows out of 21,163 Class rows).
2. Modify ONE Java file (append a comment line — content is irrelevant).
3. Run incremental analyze with `GITNEXUS_STREAM_GRAPH_EMIT_INCREMENTAL=1`.
4. Result: **18,257 of 21,163 Class rows corrupted** — identity columns (id, name, filePath) empty, startLine/endLine populated. Exit code 0. No error or warning about the corruption.

Corollary: the next (non-streamed) incremental run self-heals — drift detection matches fresh nodes against persisted ids, finds every corrupted row "drifted", and rewrites them. In our first incident this masqueraded as a mysterious 2,710-file annotation-drift storm.

## Observations that narrow the root cause

We did not root-cause to the exact line, but three pinned facts may help a maintainer do so quickly:

1. **The node CSV on disk is HEALTHY.** After the corrupted incremental run, `.gitnexus/csv/class.csv` contained 3,693 rows with zero empty ids. The corruption therefore happens **after** CSV emit — during COPY into the database, or in a later phase that rewrites rows (FTS / embedding-restore). The CSV generator and the subgraph extraction (nodes ride the real graph, never the sink) are exonerated.
2. **Both corruption incidents coincided with an FTS index build failure** ("full-text/BM25 search is disabled — the search index build failed this run"). The repair run that had no FTS failure also had no corruption. We cannot yet prove causation, but the correlation is exact across both incidents.
3. **The incremental writeback path never passes the streamed manifests** (`run-analyze.ts` incremental branch calls `loadGraphToLbug(subgraph, repoPath, storagePath, cb)` with 4 args). The full-rebuild branch's comment states the assumption outright: *"Only ever set on a full rebuild (streaming is force-gated), so the incremental branch above never carries it."* Our env flag breaks exactly that premise. Relatedly, `StreamedRelationship.reason` is the constant `'streamed'` on in-memory reads, justified by "the persisted CSV row keeps the real value" — an invariant that only holds when the manifest CSVs are the ones being COPY'd.

## What we'd suggest

1. If combining the sink with `extractChangedSubgraph`/incremental COPY is fundamentally unsound, a **runtime hard-fail** (rather than relying on the config gate alone) would have saved us a week of forensic archaeology — the corruption is silent and its downstream symptom (annotation drift) points elsewhere.
2. We're happy to share the corrupted DB artifacts or the exact env/versions for a regression test. Repro is cheap if you have any multi-module Java repo: full rebuild → touch one file → flip the incremental-streaming env → count empty `name` rows in Class.
3. If maintainers already know the mechanism, a comment near the incremental gate explaining it would be valuable — the current one says "soundness boundary" without saying what breaks.

## Environment

- GitNexus 1.6.9 (local build; patched `resolveStreamGraphEmit` only — env gate `GITNEXUS_STREAM_GRAPH_EMIT_INCREMENTAL` defaulting off, exactly as upstream ships)
- Node v22.22.3, Linux x64, 4GB RAM + zram
- Repo: 25k-file Java/Spring monorepo (multi-module Maven), `GITNEXUS_MAX_PACKAGE_FILES=5000`, `MAX_INJECTED_SIBLINGS=200`, `WORKER_POOL_SIZE=1`

title: fix(analyze): make incremental analyze skip the derived layers it can reuse (#3016)
body:
Fixes #3016.

## The problem

A warm incremental run only ever writes a handful of files, but it still paid for the whole graph on the way out:

- Leiden community detection ran over every node in the graph.
- Flow/process extraction re-derived every process.
- Every configured FTS index was dropped and rebuilt from scratch.

On a small edit that tail dominates the run, which is why "incremental" did not feel incremental.

## The change

Reuse what the previous run already derived, when the write plan allows it.

- `skipDerivedGraphPhases` holds back community detection and flow extraction whenever the persisted metadata says this run is a candidate for a surgical write. MRO and DI still run.
- The DB keeps its `Community` / `Process` rows instead of the wipe-and-rewrite, and `extractChangedSubgraph` leaves those graph-wide nodes alone.
- The FTS sweep is narrowed from "every configured index" to "the indexes this run must touch", so untouched tables keep their live index.

The optimistic skip is decided **before** the pipeline (only the persisted metadata is available then) and **settled after** it. Any plan that turns out to need a freshly derived layer — a full rebuild, an escalated write, or an incremental diff with deleted files — runs the held-back phases via the new `PipelineResult.runDeferredDerivedPhases`, against the same graph and the same phase outputs, so the result is identical to never having skipped them.

Scope resolution stays full-workspace; that is #1841, not this PR.

## Correctness details

Each of these loses data silently if it is got wrong, so they are called out explicitly:

- **Derived edges are carried across the delete.** The `MEMBER_OF` / `STEP_IN_PROCESS` edges of the changed files are snapshotted before the `DETACH DELETE` and reattached after the subgraph load, `step` column included (process traces `ORDER BY r.step`). Both endpoints are matched by an **explicit label**: `labels(n)[0]` over an unlabelled match returns an empty string on this engine, which produced a snapshot that captured 23 edges and restored none of them.
- **The FTS narrowing unions three sets**, and dropping any one strands something: what the writeback *deletes* (a DB probe — a symbol the edit removed is in no fresh graph but is still a row), what it *inserts* (the fresh graph — inserting under a live FTS index is the same #2589 hazard as deleting under one), and what is *missing right now* (otherwise the indexes a prior escalation dropped would only ever come back on the next full rebuild). An unreadable index catalog withdraws the narrowing entirely rather than guess.
- **Deletions disqualify reuse outright.** Persisted derived rows can reference nodes this run removes, and nothing short of re-deriving can tell which.

## Test plan

- [x] `npx tsc --noEmit` clean.
- [x] `npx eslint` on the changed files — 0 errors.
- [x] Full unit suite: **13,719 passed**. The one failure, `wiki-llm-client.test.ts`, reproduces identically on an unmodified baseline in the same environment (it reads ambient provider env vars) and is unrelated to this change.
- [x] `incremental-orchestration.test.ts` — including *"incremental output is byte-equivalent to a full rebuild (incremental ≡ --force on the same repo state)"*, which is the load-bearing proof that the reused derived layer matches a fresh one.
- [x] `incremental-fts-drop-ordering.test.ts` — the #2589 drop-before-delete ordering, now asserted per touched table.
- [x] `incremental-index-extension-dml-gate.test.ts` — the #2841 escalate-once path, which is what caught the missing-index case above.
- [x] New unit tests for the writeback helpers, the seeded-phase runner, and `missingSearchFTSIndexTables`.

title: java-workspace-extractor skips repos sharing a parent POM as "duplicate artifact" — breaks manifest cross-links
body:
### Area

gitnexus (CLI / core / indexing / MCP server)

### Summary

`java-workspace-extractor` skips repositories that share a common Maven parent POM, reporting them as "duplicate artifact", so `group sync` builds zero `manifest` cross-links even though every `pom.xml` is correctly parsed and artifact coordinates are recognized.

### Context

A group of independent Java/Maven git repositories that all inherit from the same `<parent>` POM — the standard layout for a portfolio of related services / shared libraries under one organization (e.g. multiple repos inheriting `spring-boot-starter-parent`). Each repo is indexed independently and added to a group. `workspace_deps` is enabled in `group.yaml`. The extractor clearly reads each repo's `groupId:artifactId` from its `pom.xml`, but then skips nearly every repo because they share the inherited parent artifact id.

This makes the `workspace_deps` cross-linking feature effectively unusable for this extremely common Maven shape.

### Expected behavior

- A shared parent POM is inherited, not the repo's own deliverable artifact. Repositories that merely share an inherited `<parent>` should not be treated as duplicates of each other or of the parent.
- The extractor should build cross-links from a repo's `<dependency>` declarations to the repo that publishes that dependency artifact — even when multiple repos share the same parent.
- In a group where `service-a` and `service-b` both declare `<dependency>` on `com.example:shared-lib`, each should get a `manifest` cross-link to the `shared-lib` repo, regardless of all of them inheriting `com.example:parent`.

### Actual behavior

`group sync --verbose` recognizes every artifact but skips all but the first repo per shared artifact id:

```
[java-workspace-extractor] duplicate artifact "com.example:parent" in "service-a" and "parent" — skipping "service-a"
[java-workspace-extractor] duplicate artifact "com.example:parent" in "service-b" and "parent" — skipping "service-b"
[java-workspace-extractor] duplicate artifact "com.example:parent" in "shared-lib" and "parent" — skipping "shared-lib"
...
```

Result:

```
Matching:
  exact:     6 cross-links (confidence 1.0)
  manifest:  0 cross-links
  wildcard:  0 cross-links
```

`manifest: 0 cross-links` — the `service-a → shared-lib` and `service-b → shared-lib` Maven dependency edges are never created, because the repos carrying those `<dependency>` declarations were skipped as "duplicate artifact".

### Steps to reproduce

Setup: independent Maven repositories sharing a common parent POM:

- `parent` — root POM, `com.example:parent`, `packaging: pom`
- `shared-lib` — `<parent>` is `com.example:parent`; publishes `com.example:shared-lib`
- `service-a` — `<parent>` is `com.example:parent`; `<dependency>` on `com.example:shared-lib`
- `service-b` — `<parent>` is `com.example:parent`; `<dependency>` on `com.example:shared-lib`
- (several more repos inheriting the same parent)

1. Index each repo independently:
   ```bash
   gitnexus analyze <repo> --force --index-only
   ```
2. Create the group and add members:
   ```bash
   gitnexus group create mygroup
   gitnexus group add mygroup parent parent
   gitnexus group add mygroup shared-lib shared-lib
   gitnexus group add mygroup service-a service-a
   gitnexus group add mygroup service-b service-b
   ```
3. Enable workspace dependency detection in `group.yaml` (off by default):
   ```yaml
   detect:
     workspace_deps: true
   ```
4. Sync:
   ```bash
   gitnexus group sync mygroup --verbose
   ```
5. Observe the "duplicate artifact ... skipping" log lines and `manifest: 0 cross-links`.

### Environment

- OS: macOS (arm64)
- Node: v24.15.0
- Commit / version: gitnexus 1.6.10

### Logs / screenshots

See the "duplicate artifact ... skipping" lines and the `manifest: 0 cross-links` summary quoted in *Actual behavior* above.

### Notes

- `pom.xml` files ARE indexed as `File` nodes and their artifact coordinates ARE parsed (the log shows the extractor reading `groupId:artifactId` correctly) — the issue is purely the duplicate-artifact skip logic, not parsing.
- The `ContractType` enum already includes `'lib'`, and `extractJavaWorkspaceLinks` + `ManifestExtractor` are wired up — so this looks like a logic gap in duplicate handling rather than a missing feature.
- `group query` (federated execution-flow search) works across repos and is a usable fallback for discovery, but it does not represent the Maven dependency edges as cross-links.

title: feat(spring): import optional Actuator runtime data with Kotlin JVM mapping
body:
## Summary

Adds an opt-in `--spring-actuator <path>` importer for Spring Boot Actuator mappings, beans, conditions, configprops, and env snapshots, and maps those runtime identities onto static Java/Kotlin graph nodes. Kotlin JVM callables (companions, file facades, getters, suspend descriptors, `@JvmName`) are matched through a language-local strategy so the shared importer stays language-agnostic.

Closes #2418.

## Motivation / context

Static Spring extraction cannot see runtime-only routes, bean types, or condition outcomes. Operators already have Actuator JSON; importing it as confirming evidence (not a replacement for static analysis) closes that gap without fetching over the network.

## Areas touched

- [x] `gitnexus/` (CLI / core / MCP server)
- [ ] `gitnexus-web/` (Vite / React UI)

- [ ] `eval/` or other tooling

## Scope & constraints

**In scope**

- Explicit `--spring-actuator` path: endpoint directory or JSON bundle. No network fetch. Watch mode remains unsupported.
- Runtime mappings and beans confirm matching static nodes; conditions and config-property keys enrich existing evidence.
- Kotlin `RuntimeSymbolStrategy`: companions, file-facade owners (including top-level properties), getter/`is` names, suspend `Continuation` arity, import/FQ `@JvmName`.
- Fail closed when an Actuator bean `type` disagrees with a static `providedTypeName` / class `qualifiedName`.
- Payload reads share one file handle with the size gate, loop until EOF, and reject over 16 MiB.
- HTTP methods are taken from the predicate text before the first `[`, so path segments like `/GET` are not treated as methods.
- Env/config values, origins, condition messages, and property-source names are never persisted or printed.
- Repo-local snapshot paths stay as normalized relative scan exclusions after enrichment is disabled.

**Explicitly out of scope / not done here**

- Network Actuator scraping or watch-mode re-import.
- Treating runtime ownership as authoritative over a conflicting static handler.
- Simple-name fallback after a qualified-name miss; duplicate indexes stay ambiguous at three or more matches.

## Implementation notes

- Structured runtime fields live only on Route; other evidence stays in descriptions and provenance edges.
- Handler conflicts are stored as unconfirmed evidence without a contradictory confidence-1 owner edge.
- Graph load/stream retries the legacy Route projection when runtime columns are missing (`SCHEMA_FINGERPRINT` mismatch forces rebuild; COPY does not hit unrebuilt tables).
- Aggregate condition status stays on the owner, not copied onto every child target.
- Kotlin file-facade metadata is cached per parse tree; synthetic `kotlin-jvm` accessors are skipped so they do not compete with property getters.

## Testing & verification

- Route gains nullable runtime evidence columns. The graph API remains compatible with pre-change indexes; a normal analyze rebuilds the derived schema.
- Runtime evidence is additive. Static ownership wins on conflicts, which are marked rather than overwritten.
- Actuator snapshot paths are excluded from later source/FTS scans even after enrichment is turned off.

title: fix(server,web): honor the grep tool contract — real regex, fileFilter, caseSensitive
body:
## Problem

The server's `/api/grep` escapes every pattern through `escapeRegExp` (a ReDoS hardening), but the web UI's grep tool schema was never synced to that: its description says "using regex", its example is `console\.log`, and it advertises `fileFilter`/`caseSensitive` parameters. An agent following that contract generates alternations like `"sign|Sign"` and fileFilter calls → guaranteed zero hits → the AI concludes "this interface does not exist in the codebase" (observed on a real monorepo). The schema's own example returns wrong results under literal semantics. The frontend handler also still had a `(?=.*filter).*pattern` lookahead concat (equally literalized).

The impact tool's grep fallback (`\\b${escapeRegex(baseName)}\\b`) was silent dead code under the old semantics and comes alive under the new one.

## Fix

- New `gitnexus/src/server/grep-params.ts`: pure parameter-parsing functions (regex construction, `literal=1` compat for the old semantics, fileFilter lowercased path-substring, limit clamping, BadRequestError paths); `api.ts` handler is a thin wire-up (follows the #2790 helper-extraction convention).
- `gitnexus-web`: grep handler drops the lookahead concat; description now tells the truth (regex/alternation/path-substring/time budget); `backend-client.grep` gains GrepOptions (fileFilter/caseSensitive → query params); useAppState passes them through.
- 20 new test cases (alternation, schema-example regex, case handling, literal compat, CJK patterns, line anchors, fileFilter normalization + array rejection, limit clamping, type-confusion guards, invalid regex, handler wiring source assertions).

## Security note (deliberate trade-off, also in SECURITY.md)

Literal-escaping was an accidental immunity; this PR restores the promised contract. The 200-char cap / per-line matching / result caps / 5s wall-clock budget (checked between files, partial results + `timedOut: true`) cannot interrupt catastrophic backtracking inside a single `regex.test()` (measured: `(a+)+$` against a 35-char line > 120s, event loop blocked throughout). Accepted on the grounds that local serve binds loopback by default and hosted deployments sit behind the edge token gate. The root fix (worker_threads + terminate, or optional re2) is explicitly listed as follow-up and NOT part of this PR.

**Repro**: `curl ".../api/grep?pattern=TODO%7CFIXME"` — 0 hits under literal semantics, both marker kinds under regex semantics.

Full-repo caller audit: `/api/grep` has exactly one HTTP caller (backend-client.grep); MCP has no grep tool; blast radius ~zero.
