title: feat(jvm): fold Java static wildcards and Kotlin star imports for route constants
body:
## Problem

Java `import static a.b.C.*` recorded only the class name, never the members, so wildcard-imported route constants failed to fold and their provider contracts were dropped. On a 24k-file Java monorepo that was ~693 unmatched `@WinPostMapping(ApiPaths.SAVE_V1)`-style paths.

Kotlin controllers have the same gap for star imports: `import com.example.api.*` (package) and `import com.example.ApiPaths.*` (object/classifier members). Those names never folded either.

Also: `resolveJavaImport` compared repo keys raw — on a Windows checkout the keys carry backslashes and the POSIX-joined class file never matched.

## Fix

**Java static wildcards**

- Extract time records `import static a.b.C.*` in `wildcardImports`.
- A language-provider `prepareRouteConstants` hook materializes bare member bindings once the repo map exists (ingestion parse phase and group `prepareRepo` share `prepareJavaRouteConstants`). The shared parse phase does not name Java.
- Members are owned by the target type only; unfoldable locals and explicit static imports win; duplicate wildcard members floor instead of first-wins.
- A static wildcard does **not** import the type name. Qualified `ApiPaths.X` still needs a type import; the bare member from the wildcard still folds.
- Harvest admits class imports and static (including on-demand) imports, not ordinary `import pkg.*`.
- `resolveJavaImport` compares in POSIX space.

**Kotlin star imports**

- Package stars (`import pkg.*`) fold top-level names and keep same-package declarations (including harvested non-constant types/`var`s) above the star.
- Classifier stars (`import Type.*`) fold object/class/companion members. The type name itself is not imported.
- Overlaying an import-only file is a cheap repo view; replacing a file that already contributed constants rebuilds `byPackage` / `byFqn`.

**Cache / CI**

- `SCHEMA_BUMP` is **88** (unfoldable-declaration metadata on the Java constants shape).
- CI benches for Java wildcard expansion and Kotlin star folding (`bench/java-wildcard-route-constants`, `bench/kotlin-star-route-constants`).

## Effect

Java graph: 1674 → 2390 route nodes on the motivating monorepo (wildcard constant routes enter the graph). Kotlin star-imported annotation paths now fold on the same skip-floor contract as named imports.

title: feat(node): wrapped-client HTTP consumers + leading-prefix template stripping
body:
## Problem

Enterprise frontends typically route everything through a wrapped axios instance: `httpClient.request({ url: \`${serviceClient}/api/v1/orders\`, method: 'post' })`. Upstream node extraction only recognizes bare `fetch`/`axios`/jQuery, and consumer-path normalization left the leading `${serviceClient}` as a `{param}` segment that never matches anything.

An earlier iteration of this took the longest `/`-leading literal segment of the url template; review confirmed that heuristic silently truncates mid-template interpolations (failure mode: a confidence-1.0 false link). This PR carries the corrected design.

## Fix

- `X.request({ url, method|type })` member form: any `.request(options)` call with url/method string props (property named `request` — no conflict with the express provider or axios member shapes).
- Leading `${...}` gateway/service-prefix variables are stripped as **consumer-path normalization semantics** (`stripLeadingTemplatePrefix` in `normalizeHttpPath`): `${client}/api/v1/x` → `/api/v1/x` for fetch/axios/wrapped shapes alike. Mid/tail interpolations still round-trip through `{param}`. A stripped remainder not starting with `/` is dropped — the same rejection static relative urls get at scan time, because whether `${c}api/x` reads as a path depends on unverifiable runtime state.
- Non-literal `method` → `*` wildcard. `%7B/%7D` unescaping on the absolute-URL branches.

## Effect

On our 16-repo frontend monorepo + backend group: sync went from 1740 contracts / **0** cross-links to 5111 / **2097** exact cross-links (16/16 frontend repos linked, confidence 1.0, frontend api function ↔ backend Controller method).

title: fix(group): impact selector pass-through, degraded links, sync failure hygiene
body:
Three fixes in the group surface, found running cross-repo groups at scale:

## 1. `@group impact` selector pass-through (dead wire)

`target_uid` / `file_path` / `kind` were accepted at the MCP boundary and then dropped in validation — the three-segment chain (MCP boundary → service port → cross-impact `impactParams`) was never wired, so disambiguating an ambiguous impact target never actually reached the per-member impact. All three segments now forward.

## 2. Degraded cross-links

Cross-links whose provider endpoint never resolves to a graph symbol are marked `degraded: true` at the single persistence boundary (post merge/dedupe, before re-export), counted in `SyncResult.degradedLinks`, and surfaced by the sync summary ("degraded links: N"). The field documents its own remedy: re-analyze the provider repo so its handlers resolve. Before this, such links were indistinguishable from healthy ones and silently failed cross-impact fan-out.

## 3. Sync failure hygiene

- A repo whose per-repo extraction throws now records `{ repo, reason }` in `SyncResult.failedRepos` (it still lands in `missingRepos`, so downstream semantics are unchanged). The old catch swallowed the exception entirely — a repo whose HTTP extractor succeeded and whose gRPC extractor threw could contribute a partial contract set while the log said "its contracts are omitted".
- Operator warnings accumulate in `SyncResult.warnings` (e.g. bridge.lbug write failure after contracts.json was already written).

Tests cover the selector threading (three-segment chain), degraded marking, and per-repo failure reporting.

title: fix(group): make degraded links, sync warnings and UID-only impact actually work
body:
Supersedes #3112 (by @ChunxueLi, whose three commits are included here unchanged). This branch adds the follow-up that makes that PR's three claims true at the boundaries that produce the values.

## Summary

PR #3112 wired `degradedLinks`, `failedRepos` and `warnings` through the types and the MCP payload, but nothing on the sync path ever set them, so all three were constant. This adds:

- **`degraded` was never set.** The flag was only ever *cleared*, inside the exported `dedupeCrossLinks` — which the sync path does not call (it has a local key-only dedupe). `degradedLinks` was therefore always `0`. Derivation now lives in one exported `applyDegradedFlag`, called both by the sync finalize step and by the post-merge re-derivation, so exact/wildcard/manifest origins share a single truth point and the `manifest::` exemption stays in one place.
- **`warnings` was always `[]`.** The `writeBridgeUnlocked` catch logged an operator warning and dropped it. It now pushes the same string it logs.
- **UID-only `@group impact` was unreachable.** `validateGroupImpactParams` rejected on a missing `target` *before* parsing `target_uid`, so the documented "re-call with `target_uid`" disambiguation loop could not work in group mode even though the selectors were forwarded correctly. It now requires `target` **or** `target_uid`.
- **`failedRepos[].repo` could not be joined to `unreadableRepos`.** The former used the registry display name, the latter the group path. Both now use the group path; the JSDoc no longer points at the wrong list (`missingRepos`).
- **Truncated tool description.** `group_sync`'s heading read `AD THE RESULT:`; restored to `READ THE RESULT:` and documented the three new fields.

## Test plan

Each value is pinned at the boundary that produces it, rather than at the type:

- [x] `test/unit/group/sync.test.ts` — degraded provider sets the flag and the count; a resolved provider leaves the key absent (not `false`).
- [x] `test/unit/group/sync-unreadable-repos.test.ts` — ENOSPC bridge-write failure populates `warnings`; unopenable index populates `failedRepos` keyed by group path.
- [x] `test/unit/group/cross-impact.test.ts` — UID-only call is accepted and forwards a non-empty `target`; a call with neither selector is rejected.
- [x] `test/unit/group/service-group-sync-payload.test.ts` — exact `toEqual` wire shape now includes all three fields (it previously omitted them, so dropping any one was silent).
- [x] `test/unit/tools.test.ts` — pins `READ THE RESULT` and the three field names in the description.

body:
Bumps [onnxruntime-common](https://github.com/Microsoft/onnxruntime) from 1.27.0 to 1.29.0.
Release notes

Sourced from onnxruntime-common's releases.

ONNX Runtime v1.29.0

Announcements & Breaking Changes

  • onnxruntime-web has announced the deprecation of WebGL and JSEP. The native WebGPU EP is the recommended path going forward. See the deprecation and migration plans for details (#29716, #31683).
  • POSIX telemetry is now available on Linux, macOS, Android, and iOS when ONNX Runtime is built with telemetry enabled. It does not change the public ABI, WebAssembly remains telemetry-free, and setting ORT_DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 before initialization disables non-Windows telemetry for the process (#27379, #29872).
  • The unused internal onnxruntime/python/tools/tensorrt dashboard tooling was removed. This does not affect the TensorRT Execution Provider APIs (#29395).

Security Fixes

Path, bounds, and input validation

  • Fixed a path traversal vulnerability in TensorRT and NvTensorRTRTX engine refitting by making external-data path validation unconditional (#29396).

title: Fatal watch error can be retried before shutdown completes
body:
## Problem

A queued streamed-incremental writeback violation is supposed to stop `analyze --watch` without retrying the pipeline. Fatal `onError` currently only resolves a promise. `WatchRefreshQueue` then requeues the failed paths and schedules backoff while `closed` is still false. `loop.close` awaits `watcher.close()` before `queue.close()`, so a slow chokidar close can let drain start another `runFullAnalysis`. Operators then pay another full pipeline and may see "Retry scheduled" after a claimed terminal stop.

This was found in code review of the #3101 fail-closed guard. It was not auto-applied: confidence 75, Codex-only (no cross-persona agreement), `autofix_class: manual`.

## Suggested fix

Mark the refresh queue closed synchronously in the fatal-error path, or close the queue before awaiting `watcher.close()`, so `runBatch` cannot schedule a retry that fires during watcher teardown.

Add a test that delays `watcher.close` and asserts zero extra `runFullAnalysis` after `StreamedIncrementalWritebackError`.

## Evidence

```
gitnexus/src/cli/watch.ts:345-347 -- close: async () => { await watcher.close(); await queue.close(); }
gitnexus/src/cli/watch.ts:469-473 -- if (shouldStopAfterWatchRefreshFailure(...)) { ... stopWatching(); return; }
gitnexus/src/cli/watch-queue.ts:147-166 -- after onError returns, if (!this.closed) re-add paths and schedule(retryDelayMs)
gitnexus/src/cli/watch.ts:500-501 -- await stopped; await loop.close();
```

## Source

Branch: `fix/3101-streamed-incremental-class-corruption`
Head: `d903bbfc9aa1f5342816bfe0f72d4a30a2029731`
Related: #3101
Review artifact: `docs/reviews/2026-08-31-streamed-incremental-writeback-ce-code-review.json`

title: fix(analyze): reject streamed incremental writeback
body:
## Summary

Incremental analysis that produced a streamed structural or PDG manifest now fails before writeback. The live graph index stays intact, and `analyze --watch` stops instead of retrying that deterministic violation.

Fixes https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/issues/3101

## Motivation / context

A local patch that bypassed the full-rebuild-only stream gate could finish as a successful incremental run while the persisted graph was already unsound. GitNexus could still have refused the write; it did not. This PR adds a fail-closed check at the final incremental decision, using actual pipeline manifests rather than request-time flags.

Plan: `docs/plans/2026-08-31-2052-fix-streamed-incremental-writeback-plan.md`

## Areas touched

- [x] `gitnexus/` (CLI / core / MCP server)
- [ ] `gitnexus-web/` (Vite / React UI)
- [ ] `.github/` (workflows, actions)
- [ ] `eval/` or other tooling
- [ ] Docs / agent config only (`AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.cursor/`, `llms.txt`, etc.)

## Scope & constraints

**In scope**

- Typed invariant at the post-pipeline incremental seam: a defined structural or PDG manifest, including zero-row, is a streamed representation and cannot be written surgically.
- Watch treats that error as terminal and reports that the live index was not changed.
- Analyze-worker IPC keeps one terminal, non-retryable error with the recovery text.

**Explicitly out of scope / not done here**

- Enabling sound incremental streaming (delta-scoped manifests and full persistence parity).
- COPY, FTS, embedding, or LadybugDB forensics for the original `Class` row shape.
- Watch queue retry during shutdown (follow-up work).

## Implementation notes

The guard runs after the final `isIncremental` decision and before writeback-owned metadata or graph-store work. Pre-pipeline compatibility reconciliation of metadata mirrors remains allowed.

Watch distinguishes this configuration violation from live-index mutation: only the latter still uses the “may have been updated in place” stop reason.

## Related

- Related: https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/issues/3120

## Testing & verification

- [x] `cd gitnexus && npx vitest run test/unit/streamed-incremental-writeback-guard.test.ts test/unit/streamed-incremental-writeback-orchestration.test.ts test/unit/watch-failure-policy.test.ts test/unit/analyze-worker-core.test.ts`
- [ ] `cd gitnexus && npm run test:integration` *(if core/indexing/MCP paths changed)*
- [x] `cd gitnexus && npx tsc --noEmit`
- [ ] `cd gitnexus-web && npm test` *(if web changed)*
- [ ] `cd gitnexus-web && npx tsc -b --noEmit` *(if web changed)*
- [ ] Manual / Playwright E2E *(note environment — see `gitnexus-web/e2e/`)*

Focused coverage: empty and populated structural/PDG/both manifests; full rebuilds still pass manifests through; ordinary incremental with neither manifest is unchanged; watch stop vs retry; worker single terminal error.

Also run: `cd gitnexus && npx vitest run test/unit/stream-graph-emit-config.test.ts test/unit/stream-pdg-emit-config.test.ts test/unit/stream-graph-emit-force-ordering.test.ts test/unit/incremental-orchestration.test.ts test/unit/incremental-fts-drop-ordering.test.ts`

## Risk & rollout

No schema, format, or default streaming-mode change. Supported full rebuilds and ordinary incrementals keep their current write paths. Operators who hit the new error should disable incremental streaming or run `gitnexus analyze --force`. No index refresh is required for a healthy repo.

## Checklist

- [x] PR body meets repo minimum length (workflow may label short descriptions)
- [ ] If `AGENTS.md` / overlays changed: headers, scope block, and changelog updated per project conventions
- [x] No secrets, tokens, or machine-specific paths committed

title: Add a CLI option to control stale-index warnings
body:
### Area

Other

### Problem or opportunity

GitNexus checks whether the indexed repository is stale relative to the current Git HEAD and surfaces staleness information. However, users running GitNexus in scripts, CI environments, or automated workflows may want different behavior depending on the context.

For example, an interactive user may want a visible warning when the index is stale, while an automated workflow may prefer to suppress the warning or explicitly fail when stale data is detected.

Currently, there is no simple CLI-level option to control how stale-index detection is handled.

### Proposed solution

Add a CLI option that allows users to control stale-index handling for commands that rely on the index.

For example:

```bash
gitnexus query "authentication" --stale-policy warn
gitnexus query "authentication" --stale-policy ignore
gitnexus query "authentication" --stale-policy error

### Alternatives considered

**Alternatives considered**
```markdown
One alternative is to rely on environment variables or configuration files for this behavior. However, a CLI option is easier to discover, works well in CI/scripts, and allows different invocations to use different policies without modifying persistent configuration.

Another alternative is to automatically re-index whenever the repository is stale. This could unexpectedly trigger expensive analysis and embedding work, so automatic re-indexing should remain separate from stale-index policy.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `--stale-policy` CLI option is available for commands that consume the repository index.
- [ ] `warn` preserves the current behavior of reporting staleness while continuing execution.
- [ ] `ignore` suppresses stale-index warnings while continuing execution.
- [ ] `error` exits with a non-zero status when the index is stale.
- [ ] The default behavior remains backward compatible.
- [ ] Invalid policy values produce a clear CLI validation error.
- [ ] CLI help documents the available policies.
- [ ] Tests cover fresh and stale indexes for each supported policy.

### Constraints

- Must not change the existing index format or analysis pipeline.
- The default behavior must remain backward compatible.
- `--stale-policy` should not automatically trigger re-indexing.
- The implementation should work consistently across supported CLI commands that consume indexed data.
- The option should not add new runtime dependencies.

### Contribution

- [x] I am willing to open a PR for this (may need design discussion first).

title: feat(ingestion): capture Spring handler annotation arguments and template publishes
body:
Non-HTTP handler recognition already resolves the annotation *name* through imports, aliases, use-site targets and package visibility. What it never captured is the annotation's **arguments**, so the destination a listener binds to was invisible: `@KafkaListener(topics = ...)` and `@RabbitListener(queues = ...)` name it with different attributes, and a producer names it by position. The publishing side was missing entirely, which left every messaging edge one-directional by construction.

## What this adds

**Consumer side.** `SpringNonHttpHandlerAnnotationFact` gains an optional `args?: readonly { name?: string; text: string }[]`. `name` is optional because positional and named arguments are genuinely different shapes, not because it is sometimes unknown.

**Producer side.** `KafkaTemplate.send`, `RabbitTemplate.convertAndSend`, `JmsTemplate.convertAndSend` and `StreamBridge.send`, for both Java and Kotlin.

Arguments are captured as **syntax, never as a resolved address**. At capture time imports are not final, a sibling file's constants do not exist yet and configuration has not been read — the same reason annotation-name resolution is deferred. Resolution belongs to a later phase; doing it here would be a layering error that happens to work on simple inputs. Verified by experiment: stripping every `import` from a file, and capturing a file that really defines the referenced constant *before* the consumer, both leave the facts byte-identical.

## Parse cache schema 88 → 89

Both new facts ride the existing worker → main side channel, which is replayed verbatim from `ParsedFile.captureSideChannel`, so a warm v82 cache would skip the workers and hand back annotation facts with no `args` and an empty producer list.

This was measured across two worktrees rather than argued. With an older cache relabelled to the new number (simulating a forgotten bump), the new code serves it entirely from disk — `usedWorkerPool: false`, `reparsedFileCount: 0` — and returns **`producers: 0`** while still returning all 22 handler annotations: exactly the silent omission the bump prevents. With honest labels the cache is rejected and all 16 files reparse. One bump covers both replay paths, since the parse cache and the durable `ParsedFile` store key on the same version.

**This already happened once.** The entry was first allocated 83; by the time the branch was rebased, five bumps
had landed upstream and `main` stood at 88. It is now 89 — please re-check again before merging, since the
same race can repeat.

## Failure modes handled deliberately

- **Recovered syntax.** tree-sitter `ERROR`/`MISSING` nodes used to reach the argument list, so `@KafkaListener(topics = "orders", groupId =` produced a `groupId` whose value `{}` appears nowhere in the source, and a truncated publish swallowed the next method's text as arguments. A producer call with an unparsed argument list now yields **no fact** — the fact exists to carry a destination and has no state meaning "published somewhere unreadable" — and an annotation reports **no args**, collapsing into the marker-annotation state. Both tell a consumer "nothing here to resolve", which is true; a fabricated value would send it somewhere real and wrong. Failing closed is scoped to the broken call: a well-formed publish elsewhere in the same file still captures.
- **Comparability.** Whitespace normalization is applied to receiver *and* argument text on all four paths, so `send(Destinations.ORDERS, p)` and the same expression wrapped across lines produce equal facts. The normalizer is literal-aware, so a text block or raw string keeps its newlines.
- **Three-state contract.** `@Scheduled` → `args` absent; `@Scheduled()` → `[]`; with arguments → the list. Likewise `send { }` / `send()` / `send("t")`. The distinction survives `structuredClone`, `v8.serialize` and JSON, and is pinned.

## Cost

The Kotlin path deliberately does not prefilter annotations by simple name, because import aliases (`EventListener as SpringEvent`) would be lost. Reading arguments unconditionally therefore doubled the side-channel payload for every annotated callable in a repository. It now runs the same two passes as Java, with the first widened by the file's import aliases: the import header states both the local name and the FQN, so the relevance question is asked about the imported name and the answer carried back to the alias. Measured on 200 annotated non-handler functions: 78797 bytes unconditional → **41069, byte-identical to `main`**. Aliased handlers keep their arguments; aliased non-handlers get none.

## Verification

- Differential over **406 repository fixtures** plus 1218 deliberately malformed mutants (40%/75% truncation, BOM, CRLF): after removing the two new fields, output is byte-identical to `main`, with no crash on either side. Node- and edge-level graph comparison on three Spring fixture apps is identical too, so nothing downstream shifted.
- A mutation harness over 19 behaviour-bearing branches kills 18; the survivor is a defensive guard documented as currently unreachable under this grammar, with the node shape that proves it.
- Full suite green apart from three files that fail identically on `main` in this environment.

## Known gaps, unchanged by this PR and verified identical on `main`

Java does not capture handlers in interface default methods, enum or record methods, or anonymous classes; Kotlin does not capture them on top-level functions or anonymous objects; neither resolves a class-level `@KafkaListener` paired with `@KafkaHandler`, where the destination lives only on the class annotation; Kotlin `@[A(...) B(...)]` keeps only the first entry. Each changes which callables are scanned at all, which is a broader entry-point change than this PR should carry.

The producer facts have no production consumer yet — they ride the side channel and the cache, and the phase that joins them to handlers is the deferred resolution step.

title: feat(kotlin): ingest Spring HTTP routes as decoratorRoutes
body:
### Area
gitnexus (CLI / core / indexing / MCP server)

### Problem or opportunity
#2865 stamps definition-level `HANDLES_ROUTE` from `ExtractedDecoratorRoute.handlerName`. Python needed a `LanguageProvider.decoratorRouteHandlerName` hook because Flask/FastAPI emit through the worker's generic `@decorator` captures. Java and Nest already set `handlerName` in dedicated `extractDecoratorRoutes` extractors (`spring.ts`, `nest.ts`).

Kotlin is the remaining gap of the same *kind*, but **not** the same seam:

- The **group** HTTP plugin already scans Kotlin Spring annotations (`gitnexus/src/core/group/extractors/http-patterns/kotlin.ts`).
- The **ingestion** Kotlin provider (`gitnexus/src/core/ingestion/languages/kotlin.ts`) does **not** implement `extractDecoratorRoutes`.
- `extractSpringRoutes` in `gitnexus/src/core/ingestion/route-extractors/spring.ts` is bound to **tree-sitter-java** node types, so it cannot be pointed at Kotlin as-is.
- `KOTLIN_QUERIES` has no generic `@decorator` captures with `arg_str` / `arg_expr`, so copying Python's `decoratorRouteHandlerName` hook would be a no-op.

Consequence: Kotlin Spring controllers do not produce ingestion `Route` nodes / `handlerSymbolId` the way Java does. Parse-impl's constant fold also runs only over `decoratorRoutes`, which is why `kotlin-const-resolver.ts` is wired on the group layer only and documents an ingestion extractor as the prerequisite:

> Kotlin is wired into the GROUP layer only, because the ingestion fold in `pipeline-phases/parse-impl.ts` runs exclusively over `decoratorRoutes` — and `languages/kotlin.ts` declares no `extractDecoratorRoutes`.

### Proposed solution
Add a **Kotlin-owned** Spring route extractor (tree-sitter-kotlin AST), registered as `extractDecoratorRoutes` on `kotlinProvider`. It should emit the same `ExtractedDecoratorRoute` shape Java already uses, including `handlerName` from the annotated function/method.

Then wire the existing Kotlin constant-resolver hooks (`extractModuleConstants` / fold operands) so composed `@GetMapping(ApiPaths.X)` paths fold the same way as Java.

Do **not** implement `decoratorRouteHandlerName` for Kotlin unless Kotlin later starts emitting HTTP routes through the generic worker decorator loop.

### Alternatives considered
- **Reuse `decoratorRouteHandlerName`.** Wrong seam: Kotlin never hits that loop.
- **Call `extractSpringRoutes` from the Kotlin provider.** The extractor walks Java grammar (`method_declaration`, Java annotations). Kotlin's `function_declaration` / annotation nodes would silently miss.
- **Leave group-only coverage.** Group sync can still see Kotlin providers, but `analyze` Route nodes, `handlerSymbolId`, definition-level `HANDLES_ROUTE`, and parse-skip/`routeCoverage: 'complete'` stay Java-only.

### Acceptance criteria
- A Kotlin `@RestController` with `@GetMapping` / `@PostMapping` / `@RequestMapping` (method-level, plus class prefix) produces `Route` nodes on `analyze` with the same identity rules as Java Spring.
- Those routes carry `handlerName` / resolved `handlerSymbolId` for same-file handler functions/methods, and emit both file-level and definition-level `HANDLES_ROUTE` when the handler node exists in the graph.
- Composed/constant annotation arguments that `kotlin-const-resolver.ts` already folds in the group layer also fold on the ingestion path.
- Class-attached / non-handler annotations do not steal an enclosing class name as `handlerName`.
- Focused pipeline tests on a small Kotlin Spring fixture (cold + warm parse cache if `handlerName` is worker output).
- No change to Python's generic-decorator hook or to Java/`spring.ts` grammar ownership.

### Constraints
- Shared `core/ingestion/` must not grow Kotlin node-type names; plug in via `LanguageProvider` (`extractDecoratorRoutes` / constant hooks), per AGENTS.md.
- Keep `routeCoverage` at `'partial'` until ingestion emits a Route for every provider the Kotlin group plugin's `scan()` finds (same trap as Python Flask `add_url_rule`).
- `SCHEMA_BUMP` if new fields are minted in the parse worker and persisted in the parse cache.

### Context
Raised from review follow-up on https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/pull/2865: other languages do not all need the Python hook; Kotlin needs a dedicated ingestion Spring extractor.

title: BUG: detect-changes reports "No changes detected" for every scope and repo form on a fresh, populated index
body:
### Area

gitnexus (CLI / core / indexing / MCP server)

### Summary

`detect-changes` returns `No changes detected.` for every invocation I can construct on this machine: unstaged working-tree edits, `--scope all`, and `--scope compare` against a base ref hundreds of commits away. The index is freshly built and demonstrably populated — `impact`, `context` and `query` resolve real symbols from it in the same session, and `status` reports up-to-date at the current commit.

It exits 0, so anything treating it as a gate passes. `AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md` mandate exactly that use:

> **MUST run `detect_changes()` before committing** to verify your changes only affect expected symbols and execution flows.

I want to be explicit about what this report is not, because #2690 describes a similar-looking symptom and its reporter retracted it. Their repro appended to the end of a file, which maps to no indexed symbol, so zero was the correct answer. Every edit below is inside the body of an indexed exported function, and the failure reproduces in the main checkout, not only in a linked worktree. I also began with the worktree framing and disproved it with the control in step 4.

### Environment

- gitnexus 1.6.9
- Node v22.22.3
- macOS 26.5.1, arm64
- Repository indexed as `kpi-tracker`; a TypeScript / Next.js repo of roughly 2,000 source files
- Six indexed entries share the name `kpi-tracker` (a main checkout plus five linked worktrees), so every command below passes `--repo` explicitly

### Steps to reproduce

1. Index the main checkout and confirm it is current.

```
$ node .gitnexus/run.cjs analyze .
$ node .gitnexus/run.cjs status
Indexed commit: 320d74d
Current commit: 320d74d
Status: ✅ up-to-date
```

2. Confirm the target symbol is in the index. `impact` resolves it, with the file path and kind:

```
Function:src/features/campaigns/server/campaign-update/status-change.ts:applyStatusChange
```

3. Edit **inside that function's body**. `applyStatusChange` begins at line 142; the two inserted lines land at 151, well inside it:

```ts
  const priorStatus = priorStatusRow?.status ?? null
  const probeMarker = String(priorStatus ?? '').trim().length   // added
  void probeMarker                                              // added
```

`git diff --name-only` lists the file.

4. Run every form. All report nothing:

```
$ node .gitnexus/run.cjs detect-changes --repo /abs/path/to/main-checkout
No changes detected.

$ node .gitnexus/run.cjs detect-changes --scope unstaged --repo /abs/path/to/main-checkout
No changes detected.

$ node .gitnexus/run.cjs detect-changes --scope all --repo /abs/path/to/main-checkout
No changes detected.

$ node .gitnexus/run.cjs detect-changes --repo kpi-tracker
No changes detected.
```

5. `compare` scope also reports nothing, against base refs that differ by a great many commits:

```
$ node .gitnexus/run.cjs detect-changes --scope compare --base-ref origin/dev --repo /abs/path/to/main-checkout
No changes detected.

$ node .gitnexus/run.cjs detect-changes --scope compare --base-ref HEAD~5 --repo /abs/path/to/main-checkout
No changes detected.
```

The same battery in a linked worktree, indexed separately with `analyze /abs/path/to/worktree`, behaves identically. That is why I no longer believe this is worktree-specific.

6. The same package's own change detection is unaffected, which is the sharpest contrast I can offer. Run against a stored index that has fallen behind the checkout, `analyze` correctly identifies the delta:

```
$ node .gitnexus/run.cjs analyze .
Incremental: changed=678, added=905, deleted=791 (skipping wipe + 3885 unchanged file rows preserved)
```

So the indexer sees 678 changed files against the same stored index from which `detect-changes` reports none.

### Expected behavior

An unstaged edit inside an indexed function is reported as a changed symbol, and `--scope compare` against a distant base ref reports the symbols that differ. Where the tool cannot map a diff it should say so, rather than returning an empty result that reads as "nothing changed".

### Actual behavior

Every scope and every repo form returns `No changes detected.` and exit code 0, on an index that other commands read successfully in the same session.

### Impact

The failure mode is silence, which is what makes it costly. A gate built on `detect_changes` reports a clean blast radius for a commit it never analysed, and the result looks identical to a genuinely clean one. This repository worked around it in a `PreToolUse` hook that cross-checks `git diff` and denies the commit when git sees changed source files and `detect_changes` reports none — a guard that would be unnecessary if an unmappable diff failed loudly.

### What I could not rule out

I have only one machine to test on, so I cannot distinguish a defect in 1.6.9 from a fault in this particular installation or index store. If there is a diagnostic that would separate the two — a verbose flag, or a way to dump the diff-to-symbol mapping step — I am happy to run it and post the output.

One observation that may or may not be related: without `--repo`, the CLI errors with `Multiple repositories indexed. Specify which one with the 'repo' parameter` and lists six entries all named `kpi-tracker`. That is correct fail-closed behaviour and matches the fix noted in #2690, but it does mean this repository always exercises the explicit-`--repo` path.

title: feat(ingestion): resolve Spring messaging destinations into Destination nodes
body:
## What

Spring async messaging is captured today but nothing reads it. `SpringNonHttpHandlerAnnotationFact.args` (listener annotation arguments) and `SpringMessageProducerFact` (template publishes) both ride the capture side-channel and survive the parse cache, and no consumer exists. The PR that added them said as much.

This adds the consumer: a `Destination` node per broker address, with `PUBLISHES_TO` / `CONSUMES_FROM` edges from the callable that publishes or consumes. It is symmetric to `Route` + `HANDLES_ROUTE` — an address is to messaging what a URL is to HTTP.

No new capture, so **no `SCHEMA_BUMP` of its own**: this only reads facts already produced on `main`, and inherits 91 from #3133.

## The invariant this is built around

An address that could not be resolved must never connect two code sites.

If an unresolved `${app.topic}` entered the graph keyed by its placeholder text, two unrelated services that each write `${app.topic}` would share a node and read as connected. A missing edge is visible; a false one enters reports as real.

A status flag does not prevent that — the key still matches. The key does:

| | node id | `address` | connects |
|---|---|---|---|
| resolved | the address | present | yes |
| unresolved | code location | **absent (SQL NULL)** | no, structurally |

Anything joining on `address` cannot match a NULL, so the separation survives the database round trip rather than depending on every future query remembering to filter. The same rule is enforced at the HTTP boundary: the graph mapper normalizes NULL to *absent*, because serializing `"address": null` would hand every unresolved destination one shared join key.

## The cascade

1. **literal** — `"orders.v1"`, plus array forms (`{"a","b"}`, `["a","b"]`, `arrayOf(...)`), which arrive as one unsplit string and are parsed here
2. **constant** — `Topics.ORDERS`, through the existing Java and Kotlin constant folds
3. **configuration key** — recorded and linked to `Property` nodes, never resolved to a value (config values are deliberately absent from the graph)
4. **specification** — a documented seam, not implemented

Every path that declines records **why**, from a closed set of named reasons. Refusals are data: the point of this feature is to make the unresolved fraction measurable, so a silent drop would hide the number that says whether it works.

## Deliberate refusals

Several shapes look resolvable and are not. Each is refused with a named reason rather than guessed:

- **SpEL** (`#{@beanName.topic}`) — a runtime bean expression, not an address
- **Kotlin string templates** (`"orders-$env"`, `"orders-${env}"`) — the language interpolates, so this is not a literal. The escaped `"\${app.topic}"`, which is how a Spring placeholder must be written in Kotlin, still resolves normally. Routed through an `interpolatesStringLiterals` capability on the provider, so no language name enters shared pipeline code.
- **`${key:default}`** — the default is written in the source, but it only holds if configuration does not override it, and configuration values are not in the graph. Reading it is fair; using it as node *identity* is not, so this is unresolved with both key and default retained.
- **`rabbitTemplate.convertAndSend` with an ambiguous overload** — at arity 3 and 4 a string literal in slot 1 is syntactically indistinguishable between routing key and message payload, so it is refused rather than read. A constant or qualified reference there is evidence and still resolves; arity 5 has no competing overload and is unaffected. This costs coverage on an idiomatic shape — `convertAndSend("exchange", "orders.created", payload)` now yields nothing — but the alternative silently publishes a payload as an address.

## One address, two brokers

**Disconnected, not merged.** A Kafka topic and a same-named Rabbit queue used to share a node with a `brokerConflict` flag — but ordinary traversal still reported that as a connection, and the flag did not undo the join. Now both sides take a location key, drop `address`, and carry `resolution: 'broker-conflict'` plus the conflicting broker names, so the diagnosis survives while the join cannot happen.

Detection is two-pass: the conflict is only observable on the second broker, by which time the first node may already carry an edge.

## Verification

Measured on `test/fixtures/spring-destination-app`, which is in this PR: **24 destinations, 16 unresolved, 0 false joins.** Both roles occur. The fixture is deliberately loaded with hard cases, so that ratio is not representative of real code.

- On a repository with **no** messaging, the graph is byte-identical to base across 899 nodes and 1327 edge triples.
- On a messaging repository the only differences are the new label and the two new edge types; nothing is removed.
- Warm parse cache is a genuine replay (`usedWorkerPool === false`), cold and warm agree.
- Incremental re-analyze is covered by a test that runs `runFullAnalysis` three times against a real repository and asserts the incremental branch actually ran, so it cannot pass on a silent full rebuild.

The schema pair table moves 482 → 509: 26 generated by the `ATTACHMENT_TARGET_LABELS` rule plus one hand-declared `Destination → Property`. The 1.5× budget in `schema.ts` is prose and has not been re-measured at this size; nothing was relaxed to make room.

## Known limitations

- Annotations are matched by simple name; a phase has no import tables, so an import-aliased `@KafkaListener` is missed. Capture already gates the same way.
- A Kotlin constant that folds to an escaped placeholder loses its escapes in the fold, so it is filed under `unescaped-interpolation` where `unresolved-config-key` would be precise. Both are unresolved — never a false address — but the reason breakdown is imprecise there. A precise diagnosis needs the fold to report whether the declaration was escaped, which the shared `ModuleConstants` shape does not carry.
- The destination layer is rebuilt on each incremental writeback rather than incrementally maintained. It is a small table, but it is new unconditional work.
- Broker attribution comes from the receiver's *name*, so a wrong guess now disconnects a pair that genuinely agrees on an address. That is the deliberate direction — a missing edge is visible, a false one is not — but nothing distinguishes "two real brokers" from "one bad name guess" beyond the recorded conflict.

title: feat(analyze): adaptive worker concurrency under a memory budget + quieter rebuild gates + persisted needsFullRebuild marker (OOM ops feedback from a 25k-file repo)
body:
## Context

Reindexing a large Java monorepo (~25.7k `.java` files, single `winning-winex-opt` repo) after a gitnexus upgrade triggered all three full-rebuild gates at once (schema fingerprint, analysis features, runner identity — expected and correct). The subsequent full re-analyze **OOM'd twice on consecutive nights** on a memory-constrained host (3 GB RAM + 17 GB swap, `--max-old-space-size=8192`):

```
[557175] 12990986 ms: Scavenge 7704.5 (8229.8) -> 7702.0 (8230.8) MB ... allocation failure
FATAL ERROR: Reached heap limit Allocation failed - JavaScript heap out of memory
```

It ran for **3.7 hours** before dying — ~2x slower than the last successful full analyze of the same repo (67 min on the previous build), thrashing in GC (mu = 0.02) for the last stretch. The worker-pool symptoms documented in README ("Analysis runs out of memory", #2649) also showed up in a follow-up run:

```
{"level":40,"workerIndex":2,"error":"Replacement worker did not report ready within 5000ms —
 likely crashed during top-of-script init ... repeated on a large repo? likely main-thread
 memory pressure — see the "Analysis runs out of memory" README section, #2649",
 "msg":"Worker 2 replacement failed to come online; dropping slot."}
```

This is a feature request born from ops reality, not a bug report — the gates themselves did the right thing. Three suggestions, in priority order.

## 1. Adaptive worker concurrency under a memory budget (`--memory-budget` or auto)

Today the worker count (and thus peak RSS) is effectively fixed, so a full analyze of a 25k-file repo needs a host-sized heap or it dies at hour 3 with nothing to show. Proposal:

- Add an opt-in memory budget (e.g. `--memory-budget-mb=4096` or env `GITNEXUS_MEMORY_BUDGET_MB`).
- When set, derive worker count from the budget (start conservative: `max(1, budget / perWorkerEstimate)`), and **drop worker slots instead of crashing** when `worker.replace` fails on memory pressure — the pool already has the "dropping slot" concept, it just arrives too late (after the replacement crashed) and the run still dies later on the main thread.
- Even without an explicit flag, a cheaper win: when a replacement worker fails to come online *and* the reason string contains "memory pressure", **halve the live worker count** once and log it, instead of retrying at the same width.

Trade-off to be explicit about: fewer workers = slower parse, but a run that finishes at 1.5x wall-clock beats a run that OOMs at 3.7h and leaves the repo unindexed.

## 2. Collapse the three rebuild gates into one diagnostic line

When schema fingerprint + analysis features + runner identity all change in one upgrade (the common case: "I pulled a new build"), the log prints three separate `forcing a full ...` lines. Operators then have to figure out whether they have three problems or one. Suggestion: detect the multi-hit and print a single summary:

```
full rebuild required — 3 gates tripped by this build change:
  - index schema changed (0061b2888f22 -> 6827b7d6b062)
  - analysis capabilities changed (missing: java.heritage-captures, ...)
  - analyzer runner identity changed
(all expected after upgrading the analyzer; one full re-analyze clears all three)
```

## 3. Persist a `needsFullRebuild` marker on failure so retries don't look mysterious

When a forced full analyze OOMs, the *old* (pre-gate) index is still on disk and the metadata still stamps the old fingerprint. The next cron run hits the same gates, tries the same full rebuild, and OOMs again — which is how we burned two consecutive nights before a human looked. Suggestion: on a failed forced rebuild, stamp something like `meta.pendingFullRebuildReason = 'schema' | 'capabilities' | 'identity'` (or reuse the existing gate evaluation, which already computes this) so that:

- `gitnexus status` can say "index awaiting full rebuild since <date>, reason: schema — last attempt failed after 3.7h" instead of looking like a fresh mystery every night;
- ops tooling can detect "failed full rebuild" as a distinct state from "index missing".

Happy to turn any of these into a PR — #1 is the one we'd actually use daily (this host reindexes 23 repos nightly on 3 GB RAM).

title: fix(cli): do not call zero-symbol detect-changes a clean tree

## Summary

`detect-changes` printed **No changes detected.** (exit 0) for two non-clean cases that #3131 hits:

title: Cypher: lower() throws "Invalid UTF-8" on multi-label node scans while every single-label scan on the same store is clean
body:
### Environment

- gitnexus **1.6.9** (npm global), macOS, Node 24
- Kuzu store, `schemaVersion: 5`, 34 node tables + `CodeRelation`
- The affected index was **built by 1.6.9 itself** (`indexedAt` is after the 1.6.9 install), default `analyze` — no `--pdg`, no embeddings
- Java repo, ~2.2k files, 27,873 nodes

### Summary

`lower(n.name)` throws `Runtime exception: Failed calling LOWER: Invalid UTF-8` when the MATCH pattern spans more than one node table — but on the **same store**, scanning each node table individually with the same expression succeeds for **all 34 tables**, and the per-table row counts sum exactly to the untyped total. There is no row with invalid UTF-8 stored anywhere.

This looks distinct from #2889 and #3031, which are analyze-time write-path issues where dirty data really does get persisted. Here nothing dirty is persisted; the bad string appears to be produced by the multi-label scan path itself, on a read-only query.

### Repro

```cypher
-- fails
MATCH (n) RETURN count(lower(n.name));
-- Runtime exception: Failed calling LOWER: Invalid UTF-8

-- every single-label scan passes, 34/34 tables
MATCH (n:Method)   RETURN count(lower(n.name));  -- 13158
MATCH (n:Property) RETURN count(lower(n.name));  --  7566
MATCH (n:File)     RETURN count(lower(n.name));  --  2241
MATCH (n:Class)    RETURN count(lower(n.name));  --  1086
MATCH (n:Function) RETURN count(lower(n.name));  --  1363
MATCH (n:Folder)   RETURN count(lower(n.name));  --   873
MATCH (n:Const)    RETURN count(lower(n.name));  --   588
MATCH (n:Interface) RETURN count(lower(n.name)); --   277
MATCH (n:Section)  RETURN count(lower(n.name));  --   217
MATCH (n:Constructor) RETURN count(lower(n.name)); -- 209
MATCH (n:Enum)     RETURN count(lower(n.name));  --   149
MATCH (n:Route)    RETURN count(lower(n.name));  --    90
MATCH (n:Variable) RETURN count(lower(n.name));  --    56
-- remaining 21 tables from CALL show_tables(): 0 rows each, no error

-- sum = 27873
MATCH (n) RETURN count(n);  -- 27873
```

### It is not arity, not cardinality, and not one poisoned table

```cypher
MATCH (n:Method|Class|File|Folder)         -- 4 labels, 17358 rows -> OK
MATCH (n:Method|Class|Interface|Function)  -- 4 labels, 15884 rows -> FAILS

-- all four 3-subsets of the failing set pass:
MATCH (n:Method|Class|Interface)   -- 14521 -> OK
MATCH (n:Method|Class|Function)    -- 15607 -> OK
MATCH (n:Method|Interface|Function)-- 14798 -> OK
MATCH (n:Class|Interface|Function) --  2726 -> OK
```

Same pattern elsewhere in the same store:

```cypher
MATCH (n:Property|Route|Enum|Constructor)       -- 8014 -> OK
MATCH (n:Property|Route|Enum|Constructor|Const) -- FAILS
MATCH (n:Const)          -- 588 -> OK
MATCH (n:Const|Route)    -- 678 -> OK
MATCH (n:Property|Const) -- 8154 -> OK
```

`Const`'s 588 names are plain ASCII SCREAMING_CASE / camelCase identifiers.

Behaviour is identical with or without `WHERE ... CONTAINS`, and with or without `LIMIT`.

### Store-dependent

Six indexes on the same server, same gitnexus version, same 34-table schema, same language:

- 4 reproduce, at **different label thresholds** — one fails as soon as 5 labels are scanned, another passes at 5 and only fails on the full untyped scan
- 2 never reproduce, even on `MATCH (n)` over all 34 tables

Presence of embeddings and the CJK segmentation mode do not correlate with which ones reproduce.

### Impact

The natural case-insensitive symbol search — `MATCH (n) WHERE lower(n.name) CONTAINS $kw` — is unusable on affected repos. It fails loudly rather than returning wrong rows, so it is not a silent-correctness hazard, but it blocks a common query shape and is easy to misread as "0 hits" when sweeping many repos programmatically.

Workaround that works on every affected store: **one node label per statement**, run separately and add the counts.

### Guess at the mechanism

Not verified — I only have the published build. The signature (every subset passes, the union fails, independent of total row count) points at the multi-label scan's string value-vector layout rather than at stored data: something appears to read across a chunk boundary when results from several node tables are combined before `LOWER` is applied.

Happy to run any narrowing query against an affected store.

title: feat(ingestion): mint Destination nodes from AsyncAPI 3.x documents
body:
## Summary

`--asyncapi-spec <path>` reads AsyncAPI 3.x documents from an explicitly configured directory or file and mints `Destination` nodes from their `operations[]` entries, keyed by the same `destinationNodeKey(broker, address)` that #3132 introduced — so a document and a source site naming one address on one broker land on **one** node rather than two.

## Motivation / context

#3132 gave GitNexus `Destination` nodes resolved from source. Where the address is a configuration placeholder — `@KafkaListener(topics = "${app.orders.topic}")` — the source cannot resolve it, so that destination keys on its source **location** and carries no `address` property. That is deliberate: two services that merely wrote the same `${placeholder}` must not join.

The address usually does exist somewhere, though: in a shipped AsyncAPI document. Reading one closes the gap without weakening the keying rule, because a document address is a *resolved* address and keys exactly like a source-resolved one.

## Areas touched

- [x] `gitnexus/` (CLI / core / MCP server)
- [ ] `gitnexus-web/` (Vite / React UI)
- [ ] `.github/` (workflows, actions)
- [ ] `eval/` or other tooling
- [x] Docs / agent config only (`README.md`, `skills/gitnexus-cli`)

## Scope & constraints

**In scope**

- `--asyncapi-spec <path>` — an explicit local path, directory or single file, inside or outside the repository. Absent = off; the feature costs nothing when unused.
- AsyncAPI **3.x** documents. `action: send` → `PUBLISHES_TO`, `action: receive` → `CONSUMES_FROM`.
- Broker resolution in a fixed order: channel/operation `bindings`, then the channel's explicit `servers`, then the document's servers.
- Enabling **or disabling** the option forces a full rebuild, because documents live outside git and incremental freshness cannot see them change.
- A per-run report of what was scanned, accepted, and refused — with a breakdown by refusal reason.

**Explicitly out of scope / not done here**

- **AsyncAPI 2.x is refused**, under its own counted reason, never mapped. Its `publish`/`subscribe` are inverted relative to 3.x `send`/`receive` (in 2.x, `publish` describes what the *application receives*). A naive mapping reverses the direction of the async graph **while leaving it connected**, which is the failure mode nobody can see. Supporting 2.x is a real follow-up; guessing at it is not.
- **OpenAPI is out of scope.** HTTP produces no `Destination` nodes — for HTTP the host is the namespace, not the address.
- **Step 4 of the address cascade (`specification`) is still not supplied.** A document names addresses but not the *method* that uses one. A `(broker, action)` bucket usually holds more than one operation, so any assignment past a bucket of size one is a heuristic that would attach an address to the wrong call site. The hook stays empty on purpose, and the reasoning is recorded next to it in `frameworks/spring/destinations.ts`.
- **No glob auto-discovery of committed documents.** Every existing index would grow nodes on its next run with no operator decision. An explicit path keeps that a choice.
- **No `.gitnexusrc` key.** The option fails closed; a config key would let a checked-in file silently change what a shared index contains.

## Implementation notes

**The invariant this change is built around.** A *resolved* destination keys on `(broker, address)` and carries `address`; an *unresolved* one keys on its source location and omits `address`. Nothing here lets an unresolved destination acquire a joinable key. A false connection is worse than a missing one: a missing edge is visible as a gap, a false one is reported as a fact. The refusal set exists to protect that property, not to validate documents for their own sake.

**Two protocol readers with opposite defaults**, in `asyncapi/protocol.ts`:

- `brokerForProtocol` reads `servers[].protocol`, a field *declared* to hold a protocol, so an unknown value passes through as a literal — it is still the document's claim.
- `brokerForBindingKey` reads `bindings` **map keys**, a namespace where non-protocol keys are legitimately expected (`$ref`, `x-` vendor extensions), so only a known-protocol allowlist answers.

One rule applied to both would be wrong in one direction or the other: pass-through on a map key mints `Destination(broker='x-scs-function')` from an ordinary vendor annotation, and an allowlist on a declared field discards protocols we simply have not enumerated.

**Bounded reading.** The reader treats documents as untrusted input: byte, operation, document, walk-entry, directory-depth, address-length and identifier-length caps; a non-blocking open so a FIFO under the configured path cannot hang the analyzer; a read loop rather than a single `read()`; symlinks skipped and counted. Every refusal is counted by reason, so a mistyped path reports as "nothing scanned" rather than quietly making the source-side unresolved fraction look better than it is.

**Forced rebuild** mirrors the existing `springActuatorPath` mechanism in `run-analyze.ts`, including on *disable* — otherwise turning the option off would leave the previously minted nodes in the graph.

**One question for a maintainer.** `destinationNodeKey` composes `` `${broker} ${address}` `` with a space. I raised this on #3132 and it is still open; it affects `routeNodeKey` symmetrically. This PR closes it defensively on its own side (a broker containing whitespace is refused), but the key encoding itself is your call, and a delimiter that cannot occur in either component would remove the question entirely.

**One note on provenance.** An earlier commit body in this branch (`43936dec`) phrases a design decision as a measured result. The measurement was on a corpus I cannot share, so the code does not claim it — the comment in `destinations.ts` argues the point structurally instead. Please read the code comment, not that commit message.

## Testing & verification

- [x] `cd gitnexus && npx tsc --noEmit` — clean
- [x] `cd gitnexus-web && rm -f tsconfig.app.tsbuildinfo && npx tsc -b --noEmit` — clean
- [x] `cd gitnexus && npm test` — full suite green apart from four files that fail identically on untouched `main` in this environment (`analyzer-identity`, `hooks` reading ambient `ps` output, `review-agent-workflow`)
- [x] New: `test/unit/asyncapi-document.test.ts` (69 cases — refusal set, protocol normalisation, direction mapping, bounds, symlink and FIFO handling), `test/unit/spring-destinations-phase.test.ts` (+26 — node keying, counters, logging), and one end-to-end case in `test/unit/incremental-orchestration.test.ts` under the `lbug-db` project proving a changed document forces the rebuild.
- [x] Manual end-to-end against `test/fixtures/spring-destination-app`: an address existing **only** in a document is minted with the right broker and direction; an address already resolved from source stays a **single** node; the same address on a different broker stays a separate node.

Two coverage gaps I would rather state than hide: neither new test file is registered in `scripts/cross-platform-tests.ts`, so they run on `ubuntu-latest` only; and a mutant that removes directory-entry sorting survives locally because APFS returns `readdir` already sorted — it would be caught on a filesystem that does not.

## Risk & rollout

- **Off by default.** No behaviour change for any existing index that does not pass the flag.
- **No schema change.** `parse-cache.ts` is untouched, so no `SCHEMA_BUMP` is claimed here — one less collision for concurrent PRs.
- Enabling or disabling the option triggers one full rebuild by design; this is reported in the log, not silent.
- The option is rejected under `--watch`, where a forced rebuild per change would be the wrong trade.

## Checklist

- [x] PR body meets repo minimum length
- [x] `AGENTS.md` / overlays unchanged; the three shipped copies of the CLI skill are updated together and their sync test passes
- [x] No secrets, tokens, or machine-specific paths committed

Release notes

Sourced from axios's releases.

v1.20.0 — August 19, 2026

This release hardens runtime option handling, adds RFC 9110 status-code aliases, fixes Node.js and XHR reliability issues, and refreshes project tooling and documentation.

⚠️ Breaking Changes & Deprecations

  • HTTP Status Naming: Added ContentTooLarge (413) and UnprocessableContent (422), while retaining PayloadTooLarge and UnprocessableEntity as backward-compatible deprecated aliases. (#11082)

🔒 Security Fixes

  • Runtime Option Handling: Hardened behavioral configuration reads against shared and foreign prototype pollution and normalized unsafe interceptor replacement objects. This also clarifies Fetch redirect and custom implementation behavior, HTTP/2 DNS and proxy handling, CIDR-based NO_PROXY matching, and malformed data URI rejection; see the PR for documented compatibility effects. (#11141)

🐛 Bug Fixes

  • Interceptor Lifecycle: Prevented unbounded handler-array growth by trimming trailing ejected interceptors without changing iteration semantics, and kept interceptor operations safe when the public handlers field is nullish. (#11087, #11118)
  • Request Error Preservation: Prevented custom Error.prepareStackTrace implementations that return non-string values from replacing the original request failure with an unrelated TypeError. (#11109)
  • XHR Reliability: Navigation-canceled requests now reject with ECONNABORTED instead of resolving with status 0, while successful downloads flush their final progress callback during the live loadend dispatch. (#11094, #11121)
  • Node.js Socket Memory: Removed request-context retention from per-socket error listeners, preventing completed response data from being pinned for the lifetime of pooled keep-alive sockets. (#11091)
  • Core Methods and HTTP Errors: Prevented structural method-header buckets from leaking into outgoing headers, standardized invalid DNS lookup and httpVersion failures as AxiosError.ERR_BAD_OPTION_VALUE, and corrected the timeoutErrorMessage merge strategy. (#11096)

🔧 Maintenance & Chores

  • Dependencies: Updated fast-uri, postcss, js-yaml, mocha, development-tooling groups, and GitHub Actions dependencies. (#11092, #11098, #11099, #11106, #11107, #11122, #11123, #11126, #11127, #11133, #11140, #11143, #11144)
  • Documentation: Applied the v1.19.0 documentation updates, added the missing fs import to the README stream example, introduced localized global search, and repaired the interceptor test link. (#11101, #11113, #11097, #11119)
  • Sponsorship: Updated sponsorship links and data and added ScrapingBee as a sponsor. (#11124, #11136, #11137)
  • CI and Release: Switched ESM smoke tests to locked dependencies and synchronized package and runtime version metadata for v1.20.0. (#11128, #11152)

  • Update default CodeQL bundle version to 2.26.3. #4085

  • Changed the default filepath for the new remote file address format that was introduced in CodeQL Action 4.37.0 / 3.37.0 to .github/codeql-config.yml to align it with the suggested path that is used elsewhere. #4070

4.37.5 - 03 Aug 2026

  • Fixed a bug where a network error while streaming the download of the CodeQL bundle could terminate the init Action instead of falling back to downloading the bundle before extracting it. #4061

4.37.4 - 29 Jul 2026

  • This version of the CodeQL Action adds support for the tools input for the codeql-action/init step to be specified using a github-codeql-tools repository property. This feature will gradually be rolled out following the release of this version. Once rolled out, this allows for the CodeQL CLI version that is used in GitHub-managed workflows, such as Default Setup, to be set to a custom value. For example, customers who run into issues with rate limits when a new CodeQL CLI version is released can set the value to toolcache to always use the CodeQL CLI version that is available in the runner toolcache. For Advanced Setup workflows, the value provided for tools in the workflow definition always takes precedence unless the value of the repository property starts with !. #4037
  • Update default CodeQL bundle version to 2.26.2. #4051

4.37.3 - 22 Jul 2026

No user facing changes.

4.37.2 - 21 Jul 2026

  • The new address format for the config-file input that was introduced in CodeQL Action 4.37.0 is now enabled by default. In addition to the format described there, the remote= prefix can now be used to explicitly indicate that the input refers to a remote file. All previous input formats continue to be accepted as well. #4023
  • The CodeQL Action can now make use of configured private registries in Default Setup to retrieve CodeQL configuration files from remote repositories that require authentication. This will allow customers to store their CodeQL configuration in a single repository that can then be referenced by Default Setup workflows in other repositories. We expect to roll this and other, related changes out to everyone in July. #4007

title: analyze --force replays cached parses; capture changes are invisible until SCHEMA_BUMP
body:
## Summary

`gitnexus analyze --force` prints "forcing a full re-analyze so the database is recreated from the current schema", but it rebuilds the database from `.gitnexus/parse-cache` / `.gitnexus/parsedfile-cache` when the cache key (file content + `PARSE_CACHE_VERSION`) still matches. Any change that only affects parse-time captures (a `query.ts` rule, an extractor tweak) is therefore invisible to `--force` until `SCHEMA_BUMP` is incremented, and the CLI gives no indication that cached parses were replayed.

This is by design per @navidemad on #1432 (the repo rule is "bump `SCHEMA_BUMP` on any capture change"), so this issue is about the ergonomics, not the mechanism: the flag's name and its own log line both promise a full re-analysis, and a developer iterating on a capture rule gets a silently stale index.

## Reproduction (real project, 394 files)

1. Build PR #1432 at `97571d23`, `gitnexus analyze . --skip-git --force --max-file-size 600` on a 199-file Zig project. Result: 9,702 nodes / 20,774 edges, `import-resolved (constructor)` = 0.
2. Check out `e2b13233` (adds a new `struct_initializer` capture in `languages/zig/query.ts`), rebuild, run the identical `analyze ... --force`. CLI prints the "forcing a full re-analyze" line. Result: byte-identical to step 1, still 0 of the new edges.
3. `rm -rf .gitnexus/parse-cache .gitnexus/parsedfile-cache`, run the same command again. Result: 9,659 nodes / 20,682 edges, `import-resolved (constructor)` = 69.

Nothing in step 2's output distinguishes it from step 3 except the numbers.

## Suggestions (any one would do)

- Make `--force` (or a new `--no-parse-cache` / `--force=full`) also invalidate the parse caches, since "force" already reads as "ignore what you have".
- Or keep the current behaviour but say so: log "reusing N cached parses (PARSE_CACHE_VERSION x); pass --no-parse-cache to re-parse" at the point where the cache is consulted.
- Or include a hash of the language query/capture sources in the cache key so a capture edit invalidates the cache without a manual bump. That removes the human from the moment of application, which is where this fails today (the PR author forgot the bump across three iterations, and the reviewer spent a round trip on it).

## Related

- #1432 (where this surfaced; the bump was applied there in the merge commit, `SCHEMA_BUMP` 91 → 92).
- Separate CLI note from the same session: `gitnexus cypher` output over ~64 KB is truncated when stdout is a pipe (complete when redirected to a file), which looks like `process.exit()` before the pipe drains. Happy to file that separately if useful.

title: fix(analyze): add cold parser rebuild option
body:
## What changed

- add `gitnexus analyze --no-parse-cache` as an explicit cold-parser rebuild
- bypass both the sharded parse cache and the sibling durable ParsedFile cache for that run
- replace the durable cache generations with the freshly parsed results afterward
- clarify that `--force` still reuses unchanged parser output

Closes #3152.

## Why

`--force` rebuilds the graph and FTS indexes, but its content-addressed parser cache is intentionally reusable. That makes capture/query edits invisible when source contents and `PARSE_CACHE_VERSION` are unchanged. The new flag gives parser developers a precise escape hatch without making every routine forced rebuild pay the full parsing cost.

## Verification

- `npm test -- --run test/unit/analyze-no-stats-bridge.test.ts test/unit/help-i18n.test.ts`
- `npx tsc --noEmit`
- `npm run build`
- `node dist/cli/index.js analyze --help`
- `git diff --check`

## Risk

Default behavior is unchanged. The flag implies a full pipeline rebuild and is rejected with `--repair-fts`; `analyze --watch` also rejects it because watch does not accept one-shot rebuild flags.

title: test(watch): raise CI timeout budget for flaky watch-filesystem test
body:
`test/integration/watch-filesystem.test.ts` intermittently failed in CI with `Error: timed out waiting for watcher event`, most recently in `reloads gitignore rules before processing subsequent file events`.

## Root cause
- This test exercises a real chokidar filesystem watcher (real writes, real `awaitWriteFinish` polling), so event delivery latency scales with CPU/I-O contention on the runner.
- The `waitFor` helper used a fixed 5s timeout regardless of environment, leaving no headroom for busy shared CI runners.
- Verified the underlying watch/gitignore-reload logic itself is correct — the test passes consistently locally, including under synthetic CPU stress — so this is real-FS timing variance rather than a functional bug.

## Fix
- **`waitFor` timeout**: raised from a fixed `5_000`ms to `process.env.CI ? 15_000 : 5_000`, matching `FIRST_FRAME_BUDGET_MS` in `mcp/server-startup.test.ts` (the same CI-gating idiom as `server-http-startup.test.ts`, which uses 30s/15s).
- **Per-test timeout**: raised from vitest's default 30s to `process.env.CI ? 90_000 : 30_000`, since two tests chain five `waitFor` calls whose combined worst case (~75s) could otherwise exceed the global test timeout after the per-call budget grew.
- **Timeout errors**: `waitFor` now reports the budget and elapsed ms so a CI miss is distinguishable from a generic vitest 90s kill.

No production code was changed — this is a test-only timing adjustment.

title: fix(watch): await a watcher re-arm barrier so gitignore reloads cannot drop events
body:
Replaces #3156 (Copilot stacked that PR on Dependabot #3141 and GitHub refused to change the base).

`test/integration/watch-filesystem.test.ts` intermittently failed in CI with `Error: timed out waiting for watcher event`, most recently in `reloads gitignore rules before processing subsequent file events`. **This turned out to be a production bug in watch mode, not CI event latency**, so this PR now fixes the watcher instead of raising the timeout.

## Root cause

After an ignore-rule reload, `startWatchFileLoop` re-armed the watcher with `watcher.add(repoPath)`. That call returns before the rescan it starts has finished, and chokidar exposes no signal for that completion — `ready` fires exactly once per instance and is replaced with a no-op afterwards, so a post-ready `add()` is fire-and-forget.

A file the reload had just unignored is therefore still unregistered when `add()` returns. Worse, the miss is permanent rather than merely late: the in-flight rescan discovers the file, but `ignoreInitial: true` suppresses the `add` event it would emit, while the scan still records the file with its post-write stats. The rewrite is swallowed and no later event replays it.

A standalone reproduction (write immediately after the re-arm, then wait 2s for any event) missed:

| chokidar | delay after `add()` | missed |
|---|---|---|
| 4.0.3 | 0 ms | 40/40 |
| 4.0.3 | 10 ms | 0/40 |
| 5.0.0 | 0 ms | 40/40 |
| 5.0.0 | 10 ms | 0/40 |

That 10 ms is exactly what CI was flipping on: `waitFor` polls every 25 ms, so the test's own polling normally supplied enough slack to hide the unarmed watcher, and only lost the race when the runner was busy. Raising the timeout would have made the flake rarer without fixing the dropped event.

## Fix

`gitnexus/src/cli/analyze-watch.ts`:

- **Awaited re-arm barrier.** Re-arming now builds a replacement watcher and awaits its `ready` — the only completion signal chokidar offers. The outgoing instance keeps reporting until the swap, so the transition has no blind window, and a replacement that fails to arm leaves the working instance in place for the queue to retry with backoff (a re-arm failure is a `WatchControlReloadError`, matching how a failed ignore-control reload is already handled).
- **Ordering invariant.** The re-arm runs *before* the refresh, never after. The refresh reads the whole repository, so a write landing while the replacement arms is still picked up by that refresh, and a write landing afterwards is reported by the armed watcher. No state can fall between them.
- **Transient watcher errors** (the Windows `EPERM` path) now request the same awaited re-arm ahead of their bounded catch-up refresh, instead of re-arming inline with the same fire-and-forget `add()`.

## Test

`reports writes issued the instant a gitignore reload re-arms the watcher` issues its rewrites from *inside* the refresh callback, so they land immediately after the re-arm returns with none of the polling slack that hid the bug. It asserts both that the newly unignored file is reported and that the swap does not drop a file the retired watcher was already tracking.

Verified to fail deterministically against the pre-fix watcher (`timed out waiting for watcher event after 5000ms`) and to pass with the fix, 10/10 consecutive runs of the file.

## Dropped from #3156

The CI timeout inflation (`waitFor` 15s and a 90s per-test ceiling) and the reindentation it required are reverted — the test is not slow, so the budget does not need to grow. The one piece kept is `waitFor` reporting its budget and elapsed ms, which is how the failure above was read.
