title: fix(go, workspace): resolve test siblings and tighten package discovery
body:
Go internal tests should resolve their package's production and test helpers through sibling bindings. Production files must not acquire test-only helpers; external test packages may access exported production declarations through package qualifiers or explicit dot imports.

This branch also ships Node workspace source-entry discovery (nested workspace roots, static Vite `lib.entry`, and memo invalidation on analyze). Nested `test/` / `tests/` / `e2e` / `spec` trees are not workspace roots unless the repo root lists them. Vite discovery uses Vite's first existing config filename and does not union leftover sibling configs.

Part 2 of the four-PR replacement for #3182, stacked on #3190. Merge the preceding PR first, then retarget this PR to main.

Validation: shared/core build, core typecheck, Go sibling tests, and workspace discovery unit tests. No dependency or CLI/MCP contract changes.

title: fix(workspace): discover nested roots and static source entries
body:
Nested workspace roots and packages whose manifests point at build output need source entries that can be established from repository files. This change discovers nested roots deterministically, honors exclusions and rootless exports, memoizes each scan, and invalidates that memo at the beginning of analysis.

Part 3 of the four-PR replacement for #3182, stacked on #3191. Merge its predecessor first, then retarget to main. The diff contains workspace discovery, its analysis-entry invalidation, and workspace regression tests.

Review fixes included: stale rejected loads cannot evict a newer memo entry; directory queues use read cursors; Vite entry discovery reads the exported static build.lib.entry structure without executing config. Comments, unrelated objects, string contents, dynamic overrides, and misleading helpers cannot select source entries. Explicit config prevents an unrelated conventional entry from taking precedence.

Validation: shared/core build and core typecheck passed; all 52 tests in nine workspace suites passed on this isolated split. Broader workspace unit tests and real barrel pipeline regressions also passed during implementation. Full-stack CI is tracked on #3193. Public CLI/MCP signatures and dependencies are unchanged. Revert this commit to restore previous discovery behavior.

title: fix(flows): exclude guessed edges from processes and communities
body:
Global-name guesses remain useful as labeled graph evidence, but must not create execution flows or join unrelated communities. Gate process tracing and community projection on edge reason as well as confidence, since guessed edges sit exactly at the existing 0.5 threshold.

Part 4 of the four-PR replacement for #3182, rebased onto current #3191 (`fix/3182-2-go-test-siblings`) after #3192 merged into that branch. Reviewers see only the three-file flow-filtering change. Merge #3191 first, then retarget this PR to main. This PR temporarily targeted main to queue full-stack CI on commit `3aa22a3db8e0d1c2255a94d94f2ff2020a5bfaed`; that run is tracked at https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/actions/runs/34014528192 and is still running.

Validation on final stack `3aa22a3d`: 5,997 tests passed, 5 skipped, zero failures across 221 resolver, extraction, workspace, flow and cache test files. Builds and core typechecks passed. The 15-language capture benchmark passed with its original performance thresholds. Full GitHub CI remains pending; the broad local run had failures documented in #3190, so this is not a claim that the entire local suite is green. Public CLI/MCP contracts and dependencies remain unchanged. Revert this commit to restore prior flow eligibility.

Part 1 now fixes Rust lexical-import provenance through extraction, scoped binding and return-type propagation, with a cache-version bump so warm indexes receive the new facts. It retains a documented limitation around complete Cargo crate/module visibility. The stack remains draft for maintainer review and full CI verification; no merges to main have been performed.

title: fix(parse): keep stable cache packs parallel
body:
## Summary
- Cold `analyze` parsing slowed down after `9718e1247` (#3093): stable `(language, hash(path) % 128)` cache packs usually fit one worker job, so dispatch stayed serial and most workers sat idle. Repeated tree-sitter query compilation on every pack amplified the cost.
- Size jobs against the live worker count (still capped by the existing file/byte ceilings), reuse compiled extraction queries per native grammar inside each worker, and keep recovery readiness across dispatches with a bounded failed-thread termination wait.
- Controlled parse of 951 TypeScript files: **56.39s → 26.66s** (2.12×) with identical graph checksum `08650335a4cf…`. Peak RSS rose roughly 10%. Bisect classified the scheduling regression, not noisy timings.

## Evidence
These files are **not** in the PR tree.

- Zip: https://github.com/magyargergo/GitNexus/releases/download/_attachments/pr-3194-evidence-20260906-063720-a320d8e2.zip
- Comment with tables + per-file links: https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/pull/3194#issuecomment-5557477544
- Browsable gist: https://gist.github.com/magyargergo/b2e9a94f3323e590dbd02efc3e3631ce

## Test plan
- [x] Worker-participation and query-reuse regressions (failed before the fix, pass after)
- [x] Focused worker suite: 229 tests (`worker-pool`, recovery, parse concurrency, caches)
- [x] Build, `tsc --noEmit`, Prettier, ESLint on the four changed files
- [x] Default vitest project: **19,961 passed** / 85 skipped / 2 failed (unrelated: `skip-git-cli` 30s timeout from heap-respawn + cold CLI start; `wiki-llm-client` picks saved `opencode` provider)
- [ ] CI full suite (includes native LadybugDB project; not re-run locally — no DB code changed)

title: perf(parse): batch cache packs into one dispatch round
body:
## Summary
- `WorkerPool.dispatch` is a barrier, so one round-trip per parse-cache pack strands most slots. Packs are keyed by `(language, hash(path) % 128)`, so the byte budget rarely binds — this repo produces **1285 packs where the budget alone needs 16**, and **549 hold a single file**. In a real `analyze`, **76 of 221 dispatched chunks carried one file and cost 15.3s — 20% of the parse phase for 3.4% of the files**.
- Chunks now accumulate into a **round** bounded by `GITNEXUS_PARSE_ROUND_BYTES` of cache-missing source (default: the chunk byte budget) and go out through a new `WorkerPool.dispatchGroups`. Jobs are still cut at pack boundaries, so each job carries exactly one `chunkHash` and every result stays attributable to the pack whose cache key owns it.
- Follow-on to #3194, which fixed fan-out *within* a pack but left the barrier *between* packs.

## Measurements
Cold `analyze --index-only`, 2234 parseable files, 16 workers:

| | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| total | 110.3s | **70.5s** |
| parse phase | 74.0s | **40.5s** |
| dispatches | 221 | **15** |
| peak main RSS | 3372MB | 3487MB (+3.4%) |

Graph output identical in both arms: **51,286 nodes / 163,092 edges / 2106 clusters / 759 flows**.

Isolated dispatch-loop A/B over 4755 files (same pool, same worker, only round size varies) — all runs returned checksum `7df23a84935a207b` / 133,158 nodes / 133,757 rels:

| rounds | merge budget | wall |
| ---: | --- | ---: |
| 1285 (today) | — | 76.0s |
| 79 | 512KB | 52.3s |
| 17 | 2MB | 41.2s |

Round size is the in-flight cap, the role Piscina's `maxQueue` plays. Bigger rounds remove more barriers but hold more in flight; the default keeps in-flight source bytes at the magnitude the loop already prefetched (`parseChunkConcurrency`, 2 chunks ahead).

## Reentrancy guard
`dispatchGroups` claims the pool synchronously and rejects a concurrent call. Two overlapping dispatches hand the same slots out twice and both stall — the first version of this change did exactly that, and the only symptom was every worker idle-timing out ~10s later with no indication of the cause. Now it fails at the call site.

## Behavior change worth flagging
Progress messages read `Parsing chunks X-Z/Y` when a round batches several chunks (still `Parsing chunk X/Y` for a single one). `parse-impl-env-reads.test.ts` inferred pack count by counting distinct progress messages; it now reads the denominator, which is stable under both shapes.

## Test plan
- [x] New: `parse-impl-dispatch-rounds.test.ts` — identical graph fingerprint batched vs one-chunk-per-round; warm-cache replay reproduces the cold graph (pins per-pack attribution, which would otherwise only surface as a corrupted warm run); a premise guard asserting the fixture really over-splits
- [x] New: `dispatchGroups` keeps results and `chunkHash` per group, aligns an all-quarantined group, rejects a reentrant dispatch
- [x] `worker-pool` + `worker-pool-resilience` + `parsing-worker-fallback`: 75 passed
- [x] `parse-impl-*` + `parse-impl-warm-cache-parsedfile-coverage` + `incremental-orchestration`: 62 passed
- [x] `tsc --noEmit`, ESLint (0 warnings on changed source), Prettier, build
- [x] `detect_changes --scope all` clean (not partial/truncated): 35 symbols, 6 processes, all `runChunkedParseAndResolve` step 1
- [ ] Full CI suite (not run locally)

Local runs need `GITNEXUS_WORKER_READY_TIMEOUT_MS=60000` on this box — worker boot exceeds the 5s default when the repo sits on a slow 9p mount. Unrelated to this change; reproduces on `main`.

title: fix(eval): give the review agent somewhere it can actually write
body:
## The bug

The review arm mounted its artifact as a writable **file** at `/workspace/review-output.json` while binding `/workspace` read-only. Claude Code's Write tool writes atomically: it creates `<target>.tmp.<n>.<hex>` beside the target and then renames it. The parent directory is read-only, so the temp create fails and the artifact is never written.

```
EROFS: read-only file system, open '/workspace/review-output.json.tmp.2.90a76e583b0c'
```

**This is conditional on how the agent writes, and I originally described it as worse than it is.** An in-place write — `open(path,'w')`, a Bash heredoc — succeeds through the bind mount. Only the atomic path fails. So the artifact comes back empty exactly when the agent reaches for the Write tool:

- Run **33912693948** (2026-09-04): every cell used the Write tool. 127 EROFS across 35 of 35 transcripts, all 41 `*.review.json` at 0 bytes, ~$3653 for zero evidence.
- Run **33962002890** (2026-09-05, the 16h run): **artifacts were written and scored** on the same mount — 321 `review-output` mentions, zero EROFS against it, zero `.tmp.` rename attempts, real quality scores.

An earlier version of this description said every run since 2026-09-04 produced zero evidence. That was wrong; 33962002890 disproves it. The defect is a latent trap that fires per cell, not a standing outage — still worth removing, because which path an agent picks is not something the harness should be gambling on.

It read as an agent-quality problem because `parse_review_output` reported every cause as `review output is not valid UTF-8 JSON`. Its `except` folded `OSError`, `UnicodeError` and `JSONDecodeError` into one string, so an artifact that was never written looked exactly like an encoding fault.

## What this does not fix

The 16h run (33962002890) failed for reasons this PR does not touch, and it is worth being explicit so nobody expects a green generation from merging it:

- It ended on `##[error]The runner has received a shutdown signal`, mid-cell, about 22 minutes into cell 52. The instance was reclaimed. Artifact upload was skipped, which is why no `results.jsonl` survives.
- Its 51 completed cells were **all `resolved=False` with `error_kind=oracle-failed`** — none `review-evidence-invalid`. Quality ran min 0.000, median 0.212, max 0.800, with all three arms alike (0.211 / 0.243 / 0.240). `oracle_passed` for a review arm demands an exact match: zero false positives, zero false negatives, correct verdict. A median of 0.21 against that bar is a hard benchmark returning an honest negative.

A clean generation will most likely still end `insufficient_evidence` with no promotion. That is the gate working.

## The fix

The artifact gets its own writable **directory**, outside the workspace, bound at `/review-output`. That is what a rename needs. The file is no longer pre-created, so its absence is evidence rather than a 0-byte decoy.

Four layers gate that path and three still named the old location:

- `build_claude_settings` — the CLI applies its own filesystem policy to its own tools; `allowWrite`/`allowRead` listed only `/workspace`, `/tmp`, `/home/agent`. Correct until the artifact moved.
- The task corpus `verify` command still ran `test -s review-output.json` from the workspace, in a separate sandbox invocation that never sees the artifact mount. Every review cell would have been stamped `verify-failed`, which also makes those rows permanently unreusable and silently disables this PR's own comparator reuse for review arms.
- `host_text`/`host_path` had no translation for the new path, so the host-unsafe backend pointed at somewhere that exists on neither backend. Adding it exposed a second defect: `host_text` substituted every occurrence of a target, and `/review-output` appears twice in `/review-output/review-output.json` — once as the directory, once inside the filename. Matching is now anchored to a path boundary.

The workspace boundary got **tighter**, not looser: the review phase may now change nothing there at all (`enforce_phase_workspace(allowed_artifact=None)`), where before it owned one path inside it. Each parse failure now names its own cause: never written, empty, not valid UTF-8, not valid JSON with the decoder position.

## Comparator reuse

Reuse had three ways to accept evidence it should have rejected, all fixed here:

- A row with no `runtime_digest` passed the drift lock, because the guard only compared when both sides were bound — and this branch's own test asserted that as correct. Absence is now a mismatch.
- `materialize_reused_row` overwrote `recorded_at` with the copy time while the age check read that field, so a row copied forward each generation refreshed its own clock and never aged out. The first measurement time is preserved and aged against; a future-dated stamp is rejected as corrupt.
- The binding ignored task-asset and sandbox-dependency digests, and this PR changes `sandbox_dependencies` in the review corpus — so a reused comparator could be measured in one environment and compared against a candidate built in another. Closing it required preparing asset snapshots before the reuse decision, which also removes the concurrent `TaskAssetCache.prepare` the prefetch thread could race.

`RUNTIME_DIGEST` never reached the runner at all: `runner_environment` builds a fixed dict and `process_control` replaces the child environment wholesale.

The broken-incumbent canary could not fire while reuse was working — it read `resolved`, which counts reused rows. It now reads `resolved_fresh`, and the sweep keeps one paid cell per incumbent arm so that count is never vacuous.

## Wall clock

Comparator reuse, one sanitized clone per SHA, and a graph prefetch that overlaps the next task's build with paid sessions. `measure_evolution_cost.py` prices these against real durations from a run artifact rather than a guessed mean.

Two structural findings from that model: the wave barrier in `sweep_task_cells` costs about 17% of a cold run, because every cell waits for the slowest in its wave and cells are far from uniform (826s median, 2976s p90, a 5400s ceiling); and wall clock is quantised by `ceil(cells_per_task / workers)`, so `workers=4` buys exactly the wall clock of `workers=3`. Documented in the workflow's rollout checklist.

`--max-runtime-seconds` derives the instance window from `/proc/uptime` so a sweep stops in-process with partial evidence instead of being killed mid-cell. That is what should prevent a repeat of the 16h shutdown — bounding the window, not proving a generation completes inside it.

## Testing

591 eval tests pass, ruff clean, 29 workflow contract tests pass. The two `test_model_gateway.py` failures are pre-existing and fail on `main`.

**Not verified end to end.** Unprivileged user namespaces are disabled in the dev container, so bwrap cannot run there. Both executed-write canaries now bind the shipped mount and perform the atomic temp-file-then-rename that caused the original EROFS, but they are `skipif`-gated locally and only run in the Ubuntu CI job. CI is the first place this is actually proven. If cells still come back empty, the message now says `review output was never written` rather than blaming the encoding.

Separately: `test_process_control.py::test_timeout_kills_term_ignoring_descendants_before_they_write` is a TERM-to-KILL timing flake on `main` (passes 2 of 3 in isolation) in a file this branch does not touch. It deserves its own issue.

title: POST /api/analyze silently ignores `branch` — returns 202, reports `complete`, indexes the default branch
body:
### Area

gitnexus (CLI / core / indexing / MCP server)

### Summary

`POST /api/analyze` accepts a `branch` field, returns `202`, and drives the job to `complete` — but always indexes the remote's default branch. There is no error, no warning, and no `tokenIgnored`-style signal, so a caller has no way to learn the selector had no effect.

### Context

We drive `gitnexus serve` from CI to keep indexes fresh for a set of repositories, some of which develop on a non-default branch. Because the job reports `complete`, the pipeline stays green while agents query an index built from the wrong branch. The mismatch only becomes visible by inspecting the checked-out clone under `GITNEXUS_HOME/repos/`.

The capability already exists on both sides of the HTTP layer:

- `CloneOrPullOptions.branch` (`gitnexus/src/server/git-clone.ts:109`) is honored — `buildBranchCloneArgs` for a fresh clone, `checkout -B <branch> origin/<branch>` for an existing one.
- `AnalyzeOptions.branch` (`gitnexus/src/core/run-analyze.ts:435`) already drives `resolveBranchPlacement`.
- The CLI exposes it as `--branch`.

Only the route is missing it. The handler never destructures `branch` (`gitnexus/src/server/api.ts:1513`) and calls:

```ts
cloneOrPull(repoUrl, targetPath, onProgress, repoToken ? { token: repoToken } : undefined);
```

so Express discards the field.

### Expected behavior

Either the requested branch is checked out and indexed, or the request is rejected. A selector that cannot take effect should not be silently discarded behind a `complete` job.

### Actual behavior

The default branch is cloned and indexed. The job reports `complete` and the response body carries no indication that `branch` was ignored.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Start the server:

   ```bash
   gitnexus serve --port 4747
   ```

2. Request a non-default branch of a public repo (`octocat/Hello-World` defaults to `master` and has a `test` branch):

   ```bash
   curl -X POST localhost:4747/api/analyze \
     -H 'content-type: application/json' \
     -d '{"url":"https://github.com/octocat/Hello-World","branch":"test"}'
   # -> 202 {"jobId":"...","status":"cloning"}
   ```

3. Poll `GET /api/analyze/<jobId>` until it reports `"status":"complete"`.

4. Inspect the clone:

   ```bash
   git -C "$GITNEXUS_HOME/repos/Hello-World" rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD
   # -> master        (expected: test)
   ```

### Environment

- OS: macOS 15 (Darwin 25.6.0), arm64
- Node: v24.19.0
- Version: 1.6.11, built from `main` @ `780cac7`

### Logs / screenshots

No error is emitted — that is the substance of the report. The job's terminal state is:

```json
{
  "id": "...",
  "status": "complete",
  "repoName": "Hello-World",
  "progress": { "phase": "done", "percent": 100, "message": "Done" }
}
```

---

**Related:** #287 asks for branch selection in the web UI. This is the server-side gap underneath it — the UI has no field to send because the route has none to receive.

**Note for maintainers:** I have a patch that threads `branch` from the route through `cloneOrPull` and `LaunchOptions` into the worker's `AnalyzeOptions`, reusing `validateBranchName` so the HTTP and CLI entry points accept identical refs. Opening it alongside this issue.

While testing it I hit a second, pre-existing problem worth its own issue: on an **already-cloned** server-managed repo, switching branches fails with `Refusing to update ...: local changes detected`, because analyze writes `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/` into the clone and those are not covered by the `.gitnexus/` exclude. That path is currently unreachable (nothing passes `branch`), so it only surfaces once the above is fixed. Happy to file it separately.

title: feat(api): honor branch on POST /api/analyze
body:
## Summary

`POST /api/analyze` accepted a `branch` field, returned `202` and reported the job `complete` — while indexing the remote's default branch. Express drops unknown body fields, so the caller saw a successful job and no warning. This threads `branch` through the serve path so the requested branch is actually cloned and indexed, and rejects a malformed ref with `400` before it reaches `git`.

Fixes #3198.

## Motivation / context

Both ends of the plumbing already existed; only the HTTP layer was missing:

- `CloneOrPullOptions.branch` (`server/git-clone.ts:109`) is honored — `buildBranchCloneArgs` for a fresh clone, `checkout -B <branch> origin/<branch>` for an existing one.
- `AnalyzeOptions.branch` (`core/run-analyze.ts:435`) already drives `resolveBranchPlacement`, so per-branch index slots (`branches/<slug>/`) come along for free.
- The CLI has exposed this as `--branch` since #2106.

So this is wiring, not new behavior: the route reads `branch`, validates it, and passes it to the two call sites that already knew what to do with it.

## Areas touched

- [x] `gitnexus/` (CLI / core / MCP server)
- [x] `gitnexus-web/` (Vite / React UI) — request-type widening only, no UI
- [ ] `.github/` (workflows, actions)
- [ ] `eval/` or other tooling
- [ ] Docs / agent config only

## Scope & constraints

**In scope**

- `server/api.ts` — read and validate `branch`; forward to `cloneOrPull` and `launchAnalysisWorker`.
- `server/analyze-launch.ts` — `LaunchOptions.branch`, forwarded in the `start` IPC message.
- `gitnexus-web/src/services/backend-client.ts` — widen the `startAnalyze` request type so a caller can send the field.
- `gitnexus/CHANGELOG.md` — `[Unreleased]` entry.

**Explicitly out of scope / not done here**

- **Web UI branch selection** — that is #287. This only makes the field reachable.
- **The analyze slot.** `JobManager.createJob` dedupes by repo (`analyze-job.ts:101-111`), so two branches of the same repo still contend for the single global analyze slot and the second gets a 409. Unchanged here.
- **Switching branches on an already-cloned repo.** Pre-existing, and now reachable: `cloneOrPull` refuses with `Refusing to update ...: local changes detected`, because analyze writes `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/` into the clone and the `.gitnexus/` exclude does not cover them. I deliberately did **not** paper over this by passing `overwriteLocalChanges: true` — that runs `git clean --force -d` inside the clone directory, which is a policy call for maintainers rather than something to slip into a wiring PR. Noted in #3198; happy to file it separately or follow whichever fix you prefer.

## Implementation notes

- **No IPC protocol change.** `StartMessage.options` is already typed as `AnalyzeOptions`, which has `branch`; the worker spreads `{ ...options }` into `runFullAnalysis`. Only the object literal in `analyze-launch.ts` needed the key.
- **Validation reuses `validateBranchName`** (`cli/analyze-config.ts:163`) — the same function behind the CLI's `--branch` — so HTTP and CLI accept identical refs instead of drifting. It throws `GitNexusRcError`, which the route maps to `400`.
- **On the `server/ -> cli/` import:** `core/run-analyze.ts:179` already imports `sanitizeDetectedBranch` from `cli/analyze-config.js`, so this follows existing practice rather than introducing a new direction. If you would rather that validator lived in a neutral module, say so and I will move it and re-export from `analyze-config.ts` so the CLI is untouched.
- **`branch` is omitted, not sent as `undefined`,** when the caller does not select one — `AnalyzeOptions.branch === undefined` is the documented signal for "target the flat workspace slot", and a test pins that.
- **The mismatch guard still applies.** `resolveWriteTarget` (`core/run-analyze.ts:1015`) refuses a label that disagrees with the checked-out branch, which is what keeps one branch's content out of another's slot. That guard lives in core, so the server path inherits it — including for `path`-based (non-clone) requests.

## Testing & verification

- [x] `cd gitnexus && npm test` — see note below
- [x] `cd gitnexus && npm run test:integration`
- [x] `cd gitnexus && npx tsc --noEmit`
- [x] `cd gitnexus-web && npx tsc -b --noEmit`
- [x] `npx eslint .` (root) — 0 errors
- [ ] Manual / Playwright E2E — no UI change

New tests:

- `test/integration/server-analyze-branch-validation.test.ts` — five rejection cases against a real spawned `serve` (non-string, whitespace, git-forbidden ref characters, a leading `-` that would read as a git option, whitespace-only). All return `400` before any clone, so the suite stays hermetic. It is a separate file from the token cases because `/api/analyze` is rate-limited to 10 req/min per IP.
- `test/unit/analyze-launch-collapse.test.ts` — `branch` reaches the worker's `AnalyzeOptions`, and is absent (not `undefined`) when unset. The first of these fails without this change.

Manual end-to-end on a locally built 1.6.11, `GITNEXUS_HOME` pointed at a scratch directory:

```bash
curl -X POST localhost:4747/api/analyze \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"url":"https://github.com/octocat/Hello-World","branch":"test"}'
# -> 202, job reaches "complete"

git -C "$GITNEXUS_HOME/repos/Hello-World" rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD
# -> test          (before this change: master)

# and the index records the label:
#   .gitnexus/gitnexus.json -> "branch": "test"

curl -X POST localhost:4747/api/analyze \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"url":"https://github.com/octocat/Hello-World","branch":"bad branch"}'
# -> 400 {"error":"\"branch\": branch name must not contain whitespace."}
```

> **On `npm test`:** 14,812 of 14,869 pass locally. Twelve failures in `analyzer-identity.test.ts`, `analyzer-identity-in-process-guards.test.ts` and `auto-sync.test.ts` are **pre-existing on my machine and unrelated to this change** — they probe `W_OK`/`EACCES` behavior, `ps` output shapes and clone-root symlink rules. I confirmed by running those files with the change stashed and again with it applied: identical 12 failures both ways. (`hooks.test.ts` adds four more only in the full parallel run, which looks like test-ordering sensitivity rather than anything this touches.) Happy to share output if useful.

## Behavior change

`branch: null`, `branch: ""` and non-string values now return **400**. They previously reached
no validation at all — the field was dropped and the request indexed the default branch — so a
client that sends the key unconditionally will start seeing errors instead of silently getting
the wrong branch. The first-party UI never sends the key.

(Noted here rather than in `gitnexus/CHANGELOG.md`: release notes are generated from the merged
PR title via `.github/release.yml`, and the changelog is written at release time.)

## Risk & rollout

Low. The field is optional and additive: omitting `branch` produces byte-identical behavior to today (the key is not even sent to the worker), and the only new failure mode is a `400` on a ref that would have failed at `git` anyway. No migration, no config, no new environment variable. Reverting is a clean revert of this commit.

The one behavior that becomes newly *reachable* is the existing branch path in `cloneOrPull` — see the out-of-scope note about re-cloning an existing repo on a different branch.

## Checklist

- [x] PR body meets repo minimum length
- [x] No `AGENTS.md` / overlay changes
- [x] No secrets, tokens, or machine-specific paths committed
- [x] No new `GITNEXUS_*` environment variable
- [x] Documentation updated (`gitnexus/CHANGELOG.md`, `[Unreleased]`)

title: perf(parse): tighten the dispatch-round memory bound and unclamp the worker-pool override
body:
## Summary

Follow-ups to #3196, which merged before these landed. All four were found by a review + simplification pass over that PR's own code, and cherry-picked cleanly onto merged `main`.

The load-bearing one is the memory bound. `main` currently ships the round-close condition as:

```ts
if (roundMissBytes >= roundByteBudget || roundBufferedBytes >= roundByteBudget)
```

`roundBufferedBytes` counts the same bytes as `roundMissBytes` **plus** the cache hits, so it is always the greater of the two and the first disjunct can never fire on its own. One counter, one reset, one check.

Worse, both counted `String.length` — UTF-16 code units, not bytes. A CJK character is one code unit but three UTF-8 bytes, so on non-ASCII-heavy source a round could hold roughly 3x its nominal budget before draining. That budget exists specifically to stop a warm run buffering unbounded content on the main thread (the #2649 large-repo OOM class), so it was looser than intended exactly where it matters. Now uses `Buffer.byteLength(content, 'utf8')`, matching the pool's existing `estimateItemBytes` convention.

## Commits

| commit | change |
| --- | --- |
| `97f38b9d1` | Document why `dispatchGroups` is required, not optional — the neighbouring `getQuarantinedPaths?` / `getStats?` markers are compatibility accommodation for shapes that predate them, not a convention for new members. Optional here would force an unreachable fallback at the single production call site. |
| `a97989c91` | Drop `roundMissBytes`; UTF-8 byte accounting; reset a round's durable ParsedFile directories concurrently instead of serially on the critical path; skip the quarantine filter entirely when nothing is quarantined; `dispatchChunkParseRound` takes `DispatchGroup<...>` instead of re-declaring its shape inline. |
| `a09bc6ffc` | `drainRound` counts miss entries with the same `filter().length` idiom `startRound` uses one function above. |
| `b1f60acaa` | `GITNEXUS_WORKER_POOL_SIZE` is no longer silently clamped by the byte-derived auto cap. |

## The pool-size bug

`DEFAULT_POOL_SIZE_CAP`'s own comment offers `GITNEXUS_WORKER_POOL_SIZE` and `--workers <N>` as equivalent operator escape hatches "on bigger machines". They were not. The env value is read inside `resolveAutoPoolSize()`, whose result then passes through `Math.min(..., workProportionalCap)`. Measured on a 30MB corpus where that byte-derived cap resolves to 16:

```
--workers 24                  -> pool: 24/24 active
GITNEXUS_WORKER_POOL_SIZE=24  -> pool: 16/16 active   (silently ignored)
```

Both are deliberate operator input, so both now bypass the cap, which returns to bounding only the auto default. After the fix, identical graph output in each case:

title: GraphQL extractor yields 0 cross-links on a real NestJS + codegen pair: provider `startLine` off by one (1-based vs 0-based graph), PascalCased `…Document` names not tried, `${FragmentDoc}` templates rejected
body:
_All names and paths below are anonymised placeholders (same convention as #3028/#3029); counts, code excerpts from GitNexus and error shapes are verbatim._

**Version:** gitnexus 1.6.11 (linux arm64, Node 24) · follow-up to #3029 / PR #3070

## Symptom

Two-repo group, NestJS GraphQL API (`demo/api`) + TypeScript client generated with graphql-codegen (`demo/web`), `detect.graphql: true`, both repos re-indexed with `--force` on 1.6.11:

```console
$ gitnexus group sync demo
Matching:
  exact:     0 cross-links (confidence 1.0)
  manifest:  0 cross-links
  wildcard:  0 cross-links
  unmatched: 368 contracts
Wrote contracts.json (376 contracts, 0 cross-links)

$ jq '[.contracts[] | select(.type=="graphql")] | group_by(.role) | map({role: .[0].role, n: length})' contracts.json
[ { "role": "consumer", "n": 158 } ]        ← zero providers
```

The API has 89 resolver files / 318 `@Query`/`@Mutation`/`@Subscription` methods, all importing from `@nestjs/graphql` on top-level `@Resolver()` classes — the exact shape PR #3070 targets. Not one of them is extracted.

## 1. Provider anchor is off by one (root cause of the 0)

`extractProviders` in `graphql-extractor.ts` resolves the method with:

```ts
await dbExecutor(RESOLVE_METHOD_QUERY, {
  name: methodName,
  filePath,
  startLine: member.startPosition.row + 1,   // ← 1-based
})
// RESOLVE_METHOD_QUERY: … AND n.filePath = $filePath AND n.startLine = $startLine …
```

but graph nodes store **0-based** lines. `src/core/ingestion/utils/line-base.ts` documents it as load-bearing:

> The graph layer stores line numbers 0-based (tree-sitter `startPosition.row`), and this is load-bearing: the taint/PDG/CFG join and the MCP consumers all add `+ 1` to recover 1-based (see `summary-harvest-driver.ts` — "Function/Method node startLine is 0-based").

Verified on the real index:

```console
$ sed -n '21,23p' src/modules/widget/graphql/widget.resolver.ts
  @UseGuards(AuthGuard)
  @Query(() => WidgetOutputDTO)
  async getWidget(                         ← source line 23

$ gitnexus cypher "MATCH (n:Method) WHERE n.name = 'getWidget' RETURN n.filePath, n.startLine, n.endLine" -r demo-api
| src/modules/widget/graphql/widget.resolver.ts | 22 | 30 |      ← stored 0-based
```

Running the extractor's own `RESOLVE_METHOD_QUERY` verbatim against that index (1.6.11):

```console
startLine = 21 (first decorator, 1-based) → 0 rows
startLine = 22 (signature, 0-based)       → 1 row   ← the node
startLine = 23 (signature, 1-based)       → 0 rows  ← what the extractor binds
```

The extractor binds 23, gets 0 rows, `uniqueRealSymbol` returns null, the method is skipped. Every provider fails identically, so the feature produces no cross-link on any real index. (Decorators are siblings in `class_body` with tree-sitter-typescript 0.23.x, so `member.startPosition.row` is already the signature row — only the `+ 1` is wrong.)

**Fix:** drop the `+ 1` in both branches (method and `public_field_definition`), or go through `toZeroBasedLine`.

**Why CI is green:** `test/integration/group/graphql-resolve-symbol.test.ts` seeds the node by hand —
`CREATE (:Method {… filePath:'src/health.resolver.ts', startLine:5 …})` for a method on source line 5. Real ingestion would store `4`. Seeding `4` (or indexing the fixture through the real TypeScript pipeline) makes the test fail on current `main` and pass with the fix.

## 2. Consumer candidates miss PascalCased generated names

`generatedCandidates` only tries `` `${operationName}Document` ``. graphql-codegen (`typescript-operations` / `typed-document-node` / string documents) PascalCases the operation name: `query widgetTimeline { … }` → `export const WidgetTimelineDocument = …`. Every operation whose name starts lowercase is therefore skipped — 41 of 314 in this client. Adding the PascalCase spelling as a second exact candidate keeps the unique-real-symbol rule intact.

## 3. Generated documents that embed fragments are rejected (`${FragmentDoc}` interpolation)

With graphql-codegen string documents, any operation that uses a fragment is emitted as a template literal that **appends the fragment document by interpolation**:

```ts
export const GetWidgetDocument = /*#__PURE__*/ `
    query GetWidget {
  getWidget {
    ...widget
  }
}
    ${WidgetFragmentDoc}`;
```

`staticGraphqlSource` → `unquote` returns `null` as soon as the template contains `${`, the object-Document branch then fails on a template literal, and `hasGeneratedDocumentProof` is `false` — although the generated symbol resolved fine (`RESOLVE_GENERATED_SYMBOL_QUERY` returns exactly one `Const` node, verified with `gitnexus cypher`). Operations without fragments (plain template, no `${`) go through. In this client that is the split behind the 151 operations (158 consumer contracts) that do get extracted: of 314 named operations, 41 are lost to the casing in §2 and **122 to this rejection** — every operation that touches a fragment, i.e. most of the real API surface.

The proof only needs the operation's **root fields**; the interpolated parts are fragment definitions, which cannot be root fields. Two safe options:

- strip `${…}` segments before `parse()` (the remaining text is a valid document: the operation plus any inline fragments), or
- resolve each interpolated identifier against the declarators of the same generated file (`WidgetFragmentDoc` is a sibling `export const WidgetFragmentDoc = …` holding the `fragment widget on …` text) and inline it — this also keeps root-level fragment spreads verifiable.

## Net effect on a real NestJS + codegen pair (1.6.11)

| side | extracted | expected | cause |
|---|---|---|---|
| providers | 0 / 318 | 318 | §1 off-by-one |
| consumers | 151 operations / 314 | ≈313 | §2 casing (41) + §3 interpolation (122) |
| cross-links | 0 | ≈300 | — |

Happy to open a PR for 1, 2 and 3 plus the integration-test seed if useful.

title: fix(typescript): resolve tsconfig `paths` aliases on Windows
body:
## What changed

`rebaseTarget` in `gitnexus/src/core/ingestion/languages/typescript/tsconfig.ts` now normalises the path separator before deciding whether a `paths` target ends in a wildcard.

`test/unit/tsconfig-index.test.ts` is added to the cross-platform lane (`scripts/cross-platform-tests.ts`) so it runs on `windows-latest`.

## Why

`readCompilerOptions` resolves every `paths` target with `path.resolve`, and `rebaseTarget` rebases the result to repo-relative. It recognised the wildcard suffix only as `/*`. On Windows the resolved target is `C:\repo\src\*`, so that check never matched, the bare-`*` branch stripped just the star, `path.relative` ate the trailing backslash, and the target came back as `src*`.

From there `resolveViaPaths` → `substituteStar('src*', 'lib/date')` builds `srclib/date`, which matches no file, so the specifier is treated as external and no edge is written. On a repo where most imports go through `@/` (the Vite/shadcn default), that is the whole shared layer:

- `MATCH (a:File)-[:CodeRelation {type:'IMPORTS'}]->(b)` for a file with two `@/` imports and one relative one returned only the relative one.
- `impact({target: "useUnsavedChangesGuard", direction: "upstream"})` returned `risk: UNKNOWN, impactedCount: 0` for a hook with two callers.
- After the fix and `analyze --force` on the same repo: 33,500 → 38,663 edges, and the same query returns `LOW`, `epistemic: exact`, both callers.

Calling the loader directly shows it:

```
> loadTsconfigIndex(repoRoot)   // tsconfig.json: "@/*": ["./src/*"]
{ pattern: "@/*", targets: ["src*"] }   // before
{ pattern: "@/*", targets: ["src/*"] }  // after
```

The existing `tsconfig-index.test.ts` already asserts the `src/*` shape, and 4 of its 13 cases fail on Windows today — but it was only ever run on Ubuntu, which is why this shipped. Adding it to `PLATFORM_LOGIC` makes the Windows matrix cover it.

Verified on 1.6.10, and `rebaseTarget` is unchanged on `main`, 1.6.11 and 1.6.12-rc.5.

## Scope: three languages, not just TypeScript

`loadTsconfigIndex` is the single alias source for all three JS-family scope resolvers, so the same broken target reached each of them:

| Caller | File |
|---|---|
| `loadResolutionConfig` | `languages/typescript/scope-resolver.ts:100` |
| `loadResolutionConfig` | `languages/javascript/scope-resolver.ts:62` |
| `loadResolutionConfig` | `languages/vue/scope-resolver.ts:91` |

`findTsconfigFiles` also discovers `jsconfig.json` and `configRank` ranks it, so a plain JavaScript or Vue project that declares its aliases there lost them on Windows exactly as a TypeScript one did. The fix restores alias resolution for all three.

## How to verify

On Windows, from `gitnexus/`:

```
npx vitest run test/unit/tsconfig-index.test.ts   # 4 failed / 9 passed before, 13 passed after
npx tsc --noEmit
npx tsx scripts/cross-platform-tests.ts | grep tsconfig
```

On any OS, index a repo whose `tsconfig.json` declares `"@/*": ["./src/*"]` and check that a file importing `@/...` has an IMPORTS edge to it.

## Risk / rollback

The change is confined to the suffix check in `rebaseTarget`. On POSIX `path.sep` is `/`, so `split('/').join('/')` is the identity and behaviour is unchanged there. Rollback is reverting the one function.

title: Invalidate stale parse cache after durable reset failure
body:
PR #3200 skips the new parse-cache write when `prepareDurableParsedFileChunk` fails, but the chunk hash has already been added to `parseCache.usedKeys`. On shutdown, `saveParseCache` can therefore copy the existing live `.v8` cache entry, while `pruneAndSaveDurableParsedFileStore` keeps valid shards from the mixed durable directory. The next warm run may accept that retained raw entry and stale shard coverage instead of re-dispatching.

The merge commit is `f48bf812`; the relevant guard is `durablePrepareFailures.has(p.chunkHash)` in `runChunkedParseAndResolve`. Skipping only `persistParseCacheChunk` is not fail-closed because it does not invalidate the pre-existing raw key or its sharded on-disk cache path.

A regression should seed an existing raw parse-cache entry plus old durable shards, force the directory reset to fail, allow the current run to finish, then assert the next run re-dispatches rather than taking a warm hit. A fix could explicitly invalidate the raw cache key and corresponding sharded file when reset fails, or use an equivalent mechanism that proves the old generation cannot survive as a valid warm entry.

This was raised on #3200 before merge in `discussion_r3949609716`; opening it separately so the merged follow-up does not get lost.

title: feat(eval): Add bounded packed-scheduler primitives and offline replay benchmarks
body:
Supersedes #3197, together with #3207.

**No production caller in this PR.** `sweep_packed_cells` is added but nothing calls it; `_run_sweep` still uses `sweep_task_cells`. Activating it is a later change that should own the production behaviour and its validation. This PR is the primitive plus the harness that measured it.

Purely additive against the base: 6 files, +1431 / -0. No existing function changes behaviour.

## What it adds

`sweep_task_cells` finishes one task before starting the next and drains a wave before refilling it, so a task with fewer cells than `workers` leaves workers idle and one slow cell stalls its whole wave. `sweep_packed_cells` feeds every task's cells through a single pool instead.

The breaker keeps its meaning. Cells carry a total submission order continued across task boundaries, a folder walks results in that order, and consecutive systemic failures are counted there — so a doomed run aborts on the same cell it would have under waves. Verified at three failure positions.

`simulate_sweep.py` drives the real schedulers with only the paid agent session stubbed. `measure_evolution_cost.py` is an offline cost model with no runtime caller; it reports `workers` from the workflow's current default, which on this base is 1.

## What the numbers are, and are not

**These are idealized replay estimates, not demonstrated speedups.** Fixed-duration scheduling replays over a trace collected at one worker. They do not model concurrent model-service behaviour, resource contention, or any change in cell duration under load. They estimate scheduling opportunity under those assumptions.

Cell durations come from `session_durations.json` — measured per-arm samples divided by a scale factor. The distribution's shape is kept deliberately (median 826s against a 5400s ceiling) because that spread is the reason a barrier costs anything; uniform sleeps would erase the effect under test. All schedulers consume one identical seeded plan.

Under those assumptions, at `workers=3` against the review corpus, packing accounts for roughly 40% of a cold sweep's replayed wall clock, and it is the only change that moves a seeded weekly run at all — there a task is three cells and a wave is never full.

The submission window is a real trade, replayed with failures injected at four positions:

| window | wall vs waves | worst overrun |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | -8% | 2 (the wave scheduler's own bound) |
| 6 | -27% | 4 |
| 12 | -42% | 9 |
| 54 | -44% | 11 |

Overrun is wasted paid sessions on an aborted sweep. The default multiplier is 2; the curve is in the constant's comment so raising it is an informed decision.

Contention was replayed separately by burning real CPU in subprocesses under `taskset`. The advantage holds between -40% and -47% from 24 cores down to an oversubscribed 2, though packing erodes faster than waves do, because packing is what creates the concurrency. The first run of that sweep measured nothing — 6 workers on 24 cores never contend — and was re-run pinned.

## Verification

Base: `f48bf8125`.

```
cd eval && .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/ -q
cd eval && .venv/bin/python -m ruff check workflow_bench tests
```

The two failures are `tests/test_model_gateway.py::test_locked_litellm_translates_messages_to_offline_responses` and `tests/test_model_gateway.py::test_openai_gateway_never_leaves_proxy_output_on_an_undrained_pipe`. Both reproduce identically on `origin/main` in the same environment, checked directly rather than carried forward as a label.

title: fix(eval): sweep evidence handling and measurement health, with guarded comparator reuse
body:
Supersedes #3197, together with #3206.

**Draft: the runtime-path coverage below is not written yet.** Reviewable now; not ready to merge.

The runtime change set from a combined skill-evolution branch — everything that alters how a sweep executes and what it records. The packed scheduler and its measurement harness were split to #3206, which is purely additive.

## Scope: three concerns, shipped together

Correctness, evidence classification and comparator reuse share `aggregate()` and `_run_sweep`. Separating them further means hunk-level surgery on functions all three modify, and I judged the risk of a silent omission worse than the reviewability gain.

**That is a risk-based packaging decision, not proof the concerns are inseparable.** Cherry-picking the health commits onto main conflicts because they build on tree state from the artifact-path fix — that establishes extraction difficulty, not an intrinsic dependency.

### 1. The review artifact could not be written

Mounted as a writable **file** inside a read-only workspace, while the agent's Write tool writes atomically — temp file beside the target, then rename. The temp create failed `EROFS` and the artifact was never written.

Four layers gate that path; three named the old location:

- `build_claude_settings` — the CLI applies its own filesystem policy to its own tools, and `allowWrite`/`allowRead` listed only `/workspace`, `/tmp`, `/home/agent`
- the task corpus `verify` command, which runs in a separate sandbox invocation that never sees the artifact mount
- `host_text`/`host_path`, which had no translation for the new path

Fixing the translator exposed a second defect: `/review-output` appears twice in `/review-output/review-output.json`, so substitution corrupted the path. Matching is now anchored to a path boundary.

`parse_review_output` folded `OSError`, `UnicodeError` and `JSONDecodeError` into one message, so an artifact that was never written was indistinguishable from an encoding fault. Each cause now names itself.

The workspace boundary gets **tighter**: the review phase may now change nothing there at all, where before it owned one path inside it.

### 2. Health was inferred from the wrong signal

`broken_incumbent_arms` inferred a broken environment from an arm resolving zero tasks. A reviewer facing a hard corpus falsifies that — Actions run `33962002890` is exactly that shape: 51 cells, all `resolved=False` with `error_kind=oracle-failed`, median score 0.212, healthy harness.

Arms are now classified from fresh execution and evidence outcomes as `UNKNOWN`, `OBSERVED_OK`, `DEGRADED` or `UNUSABLE`. Only `UNUSABLE` aborts, so eligibility and promotion thresholds are untouched — this changes what is reported, not what is allowed. Resolution count is not consulted.

The guard names no cause: an empty artifact establishes that evidence is unusable, not that a mount rejected the write, so it reports `cause=undetermined`.

### 3. Comparator reuse accepted evidence it should have rejected

- a row without a `runtime_digest` passed the drift lock, because the guard only compared when both sides were bound
- `recorded_at` was overwritten with the copy time while the age check read that field, so a row copied forward each generation refreshed its own clock and never aged out
- the binding ignored task-asset and dependency digests, although this change alters `sandbox_dependencies` in the review corpus

Closing the last one required preparing asset snapshots before the reuse decision, which also removes the concurrent `TaskAssetCache.prepare` the prefetch thread could race.

## Verification

Base: `f48bf8125`.

```
cd eval && .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/ -q
cd eval && .venv/bin/python -m ruff check workflow_bench tests
```

**592 passed, 15 skipped, 2 failed** on this branch. Lint clean.

The two failures are `tests/test_model_gateway.py::test_locked_litellm_translates_messages_to_offline_responses` and `tests/test_model_gateway.py::test_openai_gateway_never_leaves_proxy_output_on_an_undrained_pipe`. Both reproduce identically on `origin/main` in the same environment.

**On the split:** both branches were independently tested against `f48bf8125`. File and symbol inventory checks account for the archived changes — no file or `runner.py` symbol is missing from both branches. That is extraction coverage, not behavioural equivalence: it does not establish that function bodies or interactions were preserved correctly. The pre-split tip is archived for patch-level reconciliation. Before merging both, their overlapping edits to `runner.py` and `test_workflow_bench.py` should be inspected and the composed result tested.

## Merge blockers

Runtime coverage now exists. `_run_sweep` is driven directly with cell execution scripted and everything downstream real — folding, aggregation, the artifact writers, the health guard and exit selection. It does **not** need bwrap: the expensive dependencies (cell execution, graph preparation, asset snapshots, task-binding resolution) are replaced at existing module boundaries, and the earlier claim that it did was wrong.

- [x] **Caller-to-finalization coverage** — `tests/test_sweep_finalization.py`, at `74a3806f8`
  - [x] the below-breaker unusable case reaches the guard through the runtime path — `test_one_unusable_cell_below_the_breaker_reaches_the_finalization_guard` asserts its own streak stays under `DEFAULT_OUTAGE_STREAK` first, so the pre-existing breaker cannot supply the exit; it then asserts exit `1`, `review: UNUSABLE`, and no `systemic-outage` line. Mutation-checked: removing the `enforce_measurement_health` invocation fails it.
  - [x] valid negative results survive finalization with scores intact — `test_a_zero_score_stays_a_valid_negative_measurement`: `review_weighted_f1 = 0.0` reports `OBSERVED_OK`, never `UNUSABLE`
  - [x] interruption is distinguishable — `test_cancellation_without_an_outage_exits_130`. This **found a defect**: cancellation returned the breaker's own flag, so an interrupted sweep exited `1` as "Sweep aborted". Fixed in `74a3806f8`.
  - [x] exit-reason precedence (outage `1` before cancellation `130`) — `test_an_outage_keeps_exit_1_even_though_the_breaker_cancels`. Mutation-checked specifically: reordering the two checks fails with `assert 130 == 1`, the wrong exit code rather than merely some failure.
  - [x] **persisted artifacts** — `test_finalization_persists_results_and_report` covers the completed run. Interruption is covered separately at `73e9955a1`: `test_an_interrupted_sweep_keeps_the_evidence_it_already_paid_for` asserts the cell that finished before cancellation survives in `results.jsonl` with its measurement intact, and `test_an_interrupted_sweep_emits_nothing_that_authorizes_promotion` asserts the semantic condition rather than the absence of a file — `promotion.json` is still written for an aborted run, so the test requires `run_status: "aborted"` and every decision reduced to `insufficient_evidence`. Mutation-checked: forcing `complete=True` fails it with `assert 'complete' == 'aborted'`.

`enforce_measurement_health` was previously pinned by reading `_run_sweep`'s compiled code object. That structural check is superseded: the mutation now fails a runtime test because the expected finalization behaviour disappears, not because a name went missing from a code object.

- [x] **Sandbox mount contract.** `test_proposer_sandbox.py::test_real_bubblewrap_lets_a_review_artifact_be_written_atomically`, **executed and passing** on the namespace-capable `eval / containment (ubuntu)` runner at `c04d6e47b`. The job sets `GITNEXUS_REQUIRE_BWRAP_CANARY=1`, so it cannot skip; the run went from `2 failed, 160 passed, 2 skipped` to `162 passed, 2 skipped` with the skip count unchanged, which is what shows the test ran rather than skipping.

  That job had been red **before** this canary existed. The cause: this PR moves the review artifact out of the clone into the session's private root, which `prepare_sandbox` removes on scope exit, and two tests read it after the `with` block — asserting against a directory the sandbox had already deleted. Production is unaffected, because `run_arm` holds the live session and reads the artifact inside that scope. Fixed in `b4d7b5e4f`; the canary found it independently, which is what it was written for.
- [x] **Fold order.** Characterized at `e356ec385`: `keep()` folds all reused rows ahead of the paid sweep, and the breaker consumes its own sequence rather than that one. Every consumer was enumerated — medians are order-independent, arm comparison is identity-keyed, and nothing pairs reused against paid rows positionally. Current behaviour is intentional and no violation was demonstrated, so no production change. Whether reused evidence resets a failure streak is a separate policy question, left unchanged.

title: docs(bench): correct the edit-loop numbers and add the FTS per-index breakdown
body:
## Summary

`bench/analyze-phase-breakdown.md` shipped with numbers that were **full rebuilds labelled as incremental**. Rebuilding or re-copying `dist` between runs changes the analyzer runner identity, and the tool then prints `analyzer runner identity changed ...; forcing a full rebuild`. Every measurement taken across a rebuild is a full run.

That is the **third** "silently fall back to full work" guard in this pipeline — after the non-git corpus and the escalation gate — so the method section now says to read the banner on every run and to measure the incremental path by running once to stamp identity, then editing without touching `dist`.

## Corrected edit-loop numbers

Leaf file (`cli/update-notice.ts`, 2 importers), stable runner identity, incremental path genuinely taken: **31.7s**, not 36.5s. The graph write is a 3,980-node subgraph rather than the full 51,288.

| step | ms | share |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| scopeResolution | ~13900 | 44% |
| **FTS index rebuild** | **7525** | **24%** |
| graph write (subgraph) | 3566 | 11% |
| parse | ~2800 | 9% |

## The actionable finding: FTS per-index

```
 3531ms  File.file_fts        <- 35% of FTS on its own
 1558ms  Function.function_fts
  535ms  Method     491ms  Const      466ms  Property
  427ms  Interface  363ms  Class      280ms  TypeAlias
  ...
10203ms across 20 indexes
```

`File.file_fts` dominates because File nodes carry file content — that index re-tokenizes ~30MB of source to reflect one changed row.

And a two-importer leaf edit rebuilt **20** indexes while another run rebuilt **8**. `touchedFts` is meant to narrow this and has a withdrawal path: `missingSearchFTSIndexTables` returns `undefined` when the index catalog cannot be read (`fts-indexes.ts:285`), and `tables: undefined` means rebuild everything. Worth pinning before anyone optimizes against the narrowed set — a gate that silently withdraws looks like protection and is not.

Ranked next steps are in the doc; the leading one is taking the FTS rebuild off the critical path, since nothing in `analyze` reads the index and the degraded-search state is already modelled.

- [x] Docs only — no code change, no tests affected
- [x] Prettier clean

title: docs(bench): close FTS as an optimization target with measured evidence
body:
Follow-up to #3208, which landed two claims that further measurement disproved.

## Corrections

**The FTS narrowing is not inconsistent.** A true incremental leaf edit rebuilds exactly **8** of the 20 configured indexes — the tables the writeback actually DMLs. The 20-index run I compared it against was a forced full rebuild (the runner-identity trap #3208 itself documents). Per-index costs for those 8 sum to 7769ms against the 7525ms measured in-analyze. `touchedFts` is doing its job; the "fix or delete the narrowing" item is withdrawn.

**The 845ms was not `import('./platform/capabilities.js')`.** `src/cli/analyze.ts` already imports that module statically, so a cached dynamic import measures 0.035ms and `getRuntimeCapabilities()` 0.1ms. The `await` is the first yield after the native FTS build and absorbs the libuv work still queued behind it. Added to the method section as a fourth measurement trap, since it invalidates any mark placed on an `await` that follows native work.

## What replaces them

FTS is a floor, not a target. Established by probing a copy of the corpus index directly rather than through analyze:

| exit | result |
| --- | --- |
| narrow further | nothing left — the 8 tables are exactly the set holding rows for the 6 files in the write set |
| build concurrently | hard error: `Cannot start a new write transaction in the system` |
| raise connection thread count | flat — 7298 / 7133 / 7109 / 7345 ms at 4/8/16/default, min-of-3, inside the per-config spread. CPU does move (8.8s→13.6s), so the default over-subscribes ~60% for nothing |
| drop `content` from `File` | 3541ms → 241ms, but that deletes full-file keyword search (#2317/#2323). Capping is a bad trade: the size distribution is flat, so a 64KB cap still indexes 90% of the bytes while truncating the 72 largest files |

`File.file_fts` is 47% of the incremental cost because File rows carry whole-file content — 2442 rows, 32.9MB, tokenized at ~9.8MB/s. Ladybug's FTS is not incremental, so one changed row forces a whole-table rebuild.

## The one lever left

The build runs on a libuv thread and fully overlaps blocking JS:

```
index alone                 3859ms
index + 3000ms of JS burn   3337ms      (serial would be ~6859ms)
```

File rows are `{ name, filePath }` from `processStructure` with content lazy-read at CSV time, so they are determined by the file scan — before parsing, before resolution. Two things block exploiting that, and neither is small: the DB is closed for the whole pipeline, and an early write moves `liveIndexMutationStarted` ahead of it, so a pipeline failure would leave the live index with fresh File content and stale symbols instead of untouched. Documented rather than attempted.

## Code change

One comment. The `ponytail:` note in `createSearchFTSIndexes` invited a "skip when the index is already present" gate — which cannot fire, because every caller that reaches that loop has already dropped the indexes it passes (the incremental writeback drops them for #2589; a full rebuild builds into a fresh staging DB). Replaced with the measured reason so the next reader doesn't spend a session on it.

## Verification

`tsc --noEmit` clean; `fts-indexes.test.ts` + `incremental-derived-writeback.test.ts` 32/32 pass; `detect-changes` low risk, 0 affected processes.

title: perf(scope-resolution): stop re-scanning the ParsedFile store once per language
body:
Follow-up to #3209, which closed FTS and left `scopeResolution` (14.7s, 44% of the edit loop) as the largest remaining target. This breaks it down and takes the one contained win in it.

## The breakdown

`PROF_SCOPE_RESOLUTION=1` already existed and reports the internal split; marks around the phase supply the rest.

| step | ms | share |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| ParsedFile store rehydration | 4426 | 30% |
| **`emit`** | **7161** | **49%** |
| `resolve` | 966 | 7% |
| `finalize` | 552 | 4% |
| `extract` | 369 | 3% |
| teardown, misc | ~750 | 5% |

`extract` is small because the parse cache works — 2121/2121 pre-extracted hits on the TypeScript pass. Nothing re-parses.

## What this PR fixes

Scope resolution calls `loadParsedFilesForPaths` once per language, and every call walks **every** shard in the store. The skip decision needs the envelope's path listing, and that listing is only trustworthy after the payload digest is checked — so a pass that wants 50 Python files still opens and SHA-256s all 413 shards / 301MB of a TypeScript-dominated store to prove it can skip them. **A pass wanting a single file costs 335ms.** The cost scales with *language count*, not with how many files that language has, so a polyglot repo pays it worst.

`tryLoadV8Cache` now returns the listing it already parsed for that skip decision, and the store memoizes it per run.

```
before   python 411ms   typescript 2872ms   javascript 507ms  = 3834ms
after    python 415ms   typescript 2805ms   javascript 248ms  = 3484ms
```

min-of-5. −350ms here, roughly −250ms per additional language elsewhere. The first pass is unchanged by construction — it is what populates the memo.

## The failure mode, and the test for it

A listing memo can produce a **false skip**: a pass concludes a shard holds nothing it wants, and those files silently never reach the graph. That is an exit-0 wrong answer, not a crash. The new test walks four passes with disjoint wants over one store, plus a shard written after the memo is warm. Forcing the skip fails it (verified by mutation).

Keyed on size+mtime as well as name. Shard names are content-addressed so a collision should be impossible, but that invariant lives in the parse-cache keying rather than here, and one `stat` per shard is a few ms against the hundreds this saves. The memo holds one store directory at a time, so a new repo in a long-lived MCP process drops the previous set instead of accumulating.

## What is a floor, and what is next

The digest is **not** the cost: SHA-256 over all 301MB takes 134ms (2.25 GB/s, hardware-accelerated), so swapping to CRC-32 buys ~90ms and costs an envelope-format bump. Not worth it. The rest is `v8.deserialize` (~1240ms) plus the cross-shard intern walk (~1085ms), and the intern walk is not optional — dropping it regresses retained heap ~59%, which is #2649's constraint.

`emit` is the real target — 7.2s, ~21% of the edit loop, spread across a fan of passes with no hot inner loop and nothing quadratic:

```
1828ms  emitCallableValueFlow      480ms  emitFreeCallFallback
1590ms  emitReceiverBoundCalls     426ms  emitReferencesViaLookup
 681ms  resolveDefGraphId          313ms  emitUniqueNamePropertyAccesses
 529ms  lookupCore                 280ms  emitReturnShapeMemberAccesses
 472ms  tryEmitEdge                222ms  emitPropertyDispatchCalls
```

Micro-optimizing any of them is not the win. A one-file edit re-emits all 163,094 edges to write a 3,980-node subgraph, because the pipeline rebuilds the full in-memory graph every run and only the DB *write* is incremental. Making `emit` incremental is a design, not a patch.

## Verification

`tsc --noEmit` clean. 112 tests pass across `parsedfile-store` / `v8-sidecar` / `sidecar-recovery`; 127 including the warm-cache coverage and parse-impl suites. End-to-end on a true incremental run the graph is identical: 51,288 nodes / 163,094 edges / 2106 clusters / 759 flows. The other `tryLoadV8Cache` caller (`parse-cache.ts`) reads only `.kind`/`.value`, so the added `paths` field is inert there.

title: Windows FTS still fails on fresh installations: bundle required runtime dependencies instead of relying on external DLLs
body:
### Area

gitnexus (CLI / core / indexing / MCP server)

### Summary

On newly set up Windows machines, GitNexus completes repository analysis without FTS indexes. Running `gitnexus analyze --repair-fts` then fails because the LadybugDB FTS extension cannot be loaded, even though the extension file exists and installation succeeds.

This appears consistent with the Windows dependency packaging problem discussed in #2374 and LadybugDB/ladybug#685. Improved diagnostics are helpful, but the fresh-install experience remains broken in my environment.

### Context

I am integrating GitNexus into our team's standardized backend development template as part of our engineering workflow. The goal is for developers to adopt the template, index their repositories, and use GitNexus's code graph and full-text/BM25 search through CLI and MCP with minimal manual setup.

During onboarding on newly configured Windows machines, I found that initial analysis completed without FTS indexes, and `gitnexus analyze --repair-fts` failed when loading the installed extension.

This makes team-wide adoption unreliable: FTS availability depends on each developer's existing runtime dependencies and `PATH`, rather than a reproducible setup. Requiring developers to borrow OpenSSL DLLs from Git for Windows or configure different terminal and IDE environments creates additional onboarding and support work.

Relevant issues and PRs:

* [[GitNexus #2374](https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/issues/2374)](https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/issues/2374): Similar Windows FTS loading failures.
* [[GitNexus PR #2383](https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/pull/2383)](https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/pull/2383): Diagnostic improvements, with DLL distribution left as follow-up work.
* [[GitNexus PR #2689](https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/pull/2689)](https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/pull/2689): Git Bash / OpenSSL `PATH` workaround.
* [[LadybugDB #685](https://github.com/LadybugDB/ladybug/issues/685)](https://github.com/LadybugDB/ladybug/issues/685): Missing OpenSSL dependency packaging.
* [[LadybugDB PR #704](https://github.com/LadybugDB/ladybug/pull/704)](https://github.com/LadybugDB/ladybug/pull/704): Explicitly improves diagnostics without fixing the underlying issue.

For this use case, we need a reproducible Windows installation that handles required dependencies consistently across indexing, CLI queries, and IDE-launched MCP processes.

### Expected behavior

A supported Windows installation should be able to build and use FTS indexes without depending on unrelated applications exposing compatible DLLs through `PATH`.

If a system runtime must remain an external prerequisite, GitNexus should detect it explicitly and provide actionable setup instructions before indexing proceeds without FTS.


### Actual behavior

The FTS extension is present, but Windows cannot load it. Re-running `--repair-fts` does not resolve the failure.

Relevant log excerpt, with the username redacted:

```text
GitNexus Analyzer (1.6.11)

Analysis failed: Cannot repair FTS indexes:
the LadybugDB FTS extension failed to load —
LOAD fts failed after successful INSTALL:

IO exception: Failed to load library:
C:\Users\<user>/.lbdb/extension/0.19.0/win_amd64/fts/libfts.lbug_extension
which is needed by extension: fts.

Error:  Ҳ   ָ    ģ 顣 .

The extension itself was found, so a library it depends on is the one
that could not be located. Extensions link against OpenSSL 3
(libssl-3-x64.dll and libcrypto-3-x64.dll),
which is not distributed with them.
```

The localized Windows error is also garbled, making it harder to identify the underlying loader error. The OpenSSL message suggests a likely cause, but I have not independently identified the exact missing DLL on these machines.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Install GitNexus on a newly set up Windows machine.
2. Run `gitnexus analyze` in a repository.
3. Observe that analysis completes without FTS indexes.
4. Run `gitnexus analyze --repair-fts`.
5. Observe the extension loading failure.

### Environment

* OS: Windows x64
* GitNexus: 1.6.11
* LadybugDB extension version: 0.19.0, as shown in the extension path
* Installation: global npm installation 
* Location: mainland China

Although these machines are in mainland China, the reported failure occurs during `LOAD` after successful `INSTALL`, rather than during extension download.

title: fix(zig): model callable-value references, and stop reporting their absence as `exact`
body:
## The defect

A Zig function referenced as a **value** in a binding table was absent from the
graph entirely, and `impact` reported that absence as `epistemic: "exact"`.

`Element.getNamespaceUri` in lightpanda-io/browser IS the DOM
`Element.namespaceURI` accessor. It is bound at `Element.zig:2296`:

```zig
pub const namespaceURI = bridge.accessor(Element.getNamespaceUri, null, .{});
```

`impact` answered: **5 impacted, 2 direct, LOW risk, `epistemic: "exact"`** —
two in-file callers and a claim of completeness, for a public DOM API method
reachable from every page the browser loads. That combination is worse than no
answer: `lower-bound` invites the reader to look further, `exact` tells them not
to bother. It is what got the tool rejected downstream
(lightpanda-io/browser#3399).

That one line is not an outlier: `bridge.{accessor,function,indexed,…}` appears
**2,047 times across 257 files** — the project's entire JS↔Zig surface, none of
it in the graph.

## Two fixes

### D2 — stop claiming `exact` over unmodelled callable-value references

`src/mcp/tools.ts` defines `lower-bound` as "the walk provably missed callers".
A function handed somewhere as a value is registered, not called; the
registration IS modelled (a `value-ref` site becomes a `USES` edge — Kythe `ref`
vs `ref/call`, Joern `METHOD_REF`), but the invocation **through** the stored
value is not, because it happens later via a struct field, a registry lookup or
comptime reflection. That is exactly the `lower-bound` case.

`computeEpistemicBoundary` now probes for inbound `USES` edges stamped with the
value-ref reason and hedges when it finds any, adding a boundary note and a new
`causes.callableValueReferences` (unit: distinct referrer symbols).

Read from **the graph**, not from index metadata. Unlike a dropped receiver —
which leaves no edge to find and therefore needs a persisted summary — a value
reference is already in the graph. So this needs no re-index, no analyzer
change, and works on indexes written before this PR. It is language-neutral:
TypeScript, JavaScript and C++ already emit `value-ref` and participate
immediately.

The cause gets its own slot rather than joining `dispatchBoundary`, which is
documented as "implementations plus interface-level consumers". A value referrer
is neither, and the two differ in what the reader should do: a dispatch boundary
is irreducible, whereas a callable value usually becomes traceable once the
provider models the store/load that carries it.

### D1 — make the Zig provider emit `value-ref`

`mapReferenceKindToEdgeType` has handled this case since #2437. TypeScript,
JavaScript and C++ emit `value-ref`; **Zig emitted zero**. This adds three query
rules to `ZIG_SCOPE_QUERY` tagging `@reference.value-ref` on:

- a bare identifier in argument position — `bridge.accessor(_tagName, …)`
- a qualified one — `bridge.accessor(Element.getNamespaceUri, …)`
- a const binding initialiser — `pub const defaultHandler = onReset;`

Everything downstream already existed. **No new edge type, no schema change, no
capture-machinery change, no baseline edited.**

One grammar detail is load-bearing: in tree-sitter-zig, call arguments are
*direct children* of `call_expression` (there is no `arguments` node — only
builtins have one), so the callee has to be consumed explicitly by `function:`.
Without that binding the same rule also matches the callee of `foo(bar)` and
mints a `USES` edge shadowing the call's own `CALLS` edge. There is a test for
precisely that.

The rules are deliberately broad — `js.Bridge(Element)` and `register(count)`
match too — because the **callable gate** in the property-dispatch pass
(Function/Method/Constructor only) is the filter, the same design that keeps
TypeScript's `{ port: DEFAULT_PORT }` from registering anything.

### Explicitly NOT done

Resolving the terminal invoke. The value reaches `Accessor.init` → a struct
field → `Factory.zig` reflection (`inline for`, `@typeInfo`) →
`Caller.zig`'s `@call(.auto, func, args)` over `func: anytype`. That needs
comptime evaluation. The point is to stop *dropping the reference*, and to stop
calling the result exact.

## Measured, on lightpanda-io/browser (698 `.zig` files)

Baseline and after both from a wiped index (`rm -rf .gitnexus`), same command,
same build.

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| index | 30,222 nodes / 71,070 edges | 30,222 nodes / **73,859** edges |
| `getNamespaceUri` impacted / direct | 5 / 2 | 7 / 3 |
| `getNamespaceUri` risk | LOW | LOW |
| **`getNamespaceUri` epistemic** | **`exact`** | **`lower-bound`** |
| `getTagNameLower` impacted | 30 | 31 |
| `getTagNameLower` direct / risk / epistemic | 10 / HIGH / `exact` | 10 / HIGH / `exact` |

After, on `getNamespaceUri`:

```json

"boundaries": ["1 symbol references this callable as a VALUE rather than calling it …"],

```

And `context getNamespaceUri` now lists the binding that was missing:

```json

  "calls": [ "…lookupNamespaceURIForElement", "…lookupPrefixForElement" ],
  "uses":  [ { "uid": "Struct:src/browser/webapi/Element.zig:JsApi", … } ]
}
```

**The +2,789 edges are fully accounted for.** In the new index `USES` = 2,799 and
value-ref edges = 2,799 — every `USES` edge in this repo is a value reference.
The baseline had 10, all from the repo's single `.js` file, which still has

**`getTagNameLower` +1, explained rather than waved away.** The single added

accessors, three of which (`Element.getLocalName`, `Element._prefix`,

binding table genuinely does sit two hops upstream, and one node is the right
amount to add. `direct`, `risk` and `epistemic` are unchanged, and `exact` is
the meaningful half of this control: the hedge is targeted at symbols with an
**inbound** value reference, not sprayed over everything the change touches.

## Tests

- `test/integration/impact-callable-value-references.test.ts` (new, 5 cases) —
  D2, with three controls: a CALLS-only target stays `exact`, a non-value-ref
  `USES` edge does not hedge, and the `downstream` direction stays `exact`.

## Review round 1 (`gitnexus-check`) — all five findings addressed


**1. Qualified references resolved by tail name — valid, and the serious one.**
I built the fixture and it reproduced: `bridge.accessor(Element.getThing, …)`
inside a `JsApi` that declares its own `getThing` bound the *sibling*, because
`findCallableBindingInScope` never sees the receiver and `walkScopeChain` gives
local bindings precedence. A **wrong** edge — worse than the missing edge this
PR set out to fix.

`resolveValueRefTarget` now resolves a site carrying an explicit receiver
through `findClassBindingInScope` → `findOwnedMember` (the machinery
`receiver-bound-calls` already uses), gated on `CALL_TARGET_TYPES` since
`findOwnedMember` also answers with fields. Bare sites keep the lexical walk.
When the owner cannot be resolved the site is **declined**, not fallen back:
declining costs a reference, falling back mints a confident edge to the wrong
function — and the missing reference is reported as `lower-bound` anyway.

Measured cost: value-ref edges **3,169 → 2,799 (−12%)**. Those 370 were
tail-name coincidences, not registrations. Evidence: all 94 `Element.zig`
`JsApi` entries survive; the cross-container case resolves *and* is correctly
attributed (`IntersectionObserverEntry.JsApi` → `IntersectionObserverEntry.getTarget#0`,
not the enclosing observer); a source census of the corpus finds 2,010 qualified
`bridge.*` registrations (1,812 self-owner + 198 cross-container) and the
sampled cross-container ones all resolve; both acceptance probes are unchanged.

*Known limitation, pinned by a test rather than left implicit:* when a `@This()`
alias's NAME differs from its container's (`const Element = @This();` inside
`main.zig`) the receiver does not resolve and the reference is declined. The
provider has `rewriteZigThisAlias` for exactly this, but it is applied to type
nodes and extending it to reference receivers would change existing CALL-site
behaviour — out of scope here.

**2. A failed probe read as "no boundary" — valid, fixed.** `.catch(() => [])`
turned an unanswerable query into count 0 and no note, so `exact` could be
published on the strength of a question never asked. Now returns `null` and
emits a boundary note. Three outcomes, three answers: cannot run → hedge;
measured zero → no hedge; already followed → no hedge. Test injects a rejection
into that one query (keyed on the bound `$reason`), leaving every other query on
the real database.

**3. Not every value reference is an unmodelled invocation — valid, fixed.**
Where `emitPropertyDispatchCalls` sweep 2 synthesized the dispatch, the walk did
not provably miss the caller, so hedging was noise over an answer that *was*
computed — and a signal firing on every JS/TS hook table carries no information.
A second probe excludes targets with an inbound `property-dispatch` CALLS edge.
Zig never sets a property key, so the motivating case is untouched. The
exclusion is symbol-level, not per-edge (the graph does not record which
registration produced which synthesized call); that residual is documented at
the call site.

**4. `LIMIT 50` understated the count — valid, fixed.** Replaced with
`COUNT(DISTINCT other.id)`: bounded work without a bounded answer, the shape
`countByType` in the same file already uses. The cap is gone rather than merely
disclosed.

**5. The test did not pin the caller count — valid, fixed as proposed.**
`expect(result.impactedCount).toBe(2)`; the proposed value was correct.

New regression tests: a qualified reference binds the written owner and not the
nearer lexical match; an unresolvable receiver emits nothing rather than a wrong
edge; a dispatch-modelled registration stays `exact`; a probe that cannot run
hedges instead of claiming certainty.

Gates re-run after the fix: full `vitest run` **20,634 / 20,644**, the same 10
pre-existing failures verified against `origin/main`; every bench `--check` gate
still passes with no baseline edited.
