## Review round 8 — @magyargergo + `gitnexus-check` on `38de9de7`

### 1. `DECISIONS.md` — removed

Gone from the branch.

### 2. The bench gate is a ratio, no wall clock — `bench/value-ref-resolution`

`ms_budget` is removed from both arms and from `--check`. The only timing gate
left is `linear_scaling_budget`, reshaped after
`bench/parse-dispatch-rounds/baselines.json`: `_what` / `_triage` notes, a
`_measured` block that records samples for **context only**, and min-of-15 reps
to match that file's estimator (it was 7).

Budget **1.6** — 1.40x the measured maximum over 12 runs (0.907 … 1.146), the
~1.5x headroom its siblings use on ratios.

I re-verified it has teeth instead of re-quoting the old note, and the old note
was wrong: replacing `QualifiedNameIndex.get` with a full scan moves
`linear_factor` from ~1.0 to **2.07**, not the ~3.7 the file claimed. Only 1 of
the 17 value-ref sites per module reaches that workspace-wide fallback, so 2.07
is the real signal. 1.6 sits clear of both ends. (The first attempt at that
falsification patched `gitnexus-shared/src` and changed nothing — the bench
resolves the built package; the corrected method is recorded in the note.)

### 3. `@This()` aliases now resolve — "as confident as possible", "close to what a compiler would do"

`@This()` **is** the enclosing container, and `const Self = @This();` is how most
Zig files say so. The container is minted under the FILE STEM and the alias bound
nothing class-like — a file-level alias mints no Const at all (`isZigFileThisAlias`
suppresses it so it cannot shadow the type for `w: *Widget`), a container-level
one mints a `Variable` every `isClassLike` walk steps over. So `Self.member`
resolved to **nothing**: not a wrong edge, no edge. This was PR #3219's declared
"known limitation"; it is now fixed rather than documented.

`bindZigThisAliases` (new, `languages/zig/this-alias-bindings.ts`) binds the alias
name to its container in `indexes.bindingAugmentations` — the sanctioned
post-finalize channel (I8), consulted only **after** a scope's own bindings, so it
can never outrank a real local declaration. Nothing is replaced or removed. It
runs inside the existing `populateZigRangeBindings` hook, sharing that pass's
tree: a pass of its own would re-parse every Zig file on a cold tree cache. No
query change, no capture change, no `SCHEMA_BUMP`.

**Measured on two real corpora**, cold index both sides, same command, same build:

| tigerbeetle (246 `.zig`) | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CALLS | 17,066 | **17,140** (+74) |
| USES | 437 | 443 (+6) |
| MEMBER_OF | 5,131 | 5,143 (+12) |
| every other edge type | — | unchanged |
| node counts per label | — | **identical**, all 24 labels |

| mach (132 `.zig`) | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CALLS | 7,600 | **7,615** (+15) |
| MEMBER_OF | 1,860 | 1,861 (+1) |
| USES | 66 | 66 |

The +74 on tigerbeetle matches a source census of **72** `Alias.member(` call

**🟡 Honor a local non-callable before re-published members — valid, fixed.**
`findNamespaceValueRefTarget`'s local lookup applied `CALL_TARGET_TYPES` *while*
selecting, so a target module declaring a non-callable under the name answered

callable under a name the module's own declaration owns.
`findExportedDefIncludingImportedNames` does not do that, and `x.f` / `x.f()`

provider that sets `namespaceExportsIncludeImportedNames` — so it is hardening

**⚪ Lower-bound header asserts an omission — valid, fixed as suggested.**
`callableValueReferenceBoundaries` hedges on a probe that could not RUN and says
so; the header claiming "some callers are not traced" asserted an omission

may be higher" and names no cause — the per-cause bullets underneath carry that.

## Review round 9 — `gitnexus-check` on `31c6fae5`

Both findings valid; both were claims in comments the adjacent code did not
support, one of them mine from round 8.

**🟡 The alias pass does not feed the payload walk — my comment said it did.**
The call site claimed `bindZigThisAliases` ran first "so a subject spelled

Three findings, all valid; one is a real wrong-edge bug.

title: feat(eval): record provider-native usage at the gateway instead of inferring it after translation
body:
Preserve provider-native per-request usage and actual model identity, and derive cross-provider accounting without conflating provider token semantics.

## Why the current numbers cannot be trusted

The benchmark reads token counts out of Claude Code's session output. That output is Anthropic-shaped whatever actually served the request, and the two providers do not merely name their fields differently — they mean opposite things by them:

```
Anthropic:  total_input = input_tokens + cache_creation + cache_read
            (input_tokens is the UNCACHED remainder; cache fields ADD)

OpenAI:     total_input = input_tokens
            ordinary    = input_tokens - cached - cache_write
            (input_tokens is the WHOLE; cache fields are SUBSETS)
```

Adding OpenAI's three double-counts. Subtracting Anthropic's under-counts. `runner_sessions.USAGE_FIELDS` is the Anthropic set, applied to both. One test asserts the consequence directly: the same three numbers yield a total of 10,000 on OpenAI and 18,000 on Anthropic.

## The seam

At the gateway, on the far side of the translation — the only point that still knows which provider served the request, what model answered, and what the native usage meant before its fields were renamed.

```
Claude Code → Anthropic-shaped request → gateway → provider request
                                                 → provider response
                                                     ├─ append native usage  ← evidence
                                                     └─ translate for Claude Code
```

A LiteLLM callback appends each upstream request's usage **verbatim**: unflattened, unrenamed, unsummed. Normalization is derived offline from that record, so the derivation can be revisited without re-running a paid sweep.

## Two rules the tests encode literally

**The native object is authoritative.** Reasoning tokens stay the decomposition of output tokens they are, rather than being added a second time.

**A field nobody reported is unknown, never zero.** A stored `cache_read = 0` used to mean either "the provider said zero" or "our adapter never looked" — the first says caching is not working, the second says we cannot tell. `NormalizedUsage` uses `None` and refuses to compute the ordinary portion when a term is missing, rather than subtracting an invented zero.

## Mutation-checked three ways

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| Give OpenAI Anthropic's arithmetic | 4 tests fail |
| Make unknown fall back to zero | the unknown test fails |
| Drop `input_tokens_details` in the callback | end-to-end accounting fails with `assert None == 3000` — unknown, not zeros |

## Deliberately not in this PR

**No cost is stored.** Prices change; tokens plus a versioned pricing table can answer both what a past run cost and what the same usage would cost today, without rewriting historical evidence. The actual returned model is recorded separately from the requested role, because several Claude role names map onto one upstream model here and pricing must follow what answered.

**No caching configuration change**, no model, skill, or promotion change. This installs the thermometer without altering the experiment. The progression is: can we measure caching → is it happening → where are the misses → is explicit caching worth it. Only then would settings change.

**Correlation is not built yet.** `cell usage = sum(correlated upstream requests)` needs the cell id threaded through the session environment; the field is captured, the assertion is not written.

## Verification

`538 passed, 15 skipped` plus `27 passed` in the gateway tests; ruff clean. The two `test_model_gateway.py` failures are environmental — `litellm[proxy]`'s console script is absent in this venv — and predate this branch.

Independent of #3207, which stays draft on its own remaining evidence.

title: test(cli): prove detached refresh by ordering, not by wall clock
body:
## Problem

`test/integration/cli/update-notice.test.ts > lets the parent exit without waiting for a detached refresh child` fails intermittently in the platform-sensitive matrix:

```
AssertionError: expected false to be true // Object.is equality
 ❯ test/integration/cli/update-notice.test.ts:170:87
Caused by: Error: Matcher did not succeed in time.
```

The test made two independent bets on absolute wall-clock budgets, and both are machine-speed dependent.

**Bet 1 — `expect(elapsed).toBeLessThan(1_800)`.** This bounds the *parent's* cold `node --import tsx` boot, and infers "did not wait for the child" from a 1050ms margin over the mock fetch's 750ms sleep. I reproduced it failing on Linux under 40-way CPU load: `parentElapsed: 1904`.

**Bet 2 — the 15s poll for the cache file.** That budget has to cover the entire detached child: node boot, a tsx transpile of 22 source files, an `acquireFileLock` that shells out (`ps` on POSIX, `powershell.exe -Command Get-CimInstance Win32_Process` on Windows), the mocked fetch, and the atomic write. Measured breakdown of that chain on an unloaded 24-core Linux box:

| phase | ms |
| --- | --- |
| node boot + tsx + full CLI graph | ~460 |
| `acquireFileLock` incl. `readProcessStartTime` | 16 |
| mocked fetch (the test's own `setTimeout`) | 750 |
| atomic write | ~0 |
| **total** | **~1020** |

Nothing in that chain has a bounded upper limit on a contended runner, and the Windows branch of `readProcessStartTime` spawns PowerShell and queries WMI per lock acquisition.

## Fix

Replace both budgets with an ordering proof. The preloaded mock `fetch` now parks the refresh child until the test releases it, so the asserted sequence is:

1. parent exits (awaited),
2. child is provably still mid-refresh — `refresh-started` marker present, cache absent,
3. test releases the child,
4. cache appears with the expected contents.

That is strictly stronger than inferring "did not wait" from elapsed time, and it holds at any machine speed. The remaining `expect.poll` timeouts no longer carry the assertion's meaning; they are only "is the child dead" safety nets. The mock's wait is bounded at 60s so an abandoned child (test failed before releasing, temp home already removed) exits instead of spinning forever.

Test-only change. No production behavior is touched.

## Why not just speed up the child

Considered, measured, insufficient:

- Bypassing commander/i18n in the `__update-check` child saves ~185ms of ~460ms boot here (22 transpiled source files vs 10), and would require changing the spawn contract the unit tests pin.
- The Windows `Get-CimInstance` call is the only term that can plausibly consume seconds, but it is the lock owner's PID-reuse identity, shared with the analyze/watch/auto-sync locks. Switching to `Get-Process` changes the `"O"` fractional precision, so an old holder plus a new reader would mismatch and steal each other's locks.
- Neither touches bet 1 at all, which bounds the parent, not the child.

A separate, safe win exists and is deliberately **not** in this PR: memoizing `readProcessStartTime(process.pid)`, since a process's own start time is immutable, so retry loops and `reclaimStaleLock` guards currently re-spawn PowerShell on Windows.

## Validation

- `npx vitest run --project default test/integration/cli/update-notice.test.ts` — 7/7 pass, 12.5s.
- 12 concurrent runs of the file — 12/12 pass.
- `detect_changes({scope: "all"})` — 0 changed symbols, risk low, not partial or truncated.

title: perf(lock): probe this process's own start time once
body:
## What

`acquireFileLock` stamps the owner file with the acquiring process's start time, so a later reclaimer can tell a live owner from pid reuse. That value is immutable for the process's lifetime, but it was re-probed on every acquisition — each retry attempt and each `reclaimStaleLock` guard included.

The probe is not cheap. On POSIX it is `ps -p <pid> -o lstart=` (~7ms measured here). On Windows it is:

```
powershell.exe -NoProfile -NonInteractive -Command "$p = Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter ..."
```

a PowerShell spawn plus a WMI query — the single most expensive step in taking an uncontended lock, paid once per acquisition for a constant.

## Change

New `readProcessStartTimeCached`, used as the default reader in `acquireFileLock` and `resolveWatchDeps`. Only this process's own pid is cached:

- **Foreign pids are always re-probed.** That process can exit and its pid be reused, which is precisely what the stamp exists to detect. Caching it would blind the reuse check.
- **A failed probe is not cached.** `acquireFileLock` throws `Unable to determine process start time` on an empty value, so caching one transient failure would leave the process unable to take a lock for the rest of its life.

`readProcessStartTime` itself is untouched and still probes on every call. That was deliberate: putting the memo inside it would have made the existing timezone-pinning regression test (`renders the same start time regardless of the ambient timezone`) pass vacuously, since its second call would never reach `ps`.

Behavior is otherwise identical — same probe, same string, same stamp. Injected readers (`options.readProcessStartTime`) are unaffected.

## Tests

Two new cases in `test/unit/process-identity.test.ts`, both counting actual `execFileSync` calls over a freshly loaded module so "did we really shell out" is observable rather than inferred:

- self pid probed once across repeated calls; a foreign pid re-probed every call;
- a failed self probe is retried, not cached.

## Validation

- `test/unit/{process-identity,file-lock,auto-sync-runner,cli-update-notice,update-check}.test.ts` — 116 passed.
- `test/unit/{auto-sync,pool-wal-recovery,sidecar-recovery}.test.ts` + `test/integration/lbug-core-adapter.test.ts` — passed.
- `test/unit/incremental-dirty-recovery.test.ts` fails on this host with a worker-pool startup ready-timeout. Pre-existing: it fails identically with these changes stashed, and nothing here touches the parse path.
- `tsc --noEmit`, `eslint` on all four files — clean.
- `impact({target: "acquireFileLock", direction: "upstream"})` — HIGH, 10 upstream / 4 direct, `update-check.run` process. Flagged and reviewed: the edit is a default-argument swap, no logic change inside the lock.
- `detect_changes({scope: "all"})` — 4 changed symbols, medium, 2 affected processes, both via `acquireFileLock` step 2. Not partial, not truncated.

…phantom

    A Dart declaration whose value is a constructor call parses the callee as a
    SECOND (identifier) sibling of the declared name:

      final TextEditingController _title = TextEditingController();

title: serve HTTP routes expose no branch or freshness signal, though the registry and `checkStalenessAsync` already have it
body:
### Area

gitnexus (CLI / core / indexing / MCP server)

### Problem or opportunity

An operator driving `gitnexus serve` over HTTP cannot tell which branch an index is on, or whether it is behind. Both the CLI and MCP surfaces can.

**#3199 made this sharper.** Now that a branch-pinned analyze gets its own clone directory and its own registry entry, `GET /api/repos` returns two entries for one repository:

```
Hello-World
Hello-World__test-9f86d081
```

The registry knows what those are — `entry.branch` is `master` and `test` respectively — but the route drops the field, so an HTTP client is left parsing a directory-derived name to guess. That name is an implementation detail of the clone layout, not an API contract.

What already exists and is simply not wired to HTTP:

- `RegistryEntry.branch` and `.branches[]` (`gitnexus/src/storage/repo-manager.ts:159,165`) — `gitnexus list` prints them; `/api/repos` (`gitnexus/src/server/api.ts:998-1015`) omits both.
- `lastCommit` is on the entry and returned by `/api/repos`, but `/api/repo` (`gitnexus/src/server/api.ts:1021-1049`) omits it, along with `branch`.
- `checkStaleness` / `checkStalenessAsync` (`gitnexus/src/core/git-staleness.ts:23,53`) compute commits-behind with `git rev-list --count <lastCommit>..HEAD`. MCP `list_repos` already calls the async variant across repos in parallel (`gitnexus/src/mcp/local/local-backend.ts:2264`); the async form exists precisely so many repos can be checked at once (#1363). No HTTP route calls either.

We run `serve` behind a scheduled reindex pipeline. HTTP is the only surface that pipeline talks to, so "is this index stale?" currently means shelling into the host to run the CLI — and after #3199, "which branch is this entry?" means guessing from a slug.

### Proposed solution

Surface what is already computed, without adding new git logic:

1. `GET /api/repos` — include `branch` and `branches` in the projection, and call the existing `checkStalenessAsync(repoPath, lastCommit)` in parallel across repos (the same shape `local-backend.ts:2260-2282` uses), returning `commitsBehind` and `isStale` per entry.
2. `GET /api/repo` — include `lastCommit` and `branch`, keeping the existing `meta ?? entry` precedence already used for `indexedAt`, and return the same staleness fields.

That is the whole ask: a projection change plus a call to a function that is already the production path on two other surfaces.

### Alternatives considered

- **Parsing the `<repo>__<branchSlug>` directory name.** This is what a client must do today, and it is wrong on principle — the slug is a clone-layout detail (`getCloneDir`), it is trimmed for long refs, and it does not exist for `path`-based or unpinned entries.
- **Polling `gitnexus status` over SSH.** What we do now; it needs shell access on the server host that the HTTP client otherwise does not have.
- **A dedicated `/api/status` route.** More surface than needed — both repo routes already return `indexedAt`, so freshness belongs beside it.

### Acceptance criteria

- `GET /api/repos` returns `branch`, `branches`, and staleness (`commitsBehind`, `isStale`) per entry.
- `GET /api/repo` returns `lastCommit`, `branch`, and the same staleness fields.
- A repo whose `lastCommit` cannot be resolved degrades to `commitsBehind: 0` rather than failing the request — matching `checkStaleness`'s existing catch.
- Staleness is computed in parallel, so `/api/repos` does not regress on hosts with many indexed repositories.
- Tests cover the new fields on both routes, including the unresolvable-`lastCommit` case and a branch-pinned entry from #3199.

### Constraints

- Additive only — existing fields and their shapes stay as they are, so current clients are unaffected.
- No new `GITNEXUS_*` environment variable.
- `/api/repos` is unauthenticated in the default `serve` topology, so nothing beyond what the CLI already prints should be exposed. `branch`, `lastCommit` and commits-behind are all already visible via `gitnexus list` / `status`.

### Contribution

- [x] I am willing to open a PR for this (may need design discussion first).

---

title: perf: tsconfig and node-workspace repo walks dequeue with `shift()`, making the scan quadratic in the frontier
body:
## Summary

`findTsconfigFiles` and `loadNodeWorkspacePackages` both dequeue their bounded
repository walk with `Array.prototype.shift()`. Because each loop *pushes
children while it drains*, the array stays in a mode where `shift()` memmoves
the whole remainder instead of taking V8's left-trimming fast path — so the walk
is quadratic in the frontier, bounded only by `SCAN_MAX_DIRS` (20,000).

The identical defect was reported by `gitnexus-check` against the Zig twin
(`findZigPackageDirs`) in #3219 and fixed there in `f4ab270d`. These two are the
same code shape with the same bound, deliberately left out of that PR because
they are pre-existing and reach TypeScript/Node import resolution, which nothing
in that change set covers.

## Where

| file | line | bound |
|---|---|---|
| `gitnexus/src/core/ingestion/languages/typescript/tsconfig.ts` | 283-284 | `SCAN_MAX_DIRS = 20_000` (`:59`) |
| `gitnexus/src/core/ingestion/import-resolvers/node-workspace-packages.ts` | 345-352 | `SCAN_MAX_DIRS = 20_000` (`:62`) |

```ts
while (queue.length > 0 && dirsScanned < SCAN_MAX_DIRS) {
  const { dir, depth } = queue.shift()!;
```

## Measured, not estimated

A standalone probe reproducing the loop shape (push children while draining,
20,000 dequeues — i.e. exactly the `SCAN_MAX_DIRS` bound), best of three runs on
Node 26.8.1:

| fan-out | `shift()` | head index | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 53.5 ms | 0.81 ms | **66x** |
| 20 | 80.9 ms | 0.76 ms | **106x** |

So the honest figure is tens of milliseconds per walk, not the seconds a raw
move-count suggests — but it is spent before a single config file is read.

## Why it is worth more than one walk

Both loaders are called from `ScopeResolver.loadResolutionConfig`, once per
**language** pass, and three languages call **both**:

- `languages/typescript/scope-resolver.ts:100-101`
- `languages/javascript/scope-resolver.ts:62-63`
- `languages/vue/scope-resolver.ts:91-92`

A repo containing `.ts`, `.js` and `.vue` therefore pays six of these walks per
analyze, each with the quadratic dequeue.

## Suggested fix

The same one-line change applied in `f4ab270d` — a head index instead of a
dequeue:

```ts
let queueHead = 0;
while (queueHead < queue.length && dirsScanned < SCAN_MAX_DIRS) {
  const { dir, depth } = queue[queueHead++]!;
```

Note for whoever picks this up:

- **FIFO order is unchanged**, so neither loader's output moves. `loadTsconfigIndex`
  sorts its scopes afterwards by `(dir length desc, filename rank)` and never
  depended on walk order; `loadNodeWorkspacePackages` keys by package name.
  A regression test asserting *ordering* would therefore be green either way —
  the change is a performance fix and should be reviewed as one.
- **Memory is unchanged.** Those entries were already retained by the pushes;
  `shift()` only dropped the head. The queue is bounded the same way it is today.
- `node-workspace-packages.ts` checks its cap *inside* the loop in order to log a
  warning, so the condition there needs `queueHead < queue.length` in the `while`
  and the existing `if (dirsScanned >= SCAN_MAX_DIRS)` block left alone.

## Verification

`npx vitest run test/unit/node-workspace-packages.test.ts test/unit/tsconfig*.test.ts`
plus `test/integration/resolvers` should be enough; `bench/import-target/measure.mjs --check`
and `bench/receiver-resolution/measure.mjs --check` cover the resolution output
these feed.

title: feat(api): report branch and index freshness on the serve repo routes
body:
## Summary

`GET /api/repos` and `GET /api/repo` now return the branch an index was built from, its `lastCommit`, and — where it can be computed — how far behind the working tree it is. All of it already existed: the fields sit on `RegistryEntry`, and `checkStalenessAsync` is the same helper MCP `list_repos` and `gitnexus status` already use. Only the HTTP layer never asked.

Fixes #3226.

## Motivation / context

#3199 made this pointed. A branch-pinned analyze now registers its own entry, so one repository can produce two rows in `/api/repos`:

```
Hello-World
Hello-World__test-9f86d081
```

The registry knows those are `master` and `test`. The route dropped the field, so an HTTP client had no option but to pattern-match the clone-directory suffix — a layout detail that is trimmed for long refs and absent for `path`-registered repos.

## Areas touched

- [x] `gitnexus/` (CLI / core / MCP server)
- [x] `gitnexus-web/` (Vite / React UI) — response type only, no UI
- [ ] `.github/` (workflows, actions)
- [ ] `eval/` or other tooling
- [ ] Docs / agent config only

## Scope & constraints

**In scope**

- `server/repo-projection.ts` (new) — the two response projections, extracted so the field list is assertable.
- `server/api.ts` — both routes call them; `/api/repos` resolves staleness in parallel.
- `gitnexus-web/src/services/backend-client.ts` — `BackendRepo` widened to match.

**Explicitly out of scope / not done here**

- **Any UI use of the new fields.** The web type is widened so a consumer *can* read them; rendering is a separate change.
- **Changing what staleness measures.** This reports the index against the repo's checked-out HEAD — the same thing `gitnexus status` and `list_repos` report. Measuring against the remote is a different question and would put a network call on an unauthenticated route.

## Implementation notes

**A limitation worth stating plainly, because it shapes what this field is worth.** `checkStalenessAsync` runs `git rev-list --count <lastCommit>..HEAD`. A `url`-registered repo is cloned `--depth 1`, so right after an analyze HEAD *is* `lastCommit`; and if the two ever diverged, `rev-list` cannot walk a shallow history — it exits `fatal: Invalid revision range`, which `checkStaleness` self-catches to 0. Measured on a local build:

```
Hello-World                 branch=master  staleness=absent   (server clone, --depth 1)
Hello-World__test-9f86d081  branch=test    staleness=absent   (server clone, --depth 1)
localrepo                   branch=main    staleness={commitsBehind: 2}   (path repo, after 2 commits)
```

So commits-behind is meaningful for `path`-registered repositories; for server-managed clones it will read as fresh. The branch and `lastCommit` fields are unconditional and work everywhere. I documented this in `repo-projection.ts` rather than let it be discovered later. If you would rather `checkStaleness` grew a distinct "unknown" state so a client can tell "up to date" from "could not tell", I am happy to do that as a follow-up — it touches a core helper `list_repos` shares, so I did not assume it here.

**Shape.** `staleness` is present only when the index is behind, carrying `commitsBehind` and `hint` — byte-identical to what `list_repos` returns. The same fact should not have two shapes across two surfaces.

**Rate limiting.** `/api/repos` previously had no limiter. This change makes one unauthenticated GET cost one `git rev-list` per registered repo, which is the shape the repo already rate-limits elsewhere (`/api/repo`, `/api/file`, `/api/grep` all carry one for `js/missing-rate-limiting`), so it now carries the same 60 rpm/IP ceiling. Flagging it as a deliberate behavior change rather than a silent one.

**Why a separate module.** The #3199 review landed the point that route-inline logic is only reachable by booting a server, so nothing asserts it. Extracting the projections means the field list has unit tests, and the integration test below proves the routes actually call them — I confirmed it fails when the route is reverted while the unit tests stay green.

## Testing & verification

- [x] `cd gitnexus && npm test` — see note below
- [x] `cd gitnexus && npm run test:integration`
- [x] `cd gitnexus && npx tsc --noEmit`
- [x] `cd gitnexus-web && npx tsc -b --noEmit`
- [x] `npx eslint .` (root) — 0 errors
- [ ] Manual / Playwright E2E — no UI change

New tests:

- `test/unit/repo-projection.test.ts` — 14 cases: `branch`/`branches` exposure, the two-entries-per-repo case #3199 creates, `meta ?? entry` precedence, the legacy entry with no branch, an empty-stats repo, and that a fresh index omits the key entirely rather than reporting a zero.
- `test/integration/server-repo-freshness.test.ts` — spawns a real `serve` against a real two-commit git fixture registered at the *first* commit, so `commitsBehind: 1` is computed by git rather than asserted from a constant. Also pins that the pre-existing fields are unchanged.

Manual, against a running server:

```
GET /api/repos  -> branch=main  lastCommit=6802be82  staleness={commitsBehind: 1}
GET /api/repo   -> lastCommit + branch + the same staleness
                   RateLimit-Policy: 60;w=60
```

> **On `npm test`:** 14,879 of 14,928 pass locally. The 8 failures are in `analyzer-identity.test.ts`, `analyzer-identity-in-process-guards.test.ts` and `hooks.test.ts`, are pre-existing on this machine, and are unrelated to this change — they probe `W_OK`/`EACCES` behavior and `ps` output shapes. I confirmed the same set fails on an unmodified checkout.

## Risk & rollout

Low, with one caveat named above. The response changes are additive — every existing field keeps its name, type and meaning, and `staleness` is absent unless the index is genuinely behind. No migration, no config, no new environment variable. The one behavior change is the new rate limit on `/api/repos`; a client polling it faster than 60 rpm would now be throttled.

## Checklist

- [x] PR body meets repo minimum length
- [x] No `AGENTS.md` / overlay changes
- [x] No secrets, tokens, or machine-specific paths committed
- [x] No new `GITNEXUS_*` environment variable
- [x] `gitnexus/CHANGELOG.md` untouched — release notes come from the PR title

Affects: Suspense, ErrorBoundary, and Context.Provider in hono/jsx, and renderToString() / renderToReadableStream() in hono/jsx/dom/server. Fixes missing HTML escaping for a plain string placed directly as a child or fallback of these components, or as the root value of the server rendering functions, so untrusted strings could be emitted as markup. GHSA-hxh3-vqpv-xpqv

Users who render untrusted strings inside Suspense, ErrorBoundary, or Context.Provider, or pass them directly to hono/jsx/dom/server, are strongly encouraged to upgrade to this version.

v4.13.6

What's Changed

  • fix(client): keep a param value of "index" in $url() and $path() in honojs/hono#5297
  • fix(client): normalize root WebSocket URLs in honojs/hono#5291
  • fix(types): allow symbol keys in Context get and set fallbacks in honojs/hono#5300

Full Changelog: https://github.com/honojs/hono/compare/v4.13.5...v4.13.6

v4.13.5

Security fixes

This release includes fixes for the following security issues:

Query parser reads parameters after the URL fragment, causing cache-key and proxy interpretation differentials

Affects: Cache Middleware and applications behind a proxy, WAF, or logging layer that inspects query strings. Fixes query parsing that did not stop at the URL fragment, so a ? after a # was treated as the start of a query string and the application could read parameters that the other component never saw. GHSA-crvj-82cr-hjcx

Incomplete fix for CVE-2026-39408: toSSG() still writes files outside the output directory

Affects: toSSG() for Static Site Generation. Fixes a path normalization gap where consecutive parent-directory segments in ssgParams values were not fully collapsed, bypassing the containment check added in 4.12.12. GHSA-gqvv-2mrq-wpjv

Unbounded dot-notation nesting in parseBody() can cause memory exhaustion

Affects: parseBody() when dot-notation parsing is enabled. Fixes unbounded expansion of dot-separated field names, where a small request body could allocate a disproportionately large object graph and concurrent requests could exhaust the heap. GHSA-g6gw-c38x-mqfc

Users who use Cache Middleware, deploy behind a proxy or WAF that inspects query strings, use Static Site Generation, or use parseBody({ dot: true }) are strongly encouraged to upgrade to this version.

title: test(eval): run the benchmark offline against a scripted provider
body:
Run the benchmark end to end without spending money, and fix what that exposed.

## Why

Every defect this harness shipped last round was invisible to its own tests for one reason: the tests exercised a layer *below* where the code runs.

- The usage log was never written — the proxy is a subprocess with a constructed environment.
- The callback could not be imported — LiteLLM loads it by path, not as a package.
- Failures went unrecorded — only the async hook was overridden.

CI or review caught all three. No unit test could, because each called the function directly instead of driving the path that calls it.

## What this adds

**A scriptable stand-in for Anthropic and OpenAI** (`mock_provider.py`), speaking both wire protocols the harness depends on — Anthropic Messages (streaming and not) and OpenAI Responses. The runner already supports pointing at it: `--base-url` is the same path the free-model proxy docs use.

Scripted rather than simulated: a test decides what the model says, which tools it asks for, and exactly what usage it reports. That last part is what makes provider-native accounting testable at all — real cache hits are not reproducible on demand, but a declared `cache_read` of 7,000 is.

**A stand-in CLI** (`tests/fixtures/fake_claude.py`) that does what the real one does at the two boundaries that matter: it calls `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, it **executes** the tool blocks that come back, and it prints the stream-json the parent parses. Everything between stays real.

**A whole sweep, offline.** `runner.main()` driven the way the workflow drives it: real task selection, hidden-oracle capture, sandbox, CLI subprocess, artifact capture, scoring against the oracle, aggregation, health guard, promotion gate. ~18 seconds.

## What it found

**The accounting merged in #3220 does not work.** LiteLLM never hands a logger the upstream body — it normalises usage into its own object first, so an OpenAI Responses reply arrives as `prompt_tokens` / `prompt_tokens_details`, never the `input_tokens` / `input_tokens_details` the shipped adapter reads. Every field came back unknown. The observed `call_type` is `anthropic_messages`, so `canonical_provider` returned `None` and `normalize_usage` would have refused outright.

The unit tests agreed with the wrong shape because their fixture was written in it — producer and consumer consistent, and both wrong.

**An uninvoked skill moved the arm's quality median.** `aggregate`'s filter dropped `EXCLUDED_ERROR_KINDS` and `evidence_valid=False`; `skill-not-invoked` is neither. An arm could be credited for a review it never performed with the skill under test. Excluded from quality metrics only — cost still counts, because that session ran and was billed.

## Negative controls

A scorer that cannot be wrong measures nothing:

| run | tp/fp/fn | f1 | resolved | error_kind |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| correct finding | 1/0/0 | 1.0 | True | — |
| wrong location | 0/1/1 | 0.0 | False | `oracle-failed` |
| approve / none | 0/0/1 | 0.0 | False | `oracle-failed` |

All three keep `review_evidence_valid=True` — being wrong is a quality result, not a broken measurement. `precision` is `None` in the approve case, not 0, because it is undefined with no predictions.

Two tasks, each scored against **its own** oracle: the dangerous failure of interleaving cells across tasks is a mis-routed context scoring one task against another's labels, with every row still green. Mutation-checked.

## Scope and limits

- Two provisioning steps are stubbed **only where a machine cannot supply them**. `GITNEXUS_REQUIRE_FULL_SWEEP=1`, set in `eval / containment (ubuntu)`, runs the sweep with nothing stubbed — real containment, real mounts, real graph — and **fails** rather than degrading to the stubbed path.
- The CLI-identity probe is an **experiment, not an assertion**. Per-cell usage attribution is unbuilt because one proxy serves the whole sweep, so anything read from its environment is identical for every request. What the real CLI sends is undocumented, and guessing a wire format is how the three bugs above happened — so the probe drives the real pinned CLI against the mock and records what arrives.
- Packed scheduling is **not** wired in. Measured against the real `sweep_packed_cells` it is worth −27% on a cold sweep and −37% weekly, with breaker fidelity holding at three injected failure positions. It restructures a 125-line loop across ~92 names; this PR adds the cross-task test that makes that change checkable, and stops there.

## Verification

682 eval tests pass, 17 skipped. Every fix here is mutation-checked against the exact failure it claims to prevent.

One correction worth recording: the "2 environmental `test_model_gateway.py` failures" reported on #3206, #3207 and #3220 were **my invocation error**, not the environment. `litellm[proxy]` was installed throughout; running `.venv/bin/python` without `VIRTUAL_ENV` made the resolver follow a symlink to the base interpreter. With it set, the suite is fully green.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: analyze aborts on Spring constructor-to-Bean INJECTS edge: Constructor → CodeElement is undeclared
body:
## Summary

`gitnexus analyze` aborts when a Spring dependency lookup anchored in a Java constructor targets a synthetic `@Bean` provider (`CodeElement`):

```text
Relationship label pair Constructor → CodeElement is not declared in the LadybugDB relation schema.
relationship type: INJECTS
```

Observed with the published **GitNexus 1.6.11**, Node 22.18.0, macOS arm64, LadybugDB 0.19.1. The source project is private, so this report intentionally omits its identifiers and source. I will follow up with a standalone public fixture and a focused fix.

## Expected / actual

Expected: a supported Spring lookup should retain its `INJECTS` edge and complete persistence.

Actual: the extracted relation cannot pass the declared-pair check and the repository analysis terminates during persistence.

## Initial diagnosis

At upstream main `25974caf0590b54574f9ee0703b30f417fa34557`, `gitnexus/src/core/lbug/schema.ts` declares `Function`, `Class`, and `Method` → `CodeElement`, but not `Constructor` → `CodeElement`. `CodeElement` is also outside the generated attachment target set, so the generated rules do not cover this pair.

This appears to be another structural/framework-emitter gap related to #2792 / #2793, rather than a request to allow arbitrary node pairs. Static inspection of current main confirms the missing declaration; the original end-to-end failure was observed on 1.6.11, not yet reproduced on main at the time of filing.

## Proposed follow-up

- Add a sanitized Java fixture that actually emits the constructor-to-factory-provider edge.
- Cover both the emitted relation and its successful database persistence, rather than only asserting DDL text.
- Add the minimal missing supported relation pair and inspect adjacent Spring provider cases.
- Preserve undeclared-pair fail-fast behavior; do not suppress the exception or exclude the source file.
- Rebuild the index after the schema change using the existing schema-fingerprint invalidation mechanism.

title: fix(cobol): prefer copybook dirs so COPY EXTERNAL does not hit vendor decoys
body:
## Summary

Prefer well-known copybook directories when resolving COBOL `COPY EXTERNAL` so a vendor decoy with the same stem is not first-won as a live import.

## Motivation / context

Fixes #2967. Census `resolveImportTarget` first-won any `.cpy` stem, so `COPY EXTERNAL` became `vendor/EXTERNAL.cpy` even when a real `copybooks/` member exists (or should be unresolved).

## Areas touched

- [x] `gitnexus/` (CLI / core / MCP server)
- [ ] `gitnexus-web/` (Vite / React UI)
- [ ] `.github/` (workflows, actions)
- [ ] `eval/` or other tooling
- [ ] Docs / agent config only (`AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.cursor/`, `llms.txt`, etc.)

## Scope & constraints

**In scope**

- Shared `resolveCobolCopyTarget` used by census and the regex processor.
- Prefer `copybooks` / `COPYBOOKS` / `cpy` / `copy` plus the importer dir when present; fail-open first-wins otherwise.
- Drop COBOL `KNOWN_GAPS` for this EXTERNAL decoy.

**Explicitly out of scope / not done here**

- SYSLIB
- `IN` / `OF` qualifiers
- Expander signature change
- Ruby / Swift / C / Dart copy resolvers

## Implementation notes

Processor `resolveCopy` and census `resolveImportTarget` share one helper so IMPORTS and the conformance table cannot drift.

## Testing & verification

- [x] `cd gitnexus && npm test` (vitest: 53/53 including processor pin + conformance; adjacent preprocessor/expander/index-reuse 164/164)

Release notes

Sourced from @​vitejs/plugin-react's releases.

plugin-react@6.1.1

Add compiler.logDiagnostics option

Recoverable React Compiler diagnostics are no longer logged by default. Set compiler.logDiagnostics to true to log them through Vite. Fatal diagnostics are always logged and fail the transform.

Respect environment sourcemap option for React Compiler transform when builder.sharedPlugins is enabled (#1439)

The React Compiler transform was using the top-level sourcemap option instead of the environment sourcemap option. This caused a problem when the experimental builder.sharedPlugins was enabled.

plugin-react@6.1.0

Add experimental native React Compiler support (#1419)

Add experimental native React Compiler support.

You can use it by installing oxc-transform-react and enabling it via the compiler option:

npm install -D oxc-transform-react

import { defineConfig } from 'vite'
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react'

export default defineConfig({

plugins: [

react({ compiler: true })

]

})

title: python-workspace-extractor: import scanner misses function-local imports (and only tracks PascalCase symbols)
body:
**Title:** `python-workspace-extractor`: import scanner misses function-local imports (and only tracks PascalCase symbols)

**Body:**

`scanPythonImports` in `gitnexus/src/core/group/extractors/python-workspace-extractor.ts` uses:

```ts
const fromImportRegex = /^from\s+(\w[\w.]*)\s+import\s+(.+)/gm;
```

anchored to column 0 via `^` in multiline mode. This never matches a function-local (indented) import — only module-level imports are detected.

That's a real gap on real code: any codebase that defers an optional/heavy dependency's import to function scope (a common pattern specifically for the case this extractor exists to serve — an optional cross-package dependency that shouldn't break import-time if the extra isn't installed) is invisible to workspace-deps detection, even when the manifest half (`pyproject.toml` dependency + `[tool.uv.sources]` editable path) is declared correctly and parses fine.

**Reproduction**, from a real three-repo Python stack I was evaluating GitNexus against:

- Repo A declares `optional-dependencies.foo = ["bar>=1.0"]` and `[tool.uv.sources] bar = { path = "../bar", editable = true }`.
- Repo A's own code imports it as:
  ```python
  def get_thing():
      from bar.thing import Thing  # indented — deliberately not module-level
      ...
  ```
- `gitnexus group sync` with `detect.workspace_deps: true`: `manifest: 0 cross-links`, even though the dependency and its usage are both real. Manually declaring the link in `group.yaml`'s `links:` override works as a registry entry, but the point of workspace-deps auto-detection is not needing that.

**Suggested fix:** allow leading whitespace before `from`:

```ts
const fromImportRegex = /^\s*from\s+(\w[\w.]*)\s+import\s+(.+)/gm;
```

**Second, smaller finding, same function:** `isPascalCase(sym)` filters the import scan down to symbols that look like class names —

```ts
if (isPascalCase(sym)) {
  results.push({ packageName: originalName, symbolName: sym, filePath: relFile });
}
```

so a cross-repo import of a plain function (`from bar.thing import do_thing`) is never tracked regardless of the indentation fix above, only class-shaped imports are. If that's deliberate (matching against class-shaped `lib` contracts specifically), it's worth a doc note in `PIPELINE.md`; if not, it's a second real gap in the same function. Flagging both since they compound on the same code path — a function-local import of a plain function hits both filters at once.

Happy to send a PR for the regex fix if useful — it's a one-line change plus a test case using an indented import.

title: Rust name-fallback treats src/ and tests/ as one crate without cargo metadata
body:
### Area

gitnexus (CLI / core / indexing / MCP server)

### Summary

`rustCrateRootOf` returns `''` for both `src/lib.rs` and `tests/helper.rs`, so a `crate::` import can authorize a unique-name fallback across what Rust treats as separate crates.

### Context

Split out of PR #3190 (review thread https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/pull/3190#discussion_r3976217836), where it was found and deliberately not fixed. Path-only refusal is unsafe: a file under `tests/` is not always a separate crate (`#[path]`, integration-test vs unit-test layouts, workspace prefixes). The decision on that PR is to wait for crate metadata rather than guess from directory names.

Related: `rustModulePathOf` also strips a leading `src`/`tests`/`benches`/`examples` segment, so `src/foo.rs` and `tests/foo.rs` collapse to the same module path `foo`.

### Expected behavior

A library caller in `src/lib.rs` with `use crate::helper` must not authorize a global-name fallback to an item that exists only in a different Cargo target (`tests/helper.rs`, `src/bin/tool.rs`, `benches/`, `examples/`). Those are separate crates in Rust's module model.

### Actual behavior

For a single-crate tree at the analyzed root:

- `rustCrateRootOf('src/lib.rs') === ''`
- `rustCrateRootOf('tests/helper.rs') === ''`

The same-crate guard in `rustIsGlobalNameFallbackPlausible` only skips when both roots are non-empty and differ (`gitnexus/src/core/ingestion/languages/rust/name-fallback-visibility.ts`). Empty roots compare equal, so a `crate::` import on the library side can keep a labeled `global-name-fallback` edge to the integration-test item.

Workspace crates (`crates/foo/src/…`) already compare non-empty prefixes and refuse a cross-crate `crate::` guess. The hole is the top-level / empty-prefix case.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Index a crate with a unique helper only in the integration-test target:

```rust
// src/lib.rs
use crate::helper;
fn caller() { helper(); }

// tests/helper.rs
pub fn helper() {}
```

2. Confirm `rustIsGlobalNameFallbackPlausible` accepts the library call site against `tests/helper.rs` (same empty crate root, matching trailing module path after stripping `src`/`tests`).
3. The resulting CALLS edge is labeled `global-name-fallback` at 0.5 — a guess Rust itself would reject.

### Environment

- Branch / PR: `fix/3182-1-fallback-resolution` (#3190)
- File: `gitnexus/src/core/ingestion/languages/rust/name-fallback-visibility.ts` (`rustCrateRootOf`, `rustModulePathOf`)

### Scope (when crate metadata exists)

- Identify Cargo targets (lib / bin / test / bench / example) instead of treating every `src`/`tests` folder as the same crate root.
- Keep the current empty-root allowance for a true single-crate library (`src/lib.rs` calling `src/foo.rs`).
- Add a fixture that asserts `src/lib.rs` + `use crate::helper` does **not** authorize `tests/helper.rs`.
- Do **not** land a path-only `tests/` vs `src/` reject without metadata — that was declined on #3190 as unsafe.

title: bug: overrides in package.json don't dedupe nested @huggingface/transformers copies - vulnerable sharp/adm-zip/onnxruntime-node still resolve at runtime
body:
AI Generated issue-ticket

gitnexus/package.json declares overrides for sharp (>=0.35.0), adm-zip
(>=0.6.0), and a nested onnxruntime-node override under @huggingface/transformers.

Verified on a clean, from-scratch install:
  npm uninstall -g gitnexus
  npm install -g gitnexus@latest
(npm 11.19.0, Node 24.20.0)

Every copy of each package in the resulting tree:

  node_modules/sharp                                                     0.34.5
  node_modules/adm-zip                                                   0.6.0  (patched)
  node_modules/@huggingface/transformers/node_modules/adm-zip            0.5.18 (unpatched)
  node_modules/onnxruntime-node                                          1.29.0 (patched)
  node_modules/@huggingface/transformers/node_modules/onnxruntime-node   1.24.3 (unpatched, exact pin from transformers' own package.json)

sharp has only one copy in the tree and its override never applies at all.

adm-zip and onnxruntime-node each end up with two copies: one at the
overridden/patched version, and one still at the vulnerable version nested
inside @huggingface/transformers. Because Node module resolution prefers the
nearest node_modules directory, any require() originating from inside
@huggingface/transformers's own code resolves to the nested, unpatched copy -
not the overridden top-level one. So the overrides do not actually remove the
vulnerable code path that @huggingface/transformers exercises at runtime.

Root cause: npm's own overrides design (see npm/rfcs accepted/0036-overrides.md)
states a dependency is not deduplicated against another instance that is
subject to different override rules. The nested onnxruntime-node override
scoped under "@huggingface/transformers" puts that subtree under a different
rule-set than the flat, tree-wide overrides declared for sharp and adm-zip -
so npm does not dedupe the nested copies against the top-level ones. This is
documented npm behavior, not an npm bug.

Current vulnerabilities present in a fresh install:
- CVE-2026-33327, CVE-2026-33328, CVE-2026-35590, CVE-2026-35591 (sharp/libvips, patched >=0.35.0)
- GHSA-g89c-p67h-r497, GHSA-2jg2-4ch7-h545 (sharp/libheif, patched >=0.35.4)
- adm-zip "crafted ZIP triggers 4GB memory allocation" (patched >=0.6.0)
- adm-zip "extraction follows destination symlinks" (present in the 0.5.9-0.6.0 range; the nested 0.5.18 copy falls in it)

Repro:
1. npm uninstall -g gitnexus (if previously installed)
2. npm install -g gitnexus@latest
3. find "$(npm root -g)/gitnexus" -path "*/sharp/package.json" -o -path "*/adm-zip/package.json" -o -path "*/onnxruntime-node/package.json" | xargs -I{} node -e "console.log('{}', require('{}').version)"
4. Observe the nested @huggingface/transformers/node_modules copies retain the pre-override versions.

Suggested fix: scope the sharp and adm-zip overrides under
"@huggingface/transformers" explicitly too (the same treatment already given
to onnxruntime-node), so the whole subtree sits under one consistent
override rule-set and npm dedupes it correctly, e.g.:

  "overrides": {
    "sharp": ">=0.35.4",
    "adm-zip": ">=0.6.0",
    "@huggingface/transformers": {
      "sharp": ">=0.35.4",
      "adm-zip": ">=0.6.0",
      "onnxruntime-node": "$onnxruntime-node"
    }
  }

Recommend confirming with a clean from-scratch npm install -g after any
change, since the current overrides look correct in package.json but do not
take effect for the nested copies.

title: Staleness silently reverts to fresh on branch-pinned serve clones once git prunes the indexed commit
body:
### Area

gitnexus (CLI / core / indexing / MCP server)

### Problem or opportunity

This is the "unknown vs fresh" follow-up deferred in the #3232 tri-review, which named the sharpest residual as a pull-then-fail composition in which a shallow fetch drops the indexed SHA and the catch reports it as not stale. I measured that residual against real repositories. It behaves differently from how either of us described it, and fixing it requires answering one question the codebase currently answers three different ways.

**1. On branch-pinned `serve` clones, staleness is correct at first and then silently reverts to "fresh".**

`checkStaleness` / `checkStalenessAsync` (`core/git-staleness.ts`) run `git rev-list --count <lastCommit>..HEAD`, and any failure is collapsed into `{ isStale: false, commitsBehind: 0 }`. I reproduced the case where an update moves HEAD but the analyze that follows fails, so `lastCommit` stays at the old commit. This was on real repositories with git 2.40:

| Case | `rev-list <idx>..HEAD` | `rev-parse HEAD` | reported today |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) shallow clone, index == HEAD | `0` | == idx | fresh ✓ |
| (b) pinned re-index failed, reflog intact | `1` | ≠ idx | **1 behind ✓** |
| (b′) same, after reflog expiry + `gc` | `fatal: Invalid revision range` | ≠ idx | **fresh ✗** |
| (c) path is not a git repo | `fatal: not a git repository` | fails | fresh |
| (d) deep clone, recorded SHA gone from history | `fatal: Invalid revision range` | ≠ idx | fresh |
| (e) deep clone, genuinely 2 behind | `2` | ≠ idx | 2 behind ✓ |

What decides (b) vs (b′) is which update path the clone takes:

- **Pinned** (`fetchAndCheckoutRequestedBranch`: `fetch --depth 1 origin +refs/heads/<b>:refs/remotes/origin/<b>` then `checkout -B`). The fetch re-shallows at the new tip, which orphans the indexed commit. Its HEAD reflog entry keeps the commit alive, so `gc --prune=now` alone left `rev-list` still answering `1`. Once the reflog entry expires (`gc.reflogExpireUnreachable`, default 30 days) and a `gc` prunes the object (`gc.pruneExpire`, default 2 weeks), `rev-list` fails and the catch reports **fresh**. That happens while the index is still behind.
- **Unpinned** (`pull --ff-only`). Not affected. The old commit stays reachable as HEAD's parent, and `rev-list` still answered `1` after a forced `gc --prune=now`.

For monitoring, this is the worst available shape. An alert on `staleness` fires correctly for about a month, then **clears itself** with no re-index having happened. After #3199, every branch-pinned clone takes this path.

**2. The codebase already disagrees with itself about "can't tell".**

| Where | Rule | When it cannot answer |
|---|---|---|
| `core/git-staleness.ts` (MCP `list_repos`, tool staleness, HTTP repo routes) | `rev-list` count | **fresh** — pinned deliberately by four tests in `staleness.test.ts` ("Git failure → fail open") |
| `core/group/service.ts:875-877` | no `lastCommit` → `{ isStale: true, commitsBehind: -1 }` | **stale** |
| `gitnexus/hooks/claude/gitnexus-hook.cjs:524` | `git rev-parse HEAD !== lastCommit` | **stale** |

The hook's rule, "HEAD is not the indexed commit", is exactly the one that answers (b′) and (d): `rev-parse HEAD` succeeds there and disagrees with the index. The same file also already says this about the sibling-clone check `commitsAheadOfIndexed`: "The caller should treat `undefined` as 'drift unknown' rather than 'no drift'."

**3. A small concrete bug from the disagreement.** `cli/group.ts:164-165` renders `STALE (${row.commitsBehind ?? '?'} commits behind)`. `??` does not catch the `-1` that `group/service.ts` uses for "no `lastCommit`", so `gitnexus group status` prints **`STALE (-1 commits behind)`**. Nothing in `test/` covers that branch.

### Proposed solution

One shared answer in `core/git-staleness.ts`, additive, so no existing consumer changes behaviour unless it opts in:

```ts
export type StalenessStatus = 'current' | 'behind' | 'diverged' | 'unknown';

export interface StalenessInfo {
  isStale: boolean;        // unchanged
  commitsBehind: number;   // unchanged
  hint?: string;           // unchanged
  status: StalenessStatus; // new
}
```

- `current`: `rev-list` answered 0.
- `behind`: `rev-list` answered N > 0. Same result as today.
- `diverged`: `rev-list` failed, but `rev-parse HEAD` resolved and differs from `lastCommit`. The index is provably not at HEAD; only the count is unknown. This covers (b′) and (d).
- `unknown`: HEAD could not be resolved at all (not a git repo, timeout, empty `lastCommit`). This covers (c).

`isStale` and `commitsBehind` keep their current values in every case, so the four fail-open tests and the `attachToolStaleness` "leave the result untouched when fresh" contract hold unchanged. Surfaces opt into `status`:

- `staleness` stays absent for `current`, which preserves the MCP-parity rule from #3232.
- For `diverged`, the same `staleness` object carries `{ status: 'diverged', hint }` with `commitsBehind` omitted, since the count genuinely is not known. It keeps one field for one fact across MCP `list_repos`, tool staleness, and `/api/repos` + `/api/repo`, rather than a second HTTP-only flag.
- `group status` reads the shared status, so a missing count renders as unknown instead of `-1`.

I will open a PR that implements the recommendations below. If you would rather any of them went the other way, say so here and I will build it that way instead. The parts I would rather you decide than have me assume:

1. **Surface `diverged` through the existing `staleness` object?** My recommendation is yes: it is a positive proof of staleness, and it closes the residual. The cost is that "`staleness` present" would no longer always imply a numeric `commitsBehind`.
2. **Where should `unknown` appear, if anywhere?** I would keep it off the hot tool path, since a `--skip-git` repo would otherwise carry it on every read tool response, and expose it only on the listings (`list_repos`, `/api/repos`, `/api/repo`), where a monitor is looking.
3. **Should `diverged` also set `isStale: true`?** That would align core with the hook and with `group`. It would also flip the pinned "fails open with invalid commit hash" tests, so I have left it off by default.

### Alternatives considered

- **Deepen the pinned fetch** (no `--depth 1`) so the indexed commit is never orphaned. That trades clone size and fetch time on every re-index for a monitoring signal, and it does nothing for (d), where history really was rewritten.
- **Read `rev-list`'s exit status as "stale".** That would treat a non-git `--skip-git` folder as stale on every read tool response. `rev-parse HEAD` is the check that separates "index is behind" from "cannot tell".
- **Measure against the remote** (`ls-remote`). That answers a different question and puts a network call on unauthenticated routes. The #3232 review did not pick it up either.

### Acceptance criteria

- `checkStaleness` and `checkStalenessAsync` return `status` for all four cases above, and both helpers agree with each other.
- A test reproduces (b′) on a real shallow clone (pinned fetch path, reflog expired, `gc`) and asserts `diverged`, with a sibling test asserting the unpinned `pull --ff-only` path stays `behind`.
- The four existing fail-open tests pass unmodified: `isStale` and `commitsBehind` are unchanged.
- `gitnexus group status` no longer prints `-1 commits behind`, with a test covering the missing-`lastCommit` branch.
- The `staleness` shape is identical across MCP `list_repos`, tool staleness, and the HTTP repo routes.

### Constraints

- Additive only. No existing field changes meaning, and `staleness` stays absent when current.
- `diverged` costs one extra `rev-parse HEAD`, and only on the failure path. The happy path is unchanged.
- No new `GITNEXUS_*` environment variable.

### Contribution

- [x] I am willing to open a PR for this (may need design discussion first).

---

Measured on git 2.40, macOS arm64, against `main` @ `16307a1`. Related: #3226, #3232, #2655.

title: feat(staleness): report diverged and unknown index state instead of fresh
body:
## Summary

Staleness checks now say *what* they could establish — `current`, `behind`, `diverged` or `unknown` — instead of collapsing every git failure into "fresh". The new `status` is additive: `isStale` and `commitsBehind` keep their values in every case, and `staleness` stays absent when the index is current.

Fixes #3256.

## Motivation / context

#3256 measured the residual the #3232 tri-review deferred: on a branch-pinned `serve` clone (#3199), a re-index that fails after the `fetch --depth 1` leaves the recorded commit orphaned. `rev-list <idx>..HEAD` counts it correctly while the reflog holds it, then fails once the reflog expires and `gc` prunes it — and the catch reported **fresh** while the index was still behind. `rev-parse HEAD` still answers there and disagrees with the index, which is the rule the Claude hook already uses.

The issue also found `gitnexus group status` printing `STALE (-1 commits behind)`: `group/service.ts` uses `-1` for "no recorded commit" and `?? '?'` never catches it.

## Areas touched

- [x] `gitnexus/` (CLI / core / MCP server)
- [x] `gitnexus-web/` (Vite / React UI) — type of `BackendRepo.staleness` only
- [ ] `.github/` (workflows, actions)
- [ ] `eval/` or other tooling
- [x] Docs / agent config only — one line in `ARCHITECTURE.md`

## Scope & constraints

**In scope**

- `checkStaleness` / `checkStalenessAsync` return `status`. On a `rev-list` failure, one `rev-parse HEAD` separates `diverged` (HEAD resolved, ≠ `lastCommit`) from `unknown` (HEAD unresolvable, not a repo, or no `lastCommit`). The happy path is unchanged.
- A timed-out `rev-list` returns `unknown` straight away rather than probing HEAD, so the #3232 bound on a hung mount is not doubled.
- One payload builder, `stalenessPayload`, used by MCP `list_repos`, the hot read tools (`attachToolStaleness`) and `/api/repos` + `/api/repo`, so one fact has one shape:
  - `behind` → `{ status, commitsBehind, hint }`
  - `diverged` → `{ status, hint }` — no invented count
  - `unknown` → `{ status }` on the listings only (`list_repos`, `/api/repos`, `/api/repo`); **not** on hot read tools, where a `--skip-git` folder would repeat it on every response
- `gitnexus group status` renders a missing count as `?`; rows also carry the shared `status`.

**Explicitly out of scope / not done here**

- `diverged` does **not** set `isStale: true`. That would align core with the hook and `group`, but it flips the pinned fail-open tests; left for a maintainer call (question 3 in #3256).
- The `gitnexus://repo/{name}/context` resource still keys its banner on `isStale && hint`, so it does not show `diverged`. Easy follow-up if wanted.
- No change to how clones fetch (no deepening of the pinned `--depth 1`).

## Implementation notes

- The status type and the payload builder live in a new pure module, `core/staleness-status.ts`, not in `git-staleness.ts`. Five existing unit suites stub `git-staleness.js` with a fixed `vi.mock` factory so nothing shells out; any pure helper exported from that module came back `undefined` under those stubs (115 failures in `calltool-dispatch.test.ts` alone on the first attempt). Splitting keeps every existing mock valid, untouched. `git-staleness.ts` re-exports the types, so existing `StalenessInfo` imports are unaffected.
- `StalenessInfo.status` is optional on the type (both helpers always set it); `stalenessStatus(info)` derives it from `isStale` for hand-built literals.
- The `group status` cell moved to `cli/group-status-format.ts` so it is testable without booting a backend against a real group.

## Testing & verification

- [x] `cd gitnexus && npm run test:unit` (vitest 4.1.11) — 15,291 passed, 41 skipped, 11 failed, none in code this PR touches:
  - 6 in `analyzer-identity.test.ts` / `analyzer-identity-in-process-guards.test.ts` fail identically on unmodified `main` @ `16307a1` on this machine (macOS `/var` vs `/private/var` realpath in the expected `rootPath`).
  - 5 in `hooks.test.ts` (DB owner guard) and `skip-git-cli.test.ts` (30 s spawn timeouts) pass when those files are run on their own; they only failed under full-suite load.
- [x] `cd gitnexus && npm run test:integration` — 302 files / 5,834 tests passed, 0 failed (12 files skipped by their own guards; `server-repo-freshness.test.ts` confirmed running, 3/3)
- [x] `cd gitnexus && npx tsc --noEmit`
- [x] `cd gitnexus-web && npm test` — 41 files / 446 tests
- [x] `cd gitnexus-web && npx tsc -b --noEmit`
- [x] Prettier + ESLint on every changed file (0 errors)
- [x] Manual E2E against the built CLI (isolated `GITNEXUS_HOME`, `serve` on a scratch port), four local repos: one untouched; one two commits past its index; one whose indexed commit was orphaned by a reset and then removed with `reflog expire` + `gc --prune=now`; one analyzed with `--skip-git`:

  | repo | `GET /api/repos` | `GET /api/repo` | `query` tool |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | untouched | absent | absent | absent |
  | 2 commits past | `behind`, `commitsBehind: 2` | same | same |
  | indexed commit pruned | `diverged`, hint, no count | same | same |
  | `--skip-git` | `unknown` | `unknown` | absent (by design) |

  Before this change the last two rows both read as fresh.

Rebased onto `main` @ `0edf9ce` (three ingestion-only commits; none touch these files) and re-verified there: `tsc` for both packages, the staleness / mock-stub / group suites (69 files, 1,598 tests), `server-repo-freshness`, and the E2E above — all unchanged.

New tests:

- `staleness.test.ts` — both helpers, parametrized: `current`, `behind` (count 2), `diverged`, `unknown` (non-git path, empty `lastCommit`). Plus a real `--depth 1` `file://` clone: the pinned fetch + `checkout -B` path reads `behind`, then `diverged` after `reflog expire` + `gc`; the unpinned `pull --ff-only` path stays `behind 1`. The four existing fail-open tests are unmodified.
- `tool-staleness.test.ts` — `behind` is labelled, `diverged` has no count, `unknown` is not attached, `current` untouched.
- `repo-projection.test.ts` — `diverged` and `unknown` on the HTTP routes.
- `cli-group-status-format.test.ts` — `-1` and missing render as `?`; counted and `OK` cells byte-identical.

## Risk & rollout

Additive. Consumers that read `isStale` / `commitsBehind` see identical values. Two visible changes, both intended by #3256: `staleness` can now be present with `status: 'diverged'` and no `commitsBehind`; and listings carry `{ status: 'unknown' }` for a repo that cannot be measured (previously absent). No index refresh needed; no new env var.

`gitnexus detect-changes --scope all` rates this **critical**, and that rating is about how widely `LocalBackend.listRepos` is used, not a code path that breaks: it has 28 upstream dependants (MCP stdio + HTTP servers, `eval-server`, the MCP resources, repository policy, every CLI read tool), and `attachToolStaleness` is HIGH (11, all via `callTool`). I checked the consumers: nothing in `gitnexus/src`, `gitnexus-web/src`, the hooks or the plugin skills reads `staleness.commitsBehind` / `.hint` off a listing or treats a listing's `staleness` as a boolean, and `getReposResource` / `getSetupResource` do not render it. The only consumers affected are external MCP / HTTP clients that treat "`staleness` present" as "behind", which is the change this PR intends to make.

## Checklist

- [x] PR body meets repo minimum length
- [ ] If `AGENTS.md` / overlays changed — n/a
- [x] No secrets, tokens, or machine-specific paths committed

title: fix(embeddings): fail closed on foreign identity and vector-width drift in embeddings sync
body:
## Summary

Follow-up fixes for `gitnexus embeddings sync` and the HTTP embedding client, from a code review of the post-merge work on #3065. Two are fail-closed refusals for paths that silently corrupted an existing index; the rest are a config-parsing fix, one write-path extraction, and coverage for contracts that had none.

## Motivation / context

`embeddings sync` writes vectors into an index it did not create, so each guard it skipped was a way to damage someone's existing index.

- **The identity gate exempted `unverified-count` checkpoints.** `decideEmbeddingResume` abandons that kind *before* it compares identity, so the exemption was the only thing stopping a changed provider/model from filling the remaining holes beside the old model's vectors — two vector spaces in one `CodeEmbedding` table, checkpoint cleared, index reported healthy. `CodeEmbedding` rows carry no model column, so the mix is undetectable afterwards. The regression test added with that carve-out asserted the permissive run *succeeds*, encoding the behaviour as intended.
- **The command never read `meta.embeddingDims`.** The vector column is `FLOAT[N]` fixed at index creation, and the pipeline deletes each batch's stale rows immediately before inserting the replacements — so pointing GitNexus at an endpoint of a different width deleted rows it then could not re-insert, aborting mid-run on a raw LadybugDB type error. `analyze` forces a full rebuild on exactly this mismatch (`run-analyze.ts:1678`) and the MCP query path refuses on it; only `sync` did neither. The HTTP client's own dimension check does not cover it, because it compares against the env width rather than the column's recorded width.
- **`GITNEXUS_EMBEDDING_RETRY_TIMEOUTS` was parsed by an integer parser that throws on any non-digit**, so the conventional `=true` did not enable the flag and did not fall back to the documented default — it hard-failed every embedding call through `readConfig()`.

## Areas touched

- [x] `gitnexus/` (CLI / core / MCP server)
- [ ] `gitnexus-web/` (Vite / React UI)
- [ ] `.github/` (workflows, actions)
- [ ] `eval/` or other tooling
- [x] Docs — one README environment-variable row

## Change

- `embeddings-sync.ts` — the identity refusal now covers every checkpoint kind; the `unverified-count` carve-out is gone.
- `embeddings-sync.ts` — new `embeddingDimsMismatch(meta.embeddingDims, EMBEDDING_DIMS)` refusal before `initLbug`, reusing the helper `analyze` already guards with. An absent recorded width stays a non-mismatch, per that helper's contract.
- `http-client.ts` — the retry-timeouts flag parses through the repo's `parseTruthyEnv` (`1`/`true`/`yes`), so unrecognized values fall back to the documented default instead of throwing. README names the accepted spellings.
- `embeddings-sync.ts` — one `persistMeta` write path replaces three inlined metadata read-modify-writes. #2790 traced two production drifts to hand-copied writers of these exact fields.
- Tests (5 new) — the pipeline mock now invokes `onCheckpointWindowStart`/`onCheckpoint`, so the checkpoint/resume contract this feature exists for executes under test for the first time; plus the incomplete-index refusal, the vector-width refusal, the partial-checkpoint branch, and the body-read timeout retry site that the existing opt-in test never reached.

## Verification

- `npx tsc --noEmit` — clean
- `npx vitest run test/unit/embeddings-sync-command.test.ts test/unit/http-embedder.test.ts test/unit/cli-index-help.test.ts` — 99 passed (was 94)
- `npx prettier --check` — clean on all changed files

## Open question for maintainers (deliberately not fixed here)

The identity gate still sits inside `if (meta.embeddingCheckpoint)`, and a clean `analyze --embeddings` deletes that checkpoint. So on the command's headline case — a healthy index with holes — a **same-width** model swap still mixes vector spaces with no gate at all. This PR closes the sibling door (the `unverified-count` exemption); this one predates the command and `POST /api/embed` shares it, so it wants a decision rather than a drive-by patch:

1. Stamp the resolved identity into `RepoMeta` on every successful run and compare it unconditionally, treating an absent stamp as permitted (mirrors the `embeddingDims` absence precedent), and apply the same stamp-and-compare at `server/api.ts:1835` so the two in-place top-up paths cannot disagree.
2. As above, plus a `--allow-identity-change` escape hatch if you want refusal to be the default for unstamped indexes.
3. Accept the gap and drop the fail-closed claim from the comment at `embeddings-sync.ts:71-73`, so the code and its stated rule agree.

Happy to implement whichever you prefer.

title: MCP tools silently ignore unknown arguments: `depth` instead of `maxDepth` returns 200 OK with plausible but wrong results
body:
## Summary

MCP tool arguments that are **not** in a tool's `inputSchema` are **silently ignored**: the call returns
`200 OK` with a valid JSON-RPC result computed from the server's **default** value for the argument the
caller *thought* they were setting. There is no error, no warning, and no way for a client to notice.

## Where it bit me

The `impact` tool declares **`maxDepth`** (`"Max relationship depth (default: 3, server clamps to 1–32)"`).
I called it with **`depth`** — a plausible name that does not exist — and got a perfectly well-formed
response. I built on it for a while before noticing the numbers were wrong.

Same symbol, same `direction`, varying only the depth control:

| arguments sent | levels returned | symbols returned |
|---|---|---|
| `depth: 1` (not a real key) | 1, 2, 3 | 47 |
| `depth: 2` (not a real key) | 1, 2, 3 | 47 |
| `depth: 3` (not a real key) | 1, 2, 3 | 47 |
| `maxDepth: 1` | 1 | 5 |
| `maxDepth: 2` | 1, 2 | 42 |
| `maxDepth: 3` | 1, 2, 3 | 47 |

The three `depth: *` calls are **byte-identical** — which is the only clue that the key is being dropped.
I initially concluded that the **CLI** (`gitnexus impact --depth n`, which honours it: 5 / 42 / 47) and the
**MCP service** disagreed about depth semantics, i.e. that the two code paths diverged. They do not: the
argument simply never arrived.

## Why this is worth reporting

* **It is invisible by construction.** Varying an argument's *value* cannot reveal that the *key* is
  unknown. The only way to find it is to enumerate `inputSchema` — which a client has no reason to do when
  its call succeeds and returns plausible data.
* **API contracts are the wrong place to be permissive.** For a code-intelligence tool, a silently
  different traversal depth means silently different blast-radius answers — here a 42-vs-47 file
  difference, i.e. five files whose callers would not be warned about an incoming change.
* **Any client is exposed**, not just mine. This is the kind of defect every MCP consumer will hit once.

## Suggested fix

Either is fine, and I would argue for the first:

1. **Fail closed** — reject unknown top-level keys in `arguments` with a JSON-RPC error naming the
   offending key. Cheap, and it makes the schema the actual contract.
2. **Report, don't reject** — return normally but include the ignored keys in the payload
   (e.g. `"ignoredArguments": ["depth"]`), so a caller can see it in logs.

A discriminated `oneOf`/`additionalProperties: false` in the tool schema would also let clients validate
before sending.

## Environment

* `gitnexus` **1.6.11** (current latest at the time of writing)
* transport: MCP **streamable HTTP**, local `serve`
* tool: `impact` (the pattern looks general to the tool layer, not specific to this tool)

## Reproduction (no private data)

```
POST /api/mcp
  initialize → notifications/initialized → tools/call

tools/call { "name": "impact",
             "arguments": { "target": "<some symbol>", "repo": "<indexed repo>",
                            "direction": "downstream", "depth": 2 } }
  → 200, levels 1..3 returned        # `depth` ignored

tools/call { "name": "impact",
             "arguments": { "target": "<some symbol>", "repo": "<indexed repo>",
                            "direction": "downstream", "maxDepth": 2 } }
  → 200, levels 1..2 returned        # honoured
```

Compare with the CLI, which does honour it: `gitnexus impact <symbol> -r <repo> --depth 2`.

---

*Unrelated, but found while measuring this:* the MCP `impact` payload is valid JSON followed by a
markdown footer (`---\n**Next:** Review d=1 items first (WILL BREAK)…`). `json.loads()` on the text
block fails with `Extra data`, so a client that parses the block naively loses the entire response. Not a
bug in itself — just worth documenting in the tool output contract, since it is not obvious from the
schema.

title: bug(swift): nested constructor in extension resolves to unrelated top-level type
body:
### Area

gitnexus (CLI / core / indexing / MCP server)

### Summary

An unqualified nested Swift constructor inside an extension is resolved to an unrelated top-level type with the same short name, creating a false `CALLS` edge.

### Context

The standalone example below uses three Swift files and no dependencies. It reproduces with a freshly created index; `gitnexus status` reports that the index matches all three files and the current commit.

### Expected behavior

Within `extension Container`, `Entry(id:text:)` resolves to `Container.Entry` from `Types.swift`. `makeEntry` should have no call edge to the top-level `Entry` in `Standalone.swift`.

The Swift compiler accepts both the complete example and `Types.swift` plus `Builder.swift` alone. The unrelated top-level type has a different memberwise initializer (`enabled:`).

### Actual behavior

`context makeEntry` reports a call to `Struct:Standalone.swift:Entry`. Context for that unrelated type reports `makeEntry` as an incoming caller. Upstream impact reports one direct dependency through the same false edge, with confidence `0.85` and `epistemic: "exact"`.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Create a new directory containing these three files.

`Standalone.swift`:

```swift
struct Entry {
    let enabled: Bool
}
```

`Types.swift`:

```swift
struct Container {
    struct Entry {
        let id: Int
        let text: String
    }
}
```

`Builder.swift`:

```swift
extension Container {
    static func makeEntry() -> Entry {
        Entry(id: 1, text: "sample")
    }
}
```

2. Initialize a Git repository, commit the example, and check Swift's resolution:

```sh
git init
git add Standalone.swift Types.swift Builder.swift
git commit -m "Add Swift scope reproduction"
swiftc -typecheck Standalone.swift Types.swift Builder.swift
swiftc -typecheck Types.swift Builder.swift
```

Both type checks pass.

3. Build a fresh GitNexus index and query it from that directory:

```sh
gitnexus analyze --index-only .
gitnexus status
gitnexus context makeEntry --file Builder.swift --repo "$PWD"
gitnexus context Entry --file Standalone.swift --content --repo "$PWD"
gitnexus impact Entry --file Standalone.swift --direction upstream --depth 1 --repo "$PWD"
```

4. Observe the incorrect edge from `Container.makeEntry` to the top-level `Entry`.

### Environment

- GitNexus: 1.6.11
- Node.js: v26.8.2
- OS: macOS 26.6.2, arm64
- Swift compiler: Apple Swift 6.3.3
- Index: freshly generated from the three-file example; status reports current commit and matching file contents

### Logs / screenshots

Relevant excerpt from `context makeEntry` for the standalone example:

```json
{
  "epistemic": "exact",
  "outgoing": {
    "calls": [
      {
        "uid": "Struct:Standalone.swift:Entry",
        "name": "Entry",
        "filePath": "Standalone.swift"
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

This makes the unrelated top-level type appear to have a caller and makes its impact result incorrect.

title: Non-integer depth empties impact, defaults trace
body:
## Problem

A schema-legal `depth` such as `0.5` is folded onto `maxDepth`. Local callgraph impact then runs zero BFS hops (looks like no dependents) while local trace silently falls back to 10 hops and group impact/trace keep the fraction. Same MCP key, disagreeing outcomes, including a shallow blast-radius that can be misread as safe-to-edit.

This is leftover value-domain enforcement from #3261 (keys fail closed; numeric range/type beyond the `0` omitted sentinel was deferred).

## Suggested fix

After the literal-0 sentinel in `foldNumericToolArgumentAliases`, reject non-integers and values outside the advertised `maxDepth` minimum/maximum (`Number.isInteger(value) && value >= 1 && value <= cap`) instead of writing them through. Keep `0` as the omitted adapter sentinel.

## Evidence

- `gitnexus/src/mcp/tool-arguments.ts:148-155` accepts any non-NaN number except `0`.
- Local impact uses `params.maxDepth || 3` then `for (let depth = 1; depth <= maxDepth`.
- Local trace uses `Number.isInteger(params.maxDepth) && maxDepth > 0 ? params.maxDepth : DEFAULT_TRACE_DEPTH`.

## Source

Branch: `fix/issue-3261-mcp-unknown-args`
Head: `8d3373dd2`

## Metadata

- Severity: P2
- Confidence: 75
- Reviewer(s): adversarial
