title: fix(group): skip Python test doubles named like gRPC stubs
body:
## Summary

The Python gRPC scanner took every call to a name ending in `Stub` as a gRPC client. Test doubles are often named that way (`_CollectionStub`, `SessionRepoStub`), so `group sync` registered them as consumer contracts such as `grpc::_Collection/*`. That is the report in #1186.

With this PR, a `XxxStub(...)` call is a consumer only when:

- the file imports gRPC: the `grpc` or `grpclib` package, or a generated module (`auth_pb2_grpc`, or `auth_grpc` from grpclib), at top level or inside a function;
- and `XxxStub` is not a class the same file defines, unless the call goes through a name a gRPC import binds (`rpc.AuthServiceStub(channel)`), or the class extends the generated stub of its own name (`class UserServiceStub(users_pb2_grpc.UserServiceStub)`).

I checked it with the real CLI (`analyze`, `group create`, `group add`, `group sync`), run from the sources of `main` (302969291) and of this branch, on one repository with four test files and six clients:

| file | call | `main` | this branch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `tests/services/test_session_rule_service_purge.py` | `_CollectionStub()`, class defined in the test | `grpc::_Collection/*` | none |
| `tests/scripts/test_migration_purge_pre_fix_orphans.py` | `_CandidateRepoStub()`, `_MessageRepoStub()` | `grpc::_CandidateRepo/*`, `grpc::_MessageRepo/*` | none |
| `tests/services/test_session_service.py` | `SessionRepoStub()`, imported from `tests.fakes` | `grpc::SessionRepo/*` | none |
| `tests/clients/test_auth_client.py` | `_AuthServiceStub()`, class defined in a test that imports `grpc` | `grpc::_AuthService/*` | none |
| `app/clients/auth.py` | `auth_pb2_grpc.AuthServiceStub(channel)` | `grpc::AuthService/*` | the same |
| `app/clients/orders.py` | `OrderServiceStub(channel)`, from `proto.orders_pb2_grpc`, channel passed in | `grpc::OrderService/*` | the same |
| `app/clients/billing.py` | `rpc.BillingServiceStub(channel)`, `import proto.billing_pb2_grpc as rpc` | `grpc::BillingService/*` | the same |
| `app/clients/search.py` | `from grpc import aio`, `from . import search_pb2_grpc` | `grpc::SearchService/*` | the same |
| `app/clients/greeter.py` | grpclib channel, `from .helloworld_grpc import GreeterStub` | `grpc::Greeter/*` | the same |
| `app/clients/users.py` | `import grpc` and `users_pb2_grpc` inside the function | `grpc::UserService/*` | the same |

`group sync` wrote 11 unmatched contracts on `main` and 6 on this branch.

The review follow-ups, checked with the real `GrpcExtractor` on `main`, on the first commit of this PR (275702494) and on this branch, then with `group sync` on this branch (4 contracts, the first four rows):

| file | `main` | 275702494 | this branch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `rpc.AuthServiceStub(channel)` next to a `class AuthServiceStub:` | `grpc::AuthService/*` | none | `grpc::AuthService/*` |
| a `BillingServiceStub` facade over `billing_pb2_grpc.BillingServiceStub(channel)` | `grpc::BillingService/*` | none | `grpc::BillingService/*` |
| `class UserServiceStub(users_pb2_grpc.UserServiceStub)`, then `UserServiceStub(...)` | `grpc::UserService/*` | none | `grpc::UserService/*` |
| `from . import search_pb2_grpc` as the only gRPC import | `grpc::SearchService/*` | the same | the same |
| betterproto, `from .lib.helloworld import GreeterStub` and nothing else | `grpc::Greeter/*` | none | none (see below) |
| a test's `class FakeOrderServiceStub(orders_pb2_grpc.OrderServiceStub)` | `grpc::FakeOrderService/*` | none | none |
| `_CollectionStub()` | `grpc::_Collection/*` | none | none |
| `self._RepoStub()` in a test that imports `grpc` | `grpc::_Repo/*` | none | none |

## Motivation / context

Fixes #1186. In the reporter's 7-repository group, 36 of the 45 gRPC consumer contracts came from such test doubles. They also crowd the unmatched list that `group sync` prints. The issue suggests requiring a `grpc` or `_pb2_grpc` import; this PR does that, and also covers the test of a real gRPC client, which imports `grpc` and defines its own fake stub.

## Areas touched

- [x] `gitnexus/` (CLI / core / MCP server)
- [ ] `gitnexus-web/` (Vite / React UI)
- [ ] `.github/` (workflows, actions)
- [ ] `eval/` or other tooling
- [ ] Docs / agent config only (`AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.cursor/`, `llms.txt`, etc.)

## Scope & constraints

**In scope**

- `grpc-patterns/python.ts`, consumer detection only: the import check and the class check above.

**Explicitly out of scope / not done here**

- Python providers (`add_XxxServicer_to_server(...)`): unchanged. That name is specific to generated code.
- Skipping `tests/` folders, which the issue mentions as an option. A test can call a real stub, and the two checks already drop the doubles.
- Go, Java and Node scanners: unchanged.
- Cases that `main` already gets wrong, left for a follow-up: a test double imported from a helper in a test that also imports `grpc` (for `StatusCode`, say), an import check that accepts a gRPC part anywhere in a name (`configure_grpc`, `tests.grpc.fakes`), and `google.api_core`'s `ChannelStub`.

## Implementation notes

- Imports are read once per file, and only when a call is named like a stub, so files without such a call cost the same as before. The file's classes are read only after the imports show gRPC, and only for a call that does not go through a gRPC module.
- The names a gRPC import binds: `rpc` in `import a.x_pb2_grpc as rpc`, `a` in `import a.x_pb2_grpc`, `x_pb2_grpc` in `from a import x_pb2_grpc`, and every name imported from a gRPC module. A call's receiver is checked by its leftmost name, so `self._RepoStub()` still goes through the class check.
- Two cases change on purpose. A file that calls a stub imported from a module with no gRPC part in its name, and imports nothing else from gRPC, no longer gives a contract: a re-export (`from app.clients import AuthServiceStub`), or a betterproto package with the channel passed in. Such a file usually opens its channel with `grpc` or `grpclib`, or imports the generated module; that is the trade the issue asks for, and a test pins the betterproto case.

title: fix(analyze): enforce parser-worker heap caps and stop charging workers the main heap
body:
## Summary `analyze` admission charges every parse worker the full main heap, because Node's process-wide `--max-old-space-size` overrides a Worker's `resourceLimits`. This PR makes the worker cap real and then charges each worker its own cap. The automatic main heap in a 10 GiB / 4-CPU container goes from 2639 MiB to 4206 MiB, and from 4300 to 6850 MiB at 16 GiB. The admission sweep below found no newly rejected configurations. ## Motivation / context Since #3829 / #3842, `resolveAnalysisResourceBudget` sizes the automatic main heap as roughly `(total - fixed) / (workers + 1)`, capped at `0.35 * total`, and charges each worker `max(mainHeap, workerHeap) + 128`. The code comment gives the reason: the main process's heap flag overrides `resourceLimits.maxOldGenerationSizeMb`. That is true. Measured on Node 22.22.3 and 26.0.0: under `--max-old-space-size=3000` a worker capped at 512 MiB reports a 3048 MiB `heap_size_limit` and grows past 2.5 GB. The main heap peaks in scope resolution and graph build, after the parse workers have exited. The policy still holds a main-sized heap per worker for the whole run. In a 10 GiB container the main heap gets about 26% of RAM. A large single-language Kotlin/Android monorepo that indexed before #3829 now dies with `Ineffective mark-compacts near heap limit` at the start of scope resolution, with most of the container unused. An explicit `--memory-budget` cannot help: in that container admission rejects any main heap above 2639 MiB (`--memory-budget 2640` -> "requires at least 7682 MiB"). ## Implementation - The parser pool starts each worker with an old-space cap and a 96 MiB young generation. Node 24.19.0 gave a 512 MiB worker a 704 MiB heap with the implicit young generation. The explicit setting gave it 608 MiB, within the 640 MiB reservation. - A short-lived lease clears the old-space, semi-space and combined heap-size flags while Node creates a parser worker. When the process has frozen flags that would need clearing, or the parsed limits contradict the live V8 heap, it skips the lease. Initial workers and replacements use the same factory. A synchronous restore immediately after the constructor leaked the main limit into 43/160 workers on Node 22 and 58/160 on Node 26. Waiting for startup gave 0/160 in the author's runs. - Admission reserves the supervisor, pools, queues, headroom and minimum requested parser concurrency first. The main heap gets the remaining space up to 16,384 MiB. Automatic worker count and heap size share the remaining parser budget. Each worker is charged its admitted old-space size plus 128 MiB. If the lease cannot enforce that cap, admission reserves at least the main-heap allocation for each worker, plus the allowance. - A PDG build with an explicit total of at most 6 GiB uses a single native database writer when the operator selects automatic workers or requests one. The graph-writing child also runs the parse pool. It receives the two-arena glibc default even when automatic sizing admits several parser workers. Operator-supplied allocator settings take precedence. - Graphology and Icebug start after the parser pool exits. They start under the original flags unless a parser worker has already used the lease. Their heaps fall outside the parser and embedding reservations. ## Admission before / after 4 CPUs, 200 MiB supervisor, no embeddings, default env (`resolveAnalysisResourceBudget`). Each cell is main heap MiB / parse workers × worker heap MiB. | Container | workers | before | after | |---|---|---|---| | 4 GiB | auto | 957 / 1 × 958 | **1403** / 1 × 512 | | 10 GiB | auto | 2639 / 1 × 2639 | **4206** / 1 × 1072 | | 16 GiB | auto | 4300 / 1 × 4300 | **6850** / 3 × 512 | | 16 GiB | 1 | 4300 / 1 × 4300 | **6850** / 1 × 1792 | | 64 GiB, 16 CPUs | auto | 16384 / 1 × 16384 | 16384 / 15 × 1376 | `parse.reservedBytes` is unchanged at 4 and 10 GiB (3072 / 7680 MiB) and goes from 12246 to 12288 MiB at 16 GiB, always within the 75% total: the split changes, not the envelope. A sweep of 774,144 request combinations (RAM, CPUs, explicit total, main heap, workers, worker heap, local model, parsing on/off, heap-limit ceiling, supervisor) compared `upstream/main` with this branch: | Check | Count | |---|---| | newly rejected | 0 | | main heap decreased | 0 | | reservation above total | 0 | | previously rejected, now admitted | 13,512 | For `isConstrainedPdgBuild`, a sweep of 158,826 admitted requests gave: - 0 configurations lose the guard; - 1,920 gain it. These are explicit small budgets where `upstream/main` happened to fit two automatic workers. These runs use serial graph writes. The constrained child also defaults to two glibc arenas for a multi-worker parse, with operator allocator settings taking precedence. ## Testing & verification Validation on `3c70364a0` passed 300 focused tests on Node 22.23.3 and all 38 real-worker cases on Node 24.19.0 and 26.13.1. The test-only follow-up `14d14cbc6` passed 301 focused tests on Node 22 and all 39 real-worker cases on Node 24 and 26. Production and test TypeScript checks passed. The heap-reset cases also passed with Node reporting 3 GiB of RAM, and all 54 respawn cases passed with a simulated 64 KiB page-size probe. On the earlier head `a7691f8cd`, 401 tests passed across admission, worker startup, community detection, watch, embedding sync, auto-sync and CLI launch on Node 22.23.3. All eight real-worker tests also passed on Node 24.19.0 and 26.13.1. Production and test TypeScript checks, ESLint, formatting and the 26 shared-language-boundary tests passed. A full run stopped after six incremental-indexing failures. The eight-case rerun covering all six passed on both revisions used for that comparison. CI results are listed in the PR checks. Two cold runs per allocator setting on Node 22.23.3 indexed the same 210 TypeScript files with PDG enabled, four parser workers, a 6,144 MiB total budget and a 1,200 MiB main heap. From first dispatch to last completed chunk, the host defaults took 14.36 and 17.90 seconds. Two glibc arenas took 19.44 and 20.15 seconds. All four runs produced 39,972 nodes and 119,734 edges. The shared host was under load. The author’s separate 2,448-file Kotlin run measured cgroup peak memory as well. Three workers with two arenas parsed in 30–34 s at about 3,050 MiB peak. Allocator defaults took about 27 s at a peak around 480 MiB higher. - [x] `cd gitnexus && npx vitest run` on the admission, host-resources, analyze-admission, worker-heap-limit, worker-pool-resource-limits, watch, embeddings-sync, auto-sync and analyze-launch unit files: 198/198. - [x] `cd gitnexus && npm run build && npx vitest run test/integration/worker-pool-admission.test.ts`: 5/5 on Node 22.22.3. The enforcement cases also pass on Node 26.0.0. - [x] `npx tsc --noEmit`, `npm run typecheck:tests`, plus eslint and prettier on the changed files. - [ ] Full-suite status is tracked in the PR checks. The earlier local run and its focused rerun are recorded above. **Differential.** The new and updated tests also ran against `upstream/main` sources. Results there: - the enforcement test fails: a 512 MiB worker reports 3384 MiB; - the cap-exceeding test fails: the worker inherits about 3 GiB, never dies, and nothing is quarantined; - the admission pins fail (957/2639/4300 instead of 1403/4206/6850); - the 4206 / 4207 MiB boundary fails (base requires 10814 MiB for 4206). **End to end in a real cgroup.** A synthetic 4,080-file Kotlin repo (generator below) was run with `podman run --memory=6g --memory-swap=6g --cpus=4` and with `--memory=16g`. Node 22, linux/arm64, 4 KiB pages, no `--memory-budget`, two interleaved rounds: | Run | Result | Main heap limit | Parse workers × heap limit | Parse phase | Container `memory.peak` | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | `upstream/main`, 6g | **exit 1**, V8 heap OOM in scope resolution (2/2) | 1520 | 1 × 1520 | 182–195 s | 1.9 GiB | | this branch, 6g | exit 0 (2/2), identical graph | 2451 | 1 × 640 | 203–208 s | 3.6 GiB (80% of the 4.5 GiB admitted) | | `upstream/main`, 16g | exit 0 | 4300 | 1 × 4300 | 134–192 s | 3.8 GiB | | this branch, 16g | exit 0, identical graph (190,080 nodes / 400,240 edges) | 6855 | 3 × 560 | **80–85 s** | 3.8 GiB | Across all runs: no kernel OOM kill (`OOMKilled=false`, `oom_kill 0`), no worker deaths, no quarantined files. At 6g both versions run one worker, and the branch's parse phase was 6–12% slower there (its worker has a 640 MiB limit instead of 1520). The host was loaded (load average 23–34), and on macOS the same comparison went the other way in a quiet round, so this is not settled. A 7,978-file mostly-TypeScript corpus analyzed with `--pdg --workers 3 GITNEXUS_WORKER_HEAP_MB=512` had 0 worker deaths.
Fixture generator (node gen-kotlin.mjs <out> 40 100) ```js // Synthetic single-language Kotlin monorepo: N modules x M files, each file a class // that implements a shared interface, imports and calls classes in sibling modules. import fs from 'node:fs'; import path from 'node:path'; const [out, modulesArg = '40', filesArg = '100'] = process.argv.slice(2); const modules = Number(modulesArg), files = Number(filesArg); fs.rmSync(out, { recursive: true, force: true }); for (let m = 0; m < modules; m++) { const pkg = `com.example.m${m}`; const dir = path.join(out, `module${m}`, 'src/main/kotlin', ...pkg.split('.')); fs.mkdirSync(dir, { recursive: true }); fs.writeFileSync(path.join(out, `module${m}`, 'build.gradle.kts'), `plugins { kotlin("jvm") }\n`); fs.writeFileSync(path.join(dir, 'Api.kt'), `package ${pkg}\n\ninterface Api${m} {\n fun handle(input: String): String\n fun size(): Int\n}\n`); for (let f = 0; f < files; f++) { const deps = [1, 2, 3].map((d) => ({ m: (m + d) % modules, f: (f * 7 + d) % files })); const imports = deps.map((d) => `import com.example.m${d.m}.Service${d.m}x${d.f}`).join('\n'); const fields = deps.map((d, i) => ` private val dep${i} = Service${d.m}x${d.f}()`).join('\n'); const methods = Array.from({ length: 12 }, (_, k) => ` fun op${k}(value: Int): Int {\n var acc = value\n for (i in 0 until ${k + 2}) {\n acc = if (acc % 2 == 0) dep${k % 3}.size() + acc else acc - i\n }\n return acc + helper${k % 4}(acc)\n }`).join('\n\n'); const helpers = Array.from({ length: 4 }, (_, k) => ` private fun helper${k}(x: Int): Int = x * ${k + 1} + dep${k % 3}.handle("v$x").length`).join('\n'); fs.writeFileSync(path.join(dir, `Service${m}x${f}.kt`), `package ${pkg}\n\n${imports}\n\ndata class Payload${m}x${f}(val id: Int, val name: String)\n\nclass Service${m}x${f} : Api${m} {\n${fields}\n\n override fun handle(input: String): String = dep0.handle(input) + dep1.size()\n\n override fun size(): Int = ${f}\n\n${methods}\n\n${helpers}\n}\n`); } } console.log(`generated ${modules * (files + 1)} Kotlin files in ${out}`); ```
## Areas touched - [x] `gitnexus/` (CLI / core / MCP server) - [x] Docs (`README`, `RUNBOOK.md`, `MIGRATION.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `docs/cli-reference.md`) ## Risk & rollout - **Parser workers are now really capped.** On `upstream/main` every respawned `analyze` gave workers the main heap by accident. The minimum admitted old-space cap is 512 MiB. The automatic value depends on how much memory the workers share. A worker that exceeds it dies, and its in-flight file is quarantined with `worker hit its N MB heap cap — raise with GITNEXUS_WORKER_HEAP_MB`. - With the default 512 KiB `--max-file-size` and derived sub-batch size, no deaths were seen. - A single generated file above roughly 2 MB, allowed by a raised `--max-file-size`, or a large explicit `GITNEXUS_WORKER_SUB_BATCH_MAX_BYTES`, can exceed 512 MiB. README and MIGRATION now say to raise `GITNEXUS_WORKER_HEAP_MB` together with those knobs. - **`v8.setFlagsFromString` after startup.** Node documents runtime flag changes as possibly undefined behaviour. V8 reads the heap-sizing flags at isolate creation. It was exercised over 900+ spawns on Node 22 and 26, and the main isolate's `heap_size_limit` never changed. The codebase already toggles `--expose-gc` this way. If a future Node stops honouring this, the integration enforcement test fails. - **Process-global window.** While a parser worker is starting, any other Worker created in the same process would get V8's default heap. A user preload calling `module.register()` can start a loader isolate during this window. On Node 22.23.3 the probe measured a 4,144 MiB loader heap under the lease and 1,648 MiB with the original flags. Preload isolate heaps are outside admission. - The persisted index schema is unchanged. Changes under `core/ingestion` affect parser identity, so the next analysis rebuilds cached parse output. Subprocess coverage includes quoted sizes, explicit zeros, percentage restoration, combined heap limits, and frozen flags. With a combined heap limit alone, the parser cap is enforced and a later ordinary worker regains the original total. A community worker started through the lease can have an additional default young generation because V8 does not expose that limit’s split. A preload can also change V8 flags or delete `NODE_OPTIONS` without leaving a detectable inconsistency. ## Scope & constraints **Explicitly out of scope / follow-ups** - **Worker cap vs file size.** The automatic worker cap is not coupled to `--max-file-size`; admission does not receive the file-size limit today. - **Community-detection worker.** Graphology and Icebug use inherited heap settings. Neither worker has a separate admission reservation. Sizing them requires a peak-heap measurement on a representative large graph. - **Vector pool and embedding queues.** They are reserved even when no embeddings run, which is why 10 GiB stops at 4206 MiB rather than about 4.7 GiB. - **The motivating repository.** It needs about 6.85 GB of main heap, which this policy admits from 16 GiB. Fitting it into 10 GiB needs a lower scope-resolution peak (loading a language's parsed files in batches); that is a separate change. - **`--max-old-space-size-percentage`.** It still overrides the respawn's explicit `--max-old-space-size`; this is pre-existing. ## Checklist - [x] PR body meets repo minimum length - [x] No secrets, tokens, or machine-specific paths committed 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- ### 📝 Summary by GitNexus ## Summary *This appears to be a broad TypeScript change to analysis resource budgeting and worker heap management, spanning implementation, tests, and operational documentation. Its blast level is critical, despite the file risk being low.* **🔴 CRITICAL blast radius. This change adjusts parser worker heap caps and analysis heap admission across the GitNexus analysis pipeline, with 33 dependents.** The implementation centers on `gitnexus/src/core/analysis-resource-budget.ts`, the hottest changed file, alongside `gitnexus/src/cli/analyze.ts`, `gitnexus/src/core/analysis-host-resources.ts`, and the ingestion worker files. The graph places impact in `Cli`, `Embeddings`, `Ingestion`, `Pipeline-phases`, `Server`, `Lbug`, `Storage`, `Integration`, `Auto-sync`, and `Workers`. Review the resource budget and admission logic first, especially `resolveHostAnalysisResources`, `manualHeapAdmission`, and `analyzeCommandImpl`, then check the worker heap and pool tests. The change also updates architecture, migration, runbook, and CLI documentation. Review tier: Base · 4m36s · $0.60 **Merge confidence: 3/5** - Review findings need human attention. - Review coverage is incomplete or unverified; confidence is capped at 3. **Since last review** This push appears to be a TypeScript test change in `gitnexus/test/unit/analyze-heap-respawn.test.ts`, with `mockSpawnExit`, `value`, and `pending` changed. No newly reached modules or risk transition were reported. _Added by GitNexus for PR #4045. Edit freely — this block is replaced on the next review, everything above it is left untouched._

title: eval containment: SandboxError raised while the preflight reports 2/2 successful tool results (self-contradictory evidence rejection)
body:
## Symptom

`eval/tests/test_workflow_bench.py::test_all_pinned_proposal_graders` fails with:

```
SandboxError: offline CLI preflight with GitNexus failed: 2/2 successful tool results
```

The message rejects evidence while simultaneously reporting that **all 2/2 preflight tool results succeeded** — classification and outcome are contradictory.

## Evidence

- Run: 45024535499 (`fix/wiki-regroup` @ `2d42b87c`, 2026-11-22), job **137243162244**
- Blast radius: evidence rejected → `test-completeness` red → all six `protected-platform-checks` mirrors red → CI Gate red, on a PR unrelated to eval code.

## Suspected area

SandboxError classification / preflight result aggregation in the eval containment pipeline (proposer sandbox preflight counting vs the failure predicate). Likely an off-by-design check such as `if results != expected_shape` evaluated against a success payload, or a mislabeled branch that treats "preflight completed" as "preflight failed".

## Why file it

Every occurrence turns one unrelated PR fully red with a misleading first error line. Even if low-frequency, the message itself is wrong and costs a log-dive per occurrence.

title: Windows native runners: two real flakes in the 11-20..11-23 window (LadybugDB 0xC0000005 crash + EBUSY unlink node.exe)
body:
## Context

A per-run log audit of 2026-11-20 → 11-23 (100 completed runs) found exactly **2 real native-shard flakes** — everything else called "platform red" was mirror amplification. Both are Windows-native, file/process-layer issues:

## Flake 1 — native binding crash

- `gitnexus/test/integration/incremental-write-integrity.test.ts:321` (real LadybugDB)
- Run 44766674583, job **136422908292**, shard 1/11
- 120s timeout + vitest worker crashed with exit code **3221225477 (0xC0000005 ACCESS_VIOLATION)** — the LadybugDB native binding segfaulted on the Windows runner
- Low-frequency environmental; no ubuntu occurrences in the window

## Flake 2 — EBUSY on temp cleanup

- `gitnexus/test/helpers/claude-hook-launcher.test.ts:564`
- Run 44935862744, job **136946497391**, shard 10/11
- `EBUSY: resource busy or locked, unlink node.exe` while removing the temp dir — child process handle not yet released (or AV scanning lock); shard was 475 passed / 1 killed

## Proposed stopgap (not in this issue's scope to finalize)

1. hook-launcher: retry(3, backoff) around the temp-dir unlink, or ensure child handles are reaped before cleanup.
2. incremental-write-integrity: Windows-only `retry(1)` as a band-aid + keep this issue open for the native-crash root cause (a segfault in the binding is worth its own investigation; retry alone hides a real crash).

Happy to split into two issues if preferred — filed together because both are Windows-native single-occurrence flakes found by the same audit.

title: ci: rename the platform audit mirrors out of the native-shard namespace
body:
## Problem

The six `protected-platform-checks` jobs (ubuntu audit mirrors) render check names **identical in shape** to the native cross-platform shards:

- mirror: `tests / windows-latest (platform-sensitive) 1/3`
- native: `tests / windows-latest (platform-sensitive) 1/11`

We audited every failed run in the 2026-11-20 → 11-23 window (100 completed runs):

| signal | count |
|---|---|
| mirror-job (`N/3`) red | **60 occurrences / 10 runs / 4 days** |
| real native-shard (`N/11`) red | **2** (both Windows-native env flakes) |

→ **~96% of "platform red" was a mirror echoing `test-completeness` (or a downstream producer) through the gate**, not a platform failure. Mirror job logs show it explicitly (`NATIVE_RESULT: success, EXECUTION_RESULT: failure → exit 1`, run 45098222120): native was green, the mirror still went red. Same-shaped names made this look like random platform flake.

## Change

Rename the six mirror display names into their own namespace (no behavior change):

```
- tests / {os} (platform-sensitive) {n}/3          (old, ambiguous)
+ tests / platform-evidence audit: {os} {n}/3      (new, self-describing)
```

- `.github/workflows/ci-tests.yml`: `protected-platform-checks` `name:` + updated comment documenting the audit-mirror role and the rename coordination requirement.
- `eval/tests/test_workflow_bench.py`: `test_platform_ci_preserves_required_check_names_with_complete_execution_gates` expected-name set updated **in the same commit** (the guard enforces `isdisjoint` from native names, which still holds).

Gate semantics untouched: `needs: [cross-platform, test-completeness, scope-resolution-benchmark]`, `if: always()`, `permissions: {}`, single verification step.

## ⚠️ Coordination required at merge time

Branch protection on `main` lists the six mirror names as required status checks. When merging, the six required-check entries must be swapped **atomically**:

| remove | add |
|---|---|
| `tests / windows-latest (platform-sensitive) 1/3` | `tests / platform-evidence audit: windows-latest 1/3` |
| `tests / windows-latest (platform-sensitive) 2/3` | `tests / platform-evidence audit: windows-latest 2/3` |
| `tests / windows-latest (platform-sensitive) 3/3` | `tests / platform-evidence audit: windows-latest 3/3` |
| `tests / macos-latest (platform-sensitive) 1/3` | `tests / platform-evidence audit: macos-latest 1/3` |
| `tests / macos-latest (platform-sensitive) 2/3` | `tests / platform-evidence audit: macos-latest 2/3` |
| `tests / macos-latest (platform-sensitive) 3/3` | `tests / platform-evidence audit: macos-latest 3/3` |

If the old entries are left in place, they never report again and PRs block indefinitely. Native shard required checks (if configured) are unaffected by this PR.

## Verification

- `uv run pytest eval/tests/test_workflow_bench.py eval/tests/test_release_build.py` → **225 passed** (guard spec + workflow changed together).
- Workflow YAML parses; no other references to the old names exist under `.github/` (checked `git grep`).

Related: #4046 (eval SandboxError contradiction), #4047 (Windows native flakes) — same audit, separate deliverables.

title: fix(java): match javac resolution and move fixtures into conformance
body:
## Summary

GitNexus now resolves the Java calls and inheritance relationships that disagreed with javac in the 12 reported projects. Java fixtures run in a dedicated conformance pipeline that compares the production graph with the compiler.

## Motivation / context

Handwritten expectations could agree with an incorrect overload or fail to notice a missing edge. JDK 21 supplies the declaration and source range for each selected call. The comparator reports missing calls, unexpected targets and differences in the published edges. The standalone JSON format also works with other compilers, language servers and analyzers. [Original conformance job](https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/actions/runs/45484605100/job/138766875347) · [Conformance guide](https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/blob/test/java-compiler-conformance/gitnexus/tools/compiler-conformance/README.md)

## Areas touched

- [x] `gitnexus/` CLI, indexing engine and test tools
- [x] `.github/` CI and SonarCloud
- [x] Documentation

## Scope & constraints

The compiler inputs are the fixture sources and JDK 21 with an empty application classpath. GitNexus-specific checks cover Spring, rename, incremental replay, persistence and mixed-language projects in the same Java job. A separate recovery suite includes intentionally invalid projects and pins their expected compiler diagnostics. Dependency JAR indexing and a broader sweep of those recovery projects are outside this change.

## Implementation notes

- Java distinguishes colliding type declarations and variadic overloads. Receiver and argument types guide method and constructor selection, including `super(...)`, method references, SAM lambdas and enhanced `for` loops. Calls into the JDK can identify a library declaration without adding a source node.
- File-backed fixtures, inline Java snippets and virtual projects moved out of Vitest. This covers the former 86-file Java lane and 902 cases from 58 unit suites, including two rename cases. The dedicated native runner preserves product assertions and fails on skipped cases, todos and empty files. The ownership check covers actual Java parser and worker inputs. Windows and macOS run rename, parser ABI, persisted worker-cache and non-ASCII path checks.
- The Java workspace scanner reads import declarations, including static member imports. Apparent imports inside comments and text blocks no longer create dependency links.
- The four performance workflows compare against the first parent of the checkout that GitHub tested. Coverage from the Java job joins the LCOV report for SonarCloud. Vitest retains its own thresholds. The graph benchmarks record Java visibility verified with javac, including package-private declarations and public record accessors.

## Testing & verification

Set `JAVA_HOME` to JDK 21 and run these commands from `gitnexus/`.

```sh
npm run build
npm run test:conformance:java
npm run typecheck:tests
npm test
```

- The primary comparison passes across **135 projects, 483 source call sites, five library call sites and six method references**. This includes 100 generated overload calls. Javac also supplies the public modifier for each explicit source method in projects that compare method declarations. The second pass completes **10,507 compiler and graph checks across 105 projects**. Tests exercise both incorrect and missing target detection.
- The Java job retains 32 Spring and group scenarios. Its five opt-in Spring timing checks run separately from coverage collection.
- From `gitnexus/tools/compiler-conformance/`, run `node java/javac-report.mjs /path/to/fixture > compiler.json` and `node compare.mjs compiler.json analyzer.json` to check another producer.

## Risk & rollout

Java graph IDs can change for same-named nested types and colliding variadic methods or constructors. Refresh an existing index with `gitnexus analyze --force` before comparing saved node IDs or using them for rename. A rollback to an earlier analyzer also needs an index built with that version.

## Checklist

- [x] Includes compiler inputs, validation commands, graph-ID changes and rollout guidance.
- [x] Java regression cases run in compiler conformance.

title: test(java): cover 100 overload conversions and retire the javap count test
body:
## Summary

Follow-up to #4056, based on its conformance branch. The Java CI job now generates every ordered pair of distinct overload parameter types from `long`, `Integer`, `Long`, `Number`, and `Object`. Each pair gets five calls using an int literal, a long literal, an Integer parameter, a Long parameter, and null. Across the 100 generated calls, javac selects a declaration at 98 sites and reports two ambiguities.

The generator records the expected source file and range for each call before either tool runs. CI checks that javac visited those exact sites, then compares each selection and the emitted call graph against GitNexus. The existing fixtures and the generated sources run in a single JVM. The runner removes the temporary sources after each run.

## Test retirement

Remove the integration case that compiled the original overload fixture with javac and counted descriptors in javap output. The conformance job compares all nine calls in that fixture with javac individually. The existing JLS integration assertion still checks the six signatures and their original caller counts.

## Verification

- The original javap case passed before removal. The reference report for the same fixture contained all six overloads with the original counts.
- `npm run test:conformance:java` passed on JDK 21 for all 119 sites across the four fixtures.
- Temporarily making the Java resolver choose the first declared overload produced 51 site mismatches in the generated matrix. Applying the same rule to the original fixture produced three mismatches there.
- Replacing one compiler-reported site with a duplicate of another preserved the totals and failed the independent source-range check.
- The remaining Java overload suites and comparator tests passed (86 tests). TypeScript typecheck, ESLint, and Prettier passed.

title: feat(mcp): classify tools/call errors as client or server faults in _meta
body:
## Summary

Every failed MCP `tools/call` response now carries a machine-readable fault class, `_meta["io.github.abhigyanpatwari.gitnexus/fault"]` = `"client"` or `"server"`. A proxy, gateway or monitor in front of the MCP server can then tell a caller's mistake (bad Cypher, unknown symbol, wrong argument) from an engine, storage or server failure without parsing the response text. Response text and `isError` do not change.

## Motivation / context

Today the `tools/call` handler returns every failure as `{ content: [text], isError: true }`, and several tools (`cypher`, `impact`, `context`, `trace`, `query`, …) return failures as an ordinary result with a top-level `{ error }`. Nothing in the response says who is at fault. A monitor in front of the server must either alert on every error, so one client retrying a bad call in a loop pages on-call, or ignore errors, so a LadybugDB, pool or storage failure goes unnoticed. Engine failures returned as `{ error }` look like successes to anything that only reads `isError`.

## Areas touched

- [x] `gitnexus/` (CLI / core / MCP server)
- [ ] `gitnexus-web/` (Vite / React UI)
- [ ] `.github/` (workflows, actions)
- [ ] `eval/` or other tooling
- [x] Docs / agent config only (`docs/mcp-reference.md`)

## Scope & constraints

**In scope**

- Wire format: `_meta` key on `isError` results and on results with a top-level `error`. Successful results carry no key. `_meta` is the spec's place for extension metadata; the key follows the 2025-11-25 prefix rules; SDK 1.32.2 keeps unknown `_meta` keys on both server and client (covered by tests that go through the real SDK `Client`). `structuredContent` was not used: it is result data, and clients that prefer it would show the model a different payload.
- Classification by origin, never by message text:
  - errors leaving the LadybugDB read pool (`executeParameterized`, `initLbug`, `ensureVectorExtension`) get a non-enumerable `server` mark at the export boundary, so new engine errors are classified without touching a list;
  - argument, policy and repository-resolution rejections are raised as `client` where they are thrown;
  - every `catch` that turns an exception into an `{ error }` result reports the caught error's class into a per-call scope (`AsyncLocalStorage`); a structural guard test fails when a new such `catch` does not report;
  - filesystem errors from a caller-supplied path (`read_file`) are classified by `err.code` (`ENOENT`, `ENOTDIR`, `EISDIR`, `ENAMETOOLONG`, `ELOOP`, `EINVAL`, `ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE` → `client`; anything else → `server`);
  - group mode (bridge DB, `group.yaml`, contracts) follows the same rules, and a group fan-out's class does not depend on which member finishes first.
- Defaults: a thrown error nobody classified is `server` (unexpected failure); an `{ error }` result is `client` unless the tool reported a server fault during the call.
- `cypher`: the statement is the caller's, so errors from preparing or running it, including its timeout, are `client`; failing to get or open the database or load the VECTOR extension stays `server`.
- Argument type check before dispatch: a value whose JSON type does not match a property declared as `string`, `array`, or a union of the two is rejected as `client` (`null` passes through). Unknown tool names (including `constructor`, `toString`) and a non-string `repo` are rejected the same way. These are the only changes to response text; see Risk & rollout.

**Explicitly out of scope / not done here**

- Turning server-class `{ error }` results into `isError: true` (the spec's intent for tool execution errors). The class now makes that possible as a follow-up without guessing.
- A separate `retryable` hint (pool exhausted, timeout, index being rebuilt). Retryability is orthogonal to fault.
- `resources/read` and `prompts/get` errors.
- The memory watchdog exits the process (code 70) and sends no response, so it cannot carry a class; the docs tell proxies to count a closed transport as a server fault.
- `cli/tool.ts` and `cli/eval-server.ts` call the backend directly, outside MCP; they are unchanged.

## Implementation notes

- New module `gitnexus/src/core/fault-class.ts`: `markFault`/`faultOf` (a non-enumerable symbol property, read along the `cause` chain), `clientError`, query-stage marks, and the per-call scope (`createFaultScope`, `reportFault`, `reportCaughtFault`). It depends only on `node:async_hooks`; `core/lbug` does not import anything from `mcp/`.
- The pool-adapter change only adds a mark to the same error object and rethrows it: identity, message, `code`, `cause`, stack, JSON and pino output are unchanged, and the `finally` ordering (connection check-in, memory guard) is untouched. Callers outside MCP never read the mark.
- `server.ts` is the single place that writes `_meta`, so stdio, Streamable HTTP, SSE and `serve /api/mcp` all carry it.
- Known false-`client` cases, documented in `docs/mcp-reference.md`: a storage failure that first surfaces while a caller's `cypher` runs (the same failure is `server` on every other tool), and a failed `git diff` in `detect_changes` (a wrong `base_ref` and a git failure cannot be told apart without parsing stderr).
- Commits are atomic and ordered so each one builds and passes on its own; the `_meta` key becomes visible in `feat(mcp): expose the tool error fault class in tools/call _meta`.

## Testing & verification

- [x] `cd gitnexus && npm test` — full `test:unit` with an isolated `GITNEXUS_HOME` on the final head: 28814 tests. Failures on a heavily loaded machine were timeouts that all pass when their files are re-run on their own (11 files), plus four environment-specific files that fail identically on `main` on the same machine (embedding limit, hook launcher, release docker gate, review-agent workflow).
- [x] `cd gitnexus && npm run test:integration` — fault-class, MCP, LadybugDB pool and group sets: 890 passed.
- [x] `cd gitnexus && npx tsc --noEmit` and `npm run typecheck:tests`
- [ ] `cd gitnexus-web && npm test` *(web not changed)*
- [ ] `cd gitnexus-web && npx tsc -b --noEmit` *(web not changed)*
- [ ] Manual / Playwright E2E *(not applicable)*

New tests (all through the real `tools/call` handler and SDK `Client`; integration cases on a real LadybugDB fixture that inject failures on the native connection, below the pool adapter, so the real marking boundary runs):

- `test/unit/fault-class.test.ts`, `test/unit/lbug-pool-fault-class.test.ts`, `test/unit/mcp-client-fault-marks.test.ts`, `test/unit/mcp-tool-fault-class.test.ts`, `test/unit/group-fault-class.test.ts`, `test/unit/mcp-fault-report-guard.test.ts`, `test/integration/mcp-tool-fault-class.test.ts`.
- Each class is covered: client input (unknown argument, wrong type, read-only denial, Cypher syntax error, write attempt, missing symbol/repository/file) and engine or storage failure (native execute failure whose message deliberately reads like a client error, closed pool, VECTOR extension failure, WAL branch, bridge DB that cannot open, `EIO`/`EACCES` on a file).
- Text compatibility: expected response text is pinned as literals and checked byte-for-byte; `isError` is checked as absent where it was absent.
- Differential run: the feature test files on `main` fail only for class reasons (key missing, module missing, wrong type not rejected) while every text-compatibility test passes on both `main` and this branch.
- Mutation checks: removing any fault report, reverting the group-trace ordering rule, or treating only exceptions as VECTOR failures turns the matching test red.

## Risk & rollout

- **No index, schema or configuration change.** No new settings or flags. Existing clients see one extra `_meta` key on error results; text and `isError` are unchanged for every call except the argument rejections below.
- **Behaviour change — arguments of the wrong JSON type are now rejected (`isError: true`, class `client`).** Calls that used to fail with an internal `TypeError` now get a clear message. The following properties used to accept a wrong-typed value and still return a successful response; they are now rejected:

  | Property | Before |
  |---|---|
  | `query.task_context`, `query.goal`, `query.service` | value ignored |
  | `context.uid`, `context.kind`, `context.service` | value ignored |
  | `detect_changes.scope`, `detect_changes.base_ref` | value ignored |
  | `impact.target_uid`, `impact.direction`, `impact.kind`, `impact.service`, `impact.subgroup` | value ignored |
  | `rename.symbol_uid` | value ignored (preview by `symbol_name`) |
  | `pdg_query.variable` | value ignored |
  | `api_impact.file`, `group_list.name` | value ignored |
  | `explain.target` | value ignored, findings for the whole repository returned |
  | `route_map.route`, `tool_map.tool`, `shape_check.route` | value converted with `String(x)` and used as a filter |

  A caller passing, for example, `impact { direction: 5 }` silently got the default direction; it now learns the argument is wrong. `null`, union types outside `string`/`array`, booleans and numbers are not checked, so values such as `repo: null` or `include_content: "true"` behave as before.
- **Release notes:** "MCP: failed `tools/call` responses carry `_meta["io.github.abhigyanpatwari.gitnexus/fault"]` (`client` | `server`); arguments of the wrong JSON type for string/array properties are rejected as client errors."
- The `_meta` key name is the main API choice here; happy to rename it if the project prefers another prefix.

## Checklist

- [x] PR body meets repo minimum length (workflow may label short descriptions)
- [ ] If `AGENTS.md` / overlays changed: headers, scope block, and changelog updated per project conventions *(not changed)*
- [x] No secrets, tokens, or machine-specific paths committed

title: Claude Code PostToolUse stale-index hint never fires after branch switches (git checkout / switch / reset)
body:
### Area

gitnexus (CLI / core / indexing / MCP server)

### Summary

The Claude Code `PostToolUse` stale-index hint only matches `commit|merge|rebase|cherry-pick|pull`, so after the agent switches branches (`git checkout`, `git switch`) or otherwise moves `HEAD` (`git reset`, `git am`), it never compares `HEAD` against the index and never warns, even when the new branch is unindexed or behind.

### Context

Agents are told to trust `impact` / `detect_changes`, and the hook is the only thing that tells them when the graph has drifted from `HEAD`. Per-branch indexes (`.gitnexus/branches/<slug>`) and the branch-aware lookup in `registry-query.cjs` mean a branch switch is exactly when the index the agent sees changes. But the trigger list in `gitnexus/hooks/claude/git-mutation-command.cjs` doesn't include branch-moving subcommands:

```js
const SUBCOMMAND = String.raw`\s+(?:commit|merge|rebase|cherry-pick|pull)(?=[\s;&|)]|$)`;
```

(Same list in the 1.6.12 npm package's `hooks/claude/gitnexus-hook.cjs`.)

### Expected behavior

Any agent git command that can move `HEAD` triggers the existing cheap check (HEAD vs. the current branch's `lastCommit`), and the hint appears when they differ. At minimum `checkout`, `switch` and `reset`, probably also `am`, `stash pop`/`apply` and `revert`. The `git checkout -- <file>` form only touches files, but running the check is harmless there because HEAD is unchanged.

### Actual behavior

No hint after `git switch -c new-branch`, `git checkout other-branch` or `git reset --hard <older-sha>`. The agent keeps querying an index that doesn't match `HEAD` until the next `commit`/`merge`/`pull`.

### Steps to reproduce

1. `gitnexus setup` (Claude Code hooks: PreToolUse + PostToolUse) and `gitnexus analyze` on the default branch.
2. In Claude Code, have the agent run `git switch -c some-new-branch` (unindexed), or `git reset --hard HEAD~3`.
3. No stale-index hint is emitted. `gitnexus status` / `list_repos` show the index doesn't match `HEAD`.
4. Have the agent run `git commit --allow-empty -m x`. Now the hint appears.

### Environment

- gitnexus 1.6.12 (npm) and `main` as of 2026-11-23; also seen on 1.6.8
- Claude Code, Linux

### Logs / screenshots

N/A. Silent by design (no hint emitted). Related but distinct: #3897 (git global options).

Workaround we use: a small project-level hook that runs the same HEAD-vs-branch-`lastCommit` comparison on `checkout|switch|reset|am` as well. It also runs at `SessionStart` (non-Windows) to catch pulls and switches made outside the agent. Happy to send a PR extending `SUBCOMMAND` if that direction works for you.

title: analyze` hangs forever in the FTS phase: staging DB and WAL frozen, zero CPU, zero I/O, and an `await` that never settles
body:
# `analyze` hangs forever in the FTS phase

## Summary

On a large repository, a **full rebuild** (`gitnexus analyze --force`) reaches the FTS phase and then **stops permanently**:

```
  85% | Creating search indexes... (12h 15m)
```

The process is not slow — it is **frozen**. Every observable counter is flat:

- the staging database file and its WAL have not changed for **21 hours**;
- `/proc/<pid>/io` advances **40 bytes of reads in 12 minutes** and **0 bytes written**;
- the main thread is **0.0% CPU**, all 36 thread-pool threads are blocked, and process RSS does not move by a byte in 30 seconds;
- `process._getActiveRequests()` returns **`[]`** — no libuv request is in flight;
- the event loop is healthy (the 1-second progress-bar timer still fires), so the main thread is idle while **awaiting a promise that will never settle**;
- `pageFaults.IORequired === 0` — **no major faults, so no paging or memory reclaim** is involved.

This has now happened **twice independently** in the same environment, with the **same signature**: only the run that was invoked with `--skip-fts` ever completed.

## Environment

- GitNexus `1.6.13-rc.252` (Docker), also observed on `1.6.13-rc.216`
- `--memory-budget 12288` (analyze child runs with a 12 GB V8 heap)
- Full rebuild into a **staging** database (`buildPath !== lbugPath`, POSIX atomic-swap path)
- 513 parse chunks / ~28.9k files; graph phases complete normally (parse → type resolution → process detection → `Loading into LadybugDB...` at 60% → `Creating search indexes...` at 85%, where it stops)
- The corpus contains a large amount of **CJK text** in identifiers, comments and string literals
- 64 GB host, 64 GB container limit; cgroup memory is **not** constrained (`constrained_memory` reports the unbounded sentinel)

## Reproduction

```bash
gitnexus analyze --force
```

Progress reaches `85% | Creating search indexes...` and never advances. Killing it and re-running reproduces the same stop.

**Two independent occurrences in the same environment:**

| Occurrence | Version | Staging DB size | WAL size | Frozen since | Duration |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `1.6.13-rc.216` | 4,147,929,088 B | **351 B** | `Nov 9 13:13` | 13 h |
| 2 | `1.6.13-rc.252` | 4,167,692,288 B | **349 B** | `Nov 23 13:13` | 21 h |

The only successful full run in that window used `--skip-fts`, which is why the published index records `capabilities.fts.status = "unavailable"`.

## Evidence

All figures below are from the live, frozen process; nothing was killed before collection.

### Filesystem: staging DB and WAL are frozen

```
lbug.generation.<hash>.staging.<uuid>        4167692288  Nov 23 13:13
lbug.generation.<hash>.staging.<uuid>.wal         349  Nov 23 13:13
```

The WAL sitting at ~350 bytes means the last transaction record was written and then **nothing else ever happened** — no checkpoint, no further commit. Both fds (DB + WAL) are still open by the process.

### `/proc/<pid>/io` over 12 minutes

| Field | Change |
| --- | --- |
| `rchar` | +40 bytes |
| `wchar` | +382 bytes |
| `syscr` | **+5** |
| `syscw` | +11 |
| `write_bytes` | **0** (unchanged) |

Five read syscalls in twelve minutes is not a slow tokenizer — it is a stopped process.

### CPU and memory

```
VmRSS:  10875656 kB      (identical after 30 s)
VmSwap:        0 kB
Threads:        43
```

Thread census — **no thread is executing user code, and no extension-owned native thread exists**:

```
36 libuv-worker       S
 7 node               S
 1 DelayedTaskSche    S
```

Thread CPU accumulators are **byte-identical across two samples 60 seconds apart** — the whole process consumed **zero** CPU-time in that window.

`workers: []` in the diagnostic report confirms the parse worker pool has already exited, so this is not a parse-phase leftover.

### The main thread is idle, not blocked

Inspector (`SIGUSR1`, bound to `127.0.0.1:9229`) responds immediately, and a `Debugger.pause` lands in:

```
callFrames: processTimers
```

i.e. the progress-bar timer. There is no user JS frame, no `run-analyze` frame, no FTS frame on the stack.

`process._getActiveHandles()` / `_getActiveRequests()`:

```json
{"handles":["Pipe","Socket","ReadStream","Socket"],
 "requests":[],
 "timers":["PipeWrap","PipeWrap","TTYWrap","PipeWrap","Timeout","Timeout"]}
```

`requests` is **empty**: there is no fs read, no fs write, and no native query callback outstanding. The libuv handle list from the diagnostic report contains only stdio pipes, the SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers, the analysis-slot lock pipe, and one repeater-less timer.

**Together: the event loop is spinning normally and every async primitive is idle, yet `analyze` is awaiting something that never settles.**

### Not memory pressure

```json
"pageFaults": { "IORequired": 0, "IONotRequired": 13012627 },
"rss": 11140444160, "maxRss": 14272663552,
"constrained_memory": 18446744073709552000
```

`IORequired === 0` means **zero major page faults**: nothing was ever faulted in from disk, so neither the host nor the container spent time reclaiming. `VmSwap` is 0 and cgroup memory is unconstrained. Paging/reclaim is ruled out by measurement.

### The FTS extension is loaded — this is not the install path

`/proc/<pid>/maps` contains the vendored extension:

```
/app/gitnexus/vendor/lbug-fts/prebuilds/linux-x64/libfts.lbug_extension
```

There is also **no `install-duckdb-extension.mjs` child process**, so the bounded out-of-process install path (which has a 15 s timeout anyway) is not where the run is stuck.

### `meta.json` shows no phase stamp — expected on this path, not evidence of an earlier stage

```
phase: None
fts: { status: "unavailable", skipReason: "disabled-by-flag" }
indexedAt: 2026-11-10T10:29:15Z
```

This metadata belongs to the previous (successful) `--skip-fts` run. `shouldStampFtsDirtyPhase()` returns `false` for the **staging** write plan, so a staging run never writes a phase marker. The absence of `phase` here therefore says nothing about where the current run is.

## Analysis

### Where the progress bar comes from

`run-analyze.ts` emits the 85% label **before** the extension is even loaded:

```ts
progress('fts', 85, ftsDisabledReason ? 'Skipping search indexes...' : 'Creating search indexes...');
const ftsAvailable = !ftsDisabledReason &&
  (await loadFTSExtension(undefined, { policy: resolveAnalyzeInstallPolicy() }));
```

So `Creating search indexes...` covers extension loading **and** the entire per-table rebuild. The rebuild loop itself (`createSearchFTSIndexes`) is:

```ts
for (const { table, indexName, properties } of indexes) {
  await dropFTSIndex(table, indexName);
  if (!emptyTables.has(table)) await createFTSIndex(table, indexName, [...properties], stemmer);
}
```

over 24 index definitions. Each `CREATE_FTS_INDEX` re-tokenizes **every stored row** of its table. There is **no timeout and no watchdog** on these native calls, and per-table callbacks (`onIndexStart` / `onIndexReady`) are wired **only when `--verbose` is set**.

### Why the run can hang invisibly

`conn-lock.ts` serializes every operation on the single LadybugDB connection through a promise chain:

```ts
const prior = tail;
tail = new Promise<void>((resolve) => { release = resolve; });
await prior;
try { return await inCriticalSection.run(true, fn); }
finally { release(); }
```

If any holder's `fn` never settles, `release()` never runs and **every subsequent call queues forever**. That produces exactly the observed shape: a live event loop, zero CPU, zero I/O, no pending libuv requests, and one await that never resolves.

The evidence cannot distinguish *which* of the two candidate paths is responsible, because no native symbols are available in this image:

1. a JS-visible lock/await never settled (as above), or
2. a native call blocked on an internal mutex that nobody releases.

Thirty-six `libuv-worker` threads sitting in `futex_wait_queue_me` with zero CPU delta are consistent with **either** an idle thread pool **or** a native deadlock; `wchan` cannot separate them, and `strace`/`gdb` are not present in the image.

### Additional observation: FTS tokenization and CJK corpora

The bundled FTS tokenizer splits only on whitespace, so a contiguous CJK span indexes as **one very large token**. The bundled bigram mode (`GITNEXUS_FTS_CJK_SEGMENTATION=bigram`, default `none`) exists precisely for this and rewrites each CJK run into overlapping bigrams.

This is offered as a **reproduction characteristic, not a diagnosis**: if CJK runs are implicated, the frozen state (`IORequired: 0`, zero CPU, no active request) points at a **native deadlock during postings insertion**, not at a slow loop — a slow loop would burn CPU and grow RSS, and neither happens.

## Suggested directions

Not prescriptive — flagging the shapes that would have made this tractable:

1. **Bound each `CREATE_FTS_INDEX` with a watchdog.** Today there is no timeout anywhere in the FTS build path, so an unreturning native call converts the whole run into an indefinite hang with no diagnostic. A per-index deadline that degrades keyword search (the existing `buildSearchFtsIndexesOrDegrade` contract) is consistent with how every other FTS failure is already handled.
2. **Report per-table progress unconditionally.** `onIndexStart`/`onIndexReady` are gated behind `--verbose`, so a default run parks at 85% with a climbing elapsed timer and no indication of which of 24 tables is in flight. Emitting them (or a table counter) costs nothing and would have named the stuck table immediately.
3. **Make a stuck `conn-lock` holder observable.** The promise chain has no timeout and no "who has held this, and for how long" accessor. A held-duration probe on the lock tail would turn an opaque hang into one log line.
4. **Preserve native symbols in the published image.** Without `gdb` (and without unstripped symbols), neither the reporter nor a maintainer can tell an idle thread pool from a native deadlock — which is the single question that decides where this bug lives.

## Impact

A full rebuild on a large repository **cannot complete** on this host unless FTS is disabled. Since FTS runs *after* the graph is written but *before* the staging file is published, the entire 12+ hours of parse/graph work is discarded on kill, and re-running reproduces the same hang.

Current workaround in use: `analyze --force --skip-fts`, which completes but leaves keyword search unavailable (`capabilities.fts.status = "unavailable"`).

Reported as a **hang**, not a performance regression — a slow phase would show CPU and I/O progress; this shows neither, for 21 hours, with the on-disk state byte-identical.

---

### Relation to #3870

Separate issue. #3870 / #3874 concern embedding write-path throughput and are resolved by the vector-store query-plan fix. This report is about the **FTS phase hanging with zero activity**, reproduced on `rc.252`, which already contains that fix.

title: fix(resolution): link calls and accesses through private #names in JS and TS
body:
## Summary

Calls, reads and writes through a private name (`this.#log()`, `this.#items`, `this.#count = 0`) produced no edge. The scope queries matched a member name only as `property_identifier`, and a private name is a `private_property_identifier`. JavaScript also did not declare private methods and fields in its scope query, so a call made inside `#log()` was attributed to the class, and `#items` had no `Property` node.

This PR adds the private form of each member pattern:

- JavaScript scope query: private method and field declarations, and private member calls, writes, compound writes and reads.
- TypeScript scope query: private member calls (including `await this.#m<T>()`), writes, compound writes and reads. Declarations were already there.
- JavaScript parse query: a private field is a `Property`.
- JavaScript and TypeScript parse queries: a private field holding an arrow function or a function expression is a `Method`, as its public form has been since #2693, so a call through it points at a callable.

It is the first item still open in #1646 ("`#field` reads / writes / calls").

I checked it with the real CLI (`analyze`, then `cypher` on the edges), with `dist/` built from `main` (302969291) and from this branch, on one class written in `.js` and in `.ts`:

| edge | `.js` on `main` | `.ts` on `main` | both on this branch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `add → #log`, `log → #log` (`this.#log()`) | none | none | `CALLS` |
| `this.#logger.write()` inside `#log()` | from `Store` | from `#log` | from `#log` |
| `Store → #items`, `Store → #logger` | none | `HAS_PROPERTY` | `HAS_PROPERTY` |
| `add → #items`, `#log → #logger` (reads) | none | none | `ACCESSES` read |
| `reset → #count` (`=`), `#bump → #count` (`+=`) | none | none | `ACCESSES` write |
| `make → #create` (`Store.#create()`, static) | none | none | `CALLS` |
| `new Store()` inside `static #create()` | from `Store` | from `#create` | from `#create` |
| `refresh → #load` (`await this.#load()`) | none | none | `CALLS` |
| `#onClick = () => 1` | no node | `Property` | `Method`, and `click → #onClick` |

On this branch each fixture gives the same graph as the same code with the `#` names renamed to public ones: same node and edge counts, same edges, and the same confidence and reason on each edge. Two classes with their own `#bump` each get the call to their own method (`Store.#bump`, `Queue.#bump`).

## Motivation / context

Part of #1646. `impact` and `context` read these edges, so a private method looked unused and a change to it reported no caller. Classes with `#private` members are common in modern JavaScript and TypeScript.

## Areas touched

- [x] `gitnexus/` (CLI / core / MCP server)
- [ ] `gitnexus-web/` (Vite / React UI)
- [ ] `.github/` (workflows, actions)
- [ ] `eval/` or other tooling
- [ ] Docs / agent config only (`AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.cursor/`, `llms.txt`, etc.)

## Scope & constraints

**In scope**

- `languages/javascript/query.ts` and `languages/typescript/query.ts`: the private form of the member declaration and reference patterns.
- `tree-sitter-queries.ts`: private fields in the JavaScript parse query, and private closure-valued fields in the JavaScript and TypeScript parse queries.

**Explicitly out of scope / not done here**

- The other items of #1646: destructured parameters, `static { }` blocks, generator return types, tagged templates, computed keys, `Object.assign` mixins, JSDoc `@typedef` / `@extends` / `@implements`, and unions.
- `#x in obj` brand checks: they test membership and read no value, so they get no edge, as before.
- Calls made in a field initializer (`#onClick = () => this.render()`): JavaScript and TypeScript already differ there for public fields too. Not changed.

## Implementation notes

- Each private pattern is a separate pattern next to its public form, as the TypeScript declarations already are, rather than an alternation.
- JavaScript gets no awaited private call pattern: without type arguments, `await this.#m()` parses as an ordinary call, which the plain pattern matches. Only TypeScript's `await this.#m<T>()` puts the `await` inside the call's function.
- Names keep their `#`, as TypeScript already declared them, so `#log` and `log` stay two members: `log → #log` is a call, not a self-loop.

## Testing & verification

- [x] `test/integration/resolvers/javascript.test.ts`: one fixture, run as a `.js` file and as a `.ts` file (9 tests):
  - a call through `this.#name` goes to the method of the same class, with two classes that each have a `#bump`; a static `Store.#create()` and an awaited call are linked too;
  - a call made in a private method is attributed to that method;
  - reads, writes and compound writes of private fields are recorded;
  - private fields are `Property` nodes, and private fields holding an arrow function or a function expression are `Method` nodes that calls point at;
  - TypeScript only: `await this.#load<number>()`.
  - On `main`, 8 of the 9 fail. The one that passes is the TypeScript attribution test: TypeScript already declared private methods.
- [x] Mutations: 16, one per added pattern, each built and tested, then restored. Each one fails a test.
- [x] `npx vitest run test/integration/resolvers`: 5,870 tests pass and 17 are skipped.
- [x] `npx vitest run test/unit`: 28,608 tests pass and 54 are skipped. The 3 tests of `analyze-phase-handoff.test.ts` timed out (a 1 s `vi.waitFor`) under the load of the run; on their own they pass, 3 times out of 3.
- [x] `npx vitest run test/integration` outside `resolvers/`: 10,330 tests pass and 110 are skipped. `parse-cache-identity-package.test.ts` ran out of space copying the package into a 3 GB `/tmp`; with `TMPDIR` on a larger disk it passes.
- [x] `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npm run typecheck:tests` pass. prettier is clean, `npm run test:dupes` reports nothing, and eslint reports no new warning.
- [x] The real CLI: see the table above.
- [x] `detect_changes`, with the index refreshed: the four query constants and the new tests change, and no flow is affected. `impact` on `getJsScopeQuery` and `getTsScopeQuery` is LOW (12 and 6 symbols, through `emitJsScopeCaptures` and `emitTsScopeCaptures`).

Note for local runs: under Vitest the parse workers load `dist/`, so these tests need `npm run build` after a query change.

## Risk & rollout

Low to medium. JavaScript and TypeScript files with private members get new edges and nodes on the next `analyze`; nothing changes for files without them. No migration is needed.

## Checklist

- [x] PR body meets repo minimum length (workflow may label short descriptions)
- [x] If `AGENTS.md` / overlays changed: headers, scope block, and changelog updated per project conventions (not changed)
- [x] No secrets, tokens, or machine-specific paths committed

title: fix(hooks): check index freshness after branch switches and resets
body:
## Summary

Claude Code now checks the destination index after `git checkout`, `switch`, `reset`, `am`, and `revert`. The shared matcher also recognizes `git stash apply`, `pop`, and `branch`. Antigravity uses the same matcher.

## Motivation / context

Closes #4059. A switch to a branch with different code produced no hook output, even though a commit event against the same checkout immediately reported the stale index. The command filter returned an empty directory list, so the hook never read the destination index metadata.

## Scope & constraints

The hook compares the destination HEAD with its pinned index when one exists, falling back to the workspace index. A branch switch at the same commit can therefore reveal a stale pinned index. A matching commit stays quiet.

## Testing & verification

- The new regression cases failed 10 times before the fix and passed afterward. They cover command boundaries, `git -C`, and a real switch in both directions between branches at the same commit.
- The matcher, hook, setup, language-boundary and Antigravity end-to-end suites passed locally (439 tests, 43 platform-dependent skips).
- `npx tsc --noEmit`, `npm run typecheck:tests`, Prettier and the pre-commit checks passed. The full local run hit four environment-dependent assertions in the setup and worker-pool suites. All 105 tests in those two files passed when rerun with the inherited Codex home and CPU affinity overrides removed. The original full run was stopped to keep setup tests isolated from the active Codex configuration. GitHub CI runs the full suite in shards.
- A temporary repository reproduced the original silence. After the fix, switching or resetting to stale code emitted a hint. Switching to an up-to-date index and checking out a file at a current HEAD stayed quiet.

## Risk & rollout

The extra work is the existing freshness check after a newly recognized command. The hook emits an advisory and leaves reindexing to the agent.

title: fix(lbug): prevent deadlocks during node imports and full-text indexing
body:
## Summary

Fixes #4060. Use one LadybugDB execution thread when GitNexus imports graph nodes or builds a full-text index. This covers both operations in the [upstream workaround](https://github.com/LadybugDB/ladybug/issues/1669).

## Motivation / context

LadybugDB 0.22.0 bulk-builds string primary-key indexes for graph nodes and for the FTS term dictionary. With certain non-ASCII keys, two native workers can each hold a hash partition while waiting for the other's partition. In #4060 this stalls analysis at the first FTS index. The existing `PARALLEL=false` CSV option controls the reader and leaves the native index build exposed. The upstream engine issue is open.

## Areas touched

- [x] `gitnexus/` CLI and core

## Scope & constraints

The change covers graph node imports, their `IGNORE_ERRORS` retries, and full-text index creation during analysis and FTS repair. Relationship imports use the connection's configured thread count.

## Implementation notes

The connection lock covers reading the existing thread count, setting it to one, draining the native result, and restoring the prior setting in `finally`. On a COPY retry, the warning receipt stays under the same lock.

## Testing & verification

- A regression using the native database observed the execution-thread setting on the initial COPY and its retry for both nodes and relationships. It failed on the FTS-only commit and passed with this change.
- The patched graph loader imported all 600,000 non-ASCII file IDs in 2.5 seconds and restored the four-thread setting. On the FTS path, the CLI indexed 600 files with 600,000 distinct CJK terms and a keyword query returned the expected file.
- A queued query observed the original three-thread setting after both a successful FTS build and a native error.
- All 132 targeted tests passed across the combined run and an isolated rerun. One warm FTS repair test timed out during the combined run, then passed in isolation. The production build, test TypeScript check and Prettier passed. ESLint reported zero errors.

## Risk & rollout

Single-threaded string-index builds may take longer on some repositories. The index format stays compatible. Rerunning an interrupted analysis after upgrading rebuilds the index with the workaround in place. Revisit the thread limit when GitNexus ships an engine with the upstream fix.

## Checklist

- [x] Regression coverage exercises both operations and restoration of the thread setting.

Make the required CI Gate fail when an eligible PR fails its Sonar quality gate, the scanner exits unsuccessfully, or an analyzer logs an ERROR while the scanner exits successfully. The maintainer chose to keep scanner warnings advisory.

The main scan uploaded its report and passed after logging six protobuf errors. Its Python module also looked for the repository's LCOV report under `eval/coverage`. title: fix(ingestion): stop reading the callee of an awaited generic member call
body:
## Summary

`await svc.verify<T>(x)` gave a `CALLS` edge to `verify` and also a read `ACCESSES` edge to it. tree-sitter-typescript parses an awaited call with type arguments as `call_expression(function: await_expression(member_expression))`, so the member's parent is the `await`, not the call, and `shouldEmitReadMember` kept the read. Its doc comment already listed this case (number 4), but the switch had no `await_expression` branch.

This PR adds it. A member whose parent is an `await_expression` that is itself the `function:` of a `call_expression` is no longer a read, like a member that is the `function:` of a call. An awaited member that is not called, `await svc.pending`, is still a read.

nexus-check found it on #4062 ([thread](https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/pull/4062#discussion_r4682085546)), where `await this.#load<T>()` inherits it from the public pattern. The fix is in the filter, which runs on every read-member match, so it also covers the private form introduced in #4062.

## Motivation / context

`impact` and `context` read `ACCESSES` edges: every `await obj.m<T>()` made the caller look like it read `m` as a field, on top of calling it. Without type arguments, `await obj.m()` parses as an ordinary call and was already right.

## Areas touched

- [x] `gitnexus/` (CLI / core / MCP server)
- [ ] `gitnexus-web/` (Vite / React UI)

## Scope & constraints

**In scope**

- `languages/typescript/captures.ts`: the `await_expression` case in `shouldEmitReadMember`, and its doc comment.
- Bench baselines for the one edge this removes from GitNexus's own source (`await workerPool.dispatchGroups<…>()`, `parsing-processor.ts:398`): the TypeScript `scope-capture` fingerprint, a parse-cache `graphExpectations` entry, and a lexical-lookup receipt. That receipt could only pin added references, so `bench/lib/reference-additions.mjs` and `lexical-lookup/reference-migration.mjs` now also pin removed reference rows.

**Explicitly out of scope / not done here**

- JavaScript: without type arguments the `await` never sits inside the call's function, so `javascript/captures.ts` has no such case to handle.

- [x] The real CLI (`analyze`, then `cypher` on the edges) on one class with `await this.load<number>()`, `await this.load()` and `await this.pending`: `generic → load` and `plain → load` are `CALLS` only, and `waitPending → pending` is still an `ACCESSES` read.
- [x] `npx vitest run test/unit`: 28,706 tests pass and 54 are skipped.
- [x] `npx vitest run test/integration/resolvers test/unit/scope-resolution` with the TypeScript and Vue unit tests: 11,384 tests pass and 16 are skipped.
